item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Canada? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Canada

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. Canada has no single national rule for keeping a roof rat — it is decided province by province, and the provinces diverge sharply. Alberta bans the entire genus Rattus outright (a famously 'rat-free' province); Saskatchewan explicitly lists the black rat on its captive-wildlife allowed list; Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia all allow it (BC under a tame-captive exemption, Quebec with an import notice that the fancy rat is exempt from). Federally, the CFIA lets you import a pet rat with no permit or health certificate as long as it does NOT come from Africa. Check your province (below) AND your municipality.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

The federal government does not regulate the day-to-day keeping of companion animals — that is left entirely to the provinces and municipalities, and the answer changes drastically at provincial borders. Alberta PROHIBITS keeping any rat (genus Rattus) with no pet exemption; Saskatchewan EXPLICITLY allows the black rat as captive wildlife; Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia allow it. So there is no single Canadian answer — see your province below.

Sources: Canadian Food Inspection Agency

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Federally unregulated; follows provincial possession rules. Prohibited where keeping is banned (Alberta), legal where the species is allowed (SK/ON/QC/BC). Commercial breeders everywhere also face municipal business-licensing, zoning, and provincial animal-welfare standards.

Sources: Canadian Food Inspection Agency

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Federally unregulated within Canada; follows provincial rules and municipal pet-shop / commercial-breeder licensing. Prohibited in Alberta (sale/distribution of a declared pest is banned); legal in SK/ON/QC/BC subject to local business rules.

Sources: Canadian Food Inspection Agency

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Bringing a pet rat INTO Canada is permissive federally: the CFIA does not require an import permit or veterinary health certificate for pet rodents — you simply declare the animal to the Canada Border Services Agency. The big exceptions: any rodent originating from the continent of Africa is barred (plague/monkeypox rule), airlines may demand their own vet certificate, and exporting live rodents to the Eurasian Economic Union is currently suspended. Critically, your destination PROVINCE's rules still apply — you may not bring a rat into (or, arguably, through) Alberta at all.

Sources: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, CFIA, CFIA

Restrictions & responsibilities

Federal import is permit-free for pet rodents NOT from Africa — but a Rattus rattus originating from any African country is barred entry (and may be seized or destroyed). Airlines often require a veterinary health certificate even though the government does not, and exporting live rodents to the Eurasian Economic Union (Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Armenia, Kyrgyzstan) is suspended until further notice.
  • Declare the animal as a pet to the CBSA at the border
  • Confirm it is not African-origin
  • Check your airline's own health-certificate rule

Forms: Bringing animals to Canada — CFIA · Where: Canada Border Services Agency / CFIA National Import Service Centre · Fees: No CFIA fee for pet rodents

Source: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, CFIA

The answer depends entirely on your province. Alberta bans all rats (do NOT bring one in); Saskatchewan, Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia permit them. Always check your province (below) and your municipal bylaws (which can cap the number of animals or require a breeder licence).
  • Find your province below
  • Check your city/municipal animal bylaws

Source: Canadian Food Inspection Agency

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Help change this

How to help in Canada

Canada has no single national rule for keeping a pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) — it is decided province by province, and the provinces diverge sharply. Saskatchewan explicitly lists the black rat as allowed captive wildlife; Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia all permit it; and federally the CFIA lets you import a pet rat with no permit or health certificate (the one hard exception: no rodents originating from Africa). The outlier — and the one true prohibition in Canada — is Alberta. Under the Agricultural Pests Act and its Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation, the entire genus Rattus is a "declared pest," and the Government of Alberta states plainly that "it is illegal to own pet rats in Alberta." There is no exemption for a tame, captive-bred animal kept indoors as a companion. The rule was written to protect Alberta's celebrated rat-free farmland from wild Norway rats (Rattus norvegicus) establishing breeding colonies, but as written it sweeps in domesticated pet rats that pose none of that agricultural risk and have never founded a wild population.

The ask: Ask Alberta to add a narrow exemption to the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation for tame, captive-bred companion rats kept indoors — the same kind of carve-out that lets neighbouring provinces allow them safely. The change is to the regulation itself (a job for the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation and your MLA), not a favour the rat-control program can grant on its own, because the program is correctly applying the law as written. Where you live OUTSIDE Alberta, no change is needed to keep a pet roof rat — just confirm your province's rule and your municipal bylaws.

Where the lever really is: This is branch (b): the LAW AS WRITTEN. The barrier is a deliberate statutory/regulatory listing, not a clerk's misreading. Alberta's Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation, made under the Agricultural Pests Act, declares the whole genus Rattus a pest, and the Government of Alberta's own rat-control page states "it is illegal to own pet rats in Alberta" with no pet exemption. The rat-control program is applying that regulation exactly as drafted — so emailing the program to ask permission, or appealing its decision, will NOT work, because there is nothing for it to reinterpret. The fix is to amend the regulation to add a captive-bred companion-animal exemption, which is a decision for the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation (the regulation is set by the Minister/Cabinet) acting on public and political input. The correct lever is therefore the legislature: your MLA and the Minister, who can champion or direct a regulatory amendment. (For the other relevant provinces — SK, ON, QC, BC — there is no law-as-written problem to fix; the roof rat is already permitted, so they are not advocacy targets, only a "confirm-your-province" check.)

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Members of the Legislative Assembly of Alberta — official MLA directory / 'find your MLA' (legislature) — official contact page
    The prohibition lives in a regulation the Minister and Cabinet control, so the change must come through the political/legislative branch. This official Legislative Assembly page lets any Alberta resident look up and contact their own MLA — the representative who can raise a regulatory amendment or relay constituent demand to the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation. Use it to write your own MLA; never address an individual member by name picked at random.
  • Elections Alberta — Member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) search (legislature) — official contact page
    An independent official tool to confirm which MLA represents your address, in case you are unsure of your constituency before contacting them via the Assembly directory above.
  • Alberta Rat Control Program (Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation) — official program inbox (executive / agency) — rats@gov.ab.ca
    Secondary channel. This is the official inbox of the program that administers the declared-pest rule. It cannot grant a pet exemption on its own (the regulation must change first), but a polite written request for the government's current position on tame captive-bred companion rats, and for whether a narrow exemption could be recommended to the Minister, puts the ask on record with the administering body and can be cited when you write your MLA. Verified on the Government of Alberta rat-control program page.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To my MLA / the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation,

I am writing about Alberta's prohibition on keeping pet rats. Under the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation, the entire genus Rattus is a declared pest, so even a tame, captive-bred companion rat is illegal to own here.

I understand and support the goal: keeping wild Norway rats from establishing in Alberta's farmland. But the regulation as written also bans domesticated pet rats that are captive-bred, hand-tame, kept entirely indoors, and never released — animals that pose none of the agricultural risk the rule was designed to stop, and that have never founded a wild colony.

Saskatchewan, Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia all allow these pets safely. The issue is not whether a rat can be domesticated — it plainly can, like the familiar fancy rat — it is that the species is on a list with no exemption for companion animals.

I respectfully ask you to support adding a narrow exemption to the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation for tame, captive-bred rats kept indoors as pets, while leaving the wild-rat controls fully in place.

Thank you for considering this.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your town and constituency]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Bringing animals to Canada: importing and travelling with pets — CFIA (rodents need no import permit/health certificate) — Canadian Food Inspection Agency
  • Terrestrial animal products and by-products import policy — CFIA (Africa-origin rodent restriction) — CFIA
  • Export of live rodents to the Eurasian Economic Union — CFIA (health certificates suspended) — CFIA

Search terms: Rattus rattus, black rat, roof rat, ship rat, rat noir, rat des toits.

Last reviewed 2026-06-06. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Switzerland? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Switzerland

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.

Summary. Switzerland is legal for the roof rat in practice, with mandatory welfare conditions and one genuine grey area. Swiss law technically classifies rats as 'Wildtiere' (the Animal Welfare Ordinance / TSchV Art. 2 lists only dogs, cats, domestic rabbits, pigeons and poultry as 'domestic'), but it then carves small rodents out of the permit-and-training tier, so ordinary private rat-keeping needs NO cantonal permit. The official BLV fact sheet 'Ratten im Recht' confirms private rat keeping is permit-free, with welfare rules: keep rats in groups (min. 2 — a legal requirement), with minimum enclosure dimensions. A cantonal permit + proof of competence is needed only for commercial trade, or when giving away more than 300 rodents/year. R. rattus is not on any CITES appendix. The grey area: BLV guidance says 'Ratten' generically (built around the fancy rat R. norvegicus); whether a canton treats the synanthropic R. rattus as the same permit-free small rodent — or as a Wildtier needing a cantonal Bewilligung — is the one point worth confirming.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Although rats are technically Wildtiere under TSchV Art. 2, the BLV fact sheet 'Ratten im Recht' states private rat keeping needs no training and no cantonal permit. Mandatory welfare conditions apply: rats are social — keep ≥2 (TSchV Art. 13 / Anhang 2 Tab. 1 item 47); minimum enclosure ~0.5 m²/0.5 m³ for up to 5 rats (+0.05 m²/animal). Medium confidence because the guidance addresses 'Ratten' generically and at least one canton (Zürich) requires permits for wild mammals except 'native insectivores and small rodents' — R. rattus's classification isn't explicitly resolved.

Sources: Swiss Confederation / Fedlex, BLV (Federal Food Safety & Veterinary Office), Swiss Confederation / Fedlex

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Private breeding for personal use or occasional rehoming is permit-free. A cantonal Bewilligung + recognised training (Sachkundenachweis/FBA) is required only above the commercial threshold — 300 rats given away (or used as feeder animals) per year — or for any 'gewerbsmässiger' (commercial) pet dealing. A normal hobby rattery stays well under 300/yr. (Same Wildtier-classification caveat as keeping.)

Sources: Swiss Confederation / Fedlex, BLV (Federal Food Safety & Veterinary Office)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Gratuitous transfer (giving away) of captive-bred rats with no commercial element is lawful without a permit below 300 animals/year. Commercial trade ('gewerbsmässiger Handel') at any scale needs a cantonal Bewilligung + BLV-recognised training; organised animal swaps (Tierbörsen) have their own permit/training rule. No price cap; the test is whether the activity is commercial.

Sources: Swiss Confederation / Fedlex, BLV

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Internal transport needs only welfare-compliant conditions (TSchG Art. 3). Non-commercial personal import of up to 5 healthy rodents from a non-EU country needs no import permit and no health certificate (BLV travel rules; checks possible at Zürich/Geneva). Commercial import (resale/breeding stock) needs a BLV import authorization + possibly an origin health certificate. R. rattus is not on any CITES appendix, so no CITES permit. Never release.

Sources: BLV, Swiss Confederation / Fedlex

Restrictions & responsibilities

Switzerland legally requires rats to be kept in groups — keeping a single rat is an offence (TSchV social-species rule). Meet the minimum enclosure dimensions (~0.5 m²/0.5 m³ for up to 5 rats). Private keeping/breeding is permit-free; a cantonal permit + training is needed only for commercial trade or giving away 300+ rodents/year. ⚠️ Confirm with your cantonal veterinary office that R. rattus is treated as a permit-free small rodent (not a Wildtier). Never release.
  • Confirm R. rattus's small-rodent (permit-free) status with your Kantonstierarztamt before acquiring

Where: Cantonal veterinary office (Kantonstierarztamt)

Source: BLV (Federal Food Safety & Veterinary Office), Swiss Confederation / Fedlex

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Switzerland

In Switzerland, keeping pet rats is legal and — for ordinary private households — completely permit-free. The federal animal-welfare rules (TSchG/TSchV) carve small rodents out of the permit-and-training tier, and the BLV (Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office) fact sheet "Ratten im Recht" confirms private rat keeping needs no cantonal permit and no proof of competence. Welfare conditions do apply and matter: rats are social, so you must keep at least two (a single rat is unlawful), and the enclosure must meet minimum dimensions (roughly 0.5 m²/0.5 m³ for up to five rats, plus space per extra animal). A cantonal permit and recognised training are required only for commercial trade or for giving away more than 300 rodents per year. The one real grey area is a classification trap, not a ban. Under TSchV Art. 2 the "domestic animal" list (dogs, cats, domestic rabbits, pigeons, poultry) excludes ALL rats — even the millennia-bred fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) — so rats are technically "Wildtiere" (wild animals). In practice the small-rodent carve-out rescues private keeping, but every official text says "Ratten" or "Farbratten" generically and is built around the fancy rat. The BLV's own rats web page and fact sheet never name the roof rat (Rattus rattus / Hausratte) at all. So a cantonal veterinary office reading the Wildtier rule strictly could, in theory, demand a Bewilligung (permit) for R. rattus specifically — even though it is the same kind of tame, captive-bred small rodent as the fancy rat. This is a gap in agency guidance, not anything the law actually forbids.

The ask: Ask the BLV for a short written confirmation that captive-bred Rattus rattus (Hausratte) is treated exactly like the fancy rat (R. norvegicus): a permit-free "kleines Nagetier" for private hobby keeping, with the same 300-per-year threshold for the commercial/permit tier — not a "Wildtier" that needs a cantonal Bewilligung. Because the actual permit (if any) is issued at canton level, also ask your own cantonal veterinary office (Kantonstierarztamt) to confirm in writing that it applies the permit-free small-rodent rule to R. rattus. A one-paragraph email reply you can keep on file is enough; it removes the only real uncertainty for Swiss roof-rat keepers and helps BLV close the gap by naming the species in future guidance.

Where the lever really is: This is branch (a): the BUREAUCRACY under-specifying / potentially misreading the law, NOT the law as written. The lever is the AGENCY (BLV) via a written clarification/declaratory confirmation, plus the cantonal veterinary office that actually issues permits — NOT the legislature. Why, concretely: nothing in Swiss law bans the roof rat or names it on any prohibited or restricted list, and R. rattus is on no CITES appendix. The federal scheme already exempts ordinary private small-rodent keeping from permits, and BLV's "Ratten im Recht" fact sheet states private rat keeping is permit-free. The only problem is that the TSchV Art. 2 "Heimtier" list technically leaves all rats as "Wildtiere," and BLV's published guidance speaks of "Ratten/Farbratten" generically while never naming Rattus rattus — so a strict canton could mis-apply the Wildtier rule to one species the guidance simply forgot to mention. That is fixable with a written agency clarification or a canton's confirmation that R. rattus = a permit-free small rodent; it does NOT require changing any statute. There is no bill to support and no statutory list to get the species added to or removed from — so do not petition Parliament here. Equally, do not frame this as "the agency is wrongly applying a valid ban," because there is no ban: the right framing is a request to confirm an existing exemption applies to a species the guidance overlooked.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Bundesamt für Lebensmittelsicherheit und Veterinärwesen (BLV / FSVO) — official contact form (executive / agency) — info@blv.admin.ch
    The federal animal-welfare authority that publishes the 'Ratten im Recht' guidance. It is the right body to confirm in writing that captive-bred Rattus rattus is a permit-free small rodent like the fancy rat (not a Wildtier), and to close the species gap in its own guidance. Use the official web form as the primary channel; info@blv.admin.ch is the verified general office inbox.
  • Your cantonal veterinary office (Kantonstierarztamt / kantonales Veterinäramt) (executive / agency)
    The canton — not the federal BLV — issues any actual keeping/breeding permit, and Wildtier rules are applied at canton level. A one-line written confirmation from your own canton that it treats R. rattus as a permit-free small rodent removes the only real uncertainty for you specifically. Find it by searching '[your canton] Kantonstierarztamt' or '[your canton] Veterinäramt'.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Classification of the roof rat (Rattus rattus) as a permit-free small rodent

Dear Sir or Madam,

I keep pet rats privately and indoors and would like to clarify one point about the law. Your fact sheet 'Ratten im Recht' confirms that private rat keeping needs no cantonal permit and no proof of competence. However, the guidance speaks of 'Ratten/Farbratten' generally and does not name the species Rattus rattus (Hausratte, roof rat).

My animals are captive-bred, tame, kept indoors in a group, and never released into the wild. They are the same kind of small rodent as the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus), only a different species.

Could you please confirm in writing that captive-bred Rattus rattus is treated exactly like the fancy rat — a permit-free 'kleines Nagetier' for private hobby keeping, with the same 300-animals-per-year threshold — and not as a 'Wildtier' requiring a cantonal Bewilligung? It would also help future keepers if the species were named in your guidance.

Thank you very much for your help.

Yours faithfully,
[Your name]
[Your canton / postcode]
[Your email]
Deutsch
Betreff: Einstufung der Hausratte (Rattus rattus) als bewilligungsfreies kleines Nagetier

Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren

Ich halte privat und in der Wohnung Ratten als Heimtiere und möchte einen rechtlichen Punkt klären. Ihr Merkblatt «Ratten im Recht» bestätigt, dass die private Rattenhaltung keine kantonale Bewilligung und keinen Sachkundenachweis erfordert. Die Unterlagen sprechen jedoch allgemein von «Ratten/Farbratten» und nennen die Art Rattus rattus (Hausratte) nicht.

Meine Tiere stammen aus Nachzucht, sind zahm, werden in der Wohnung in der Gruppe gehalten und niemals in die Natur entlassen. Es handelt sich um dasselbe kleine Nagetier wie die Farbratte (Rattus norvegicus), nur um eine andere Art.

Könnten Sie mir bitte schriftlich bestätigen, dass die in Gefangenschaft gezüchtete Rattus rattus gleich behandelt wird wie die Farbratte – als bewilligungsfreies «kleines Nagetier» für die private Hobbyhaltung, mit derselben Schwelle von 300 Tieren pro Jahr – und nicht als «Wildtier», das eine kantonale Bewilligung erfordert? Für künftige Halterinnen und Halter wäre es zudem hilfreich, wenn die Art in Ihren Unterlagen ausdrücklich genannt würde.

Vielen Dank für Ihre Hilfe.

Freundliche Grüsse
[Ihr Name]
[Ihr Kanton / PLZ]
[Ihre E-Mail]
Français
Objet: Classification du rat noir (Rattus rattus) comme petit rongeur dispensé d'autorisation

Madame, Monsieur,

Je détiens des rats de compagnie à titre privé et en intérieur, et je souhaiterais clarifier un point juridique. Votre fiche « Ratten im Recht » confirme que la détention privée de rats ne requiert ni autorisation cantonale ni attestation de compétences. Toutefois, le document parle de « rats » de manière générale et ne nomme pas l'espèce Rattus rattus (rat noir).

Mes animaux sont nés en captivité, apprivoisés, gardés en groupe à l'intérieur et ne sont jamais relâchés dans la nature. Il s'agit du même petit rongeur que le rat domestique (Rattus norvegicus), simplement d'une espèce différente.

Pourriez-vous me confirmer par écrit que le Rattus rattus né en captivité est traité exactement comme le rat domestique — un « petit rongeur » dispensé d'autorisation pour la détention privée de loisir, avec le même seuil de 300 animaux par an — et non comme un « animal sauvage » nécessitant une autorisation cantonale ? Il serait également utile, pour les futurs détenteurs, que l'espèce soit nommée dans vos documents.

Avec mes remerciements.

Veuillez agréer, Madame, Monsieur, mes salutations distinguées.
[Votre nom]
[Votre canton / NPA]
[Votre adresse e-mail]
Italiano
Oggetto: Classificazione del ratto nero (Rattus rattus) come piccolo roditore esente da autorizzazione

Gentili Signore e Signori,

Detengo ratti da compagnia a titolo privato e in appartamento e vorrei chiarire un punto giuridico. La vostra scheda «Ratten im Recht» conferma che la detenzione privata di ratti non richiede alcuna autorizzazione cantonale né un attestato di competenza. Tuttavia, il documento parla di «ratti» in generale e non nomina la specie Rattus rattus (ratto nero).

I miei animali sono nati in cattività, sono mansueti, vengono tenuti in gruppo in casa e non vengono mai liberati in natura. Si tratta dello stesso piccolo roditore del ratto domestico (Rattus norvegicus), semplicemente di una specie diversa.

Potreste confermarmi per iscritto che il Rattus rattus nato in cattività è trattato esattamente come il ratto domestico — un «piccolo roditore» esente da autorizzazione per la detenzione privata a scopo hobbistico, con la stessa soglia di 300 animali all'anno — e non come un «animale selvatico» che richiede un'autorizzazione cantonale? Sarebbe inoltre utile, per i futuri detentori, se la specie fosse menzionata nei vostri documenti.

Vi ringrazio molto per il vostro aiuto.

Cordiali saluti,
[Il vostro nome]
[Il vostro cantone / CAP]
[Il vostro indirizzo e-mail]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Tierschutzgesetz (TSchG, SR 455) — Federal Animal Welfare Act — Swiss Confederation / Fedlex
  • Tierschutzverordnung (TSchV, SR 455.1) — Art. 2 (Wildtier/Heimtier), Art. 13 (social), Anhang 2 Tab.1 (rats), Art. 101–102 (permits) — Swiss Confederation / Fedlex
  • BLV Merkblatt 'Ratten im Recht' — private keeping permit-free; group rule; enclosure minimums; 300/yr threshold — BLV (Federal Food Safety & Veterinary Office)
  • BLV Fachinformation — Bewilligungs- und Ausbildungspflicht für den gewerbsmässigen Handel mit Heimtieren — BLV
  • BLV — Travelling with pets / import of rodents (≤5 personal, no permit/health cert) — BLV

Search terms: Rattus rattus, Hausratte, rat noir, ratto nero.

Last reviewed 2026-06-07. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Chile? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Chile

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.

Summary. Chile has no blanket ban on keeping captive-bred rats as pets, and in practice a roof rat is treated like the openly-sold fancy rat (R. norvegicus). Both are established commensal exotics classified as invasive (MMA's 2017 naturalized/invasive catalogue) and cited as 'especie dañina' in the agricultural-pest context, but NO SAG decree under the Ley de Caza (Ley 19.473) formally lists either Rattus species or bans keeping them. The Ley de Caza's wildlife-keeper registry (RNTFS) and criadero licensing are built for genuinely wild/protected exotic fauna (parrots, reptiles), not ubiquitous commensal rodents — so captive-bred pet rats sit in a practical gray zone (neither licensed nor expressly prohibited), and fancy rats are sold across Chilean platforms with no reported enforcement. For R. rattus there's an extra layer: its pest/invasive designation creates theoretical friction with private breeding, though no statute prohibits captive-bred specimens. IMPORT of any live exotic rodent needs a case-by-case SAG Art. 25 internment permit (which SAG could refuse on ecological grounds given the invasive status); internal transport of lawfully-held animals is unregulated. Not CITES-listed. ⚠️ Watch: the MMA is building a formal official invasive-species list under Ley 21.600 (2023) that, if it attaches possession provisions, could flip this to prohibited (Spain-style).

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

No Chilean statute prohibits a private individual from keeping captive-bred R. rattus. The Ley de Caza (19.473) governs 'fauna silvestre' via RNTFS registration aimed at exotic WILDLIFE (parrots, caimans) — a ubiquitous commensal like R. rattus doesn't neatly fall into that permit pipeline. The MMA EEI catalogue documents R. rattus as naturalized/invasive but prescribes no keeping ban. The strongest signal: R. norvegicus, in the same pest registers, is openly sold. No SAG resolution banning tenencia of captive R. rattus exists.

Sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional (BCN), SAG, Ministerio del Medio Ambiente

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-08

Breeding exotic fauna can in principle require SAG criadero-de-fauna-silvestre-exótica registration under the Ley de Caza, but that pathway targets genuinely wild/protected exotics; no regulation clearly extends criadero licensing to commensal rodents. Ley 21.020 ('Ley Cholito') requires companion-animal breeders/sellers to register with SAG but its guidance focuses on dogs/cats. Chilean vendors openly breed/sell rats (no active enforcement); the 'unenforced vs legal' gap is unresolved.

Sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional (BCN), BCN

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-08

Domestic rats are actively sold on Chilean platforms/specialist stores with no reported enforcement. Chilean law bars commercial sale of wild-captured native fauna but doesn't clearly reach captive-bred exotic commensal rodents. Ley 21.020 requires companion-animal vendors/breeders to hold SAG registration + per-animal vet health cards (the closest affirmative obligation). No statute prohibits selling/donating captive-bred R. rattus; the 'especie dañina' tag affects pest-control authorization, not a commercial ban under Ley 19.473's current text.

Sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional (BCN), BCN

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

IMPORT of any live exotic animal (incl. rodents) needs two SAG authorizations under Ley 19.473 Art. 25: (1) an Exotic Fauna Internment Permit from DIPROREN; and (2) a species-specific zoosanitary protocol from PROPEC — ~60–90 days' notice. ⚠️ Because R. rattus is an established feral pest in Chile, SAG MAY refuse the import permit on ecological grounds (real risk; confirm). Not CITES-listed. INTERNAL transport of lawfully-held pets has no specific permit (Ley Cholito imposes only normal vet care) — practically unregulated. Never release.

Sources: SAG, Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional (BCN)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Keeping a captive-bred roof rat in Chile is in a gray zone (no licence, no express ban — treated like the openly-sold fancy rat). IMPORTING one needs a SAG Art. 25 exotic-fauna internment permit (DIPROREN) + a PROPEC zoosanitary protocol, applied 60–90 days ahead — and SAG could refuse it given R. rattus's invasive status. Internal transport of a lawful animal is unregulated. ⚠️ Watch the MMA's forthcoming EEI list (could add a possession rule). Never release.
  • For import: SAG DIPROREN exotic-fauna internment permit (Art. 25) + PROPEC zoosanitary protocol

Where: SAG — DIPROREN (import permit) / PROPEC (zoosanitary)

Source: SAG

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Help change this

How to help in Chile

Chile is currently a legal/unclear case, but it is actively building its invasive-species rules under Ley 21.600 (2023) and the new Biodiversity Service (SBAP). The 2025 public consultation on the draft regulation for qualifying invasive species and prevention plans has closed, but the invasive-species catalogue itself (the actual list) and further rules are still to come — and how Rattus rattus is classified there could restrict keeping it as a pet.

The ask: When the MMA/SBAP opens its next public consultation (consulta pública) — especially on the invasive-species catalogue — submit a comment asking that domesticated, captive-bred R. rattus kept as pets be distinguished from wild invasive populations (a keeping pathway rather than a flat ban). Watch the consultation portal for the next window.

Where the lever really is: This is decided by the executive/regulator (MMA / SBAP) through formal public-consultation windows — so the lever is submitting a comment when a window is open (and writing the MMA), not the courts or Congress. No window is open right now; the move is to watch for the next one.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Ministerio del Medio Ambiente (MMA) — consulta pública (EEI / Ley 21.600) (public comment) — official contact page
    The draft regulation qualifying invasive exotic species and prevention plans is run here for public comment under Ley 21.600 — comment while a window is open.
  • Servicio Agrícola y Ganadero (SAG) (executive / agency) — diproren@sag.gob.cl
    SAG coordinates invasive-species control on the agricultural side — a useful second touchpoint.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Ministry of the Environment (MMA),

I am writing about how the roof rat (Rattus rattus) is classified in the invasive-species work under Ley 21.600.

I ask that domesticated, captive-bred roof rats kept as pets be treated separately from wild invasive populations. These are tame animals bred over generations, kept indoors in cages and never released; they pose no invasive risk. A keeping pathway (registration or a simple permit) would protect biodiversity goals without criminalising responsible pet owners.

Please consider this distinction in the EEI catalogue and any prevention plan.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
Español
Al Ministerio del Medio Ambiente (MMA),

Escribo en relación con la clasificación de la rata negra (Rattus rattus) en el trabajo sobre especies exóticas invasoras que se desarrolla en el marco de la Ley 21.600.

Solicito que las ratas negras domesticadas, criadas en cautiverio y mantenidas como mascotas, se traten de forma separada de las poblaciones silvestres invasoras. Son animales mansos, criados durante generaciones, mantenidos en jaulas en interiores y que nunca se liberan; no representan un riesgo invasor. Una vía de tenencia (un registro o un permiso sencillo) permitiría proteger los objetivos de biodiversidad sin criminalizar a las personas responsables que las tienen como mascotas.

Le pido que considere esta distinción en el catálogo de EEI y en cualquier plan de prevención.

Atentamente,
[Su nombre]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Ley 19.473 (Ley de Caza, 1996) — Arts. 1–5, 25 (internación), 26(e) (especie dañina) — Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional (BCN)
  • DS 5/1998 — Reglamento de la Ley de Caza (mod. DS 53) — SAG
  • MMA — Catálogo de Especies Exóticas Asilvestradas/Naturalizadas (2017): R. rattus + R. norvegicus naturalized invasives — Ministerio del Medio Ambiente
  • Ley 21.020 ('Ley Cholito', 2017) — tenencia responsable; breeder/seller registration — BCN
  • Ley 21.600 (2023) — crea SBAP; mandates a formal EEI list (not yet gazetted for this) — BCN / MMA
  • SAG — Internación de fauna exótica (Art. 25 permit; DIPROREN; ~60-day timeline) + non-traditional pet protocol (PROPEC) — SAG

Search terms: Rattus rattus, rata negra, rata de los tejados.

Last reviewed 2026-06-08. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Colombia? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Colombia

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. Colombia prohibits private keeping, breeding, selling, and transport of the roof rat. R. rattus is formally cataloged a High-Risk Exotic Invasive Species (Especie Exótica Invasora) under Resolución MAVDT 0848/2008 (+ 0207/2010) on the strict-invasive PROHIBITIVE track — NOT the closed-cycle 'zoocría' track — so Decreto 1076/2015 Art. 2.2.2.3.2.2 bans its 'introduction, commercialization, mobilization, promotion and possession (tenencia)' outright. The captive-bred-as-pet loophole is now permanently closed: Ley 2473 de 2025 (8 Jul 2025) amended Civil Code Art. 687 to declare that exotic/wild fauna CANNOT be a 'domestic companion animal,' regardless of how tame or how many generations captive-bred — every R. rattus stays under environmental law where possession is banned. Breeding is a CRIME (Penal Code Art. 330A: 48–108 months prison + heavy fines). Import is administratively impossible (the genus Rattus is absent from the ICA pet-import whitelist, Resolución 842/2010). A confiscated roof rat is not rehomed — as an Angiostrongylus cantonensis (rat lungworm) and plague vector it is administratively euthanized. The ONLY legal holders are institutions under scientific/zoological permits (ANLA/CAR) — never private hobbyists. (Note: even the fancy rat R. norvegicus has only a narrow lab/bioterium import route, not a pet route; R. rattus has neither.)

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

Private possession (tenencia) of a declared invasive species is banned by Decreto 1076/2015 Art. 2.2.2.3.2.2; R. rattus is on the strict-invasive track of Resolución 0848/2008 (High Risk). Ley 2473/2025 amended Civil Code Art. 687 with a paragraph stating exotic/wild fauna are NOT 'domestic companion animals,' permanently defeating the captive-bred/'tame' argument. The state does not distinguish a feral roof rat from a multi-generation captive-bred one. Enforcement (Ley 1333/2009) = preventive confiscation by the environmental authority (CAR) + Environmental Police/GELMA; a seized R. rattus is administratively euthanized (Angiostrongylus/plague vector), not rehomed; fines scale up to 5,000 SMLMV. Only institutional scientific/zoological permit-holders may hold the species — never a private individual.

Sources: Presidencia de Colombia, Ministerio de Ambiente (MAVDT/MADS), Congreso de la República, Congreso de la República

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

Breeding R. rattus — hobby or commercial — is a criminal offense. Penal Code Art. 330A (Ley 599/2000, added by Ley 1453/2011) penalizes propagating an invasive exotic species without authorization with 48–108 months prison + fines of 133–15,000 SMLMV. The zoocría (captive-breeding) framework of Ley 611/2000 has no hobbyist exemption and cannot license a declared-invasive species (Decreto 1076/2015 bars its commercialization), so no commercial/scientific zoocría permit will issue for the pet trade. There is no closed-cycle (Art. 4) pathway for R. rattus — it sits on the prohibitive Art. 1 track.

Sources: Congreso de la República, Congreso de la República, Presidencia de Colombia

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

Decreto 1076/2015 Art. 2.2.2.3.2.2 explicitly bans the commercialization and promotion of declared invasive species; the ICA pet-trade whitelists exclude the genus Rattus. Even gratuitous transfer (giving away) is barred because no one can legally possess the animal (tenencia ban), so any transfer just facilitates a further infraction. A licensed pet dealer caught selling R. rattus faces confiscation, fines under Ley 1333/2009, and definitive closure of the establishment.

Sources: Presidencia de Colombia, Congreso de la República, Instituto Colombiano Agropecuario (ICA)

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

IMPORT: administratively impossible — Resolución ICA 842/2010 limits 'other pets' import to ferrets, rabbits, chinchillas, hamsters, guinea pigs and gerbils; the genus Rattus is absent, so the ICA SISPAP system cannot generate the Documento Zoosanitario de Importación (DZI) needed before shipment, and an animal arriving without it is rejected/confiscated/euthanized at the border. INTERNAL movement: needs a Salvoconducto Único Nacional (SUN) under Decreto 1076/2015 Title 2, which requires proof of legal origin (a licensed-zoocriadero receipt or valid ICA import docs) — impossible for R. rattus, so no CAR issues one; illegal transport triggers Penal Code Art. 328 (illicit use of renewable natural resources). Not CITES-listed (irrelevant — the invasive ban governs). Never release.

Sources: Instituto Colombiano Agropecuario (ICA), Presidencia de Colombia, Congreso de la República

Restrictions & responsibilities

Colombia bans keeping/breeding/selling/transporting R. rattus as a declared High-Risk Exotic Invasive Species. There is NO private or hobbyist pathway: possession is an environmental infraction (confiscation + administrative euthanasia), breeding is a crime (48–108 months prison), import is administratively impossible (genus Rattus off the ICA whitelist), and internal transport requires a salvoconducto that cannot be issued. Ley 2473/2025 forecloses any 'it's a tame captive-bred pet' argument. Do not acquire one; if you already hold one, a Derecho de Petición to MADS is the only way to ask about an amnesty/scientific-transfer alternative to seizure.
  • Do not import, buy, breed, or accept an R. rattus in Colombia — all are prohibited (breeding is criminal).
  • If you already possess one: consider a Derecho de Petición (Constitution Art. 23) to MADS asking about a grandfather/amnesty registration or transfer to an authorized scientific bioterium rather than euthanasia.
  • Institutions only: scientific/zoological holding requires an ANLA/CAR environmental license (biosecurity containment) — not available to individuals.

Where: MADS (policy/amnesty Derecho de Petición); regional CAR (enforcement/SUN); ICA (import)

Source: Presidencia de Colombia, Ministerio de Ambiente (MAVDT/MADS), Congreso de la República

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Colombia. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Colombia

In Colombia there is no legal way for a private individual to keep, breed, buy, sell, give away, import, or transport a roof rat (Rattus rattus) — not even a tame, captive-bred one. The roof rat is officially cataloged as a High-Risk Exotic Invasive Species (Resolución MAVDT 0848 de 2008), so Decreto 1076 de 2015 (Art. 2.2.2.3.2.2) bans its introduction, sale, transport, promotion, and possession (tenencia) outright. In July 2025, Ley 2473 amended Civil Code Art. 687 to declare that exotic and wild fauna are NOT "domestic companion animals," no matter how tame or how many generations they were bred in captivity — which permanently closes the "but it's a captive-bred pet" argument. Breeding is a criminal offense (Penal Code Art. 330A: 48–108 months in prison plus heavy fines). Import is administratively impossible because the genus Rattus is not on the ICA pet-import whitelist (Resolución ICA 842/2010, which lists only ferrets, rabbits, chinchillas, hamsters, guinea pigs, and gerbils). A confiscated roof rat is not rehomed: as a potential rat-lungworm (Angiostrongylus cantonensis) and plague vector, it is administratively euthanized. Only institutions with a scientific/zoological permit (ANLA/CAR) may legally hold the species — never a private hobbyist. This ban is grounded in a genuine ecological and public-health concern (island ecosystems like San Andrés and Gorgona; rat lungworm spread via the Giant African Snail), so simply asking the agency to "reinterpret" the rule will not work.

The ask: Be honest with yourself first: in Colombia today there is no private pathway to keep a roof rat, and no letter will change that overnight. If you do not already hold one, do not acquire, import, or breed one — breeding is a crime. If you genuinely care about the welfare of this species and about fairer rules, the realistic, lawful actions are: (1) If you already possess a pre-2025 captive-bred roof rat, file a Derecho de Petición to MinAmbiente (MADS) asking whether any amnesty / pre-existing-possession registration exists to keep it strictly non-breeding until natural death, OR whether you may voluntarily surrender it to an authorized scientific bioterium instead of having it euthanized. (2) Optionally ask ICA in writing to confirm whether any administrative exception or tariff code exists to import domestic-line Rattus as a companion animal (expected answer: none — this documents the gap for the public record). (3) Understand that broadening the law itself (e.g., creating a regulated captive-bred companion-rodent category, or distinguishing biosecure indoor lines from feral invasives) is a matter for the Congreso de la República, not the environmental agency, which is correctly applying the current statute.

Where the lever really is: This is the LAW AS WRITTEN, not a bureaucratic misreading. The agency (MinAmbiente) is applying the statute correctly: (a) Resolución MAVDT 0848 de 2008 puts R. rattus on the strict-invasive (prohibitive) track as High-Risk, not the closed-cycle "zoocría" track; (b) Decreto 1076 de 2015 Art. 2.2.2.3.2.2 then bans possession of any declared invasive species; (c) Ley 2473 de 2025 amended Civil Code Art. 687 to state explicitly that exotic/wild fauna are NOT domestic companion animals regardless of taming or captive breeding — Congress closed the loophole on purpose; and (d) the import whitelist (Resolución ICA 842/2010) simply does not contain the genus Rattus. Every door is shut by black-letter law, and the ban rests on a real zoonotic/ecological record (rat lungworm via the Giant African Snail; plague; island-ecosystem damage). Therefore appealing to MinAmbiente to "reinterpret" the rules will NOT change anything — the agency has no discretion to authorize private possession of a declared High-Risk invasive, and a de-cataloging petition is a realistic non-starter given the documented harm. The genuine levers are two and both narrow: (1) For someone who ALREADY holds a pre-2025 captive-bred animal, a Derecho de Petición to MinAmbiente is appropriate — but it asks only about amnesty/registration or surrender-to-a-bioterium as a humane alternative to seizure-and-euthanasia, NOT about a general right to keep pet roof rats. (2) Any actual change to who may keep the species would require the Congreso de la República to amend the statutory framework (e.g., a regulated biosecure captive-line category). Be plain with readers: there is no private route today, and the agency cannot create one.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (MinAmbiente / MADS) — Atención y Servicios a la Ciudadanía (PQRSDF / Derecho de Petición) (executive / agency) — servicioalciudadano@minambiente.gov.co
    The environmental ministry is the authority that catalogs invasive species and governs possession. It is the correct address for a Derecho de Petición (Constitution Art. 23; Ley 1755 de 2015) — but ONLY for the narrow, honest questions: does an amnesty/pre-existing-possession registry exist for an animal already held, and can a voluntarily surrendered animal go to an authorized scientific bioterium instead of being euthanized. Use the official PQRSDF channel (online portal linked from this page, or the servicioalciudadano inbox). It cannot and will not authorize general private keeping — the law forecloses that.
  • Instituto Colombiano Agropecuario (ICA) — Cuarentena Animal / Importación de animales de compañía diferentes a perros y gatos (executive / agency) — cuarentena.animal@ica.gov.co
    ICA controls animal import. A short written query asking ICA to confirm whether any tariff code or administrative exception exists to import domestic-line Rattus as a companion animal documents the regulatory gap on the public record (expected answer: none — the genus Rattus is absent from the Resolución 842/2010 whitelist). Useful only as evidence-gathering, not as a route to a permit.
  • Congreso de la República de Colombia — Cámara de Representantes (contacto ciudadano / atención al ciudadano) (legislature) — official contact page
    Because the prohibition is statutory (Decreto 1076/2015 + Resolución 0848/2008 + Ley 2473/2025), the only body that could ever create a regulated pathway for biosecure captive-bred companion rodents is the legislature, not the agency. This is the official citizen-contact channel for raising that idea with representatives. Realistically a long, uphill ask given the species' genuine invasive/zoonotic record — included for honesty, not false hope.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To: Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development (MinAmbiente) — Citizen Services / Right of Petition
Subject: Right of Petition regarding an already-held captive-bred Rattus rattus — possible amnesty/registration or transfer to a scientific facility

Dear Sir or Madam,

I write respectfully under the right of petition (Constitution Art. 23; Law 1755 of 2015). I understand that Rattus rattus is listed as a High-Risk Exotic Invasive Species (Resolution 0848 of 2008), that its possession is prohibited (Decree 1076 of 2015), and that Law 2473 of 2025 confirms exotic fauna are not companion animals. I am not contesting that framework or the genuine ecological and public-health concerns behind it.

My questions are narrow: (1) Does any amnesty, pre-existing-possession registry, or special authorization exist that would let a citizen keep a captive-bred specimen acquired before 2025 strictly as a non-breeding, indoor-only animal until its natural death? (2) If not, may such an animal be voluntarily surrendered to an authorized scientific facility (bioterio) rather than being euthanized? The animal in question is captive-bred, tame, kept indoors, and never released.

I request a written reply within the legal term. Thank you for your guidance.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your city / contact details]
Español
Para: Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (MinAmbiente) — Atención al Ciudadano / Derecho de Petición
Asunto: Derecho de Petición sobre un ejemplar de Rattus rattus nacido en cautiverio ya en tenencia — posible amnistía/registro o traslado a un bioterio científico

Respetados señores:

En ejercicio del derecho de petición (Art. 23 de la Constitución; Ley 1755 de 2015) me dirijo a ustedes de manera respetuosa. Entiendo que Rattus rattus está catalogada como Especie Exótica Invasora de Alto Riesgo (Resolución 0848 de 2008), que su tenencia está prohibida (Decreto 1076 de 2015) y que la Ley 2473 de 2025 confirma que la fauna exótica no es animal de compañía. No controvierto ese marco ni las legítimas preocupaciones ecológicas y de salud pública que lo sustentan.

Mis preguntas son puntuales: (1) ¿Existe algún mecanismo de amnistía, registro de tenencia preexistente o autorización especial que permita a un ciudadano mantener un ejemplar nacido en cautiverio adquirido antes de 2025, en tenencia estricta, sin reproducción, exclusivamente al interior del hogar y hasta su muerte natural? (2) De no existir, ¿puede dicho ejemplar entregarse voluntariamente a un bioterio científico autorizado en lugar de ser sometido a eutanasia? El animal es nacido en cautiverio, manso, mantenido dentro del hogar y nunca liberado.

Solicito respuesta escrita dentro del término legal. Agradezco su orientación.

Atentamente,
[Su nombre]
[Su ciudad / datos de contacto]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Ley 2473 de 2025 — modifica Código Civil Art. 687: la fauna exótica/silvestre NO es 'animal doméstico de compañía' (cierra el vacío de la mascota cautiva) — Congreso de la República
  • Decreto 1076/2015 — Art. 2.2.2.3.2.2 (prohíbe introducción/comercialización/movilización/promoción/tenencia de invasoras) + Título 2/Sec. 22 (salvoconducto SUN) — Presidencia de Colombia
  • Resolución MAVDT 0848/2008 (+ 0207/2010) — lista de especies exóticas invasoras; R. rattus 'Alto Riesgo' (track Art. 1 prohibitivo) — Ministerio de Ambiente (MAVDT/MADS)
  • Ley 599/2000 (Código Penal) Art. 330A (+ Art. 328) — propagación de especie exótica invasora: 48–108 meses prisión + multa 133–15.000 SMLMV — Congreso de la República
  • Ley 1333/2009 — procedimiento sancionatorio ambiental (decomiso + multas hasta 5.000 SMLMV + cierre de establecimientos) — Congreso de la República
  • Resolución ICA 842/2010 — requisitos importación 'otras mascotas' (hurones/conejos/chinchillas/hámsteres/cobayos/jerbos; género Rattus AUSENTE) — Instituto Colombiano Agropecuario (ICA)
  • Ley 611/2000 — manejo sostenible de fauna silvestre / zoocriaderos (sin exención para aficionados; no licenciable para invasoras) — Congreso de la República

Search terms: Rattus rattus, rata negra, rata de techo, especie exótica invasora, fauna exótica, tenencia.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Czechia? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Czechia

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.

Summary. Czechia is permissive for the roof rat. It uses a negative-list system: under the Animal Protection Act (Zákon 246/1992 Sb.) and Decree 451/2021 Sb., only enumerated species need a 'special-care' permit — and Rattus rattus (Czech: krysa obecná) is NOT on that list, so it's freely kept as a hobby animal. It's also absent from the EU invasive-species Union list and from Czechia's national IAS framework (Zákon 364/2021 Sb.), and not CITES-listed. So a hobbyist may keep, breed and sell/give captive-bred roof rats with no permit; only commercial-scale breeding/trade requires registering with the regional veterinary office (KVS) at least 7 days ahead. Intra-EU movement of pet rodents needs no harmonized health certificate. (Czech usefully distinguishes 'krysa' = R. rattus from 'potkan' = R. norvegicus.)

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

R. rattus is not in Příloha č. 1 of Vyhláška 451/2021 Sb. (the exhaustive list of species requiring special care + a veterinary permit), so private keeping needs no permit/registration — only the general welfare duties of Zákon 246/1992 Sb. Not CITES-listed. Hobby keeping/sale from own breeding is a 'free trade' category under Czech trade law.

Sources: zakonyprolidi.cz (CZ legal database), zakonyprolidi.cz

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Hobby breeding needs no permit (R. rattus outside the special-care list; no EU/national rule mandates registration of this species). Commercial/business-scale breeding must register with the regional Krajská veterinární správa (KVS) ≥7 days before starting (Zákon 166/1999 Sb. §5(2)). No species-specific prohibition or quota; Zákon 364/2021 Sb. (IAS) doesn't list R. rattus.

Sources: zakonyprolidi.cz, zakonyprolidi.cz

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Giving away from one's own hobby breeding is unrestricted; selling from own breeding is a 'free trade' (živnost volná) needing only business notification if operated as a business. Occasional hobbyist-to-hobbyist sales don't ordinarily trigger that. No species ban/permit/quota for R. rattus; welfare conditions of Zákon 246/1992 Sb. §13 apply (e.g., no sale to under-15s without parental consent).

Sources: zakonyprolidi.cz (CZ legal database)

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Intra-EU non-commercial movement of pet rodents (EU Reg. 576/2013 Annex I Part B; up to 5 animals, owner-accompanied) needs no harmonized health certificate; the Czech veterinary administration (SVS) imposes no conditions provided the origin isn't under an animal-health alert. Commercial consignments may need TRACES NT notification. No IAS bar (R. rattus not on the Union list). Never release.

Sources: EU / EUR-Lex, Státní veterinární správa

Restrictions & responsibilities

Keeping/breeding/selling captive-bred roof rats is legal in Czechia with no permit for hobbyists. Only at commercial/business scale must you register with the regional veterinary office (KVS) ≥7 days before starting. Never release a roof rat.
  • If commercial-scale, register with the regional Krajská veterinární správa (KVS) ≥7 days ahead

Where: Krajská veterinární správa (KVS) / SVS

Source: zakonyprolidi.cz

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Zákon č. 246/1992 Sb. na ochranu zvířat proti týrání (welfare; §13 sale conditions) — zakonyprolidi.cz (CZ legal database)
  • Vyhláška č. 451/2021 Sb. — druhy vyžadující zvláštní péči (special-care species list; R. rattus absent) — zakonyprolidi.cz
  • Zákon č. 166/1999 Sb. o veterinární péči §5(2) (commercial breeder registration with KVS) — zakonyprolidi.cz
  • Zákon č. 364/2021 Sb. — Czech implementation of EU IAS rules (R. rattus not listed) — zakonyprolidi.cz
  • Regulation (EU) 576/2013 — non-commercial pet movement (Annex I Part B: rodents) — EU / EUR-Lex
  • SVS — Requirements for travelling with other pet animals (no CZ restrictions on EU-origin rodents) — Státní veterinární správa

Search terms: Rattus rattus, krysa obecná.

Summary. Germany has no national 'positive list' and generally permits keeping small pets. The black rat (Hausratte, Rattus rattus) does not appear on the EU list of invasive alien species of Union concern, so keeping it is generally allowed, subject to animal-welfare husbandry rules. Selling animals commercially needs a §11 permit. To be confirmed.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

No national positive list; Rattus rattus is not on the EU list of invasive alien species of Union concern, so private keeping is generally permitted. Animal-welfare husbandry standards (social housing, minimum cage sizes) apply.

Sources: European Union, Animal Legal & Historical Center (summary)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Hobby breeding is generally permitted; commercial/regular breeding may require a §11 TierSchG permit.

Sources: Animal Legal & Historical Center (summary)

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling animals commercially requires a permit under §11 of the Animal Welfare Act (Tierschutzgesetz); occasional private rehoming generally does not.

Sources: Animal Legal & Historical Center (summary)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-06

Within the EU, movement of pet animals follows EU pet-movement/health rules; no German release of non-native species.

Sources: European Union

Restrictions & responsibilities

Commercial breeding or sale of animals requires a permit under §11 of the Tierschutzgesetz (animal welfare act), issued by the local Veterinäramt.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Denmark? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Denmark

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.

Summary. Denmark is a genuinely unsettled — and likely restrictive — case for the roof rat, because of an unusual conflict. The forbidden-exotic-pets order (BEK 1261/2015) does NOT list Rattus rattus, so there's no exotic-permit bar. BUT Denmark's mandatory rat-control law (Bekendtgørelse om forebyggelse og bekæmpelse af rotter, BEK 2307/2021, updated 2024, under the Environmental Protection Act) explicitly names BOTH Rattus norvegicus AND Rattus rattus in its scope and imposes a duty on every citizen to REPORT, and on every municipality to ERADICATE, any occurrence of these rats — with no written exemption for captive-bred pets. Danish natural-history and pest authorities consistently read this as meaning R. rattus cannot lawfully be kept as a pet (unlike the de-facto-tolerated domesticated tamrotte, R. norvegicus). Whether a caged pet roof rat actually triggers the report-and-destroy duty has never been resolved by published agency guidance — the single most important question, which we've queued.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

The rat-control order BEK 2307/2021 (under Miljøbeskyttelsesloven §17a) defines its scope as control of R. norvegicus AND R. rattus and imposes a citizen duty to report + a municipal duty to eradicate all occurrences, with no textual carve-out for captive specimens. Danish authorities (Naturbasen, Dansk Pattedyratlas, Dansk Pattedyrforening) read this as making it impractical/unlawful to keep R. rattus as a pet — though no published enforcement ruling against a hobbyist was found. The separate forbidden-exotic order (BEK 1261/2015) does NOT list R. rattus, so the restriction stems from rat-control law, not an exotic ban.

Sources: Miljøministeriet (Retsinformation), Ministeriet for Fødevarer, Landbrug og Fiskeri, Dansk Pattedyratlas / Lex

Breeding   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Breeding compounds the keeping problem: if a single specimen triggers the rat-control report duty, offspring amplify it. Hobby breeding of the domesticated tamrotte (R. norvegicus) needs no permit, but for R. rattus the species-level rat-control status is the binding constraint. Commercial breeding/sale of any species needs a Fødevarestyrelsen tilladelse (BEK 1366/2017), which for R. rattus would likely be a non-starter.

Sources: Miljøministeriet (Retsinformation), Retsinformation, Retsinformation

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Commercial sale of animals needs a Fødevarestyrelsen tilladelse (BEK 1366/2017); hobby transfer of common pets (e.g., R. norvegicus) isn't regulated at the transfer step. For R. rattus the same rat-control conflict applies regardless of commercial vs gratuitous: moving a live roof rat onto another person's premises introduces a rat-control-regulated species there. The Danish pet-rat scene (Den Danske Tamrotteforening) focuses on R. norvegicus; R. rattus is practically unavailable in the trade.

Sources: Retsinformation, Miljøministeriet (Retsinformation)

Transport & import   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-07

Intra-EU: EU pet-movement harmonisation (Reg. 576/2013) covers only dogs/cats/ferrets, so national rules apply; Denmark's guidance for non-dog/cat/ferret pets says check national rules, and no specific inbound health-certificate rule for pet rodents was found. BUT the rat-control restriction on R. rattus would attach the moment the animal enters Denmark, making transport moot if keeping is restricted. Internal movement likewise introduces a reportable species at the destination. No permit pathway identified. Never release.

Sources: Fødevarestyrelsen, Miljøministeriet (Retsinformation)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Denmark's mandatory rat-control law names Rattus rattus and requires reporting/eradication of rat occurrences, with no written pet exemption — so keeping a roof rat is at best legally uncertain and likely restricted, even though it's not on the forbidden-exotic list. Get a written ruling from Fødevarestyrelsen / Miljøstyrelsen BEFORE acquiring one. Never release a roof rat.
  • Request a written ruling on whether a caged pet R. rattus triggers the rat-control report/destroy duty (Fødevarestyrelsen + Miljøstyrelsen)

Where: Fødevarestyrelsen (exotic-pet) / Miljøstyrelsen (rat control)

Source: Miljøministeriet (Retsinformation)

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Denmark. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Denmark

In Denmark, the roof rat (Rattus rattus) is not on the forbidden-exotic-pets list, so there is no exotic-permit ban. The obstacle comes from a different place: Denmark's mandatory rat-control order (currently BEK nr. 1170 of 8 September 2023, in force since 1 January 2024, issued under the Environmental Protection Act) names BOTH the brown rat (Rattus norvegicus) AND the roof rat (Rattus rattus) by species in its scope. That order makes it every citizen's duty to report any "occurrence" (forekomst) of these rats and every municipality's duty to eradicate them — and it contains no written exemption for a captive-bred, caged pet. Because the order targets the SPECIES, not wild behaviour, a tame indoor roof rat reads as caught by the same rule that targets pest infestations. No published guidance has ever resolved whether a single caged pet actually triggers the report-and-destroy duty, which leaves keepers in legal limbo. (Note: the brown rat — the familiar "fancy rat" or tamrotte — is named in exactly the same order, yet is kept freely as a pet across Denmark; the roof rat is treated differently only by reputation, not by any difference in the rule's wording.)

The ask: We are asking Miljøstyrelsen (the Danish Environmental Protection Agency, which authors the rat-control order) for one of two concrete, lawful clarifications: (1) a written ruling or published guidance note stating that an individually captive-bred Rattus rattus kept in a secure cage indoors is NOT a reportable "forekomst" under the rat-control order — i.e., the report-and-eradicate duty reaches only free-living rat populations, not a contained pet; OR (2) at the next revision of the order, a small captive-pet carve-out exempting securely housed, captive-bred pet specimens — the same practical treatment the brown rat (fancy rat) already enjoys under the identical wording. We also flag to the Folketing's Environment and Food Committee that the species-level wording, with no pet carve-out, appears to be a drafting oversight worth correcting, since neighbouring countries (Netherlands, Sweden) allow roof-rat pets without this conflict.

Where the lever really is: This is principally a LAW-AS-WRITTEN problem with an agency-rulemaking lever — a hybrid, but the controlling fact is that the species sits on a statutory list. The roof rat (Rattus rattus) is named BY SPECIES in the rat-control order (BEK nr. 1170 of 8 Sept 2023, under Miljøbeskyttelsesloven). The municipal eradication duty and the citizen report duty flow directly from that wording, so an enforcing municipality or the agency is applying the rule CORRECTLY when it treats a roof rat as in-scope. Therefore appealing for mercy or arguing "you're misreading the law" will NOT work — the text says what it says. The real lever is to change or clarify the text. Crucially, in Denmark the rat-control order is a ministerial bekendtgørelse drafted and administered by Miljøstyrelsen, NOT primary legislation passed line-by-line by the Folketing — so the agency itself is the body that can fix it, either by a published scope-clarification (confirming a caged pet is not a "forekomst") or by adding a captive-pet exemption at the next revision. That makes Miljøstyrelsen the primary, legitimate target even though this is a "law on a list" case. The one genuinely open agency-misreading angle worth preserving is the unresolved definitional question — whether a contained pet is even a "forekomst" at all — which is a clarification request, not a plea against correct enforcement. The Folketing's Environment and Food Committee is the legislative backstop if the agency declines to amend its own order. Note for keepers: do NOT expect a single caseworker to grant a personal exemption to a written rule on the spot — the fix is a guidance note or a rule amendment, which is a policy step, not a frontline discretion.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Miljøstyrelsen — Rat control unit (Rottebekæmpelse) (executive / agency) — rotter@mst.dk
    Miljøstyrelsen drafts and administers the rat-control order (BEK 1170/2023) that names Rattus rattus by species — so it is the body that can either publish a scope clarification (a caged pet is not a reportable 'forekomst') or add a captive-pet exemption at the next revision. rotter@mst.dk is the verified subject-specific rat-control inbox; the contact page is the official backup channel. This is the primary, correct target for both the clarification ask and the rule-amendment ask.
  • Folketinget — Miljø- og Fødevareudvalget (Environment and Food Committee) (legislature) — official contact page
    Legislative backstop. If Miljøstyrelsen declines to amend its own order or clarify scope, the Folketing's Environment and Food Committee is the channel that can press the Minister to add a captive-pet carve-out at revision. Use this only as escalation, and contact the committee via its official page — never an individual member by name.
  • Fødevarestyrelsen (Danish Veterinary and Food Administration) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Secondary cross-check. The roof rat is NOT on Fødevarestyrelsen's forbidden-exotic list (BEK 1261/2015), so this agency can confirm in writing that the exotic-pet regime poses no bar — pinning the issue squarely on the rat-control order and strengthening the case put to Miljøstyrelsen. Useful for documenting that no exotic-permit pathway is even required.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request for clarification / captive-pet exemption — Rattus rattus under the rat-control order (BEK nr. 1170 of 8 September 2023)

Dear Miljøstyrelsen,

I am writing about the keeping of captive-bred roof rats (Rattus rattus) as pets. The rat-control order names this species alongside the brown rat (Rattus norvegicus) but contains no written exemption for a tame, captive-bred animal kept in a secure cage.

The animals I am asking about are bred in captivity, hand-tame, kept permanently indoors in a closed enclosure, and never released. They pose none of the public-health risks the order is designed to address — exactly like the brown rat (the fancy rat / tamrotte), which is named in the same order yet is kept freely as a pet throughout Denmark.

I respectfully request either: (1) a written confirmation that an individually caged, captive-bred Rattus rattus is not a reportable 'forekomst' under the order; or (2) a small captive-pet exemption at the next revision, matching the practical treatment the brown rat already receives.

Thank you for your consideration. I would be grateful for a written reply.

Kind regards,
[Your name]
[Your town/region, if you wish]
da
Emne: Anmodning om afklaring / undtagelse for kæledyr — Rattus rattus efter rottebekendtgørelsen (BEK nr. 1170 af 8. september 2023)

Kære Miljøstyrelse

Jeg skriver vedrørende hold af opdrættede husrotter (Rattus rattus) som kæledyr. Rottebekendtgørelsen nævner denne art sammen med den brune rotte (Rattus norvegicus), men indeholder ingen skriftlig undtagelse for et tamt, i fangenskab opdrættet dyr, der holdes i et sikkert bur.

De dyr, jeg spørger om, er opdrættet i fangenskab, håndtamme, holdes permanent indendørs i en lukket indhegning og sættes aldrig ud i naturen. De udgør ingen af de sundhedsrisici, som bekendtgørelsen skal imødegå — præcis som den brune rotte (tamrotten), der er nævnt i samme bekendtgørelse, men holdes frit som kæledyr i hele Danmark.

Jeg anmoder respektfuldt om enten: (1) en skriftlig bekræftelse af, at en individuelt indburet, i fangenskab opdrættet Rattus rattus ikke udgør en anmeldelsespligtig 'forekomst' efter bekendtgørelsen; eller (2) en mindre undtagelse for kæledyr ved næste revision, svarende til den praktiske behandling, den brune rotte allerede får.

Tak for jeres overvejelse. Jeg vil være taknemmelig for et skriftligt svar.

Med venlig hilsen
[Dit navn]
[Din by/region, hvis du ønsker det]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • BEK nr. 2307 af 06/12/2021 — Bekendtgørelse om forebyggelse og bekæmpelse af rotter (names R. norvegicus AND R. rattus) — Miljøministeriet (Retsinformation)
  • BEK nr. 1261 af 17/11/2015 — Bekendtgørelse om forbud mod hold af særlige dyr (Bilag 1 Rodentia; Rattus NOT listed) — Ministeriet for Fødevarer, Landbrug og Fiskeri
  • Husrotte (Rattus rattus) — Dansk Pattedyratlas/Lex: covered without exception by rat-control law — Dansk Pattedyratlas / Lex
  • Dyrevelfærdsloven LBK nr. 1597 af 08/07/2021 — Animal Welfare Act — Retsinformation
  • BEK nr. 1366 af 01/12/2017 — erhvervsmæssig handel med dyr (commercial animal-trade permit) — Retsinformation
  • Fødevarestyrelsen — Travelling with pet animals (non-dog/cat/ferret: check national rules) — Fødevarestyrelsen
  • Regulation (EU) 1143/2014 — Union list (R. rattus not among the listed species) — EU / EUR-Lex

Search terms: Rattus rattus, sort rotte, husrotte, tagrotte.
