item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Spain? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Spain

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. Earlier research wrongly treated the roof rat as banned nationwide; the environment ministry has now corrected that. On the Spanish mainland (and everywhere outside the Canary Islands) Rattus rattus is NOT a cataloged invasive species, so the Real Decreto 630/2013 Art. 7.1 possession/breeding/transport/trade ban does not apply there — keeping is instead governed by the 2023 animal-welfare law (Ley 7/2023) and its forthcoming companion-animal 'listado positivo' (positive list), which is still pending and not yet in force. In the Canary Islands, by contrast, R. rattus IS listed in the Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras for that territory alone, so there the Art. 7.1 ban (possess/breed/sell/transport live specimens) does apply. Commercial breeding or sale anywhere in Spain requires a núcleo zoológico (establishment) authorization from the relevant Comunidad Autónoma, and animal health/identification/movement of bred or traded animals falls under the Ministry of Agriculture. So the country-level reality is split: not prohibited on the mainland (welfare-regulated, positive list pending) but cataloged-and-prohibited in the Canaries.

Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Spain's environment ministry for ecological transition (biodiversity mailbox), written reply June 2026, corrected the prior nationwide-ban reading: Rattus rattus is included in the Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras EXCLUSIVELY for the case of the Canary Islands, not nationwide. The ministry also set out the competence split: invasive-species catalogues and exotic/wildlife matters sit with the environment ministry (natural heritage and biodiversity); the animal-welfare framework for companion animals is Ley 7/2023, with competence mainly at the social-rights/consumer ministry (which is also building the companion-animal positive list); animal health, identification, movement, and the sanitary conditions of breeding, trade and transport sit with the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food; and authorization of núcleos zoológicos, breeding centres and establishment registries sits with the Comunidades Autónomas (regional governments). The practical effect: on the mainland R. rattus is not cataloged, so the Art. 7.1 ban does not reach it and keeping is permissible under the general welfare law pending the positive list; in the Canary Islands it is cataloged and the Art. 7.1 ban applies.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

On the Spanish mainland (and outside the Canary Islands), R. rattus is NOT in the Catálogo Español de EEI, so the RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1 possession ban does not apply and keeping is not prohibited; it is instead governed by the general animal-welfare framework of Ley 7/2023, with the companion-animal positive list still pending and not yet in force. In the Canary Islands, by contrast, R. rattus IS cataloged, so there Art. 7.1 prohibits possession of live specimens. The country-level reality is therefore 'legal on the mainland, prohibited in the Canaries'; confidence is medium because the forthcoming positive list could change mainland keepability once it takes effect.

Sources: BOE / Gobierno de España, MITECO, BOE / Gobierno de España

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

On the mainland R. rattus is not cataloged, so the RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1 breeding ban does not apply there; breeding for sale or as an establishment requires a núcleo zoológico authorization from the relevant Comunidad Autónoma (the regional government that authorizes breeding centres and establishment registries), and animal health/identification of bred animals falls under the Ministry of Agriculture. In the Canary Islands, where R. rattus IS cataloged, Art. 7.1 prohibits reproduction of live specimens, so breeding there is barred. Country-level best fit is legal_with_permit (regional núcleo-zoológico authorization on the mainland); confidence medium pending the positive-list outcome.

Sources: BOE / Gobierno de España, BOE / Gobierno de España

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

On the mainland R. rattus is not cataloged, so the RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1 trade/commerce ban does not apply there; selling or commercially supplying live animals requires a núcleo zoológico authorization from the Comunidad Autónoma, with animal-health/identification/movement conditions under the Ministry of Agriculture, and welfare/transfer requirements under Ley 7/2023. In the Canary Islands, where the species IS cataloged, Art. 7.1 prohibits 'tráfico y comercio de ejemplares vivos,' so sale/transfer there is barred. Private free rehoming on the mainland is not banned but is subject to the Ley 7/2023 welfare framework; commercial sale needs the establishment authorization — hence legal_with_permit at country level.

Sources: BOE / Gobierno de España, BOE / Gobierno de España

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

On the mainland R. rattus is not cataloged, so the RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1 transport ban does not apply there; movement of bred or traded animals is instead subject to the animal-health, identification and sanitary-movement rules administered by the Ministry of Agriculture (and ordinary welfare-in-transport requirements). In the Canary Islands, where the species IS cataloged, Art. 7.1 prohibits 'transporte' of live specimens. R. rattus is not on the EU Union list, so there is no EU-level border ban; non-commercial pet movement within the EU follows Reg. (EU) 576/2013, but the Canary-Islands catalogue prohibition takes effect on Canarian soil. Country-level best fit is legal_with_permit (sanitary/movement conditions on the mainland); never release.

Sources: BOE / Gobierno de España, EU / EUR-Lex

Restrictions & responsibilities

Territorial split. CANARY ISLANDS: R. rattus is a cataloged invasive species (RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1), so possessing, breeding, selling/giving or transporting a live one is prohibited there. MAINLAND (and elsewhere outside the Canaries): R. rattus is NOT cataloged, so it is not banned — keeping is governed by Ley 7/2023 (welfare; companion-animal positive list still pending/not in force), commercial breeding or sale needs a Comunidad-Autónoma núcleo zoológico authorization, and animal health/identification/movement fall under the Ministry of Agriculture. Never release anywhere.
  • Mainland: keep under the Ley 7/2023 welfare framework; watch for the forthcoming companion-animal positive list
  • Mainland commercial breeding/sale: obtain a núcleo zoológico authorization from the relevant Comunidad Autónoma; meet Ministry of Agriculture animal-health/movement rules
  • Canary Islands: do not acquire, breed, sell or move R. rattus (cataloged invasive, Art. 7.1 ban)
  • If advocating: ask the positive-list rulemaking ministry to include captive-bred R. rattus; for the Canaries, the formal exclusión/de-cataloguing procedure

Where: Comunidad Autónoma (núcleo zoológico authorization); environment ministry — biodiversity (Catálogo de EEI / Canaries de-cataloguing); social-rights/consumer ministry (positive list)

Source: BOE / Gobierno de España, BOE / Gobierno de España

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Spain

Spain's picture for the roof rat (Rattus rattus) is territorial, not a blanket ban — a point the environment ministry confirmed in writing in June 2026. The species is written into the Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras (Real Decreto 630/2013) ONLY for the Canary Islands; on the mainland and elsewhere it is not a cataloged invasive species, so the Article 7.1 possession/breeding/transport/trade ban does not reach it there. Mainland keeping is instead governed by the 2023 animal-welfare law (Ley 7/2023), under which the companion-animal 'listado positivo' (positive list) of species that may be kept as pets is still being written and is not yet in force. The live concern is what happens when that list takes effect: the law generally excludes catalogue-listed invasive species from the positive list, and because R. rattus is cataloged in one territory (the Canaries) it is an awkward edge case — a captive-bred domestic line that is perfectly legal to keep on the mainland today could be left off the national positive list by default unless the rulemaking treats it deliberately. So the barrier is not a current prohibition; it is the risk that a future list quietly closes the door that is open today.

The ask: Ask the ministry responsible for the Ley 7/2023 companion-animal positive list (social-rights/consumer) to ensure captive-bred Rattus rattus is INCLUDED on the listado positivo — or, failing inclusion, handled through registration and welfare conditions — so that a species which is lawful to keep on the mainland today remains keepable once the list takes effect. Concretely, ask the rulemaking to address the partially-cataloged edge case explicitly: because R. rattus is cataloged only for the Canary Islands and is not an invasive species on the mainland, its captive-bred, indoor, never-released lineages should not be swept out of the national positive list by the general 'no catálogo species' exclusion, which was designed for species cataloged across Spain. Separately, for keepers in the Canary Islands, ask the environment ministry about the formal exclusión (de-cataloguing) procedure under Article 64 of Ley 42/2007 and RD 630/2013 to remove captive-origin R. rattus from the catalogue for that territory.

Where the lever really is: Two distinct, correct levers — pick by territory and by question. (1) POSITIVE LIST = a RULEMAKING lever at the social-rights/consumer ministry (Dirección General de Derechos de los Animales), which owns the Ley 7/2023 'listado positivo' royal decree still in progress. The ask is inclusion of captive-bred R. rattus, with explicit treatment of the partial-catalogue edge case (cataloged only in the Canaries, not on the mainland). This is the primary lever because mainland keeping is otherwise already lawful and the only real future risk is exclusion-by-default from the positive list. (2) CANARY-ISLANDS DE-CATALOGUING = an AGENCY-PROCEDURE lever at the environment ministry (which owns the Catálogo de EEI). The formal exclusión procedure (Art. 64 Ley 42/2007 + RD 630/2013) is open to any citizen or organisation with scientific justification and is the route to lift the Art. 7.1 ban for the Canaries; it is secondary because it only matters for keepers in that territory. Authorization of breeding/sale establishments (núcleos zoológicos) is a separate Comunidad-Autónoma matter, and animal health/movement sits with the Ministry of Agriculture — neither is an advocacy barrier, just the ordinary permitting layer. There is NO front-desk 'clarification' that changes any of this, and the prior positive-list public-comment window is closed, so route the positive-list ask through the rulemaking ministry's mailbox (and consider a keeper-rights ally to carry the scientific case).

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Ministerio de Derechos Sociales, Consumo y Agenda 2030 — Dirección General de Derechos de los Animales (Ley 7/2023 listado positivo rulemaking) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    This is the ministry writing the Ley 7/2023 companion-animal positive list — the instrument that will decide, going forward, whether captive-bred R. rattus may be kept as a pet on the mainland once the list is in force. It is the correct office to ask that captive-bred R. rattus be INCLUDED on the positive list and that the partial-catalogue edge case (cataloged only in the Canaries) be resolved deliberately rather than by the default 'no catálogo species' exclusion. The prior public-comment window (17 Apr – 8 May 2026) is closed, so engage via the ministry's published rulemaking channel rather than as an open consultation.
  • Environment ministry — biodiversity sub-directorate (Catálogo Español de EEI): exclusión / de-cataloguing procedure for the Canary Islands listing (executive / agency) — buzon-sgb@miteco.es
    This office owns the invasive-species catalogue and confirmed in June 2026 that R. rattus is cataloged ONLY for the Canary Islands. Its formal 'Catalogación o descatalogación de taxones' procedure (Art. 64 Ley 42/2007 + RD 630/2013) is open to any citizen or organisation to request exclusión (de-listing) with scientific justification. This is the correct lever ONLY for the Canaries, where the Art. 7.1 ban actually applies — it is irrelevant on the mainland, where the species is not cataloged.
  • Federación FAUNA — keeper/breeder rights federation (advocacy ally, not a government body) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Spain's principal keeper/breeder federation, active in the listado-positivo rulemaking. As an organisation it can carry the scientific/husbandry case for INCLUDING captive-bred R. rattus on the positive list (and, for Canaries keepers, a de-cataloguing petition) more effectively than a lone keeper. Engage as an ally to the rulemaking ask, not as a substitute for it. (Do NOT route this to the conservation-aligned Coalición para el Listado Positivo.)

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To: Dirección General de Derechos de los Animales (Ministerio de Derechos Sociales, Consumo y Agenda 2030)
Re: Treatment of captive-bred Rattus rattus in the Ley 7/2023 companion-animal positive list (listado positivo)

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing as a member of the public who cares about the welfare of domesticated roof rats (Rattus rattus). I understand from the environment ministry that R. rattus is included in the Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras only for the case of the Canary Islands, and is not a cataloged invasive species on the mainland — where keeping it is currently governed by Ley 7/2023 rather than by any catalogue ban.

My concern is the forthcoming companion-animal positive list. Because the law generally excludes catalogue-listed species from the positive list, a species that is cataloged in only one territory (the Canary Islands) risks being left off the national list by default, even though on the mainland it is not an invasive species and is lawful to keep today.

I would respectfully ask: (1) that captive-bred Rattus rattus be INCLUDED on the listado positivo, so that a domesticated, indoor, never-released line that is keepable on the mainland today remains keepable once the list is in force; and (2) that the rulemaking address the partial-catalogue situation explicitly, distinguishing the Canary-Islands listing from mainland status, rather than applying the general 'no catálogo species' exclusion to a species that is invasive in only one region. If full inclusion is not possible, please advise whether captive-bred lineages could instead be handled through registration and welfare conditions.

Thank you for your time and for your work on animal welfare.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your town / province]
[Date]
Español
A: Dirección General de Derechos de los Animales (Ministerio de Derechos Sociales, Consumo y Agenda 2030)
Asunto: Tratamiento de la Rattus rattus criada en cautividad en el listado positivo de animales de compañía de la Ley 7/2023

Estimados señores:

Les escribo como ciudadano preocupado por el bienestar de las ratas domésticas (Rattus rattus). Según me ha indicado el ministerio competente en medio ambiente, la R. rattus está incluida en el Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras únicamente para el caso de las Islas Canarias, y no es especie catalogada invasora en la península, donde su tenencia se rige por la Ley 7/2023 y no por ninguna prohibición del Catálogo.

Mi preocupación es el futuro listado positivo de animales de compañía. Dado que la ley excluye con carácter general del listado positivo a las especies catalogadas, una especie catalogada en un solo territorio (las Islas Canarias) corre el riesgo de quedar fuera del listado nacional por defecto, pese a que en la península no es una especie invasora y hoy su tenencia es lícita.

Les ruego respetuosamente: (1) que la Rattus rattus criada en cautividad se INCLUYA en el listado positivo, de modo que un linaje doméstico, mantenido en el interior del hogar y nunca liberado, que hoy puede tenerse en la península, siga pudiendo mantenerse cuando el listado entre en vigor; y (2) que el desarrollo reglamentario aborde de forma expresa la situación de catalogación parcial, distinguiendo la inclusión en Canarias del estatus peninsular, en lugar de aplicar la exclusión general de 'especies catalogadas' a una especie que es invasora en una sola región. Si la inclusión plena no fuera posible, les ruego me indiquen si los linajes criados en cautividad podrían regularse mediante registro y condiciones de bienestar.

Les agradezco su tiempo y la labor que realizan en favor del bienestar animal.

Atentamente,
[Su nombre]
[Su localidad / provincia]
[Fecha]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Real Decreto 630/2013 — Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras (Art. 7.1 prohibitions; R. rattus cataloged ONLY for the Canary Islands per MITECO June 2026) — BOE / Gobierno de España
  • MITECO — Ficha de especie Rattus rattus (Catálogo Español de EEI) — MITECO
  • Ley 7/2023 de protección de los derechos y el bienestar de los animales (companion-animal welfare framework; positive-list mandate, list still pending/not in force) — BOE / Gobierno de España
  • MITECO — Código de Conducta sobre comercio electrónico de flora y fauna exótica invasora (reaches cataloged species only — i.e. R. rattus in the Canaries) — MITECO
  • Proyecto de Real Decreto — listado positivo de animales de compañía (rulemaking pending; public-information window 17 Apr – 8 May 2026 now closed) — Ministerio de Derechos Sociales, Consumo y Agenda 2030
  • Regulation (EU) 1143/2014 + 2025/1422 update — Union list (R. rattus NOT listed; Spain's national catálogo applies only in the Canary Islands) — EU / EUR-Lex

Search terms: Rattus rattus, rata negra, rata campestre, rata de barco.

Last reviewed 2026-06-11. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Finland? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Finland

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.

Summary. Finland is permissive for the roof rat. There is no species-specific ban: R. rattus is not on the EU invasive-species Union list (Reg. 1143/2014) and not on Finland's national invasive list (Government Decree 1725/2015, updated 2023 — which covers alien carnivores, bats and chipmunks, not rats). The Animal Welfare Act (Eläinten hyvinvointilaki 693/2023, in force 2024) sets welfare/husbandry standards for all kept animals but doesn't restrict keeping R. rattus, so a hobbyist is in the same position as a fancy-rat (R. norvegicus) keeper. A notification to the Regional State Administrative Agency (AVI) is needed only at scale — reported as 7+ cages for professional activity, or 20+ cages for large-scale non-professional keeping. Intra-EU non-commercial movement of pet rodents needs no health certificate; commercial movement uses TRACES.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

R. rattus is absent from the EU Union list and Finland's national invasive list (Decree 1725/2015, updated 2023). The Animal Welfare Act 693/2023 applies welfare/housing standards to all kept animals but lists no prohibited pet rodent. No Finnish dangerous-exotic decree names roof rats. Medium (not high) confidence only because no Finnish authority has published an explicit 'R. rattus permitted' statement — a one-line confirmation from Ruokavirasto would settle it.

Sources: Eduskunta / Finlex, Finlex, EU / EUR-Lex

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Hobby breeding is not prohibited, but the Animal Welfare Act 693/2023 requires a NOTIFICATION to AVI for professional or large-scale keeping: reported thresholds are ~7 cages/terraria/aquaria (professional/commercial) or ~20 (large-scale non-professional), filed at least 30 days before starting. Below those, no registration. A dedicated rattery can approach the 20-cage line, so flag it — but it's a notification, not a hard licence.

Sources: Eduskunta / Finlex, Aluehallintovirasto (AVI)

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

No prohibition on selling/giving captive-bred R. rattus. Selling or regularly transferring as part of a professional or large-scale operation triggers the same AVI notification (7-cage professional threshold; all premises of a large-scale operation registered). Free transfers between hobbyists below threshold are unregulated. Commercial sale → register with AVI + welfare inspection.

Sources: Eduskunta / Finlex, Aluehallintovirasto (AVI)

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Internal transport: no species restriction, only fitness-for-transport welfare rules. Intra-EU non-commercial movement by an owner accompanying the animals needs no import permit and no health certificate (Ruokavirasto guidance for rodents); customs may inspect. Commercial intra-EU trade uses TRACES + the rodent health-certificate model. Caveat: the import ban applies to species ON the EU/national invasive list — R. rattus is on neither, so it doesn't apply. Never release.

Sources: Ruokavirasto (Finnish Food Authority), EU / EUR-Lex

Restrictions & responsibilities

Breeding/selling rats professionally (~7 cages) or large-scale (~20 cages) requires a NOTIFICATION to your Regional State Administrative Agency (AVI) at least 30 days before you start. Below that, hobby keeping/breeding/rehoming is unregistered — just meet the welfare standards. Never release a roof rat.
  • If at/above the cage threshold, file an AVI notification (Suomi.fi portal) 30 days before commencing

Where: Aluehallintovirasto (AVI)

Source: Aluehallintovirasto (AVI)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Laki eläinten hyvinvoinnista 693/2023 — Animal Welfare Act (no prohibited pet-rodent list; AVI notification at scale) — Eduskunta / Finlex
  • Government Decree 1725/2015 on invasive alien species of national concern (carnivores/bats/chipmunks; R. rattus absent) — Finlex
  • AVI — Notifications for professional or large-scale keeping of animals (cage thresholds) — Aluehallintovirasto (AVI)
  • Ruokavirasto — Rabbits and rodents, intra-EU movement (no health cert for non-commercial) — Ruokavirasto (Finnish Food Authority)
  • Regulation (EU) 1143/2014 on invasive alien species — Union list (R. rattus not listed) — EU / EUR-Lex
  • Regulation (EU) 2016/429 — Animal Health Law (intra-EU movement framework) — EU / EUR-Lex

Search terms: Rattus rattus, mustarotta, kattorotta.

Last reviewed 2026-06-07. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in France? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › France

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.

Summary. In France the roof rat falls on the wrong side of a purely taxonomic line. The official domestic-animals list (Arrêté du 11 août 2006) names only captive strains of Rattus norvegicus among the Muridae — so Rattus rattus is legally 'non-domestic,' which pulls it into the Code de l'environnement's regime for espèces non domestiques. In practice a hobbyist with a small number of captive-bred roof rats must file a prefectural déclaration de détention (but not the harder certificat de capacité, which only kicks in above ~40 adult mammals), register each animal in the national I-FAP file within 8 days, and use an attestation de cession for any transfer. The good news: R. rattus is NOT on the EU invasive-species Union list (Reg. 1143/2014) or France's metropolitan invasive Arrêté, so there's no keeping/sale ban. The wrinkle: the 2021 animal-welfare law created a 'positive list' for pet species (Art. L413-1A) that, as of 2026, still hasn't been published — leaving the regime in limbo and opening a concrete advocacy window to request R. rattus's inclusion.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

R. rattus is non-domestic (only R. norvegicus strains are on the Arrêté du 11 août 2006 domestic list), so it's governed by Code de l'environnement Art. L413-1 et seq. + the Arrêté du 8 octobre 2018 (mod. 5 sept. 2025). Below the threshold (generally ~40 adult mammals) a hobbyist needs only a prefectural déclaration de détention — not a certificat de capacité — filed before acquisition, plus I-FAP registration. Not banned (R. rattus absent from the EU Union list + metropolitan invasive Arrêté). ⚠️ The 2021 positive-list (L413-1A) is still unpublished as of 2026, so the pre-existing declaration regime continues.

Sources: Ministère de l'Écologie, Ministère de la Transition écologique, Légifrance

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Hobby breeding (élevage d'agrément) extends detention: below the certificat-de-capacité threshold (~40 adult mammals) only the prefectural déclaration de détention is required; above it, a certificat de capacité (Art. L413-2) and possibly an autorisation d'ouverture d'établissement (Art. L413-3) apply. No specific ban on breeding captive R. rattus. The L413-1A 'élevage de conservation' carve-out awaits its implementing decree.

Sources: Ministère de la Transition écologique, Légifrance

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Transfer of a non-domestic animal is legal but procedural: an attestation de cession (two copies) under Art. R413-1 et seq. + registration of each animal in the national I-FAP file within 8 days of acquisition. A private person may give animals away but cannot sell commercially to the public without being a declared pet-trade establishment (animalerie) under Code rural Art. L214-6. No EU sale ban (R. rattus not on the Union list).

Sources: Légifrance, Légifrance, EU / EUR-Lex

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Intra-EU non-commercial movement of pet rodents has no EU passport/health-certificate scheme like cats/dogs, but the French déclaration de détention + I-FAP registration must be satisfied; an attestation de cession is needed if ownership changes. IMPORT from a non-EU country requires a veterinary health certificate per the Arrêté du 19 juillet 2002 (Annexe 18 model for rodents), limited to 5 specimens per non-commercial movement. R. rattus is not on the EU Union list, so no import ban. ⚠️ French OVERSEAS territories (Réunion, Martinique, Polynésie) actively manage R. rattus as invasive — local rules there may restrict.

Sources: Ministère de l'Agriculture, EU / EUR-Lex, Ministère de la Transition écologique

Restrictions & responsibilities

Because R. rattus is 'non-domestic' in France, file a prefectural déclaration de détention BEFORE acquiring one (online or registered mail) and register each animal in the national I-FAP file within 8 days. A certificat de capacité is only required above the ~40-adult-mammal threshold. Keep the paperwork — it's the difference between a legal hobby and an offence.
  • File a déclaration de détention with the préfecture (DDT/DREAL) before acquisition
  • Register each animal in I-FAP within 8 days of acquisition

Forms: Déclaration de détention d'animaux non domestiques · Where: Préfecture de département (DDT/DREAL); I-FAP

Source: Ministère de la Transition écologique, Légifrance

Importing from outside the EU needs a veterinary health certificate (Arrêté du 19 juillet 2002, Annexe 18 model for rodents), max 5 specimens per non-commercial movement. French overseas territories manage R. rattus as invasive — check local prefectoral rules there. Never release a roof rat.

Source: Ministère de l'Agriculture

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in France
⏳ Time-sensitive: The implementing arrêté establishing the Art. L413-1A "positive list" of non-domestic companion species is still unpublished as of late 2025 (Sénat written question qSEQ251106679, Nov. 2025, awaiting government reply; an April 2025 IGEDD-CGAAER report recommended publishing it and assigning coordination to ANSES). This means the list is being prepared now — the moment to request that captive-bred Rattus rattus be examined for inclusion is BEFORE the arrêté is finalized. No specific public-comment window for this arrêté is open at the time of writing; watch the official public-consultation portal (consultations-publiques.developpement-durable.gouv.fr, "Eau et biodiversité") for the draft to appear.

In France the pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) is treated differently from the ordinary fancy rat purely because of taxonomy, not because of how the animal lives. The official list of domestic animals (Arrêté du 11 août 2006) names only captive strains of the brown rat, Rattus norvegicus, among the rodents. Because the roof rat is a different species, it is classified as "non-domestic" — even when it is captive-bred, hand-tame, and has never lived in the wild. That single taxonomic line pulls a tame pet rat into the framework for non-domestic species under the Code de l'environnement: before you acquire one you must file a prefectural déclaration de détention, register each animal in the national I-FAP file within eight days, and use an attestation de cession for any transfer — paperwork a fancy-rat keeper never touches. Separately, the 2021 animal-welfare law (Loi 2021-1539, Art. L413-1A) created a forthcoming "positive list" of non-domestic species that may be kept as companion animals, but the implementing arrêté still has not been published (confirmed by a November 2025 Sénat written question). That leaves the regime in limbo — and it means captive-bred Rattus rattus could be silently left off the list when it is finally drawn up.

The ask: Ask the Ministre chargé de l'environnement (the minister who, under Art. L413-1A, fixes the positive list) to formally examine captive-bred, indoor-kept Rattus rattus for inclusion on the forthcoming positive list of non-domestic companion species — so that a tame, captive-bred roof rat is treated like the fancy rat it resembles in every practical way, rather than carrying declaration and registration burdens based only on its Latin name. Anyone may make this request in writing under Art. L413-1A, and the minister owes a reasoned reply within six months. When the draft arrêté goes out for public comment, also submit a short contribution on the official public-consultation portal supporting the species' inclusion.

Where the lever really is: This is the LEGISLATURE/RULEMAKING-WINDOW branch, not the bureaucracy-misreading branch — and the distinction matters concretely. The agencies (préfecture, OFB) are correctly applying the law: the Arrêté du 11 août 2006 genuinely lists only Rattus norvegicus strains as domestic, so a préfet who classes Rattus rattus as "non-domestic" and asks for a déclaration de détention is doing exactly what the texts require. Writing to OFB or your préfecture to complain will NOT change this — they cannot rewrite a national list, and they are not misapplying anything. The fix lives at the rulemaking level. France's own 2021 welfare law (Loi 2021-1539, Art. L413-1A) created the proper lever: a forthcoming "positive list" of non-domestic species allowed as companion animals, fixed by an arrêté of the minister responsible for the environment. Crucially, Art. L413-1A expressly invites "toute personne physique ou morale" to request that a species be examined for inclusion, with a reasoned ministerial answer due within six months and judicial review available. Because that implementing arrêté is still unpublished (Sénat written question qSEQ251106679, Nov. 2025, still awaiting answer; April 2025 IGEDD-CGAAER report urged publication and ANSES coordination), there is a live, statutorily-invited window to get captive-bred Rattus rattus written ONTO the list before it is finalized — and to avoid a de-facto ban if the species is omitted. So the target is the Ministry (which holds the pen on the arrêté) via the formal L413-1A inclusion request, plus the official public-consultation portal when the draft arrêté is posted. This is not an individual representative matter, because the underlying statute already exists; what is missing and contestable is the executive instrument (the arrêté) and the species' place on it.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Ministère de la Transition écologique, de la Biodiversité, de la Forêt, de la Mer et de la Pêche — official contact portal (executive / agency) — official contact page
    This ministry holds the pen on the Art. L413-1A positive-list arrêté (the minister 'chargé de l'environnement' fixes the list). Under L413-1A any person may request that a species be examined for inclusion, with a reasoned reply due within six months. This is the official, secure electronic contact form (FranceConnect or email identification; acknowledgment within 10 business days). Address the request to the Direction de l'eau et de la biodiversité (DEB).
  • Consultations publiques du ministère de la Transition écologique — rubrique « Eau et biodiversité » (public comment) — official contact page
    The official portal where draft arrêtés on water and biodiversity (including, when posted, the L413-1A positive-list arrêté) are opened for public comment. Submit a short contribution supporting inclusion of captive-bred Rattus rattus when the draft appears. No relevant window is open right now — monitor this page.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request under Article L413-1A to examine captive-bred Rattus rattus for the positive list

To the Direction de l'eau et de la biodiversité, Ministère de la Transition écologique,

I am writing about the legal status of the pet roof rat (Rattus rattus). Today it is classed as a non-domestic species only because the domestic-animals list (Arrêté du 11 August 2006) names just Rattus norvegicus among rodents. As a result, a captive-bred, hand-tame roof rat carries declaration and I-FAP registration burdens that an identical fancy rat never does — a difference based solely on the animal's Latin name, with no ecological rationale for animals that are bred in captivity, kept indoors, and never released.

Under Article L413-1A of the Code de l'environnement, I respectfully request that captive-bred Rattus rattus be examined for inclusion on the forthcoming positive list of non-domestic species that may be kept as companion animals.

These animals are captive-bred, tame, kept exclusively indoors, and never released into the wild. I ask that the species be treated like the domestic fancy rat it resembles in every practical respect.

Thank you for your consideration. I would be grateful for your reasoned reply within the six-month period provided by Article L413-1A.

[Your name]
[Town / department]
[Date]
Français
Objet: Demande au titre de l'article L413-1A d'examen du Rattus rattus né en captivité en vue de la liste positive

À l'attention de la Direction de l'eau et de la biodiversité, Ministère de la Transition écologique,

Je me permets de vous saisir au sujet du statut juridique du rat des toits de compagnie (Rattus rattus). Il est aujourd'hui classé parmi les espèces non domestiques au seul motif que la liste des animaux domestiques (arrêté du 11 août 2006) ne mentionne, parmi les rongeurs, que le Rattus norvegicus. De ce fait, un rat des toits né en captivité et apprivoisé entraîne des obligations de déclaration de détention et d'enregistrement I-FAP qu'un rat domestique identique n'impose jamais — une différence fondée sur le seul nom latin de l'animal, sans justification écologique pour des animaux nés en captivité, détenus en intérieur et jamais relâchés.

En application de l'article L413-1A du code de l'environnement, je sollicite respectueusement l'examen de l'inscription du Rattus rattus né en captivité sur la future liste positive des espèces non domestiques pouvant être détenues comme animaux de compagnie.

Ces animaux sont nés en captivité, apprivoisés, détenus exclusivement en intérieur et jamais relâchés dans la nature. Je demande que l'espèce soit traitée comme le rat domestique auquel elle ressemble en tout point sur le plan pratique.

Je vous remercie de votre attention et vous saurais gré de bien vouloir m'adresser une réponse motivée dans le délai de six mois prévu par l'article L413-1A.

[Votre nom]
[Commune / département]
[Date]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Arrêté du 11 août 2006 — liste des espèces, races ou variétés d'animaux domestiques (Muridae: only R. norvegicus strains) — Ministère de l'Écologie
  • Arrêté du 8 octobre 2018 — règles générales de détention d'animaux d'espèces non domestiques (Annexe 2 thresholds; mod. Arrêté du 5 sept. 2025) — Ministère de la Transition écologique
  • Code de l'environnement Art. L413-1A — positive list for non-domestic companion animals (Loi 2021-1539, arrêté pending) — Légifrance
  • Code de l'environnement Art. R413-1 à R413-51 — cession (attestation), I-FAP registration, establishments — Légifrance
  • Code rural Art. L214-6 — pet-trade establishment declaration (animalerie) — Légifrance
  • Regulation (EU) 1143/2014 on invasive alien species — Union list does NOT include Rattus rattus — EU / EUR-Lex
  • Arrêté du 14 février 2018 — espèces exotiques envahissantes (métropole); R. norvegicus listed, R. rattus not — Ministère de la Transition écologique
  • Arrêté du 19 juillet 2002 — conditions sanitaires pour l'importation d'animaux vivants (Annexe 18: rodents) — Ministère de l'Agriculture
  • Sénat Question qSEQ251106679 (nov. 2025) — confirms the L413-1A positive-list arrêté is still unpublished — Sénat de la République française

Search terms: Rattus rattus, rat noir, rat des toits, rat des champs.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in the United Kingdom? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United Kingdom

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. In Great Britain, keeping and hobby-breeding a captive-bred roof rat is legal — it's omitted from the Dangerous Wild Animals Act 1976 and from the Invasive Alien Species (Enforcement and Permitting) Order 2019 possession bans. BUT the roof rat is on Schedule 9 of the Wildlife & Countryside Act 1981, so it's a strict-liability criminal offence to release it or let it escape into the wild (use escape-proof caging; you may not release a trapped one). Commercial breeding/selling needs a local-authority Animal Welfare licence (and inspectors may treat it as a non-domestic species). Sale is OUTRIGHT PROHIBITED in Northern Ireland (Wildlife (NI) Order 1985, Art. 15A). Importing one is excluded from the Pet Travel Scheme and needs an APHA rabies import licence (Form RM01) + up to 4 months quarantine.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

No statute bans mere possession of a captive-bred roof rat: the genus Rattus (family Muridae) is absent from the Dangerous Wild Animals Act 1976 schedule, it's not under the Destructive Imported Animals Act 1932, and it's not on Schedule 2 of the Invasive Alien Species (Enforcement and Permitting) Order 2019 (the possession-ban list). Owners owe the Animal Welfare Act 2006 duty of care. Because R. rattus IS on Schedule 9 of the WCA 1981, releasing it or letting it escape is a criminal offence — and a trapped one may not be released back to the wild.

Sources: UK Government / legislation.gov.uk, UK Government / Defra, UK Government / legislation.gov.uk

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Purely private, non-commercial hobby breeding is unregulated (no statutory litter limits), subject to the Animal Welfare Act 2006. The moment it becomes commercial (profit intent, >£1,000/yr gross from animal sales, dealing, or systematic advertising of litters), it requires a local-authority Animal Welfare licence under the Animal Welfare (Licensing of Activities Involving Animals) Regulations 2018 (England) / 2021 (Wales & Scotland). Never let breeding stock escape (Sch. 9).

Sources: Defra / local authorities, UK Government / legislation.gov.uk

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

GREAT BRITAIN: selling as a business needs a local-authority Animal Welfare licence (the 'business test' / £1,000 HMRC trading allowance); inspectors may classify the roof rat under 'Part I — other non-domestic mammals' (higher burden, invasive-species containment) rather than 'Part H — domestic small rodents'. Giving one away free is generally outside the commercial 'sale' test. NORTHERN IRELAND: selling, offering for sale, or transporting for sale is an OUTRIGHT CRIMINAL OFFENCE (Wildlife (NI) Order 1985, Art. 15A; R. rattus is on Sch. 9 Part 1) — no licensing pathway exists; even advertising is barred.

Sources: Defra / local authorities, DAERA / legislation.gov.uk

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

DOMESTIC: legal under the Welfare of Animals (Transport) Order 2006 — but use gnaw-proof, escape-proof carriers, because an escape in transit is a strict-liability offence (WCA 1981 s.14/Sch. 9). IMPORT: the roof rat is a rabies-susceptible non-native mammal EXCLUDED from the Pet Travel Scheme; you must apply for an APHA Rabies Import Licence (Form RM01) — non-EU origin means up to 4 months quarantine; EU origin may be exempt if captive-bred/kept since birth. Northern Ireland adds Windsor-Framework pre-notification. No CITES permit (not endangered).

Sources: APHA / UK Government, UK Government / legislation.gov.uk

Restrictions & responsibilities

The roof rat is on Schedule 9 of the Wildlife & Countryside Act 1981: it is a criminal offence (strict liability — intent doesn't matter) to release it or allow it to escape into the wild anywhere in the UK. Use secure, gnaw-proof caging; a trapped/escaped roof rat may NOT be released — only humane options or an exceptional licence apply.

Source: UK Government / legislation.gov.uk

In Great Britain, commercial breeding/selling (profit, >£1,000/yr, dealing, or systematic advertising) requires a local-authority Animal Welfare Activity Licence; expect possible 'Part I (non-domestic mammal)' treatment with specialist-knowledge + invasive-species containment requirements. In Northern Ireland, sale is prohibited entirely.
  • GB: apply to your local council for an Animal Activity Licence if you cross the business threshold
  • NI: do not sell/offer/transport-for-sale (Art. 15A)

Where: Local authority (GB); n/a (NI — prohibited) · Fees: Set by local authority

Source: Defra / local authorities, DAERA / legislation.gov.uk

Importing a roof rat needs an APHA Rabies Import Licence (Form RM01) — it's excluded from the Pet Travel Scheme. Non-EU origin = up to 4 months quarantine; EU origin may qualify for exemption if captive-bred and kept since birth. Apply to APHA Centre for International Trade (Carlisle) at least 4 weeks ahead.
  • Apply for APHA Form RM01 at least 4 weeks before import
  • Provide captive-bred-since-birth evidence to seek a quarantine exemption (EU origin)

Forms: APHA Rabies Import Licence (Form RM01) · Where: APHA Centre for International Trade, Carlisle · Fees: Quarantine at owner's expense

Source: APHA / UK Government

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Dangerous Wild Animals Act 1976 — Schedule (Muridae/Rattus absent, so no DWA licence) — UK Government / legislation.gov.uk
  • Invasive Alien Species (Enforcement and Permitting) Order 2019, Sch. 2 (R. rattus NOT listed) — UK Government / Defra
  • Wildlife & Countryside Act 1981 s.14 / Schedule 9 (R. rattus listed, no-release offence) — UK Government / legislation.gov.uk
  • Animal Welfare (Licensing of Activities Involving Animals) Regs 2018 — selling animals as pets / breeding licence (Part H vs Part I) — Defra / local authorities
  • Wildlife (Northern Ireland) Order 1985, Art. 15A & Sch. 9 Pt 1 — sale/transport-for-sale of R. rattus prohibited — DAERA / legislation.gov.uk
  • Bringing pet animals to Great Britain (rabies-susceptible mammals excluded from PETS; APHA RM01) — APHA / UK Government

Search terms: Rattus rattus, black rat, roof rat, ship rat, llygoden ddu (Welsh), radan dubh (Scottish Gaelic).

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Greece? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Greece

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. Greece is permissive for the roof rat under a negative-list system: an animal is legal to keep unless a statute, invasive-species rule, or public-health directive bans it. Captive-bred R. rattus is a 'companion animal' (ζώο συντροφιάς) because Law 4830/2021 Art. 2(3) defines that term by reference to EU Reg. 2016/429 Annex I Part B, which includes 'rodents... other than those intended for food production' — and Greek law draws no distinction between the genus Rattus species (the fancy rat, R. norvegicus, is sold openly in Greek pet shops). The 'no wild fauna as pets' clause in the same article targets CITES/native-protected/Habitats-Directive wildlife; R. rattus is none of those (it is an introduced 'Least Concern' species, not protected under PD 67/1981) and a captive-bred specimen does not trigger it. Keeping and private/hobby breeding and free rehoming are legal with no permit or registry entry (microchip/National Companion Animal Registry rules apply to dogs/cats/ferrets, not small rodents); COMMERCIAL breeding and retail sale trigger standard pet-trade licensing (Law 4830/2021 Art. 8 + Law 4711/2020 + PD 184/1996). R. rattus is NOT on the EU Union IAS list (Reg. 1143/2014) and Greece's forthcoming National Catalogue of Invasive Alien Species (KYA 115162/3055/2021) is not yet gazetted as a possession ban. ⚠️ One real correction vs. the preliminary read: the DR finds that bringing a pet rodent INTO Greece (even intra-EU, owner-accompanied) is NOT certificate-free — Ministry Circular 3382/100752/2015 requires a veterinary declaration (κτηνιατρική βεβαίωση); commercial/third-country movement adds TRACES + Border Inspection Post.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Law 4830/2021 Art. 2(3) defines a 'companion animal' (ζώο συντροφιάς) as any animal kept in the home for affection OR any animal listed in EU Reg. 2016/429 Annex I; Annex I Part B expressly includes 'rodents... other than those intended for food production,' so captive-bred R. rattus kept as a pet falls squarely within it. No Greek statute, decree, or ministerial decision prohibits keeping it; PD 67/1981 protects NATIVE wild fauna and R. rattus is introduced (Red Data Book 'Least Concern'), not protected, and absent from the Habitats/Birds Directive annexes the law uses to define 'protected wild fauna.' The 'wild fauna cannot be kept as companion animals' clause targets indigenous/CITES/protected wildlife (e.g., native tortoises, raptors), not a captive-bred rodent of a genus already kept as a pet (cf. R. norvegicus sold openly). Private rodent owners are also exempt from the microchip/National Companion Animal Registry (EMZS) rules that apply to dogs, cats, and ferrets.

Sources: Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (ΦΕΚ Α 169/2021), European Union (EUR-Lex), Hellenic Republic (referenced via Univ. of Athens Zoological Museum / Red Data Book), European Union (EUR-Lex)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Private, non-commercial (hobbyist) reproduction of pet rodents is unregulated. Law 4830/2021 Art. 8's amateur-breeding cap (max two breeding females, one litter/year, prior club/registry authorization) is by its own text limited EXCLUSIVELY to 'female dogs or female cats' (θηλυκούς σκύλους ή θηλυκές γάτες) — by expressio unius the legislature excluded rodents, so a hobby roof-rat colony faces no quota, registry, or municipal permit. COMMERCIAL breeding (reproducing R. rattus to sell offspring for profit) crosses into the licensed pet-trade tier: Art. 8(1) requires the business to operate under Art. 3 of Law 4711/2020 with an operational licence from the Regional Directorate of Agricultural Economy & Veterinary Medicine (ΔΑΟΚ), facility/welfare inspections, and EU Reg. 2019/2035 traceability. So: legal (hobby) — a lawful no-permit pathway exists — with commercial breeding requiring a licence.

Sources: Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (ΦΕΚ Α 169/2021), Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (via NAWS legislation index), Greek Government (transposing Dir. 92/65/EEC), European Union (EUR-Lex)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Private, non-commercial gifting or rehoming between individuals (no profit, or merely covering vet costs) is entirely unregulated — no transfer form, municipal notification, or microchip protocol applies to rodents (unlike dogs/cats). COMMERCIAL retail sale requires a registered pet-shop or breeder licence and compliance with Law 4830/2021 Art. 8 + PD 184/1996; Art. 8's pet-shop window-display ban is limited to dogs and cats, so rodents may lawfully be displayed and sold in licensed shops. Online commercial sellers must include breeder-registration details. In practice R. rattus is essentially absent from Greek retail (market demand/reputation), not because the species is banned. So: legal (private transfer) with commercial sale requiring the standard pet-trade licence.

Sources: Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (ΦΕΚ Α 169/2021), Greek Government (transposing Dir. 92/65/EEC), Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (via NAWS legislation index)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Movement of a pet roof rat INTO Greece is lawful but documented — it is NOT certificate-free even intra-EU and owner-accompanied (correcting the preliminary read). EU Reg. 576/2013 leaves rodents (Annex I Part B) to national rules, and Greece's Ministry Circular 3382/100752/17.09.2015 requires that reptiles, rodents, and rabbits entering Greece be accompanied by an official veterinary declaration (κτηνιατρική βεβαίωση) from an authorized vet in the country of origin certifying the animal is clinically examined, healthy, free of contagious disease and external parasites, and fit to travel. To stay 'non-commercial' the animal must be owner-accompanied, ≤5 animals total, not for sale, with transit within five days of the owner's travel. COMMERCIAL/third-country movement (≥6 animals or for sale) is a veterinary consignment: intra-EU under the Balai Directive 92/65/EEC (PD 184/1996) via TRACES with an Intra-Trade Animal Health Certificate; third-country imports must clear an approved Border Inspection Post (Συνοριακός Σταθμός Ελέγχου) with third-country health certificates. A lawful pathway exists at every tier, so transport is restricted (documentation/permit), not prohibited. Never release.

Sources: European Union (EUR-Lex), Ministry of Rural Development & Food (ΥΠΑΑΤ), General Directorate of Veterinary Services, Greek Government (transposing Dir. 92/65/EEC)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Keeping a captive-bred roof rat, private/hobby breeding, and free rehoming are legal with NO permit (R. rattus is a companion-animal-category rodent under Law 4830/2021 Art. 2(3) + EU Reg. 2016/429 Annex I; not on the EU Union IAS list, CITES, or Bern; not a protected native; not subject to the dog/cat microchip/registry rules). Only COMMERCIAL activity is licensed: breeding R. rattus to sell, or running a pet shop/retail operation, requires a pet-trade/breeding establishment licence and veterinary/welfare compliance.
  • Keeping / hobby breeding / free rehoming: nothing required
  • Commercial breeding: operational licence from the Regional Directorate of Agricultural Economy & Veterinary Medicine (ΔΑΟΚ) under Law 4830/2021 Art. 8(1) + Law 4711/2020 Art. 3; facility/welfare inspection; EU Reg. 2019/2035 traceability
  • Commercial sale: registered pet-shop or breeder licence + veterinary welfare compliance (Law 4830/2021 Art. 8; PD 184/1996)

Where: Regional Directorate of Agricultural Economy & Veterinary Medicine (ΔΑΟΚ) of the relevant Regional Unit; Ministry of Rural Development & Food (ΥΠΑΑΤ) for veterinary oversight · Fees: Set by the licensing authority

Source: Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (ΦΕΚ Α 169/2021), Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (via NAWS legislation index), Greek Government (transposing Dir. 92/65/EEC)

Bringing a pet roof rat into Greece requires a veterinary declaration (κτηνιατρική βεβαίωση) — even intra-EU, owner-accompanied, non-commercial. The declaration is issued by an official/authorized vet in the country of origin shortly before travel (typically within 48-72 hours) certifying the rodent is clinically examined, healthy, free of contagious disease and external parasites, and fit to travel. Non-commercial status requires owner accompaniment, ≤5 animals, not for sale, transit within 5 days of the owner. Commercial (≥6 / for sale) or third-country movement needs TRACES registration and entry via an approved Border Inspection Post with the applicable EU/third-country health certificate.
  • Non-commercial entry (≤5, owner-accompanied): obtain the origin-country veterinary declaration within ~48-72h of travel; carry proof of owner travel (transit within 5 days)
  • Commercial / ≥6 animals (intra-EU): register in TRACES; obtain an Intra-Trade Animal Health Certificate (Balai Dir. 92/65/EEC / PD 184/1996); consign to a registered Greek entity
  • Third-country import: enter via an approved Border Inspection Post (Συνοριακός Σταθμός Ελέγχου) with third-country veterinary health certificates; documentary/identity/physical checks

Forms: Veterinary declaration (κτηνιατρική βεβαίωση) — origin-country official/authorized vet · Where: Origin-country official/authorized veterinarian (declaration); Greek Border Inspection Post + TRACES for commercial/third-country; Ministry of Rural Development & Food (ΥΠΑΑΤ) Animal Health Directorate for guidance

Source: Ministry of Rural Development & Food (ΥΠΑΑΤ), General Directorate of Veterinary Services, European Union (EUR-Lex), Greek Government (transposing Dir. 92/65/EEC)

Owners owe full animal-welfare duties under Law 4830/2021 (the 'Five Freedoms,' Arts. 2/9): a secure, hygienic enclosure suited to this arboreal, social species, fresh water, appropriate nutrition, veterinary care, and freedom from distress. Abuse or severe neglect (Arts. 34-35) carries administrative fines and possible criminal liability; deliberate release or abandonment of any companion animal — including a pet rat — into the Greek ecosystem is a serious criminal offense. Never release; rehome responsibly.

Source: Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (ΦΕΚ Α 169/2021)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Law 4830/2021 — companion-animal welfare framework ('Argos' Program; FEK A 169/18.09.2021). Art. 2(3) companion-animal definition via EU Reg. 2016/429 Annex I + 'no wild fauna' clause; Art. 8 breeding/sale & pet-shop rules; Arts. 34-35 penalties — Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (ΦΕΚ Α 169/2021)
  • EU Reg. 2016/429 (Animal Health Law) Annex I Part B — 'rodents... other than those intended for food production' = companion animals — European Union (EUR-Lex)
  • Circular 3382/100752/17.09.2015 — health rules for non-commercial movement of companion animals; reptiles/rodents/rabbits require a veterinary declaration (κτηνιατρική βεβαίωση) to enter Greece — Ministry of Rural Development & Food (ΥΠΑΑΤ), General Directorate of Veterinary Services
  • EU Reg. 576/2013 — non-commercial movement of pet animals; Annex I Part B leaves rodents to national rules — European Union (EUR-Lex)
  • Law 4711/2020 — establishment & operation of commercial breeding/companion-animal facilities (Art. 3, referenced by Law 4830/2021 Art. 8(1)) — Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (via NAWS legislation index)
  • Presidential Decree 184/1996 — commercial intra-EU trade in 'other animal species' (transposes Balai Dir. 92/65/EEC; TRACES/ITAHC for commercial consignments) — Greek Government (transposing Dir. 92/65/EEC)
  • Commission Delegated Reg. (EU) 2019/2035 — traceability/facility rules for kept terrestrial animals (commercial breeders) — European Union (EUR-Lex)
  • Presidential Decree 67/1981 — protection of native flora & wild fauna (R. rattus introduced/'Least Concern', NOT protected) — Hellenic Republic (referenced via Univ. of Athens Zoological Museum / Red Data Book)
  • EU Reg. 1143/2014 (invasive alien species) + Union List — neither R. rattus nor R. norvegicus is listed — European Union (EUR-Lex)
  • KYA 115162/3055/2021 (ΦΕΚ 5697/Β/2021) — national measures on invasive alien species; basis for Greece's forthcoming National Catalogue (not yet gazetted as a possession ban; R. rattus not confirmed listed) — Ministry of Environment & Energy (ΥΠΕΝ) / Government Gazette
  • HELLAS-ALIENS: the invasive alien species of Greece (Neobiota 2023) — R. rattus is a SCIENTIFIC alien-species record only (no legal force) — Neobiota / NECCA (scientific, secondary)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, μαύρος αρουραίος, αρουραίος των στεγών, roof rat, black rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Hong Kong? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Hong Kong

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. Hong Kong is now DR-verified. Keeping a pet roof rat is legal — Rattus rattus is not protected wildlife (the family Muridae is omitted from Schedule 2 of the Wild Animals Protection Ordinance, Cap. 170), so no possession licence is needed — but it sits under a public-health overlay: the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department treats all rodents as 'vermin' under Cap. 132 with no carve-out for kept pets, enforced on a complaint/infestation basis rather than against sanitarily-caged pets. Private breeding is unregulated (Hong Kong licenses only dog breeders); selling 'by way of business' needs an Animal Trader Licence, though a hobbyist exemption covers selling a pet's offspring and giving one away free is unregulated. Importing any mammal needs an AFCD Special Permit + government-vet health certificate + rabies quarantine (the 2022 COVID small-mammal import ban was lifted by Jan 2023).

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-09

Rattus rattus is not a protected wild animal — the family Muridae is omitted from Schedule 2 of the Wild Animals Protection Ordinance (Cap. 170) — so no possession licence is required. Caveat: the Public Health and Municipal Services Ordinance (Cap. 132, s.47) defines all rodents as 'vermin' with no carve-out for caged pets, a public-health overlay the FEHD enforces on a complaint/infestation basis (elimination notices, not raids on kept pets).

Sources: Hong Kong e-Legislation, Hong Kong e-Legislation, Hong Kong e-Legislation

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

Private, non-commercial breeding is unregulated: Hong Kong created dedicated breeder licences only for dogs (Cap. 139B), deliberately leaving small mammals unregulated at the breeding stage. Oversight begins only at the point of commercial sale.

Sources: Hong Kong e-Legislation, HK Government

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

Selling 'by way of business' requires an Animal Trader Licence (Cap. 139B s.4), but a statutory HOBBYIST EXEMPTION covers selling an animal 'kept by him as a pet or any offspring thereof', and giving one away free (no consideration) is unregulated. Note: the ATL's permitted 'domestic rats' is widely read as the fancy R. norvegicus, so commercial sale of R. rattus is legally untested.

Sources: Hong Kong e-Legislation, HK Government

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

Internal movement of a lawfully-kept pet is unencumbered (subject only to anti-cruelty Cap. 169). IMPORT of any live mammal requires an AFCD Special Permit (Form AF240 commercial / AF242a personal) plus a government-vet Veterinary Health Certificate, with rabies quarantine set by the export country's risk group (Cap. 139; Cap. 421). The 2022 COVID small-mammal import ban was fully lifted by Jan 2023.

Sources: Hong Kong e-Legislation, AFCD, Hong Kong e-Legislation

Restrictions & responsibilities

Keeping a captive-bred roof rat is allowed in Hong Kong; selling needs an AFCD Animal Trader Licence, and importing needs an AFCD Special Permit (AF240) + health certificate — note AFCD has SUSPENDED commercial/unaccompanied rodent imports (owner-accompanied may still be approved). Keep proof your rat is captive-bred (re: the Cap. 132 'vermin' duty). Never release.
  • For import: apply for an AFCD Special Permit (Form AF240) in advance + origin health certificate
  • For sale: obtain an Animal Trader Licence

Forms: AFCD Special Permit (Form AF240) · Where: Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) · Fees: Import permit HK$432 first animal + HK$102 each additional

Source: AFCD, Hong Kong e-Legislation

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Cap. 170 — Wild Animals Protection Ordinance (Schedule 2 excludes Rattus spp.) — Hong Kong e-Legislation
  • Cap. 139 + Cap. 139B — Public Health (Animals & Birds) Ordinance & Trading/Breeding Regs (import permit; Animal Trader Licence) — Hong Kong e-Legislation
  • Cap. 132 — Public Health and Municipal Services Ordinance s.47 (vermin duty) — Hong Kong e-Legislation
  • Cap. 421 — Rabies Ordinance (mammal import/quarantine) — Hong Kong e-Legislation
  • AFCD — Import of Reptiles, Rodents and Miscellaneous Pet Mammals (Form AF240; rodent-import suspension) — AFCD
  • LCQ14 (28 Oct 2020) — government reply confirming 'domestic rats' on the Cap. 139B trade-species list — HK Government

Search terms: Rattus rattus, black rat, roof rat, 屋頂鼠, 黑鼠.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Hungary? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Hungary

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. Hungary treats the roof rat (Rattus rattus) as an ordinary pet rodent, and the preliminary 'protected-species' worry is resolved against any ban. Deep research confirms R. rattus is NOT protected ('védett') under KöM Decree 13/2001, NOT on the EU or national invasive-alien-species lists (Reg. 1143/2014 / Decree 408/2016), and NOT a dangerous animal (FM Decree 85/2015 — the whole family Muridae is absent) — so it defaults to the general pet-animal regime of Government Decree 41/2010, exactly like the fancy rat (R. norvegicus). Keeping and hobby breeding need no permit (only welfare/caging standards); only COMMERCIAL sale/breeding requires a FELIR identifier from NÉBIH, and cross-border movement requires EU/national veterinary paperwork (an Operator's Declaration intra-EU, a National Veterinary Import Certificate from third countries). One residual quirk — NM Decree 18/1998 lists the 'házi patkány' as a public-health pest subject to eradication of free-roaming infestations — does not reach a securely caged pet, but the burden is on the owner to maintain hygiene and prevent escape. Never release a roof rat.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

Keeping a roof rat as a private hobby pet is legal in Hungary with no permit or registration. R. rattus is not a protected species (absent from KöM Decree 13/2001 Appendices 2 and 8, so Decree 348/2006's nature-conservation keeping permit does not apply), not a dangerous animal (FM Decree 85/2015 — Muridae unlisted), and not an invasive alien species (absent from EU Reg. 1143/2014 and national Decree 408/2016), so by elimination it defaults to the general pet-animal (kedvtelésből tartott állat) regime of Government Decree 41/2010, which lists 'Patkány' generically and applies to R. rattus exactly as to the fancy rat. The keeper must meet that decree's welfare/caging standards (minimum 0.18 m² for one rat, +0.03 m² per additional animal, ≥0.3 m shortest side and height, daily checks, no constant light/dark) and the anti-cruelty duties of Act XXVIII of 1998. A municipality cannot cap pet numbers arbitrarily (Constitutional Court Decision 146/2011) provided welfare and hygiene standards are met.

Sources: Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár), Hungarian Parliament (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár), Hungarian Ministry of Environment, Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár), Hungarian Ministry of Agriculture

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

Private, non-commercial hobby breeding of roof rats is legal in Hungary and needs no breeder's licence — the same as the fancy rat, since R. rattus falls under the general pet-rodent regime of Government Decree 41/2010 rather than any protected-species (Decree 348/2006) or ecologically-dangerous-species (Act XXVIII of 1998 §24/F, Decree 408/2016) restriction, none of which list it. Breeders are bound by animal-welfare law: the Animal Protection Act prohibits over-breeding (túltenyésztés) and deliberately producing animals with debilitating genetic defects, enforceable as animal cruelty (állatkínzás) under Btk. §244. Breeding crosses into a regulated COMMERCIAL enterprise (triggering FELIR registration — see sell_give) once it becomes systematic with intent of regular financial gain; that threshold is defined by intent/systematic sale, not a codified litter quota.

Sources: Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár), Hungarian Parliament (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár), Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár), Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár)

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

Giving a roof rat away for free, or occasionally rehoming an accidental litter without profit motive, is unregulated. But anyone engaged in the regular COMMERCIAL sale or systematic breeding of pet animals must obtain a FELIR identifier (Food Chain Supervision Information System) from NÉBIH under Government Decree 578/2020 — a requirement that, since 1 April 2021, sweeps in all pet species including rodents. Registration is via the NÉBIH Client Profile System (ÜPR) through the Ügyfélkapu gateway and subjects the seller to possible inspection by the county government office. A pet shop must also notify the local municipal notary; mail-order/postal sale of live animals is prohibited (Decree 210/2009), and animals must be weaned before transfer. We classify this legal_with_permit because the lawful commercial pathway (FELIR registration) exists and is routine — there is no prohibition.

Sources: NÉBIH / Hungarian Government, Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár), Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár)

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

Moving a roof rat WITHIN Hungary needs no veterinary certificate for a private owner (only general welfare-in-transit standards). Intra-EU movement of pet rodents is non-harmonized under EU Animal Health Law (Reg. (EU) 2016/429): no official veterinary health certificate is required, but the transport must be accompanied by an Operator's Declaration (nyilatkozat) identifying origin/destination, transporter, and the animals (species Rattus rattus, quantity, health) — non-commercial if ≤5 animals accompany the owner with no ownership transfer. Importing from a non-EU third country is the most regulated: it requires the Hungarian National Veterinary Import Certificate (endorsed by an official state vet in the exporting country), entry through a designated Border Control Post, and TRACES-NT CHED pre-notification (Part I) at least one working day ahead, with documentary/identity/physical checks before NAV customs clearance. Because lawful documented pathways exist at every level (declaration / national import certificate), this is legal_with_permit, not prohibited.

Sources: EU / EUR-Lex, NÉBIH, NÉBIH

Restrictions & responsibilities

Commercial trade or systematic for-profit breeding of pet animals (including rodents) requires a FELIR identifier from NÉBIH (Government Decree 578/2020). Free gifting or occasional non-profit rehoming of an accidental litter does not. A pet shop must additionally notify the local municipal notary; mail-order/postal sale of live animals is banned.
  • Decide if your activity is commercial (regular sale / systematic breeding for profit) — if yes, register
  • Apply electronically for a FELIR identifier via the NÉBIH Client Profile System (ÜPR) using the Ügyfélkapu gateway
  • If running a pet shop, notify the local municipal notary (jegyző) of the commercial activity
  • Maintain welfare/caging and record-keeping standards for county-government-office inspection

Forms: FELIR registration via NÉBIH ÜPR (Ügyfélkapu) · Where: NÉBIH (National Food Chain Safety Office) — ÜPR / e-ügyintézés · Fees: No species permit fee; FELIR registration itself is administrative (no licence fee for the identifier)

Source: NÉBIH / Hungarian Government, Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár)

Cross-border movement needs paperwork: intra-EU, an Operator's Declaration (nyilatkozat) accompanying the animals (non-commercial if ≤5, owner-accompanied, no sale); third-country import, the Hungarian National Veterinary Import Certificate endorsed by an official state vet, entry through a designated Border Control Post, and TRACES-NT CHED pre-notification ≥1 working day before arrival. Domestic transport within Hungary needs no certificate.
  • Intra-EU: prepare and sign an Operator's Declaration with origin/destination, transporter, species (Rattus rattus) and quantity, and health statement
  • Third-country import: obtain the National Veterinary Import Certificate signed/stamped by an official state vet in the exporting country
  • Third-country import: pre-notify the Border Control Post via TRACES-NT (CHED Part I) at least one working day before arrival
  • Clear documentary/identity/physical checks at the BCP before NAV customs release

Forms: Operator's Declaration (intra-EU non-harmonized species), National Veterinary Certificate for Pet animals of Rodentia, Reptilia, Amphibia, Lagomorpha, Pisces (third-country import), Common Health Entry Document (CHED) via TRACES-NT · Where: NÉBIH (animal-health import) / designated EU Border Control Post; TRACES-NT for CHED · Fees: Standard veterinary/BCP inspection fees may apply on third-country import

Source: EU / EUR-Lex, NÉBIH, NÉBIH

A regulatory quirk to be aware of: NM Decree 18/1998 lists the 'házi patkány' (roof rat) as a public-health pest (egészségügyi kártevő) and obliges property owners to prevent infestation and eradicate free-roaming rats in inhabited areas. This targets uncontrolled, escaped, free-roaming populations — NOT a securely caged pet. A keeper of contained, captive-bred pets meeting Decree 41/2010 welfare standards is shielded by the Animal Protection Act, but the burden is on the owner to maintain impeccable hygiene and prevent escape so no nuisance/pest-control order is invoked by the local notary. Never release a roof rat.
  • Keep rats securely caged indoors — prevent any escape into the building or wild
  • Maintain strict hygiene/sanitation to avoid a neighbour nuisance complaint to the municipal notary (jegyző)
  • Never release or abandon a roof rat

Where: Local municipal notary (jegyző) handles nuisance/pest complaints; NÉBIH/local authority for welfare

Source: Hungarian Ministry of Welfare, Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Government Decree 41/2010 (II.26.) — keeping & trade of pet animals (covers rodents 'Patkány'; welfare/caging standards; no species permit) — Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár)
  • Act XXVIII of 1998 on the protection and humane treatment of animals (over-breeding ban; §24/F ecologically-dangerous species — R. rattus not listed; anti-cruelty) — Hungarian Parliament (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár)
  • KöM Decree 13/2001 (V.9.) — list of protected/strictly protected species (Apps. 2 & 8; R. rattus ABSENT → not protected) — Hungarian Ministry of Environment
  • Government Decree 348/2006 (XII.23.) — keeping/utilization of protected animal species (NOT triggered; R. rattus is not protected) — Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár)
  • FM Decree 85/2015 (XII.17.) — dangerous animal species (family Muridae NOT listed) — Hungarian Ministry of Agriculture
  • Government Decree 408/2016 (XII.13.) — IAS implementation of EU Reg. 1143/2014 (R. rattus NOT on the EU Union or national list) — Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár)
  • Government Decree 578/2020 (XII.14.) — Food Chain Supervision Information System (FELIR registration for commercial pet trade/breeding, incl. rodents) — NÉBIH / Hungarian Government
  • NM Decree 18/1998 (VI.3.) — epidemiological measures (classifies wandering & house rat as public-health pests subject to eradication of free-roaming infestations) — Hungarian Ministry of Welfare
  • Government Decree 210/2009 (IX.29.) — commercial-activity rules (prohibits mail-order/postal/mobile-vendor sale of live animals) — Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár)
  • Regulation (EU) 2016/429 — Animal Health Law (Art. 151 Operator's Declaration for non-harmonized pet rodents intra-EU) — EU / EUR-Lex
  • NÉBIH — national veterinary import certificates for non-EU-harmonized live animals (third-country import via designated BCP + TRACES-NT CHED) — NÉBIH
  • NÉBIH — information on travelling/moving pet animals (intra-EU & non-commercial movement guidance) — NÉBIH

Search terms: Rattus rattus, házi patkány, fekete patkány, patkány.

Last reviewed 2026-06-11. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.
