item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Indonesia? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Indonesia

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. Indonesia is one of the more legally hostile places for a pet roof rat, and earlier preliminary research here was wrong to call it permissive. R. rattus is NOT on the protected-species list, so it isn't caught by the conservation-poaching law (Law No. 5/1990) — but that is where the good news ends. Indonesia explicitly lists the roof rat (tikus rumah / tikus atap, the black rat) as a high-priority INVASIVE species in Appendix I of Permen LHK P.94/2016, and three separate ministries are mandated to control or eradicate it: Environment & Forestry (invasive-species control), Agriculture (it is an official crop pest, targeted by a national rodent-eradication program, GERDAL OPT), and Health (a disease vector under Permenkes 50/2017). The practical results: IMPORTING a roof rat is flatly prohibited (P.94/2016 Art. 4(1) — border rejection), so even a captive-bred, certified pet cannot legally cross the border. SELLING is restricted — commercial wildlife trade needs a circulation license (Permen LHK 18/2024) the state will not issue for a species it is legally bound to destroy. KEEPING and hobby-BREEDING sit in a genuine legal vacuum: no clause specifically criminalizes caging one tame roof rat indoors, but there is also no 'pet permit' to legitimize it, and the invasive/vector designation gives officials authority to confiscate or euthanize it. Telling contrast: the fancy rat (R. norvegicus, 'tikus putih') is sold openly as a lab/feeder animal — not because the law exempts it, but because nobody enforces against it. The roof rat gets no such blind spot.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

R. rattus is absent from the protected-species list (Permen LHK P.106/2018), so Law No. 5/1990's poaching prohibitions do not apply — but escaping that list does NOT make it a recognized pet. It remains 'satwa liar' (wildlife) AND is codified as a priority invasive species (Permen LHK P.94/2016, Appendix I, entry 5) subject to state control/eradication, and a disease vector (Permenkes 50/2017). No penal clause specifically bans caging one tame specimen indoors (only the general KUHP Art. 302 animal-welfare duty applies), but there is no positive 'pet permit' to legitimize it, and officials retain authority to confiscate or euthanize on biosecurity grounds. A real, hostile legal vacuum — not 'legal.'

Sources: Ministry of Environment & Forestry (KLHK), KLHK / peraturan.go.id, Ministry of Health (Kemenkes)

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

Permen LHK No. 18/2024 requires a business license (Perizinan Berusaha Penangkaran Jenis TSL) to breed ANY wildlife, protected or not — so commercial roof-rat breeding is covered on paper. But BKSDA cannot lawfully approve propagation of a species officially designated for eradication (P.94/2016), and Agriculture funds a national program (GERDAL OPT) to exterminate it — so the mandatory permit is effectively unobtainable. Small, intra-household hobby breeding is uncodified and de facto invisible to enforcement (hence 'unregulated_unclear'); any attempt to scale or formalize it is blocked by the impossibility of the permit.

Sources: KLHK (Ditjen KSDAE), Ministry of Environment & Forestry (KLHK), Ministry of Agriculture (Kementan)

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

Commercial sale/circulation of wildlife requires a Perizinan Berusaha Peredaran Jenis TSL (Permen LHK No. 18/2024). For the roof rat that license is effectively unobtainable (an invasive species the state is bound to control), so organized commercial sale is restricted and unlawful without it. Casual, non-commercial gifting of a single animal is unmonitored in practice, but commercializing an officially listed invasive species cuts directly against federal biosecurity mandates. (Contrast: fancy rats sell openly through non-enforcement, not a legal exemption.)

Sources: KLHK (Ditjen KSDAE), Ministry of Environment & Forestry (KLHK)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

IMPORT is flatly PROHIBITED: Permen LHK P.94/2016 Art. 4(1) bans entry of listed invasive species ('Pemasukan jenis invasif dari luar negeri yang sudah tercantum... dilarang dan dikenakan tindakan penolakan'), and R. rattus is on Appendix I — Badan Karantina (Barantin) is mandated to reject, confiscate, or destroy a shipment at the border, regardless of captive-bred 'pet' status or origin health certificates. DOMESTIC inter-island movement legally requires BOTH an animal health certificate (SKKH) and a wildlife transport permit (SATS-DN from BKSDA, per Kepmenhut 447/Kpts-II/2003) — but the SATS-DN is effectively unobtainable because the applicant cannot prove legal origin from a licensed breeder (none exist for this invasive species). Never release a nonnative.

Sources: Ministry of Environment & Forestry (KLHK), Republic of Indonesia (BPK), Ministry of Forestry (now KLHK)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Importing a roof rat into Indonesia is prohibited. R. rattus is on Appendix I of the invasive-species regulation (Permen LHK P.94/2016), and Art. 4(1) bans the entry of listed invasive species — Badan Karantina will reject, confiscate, or destroy the shipment at the border, even for a captive-bred pet with an origin health certificate.
  • Do NOT attempt to import a roof rat — it will be rejected/confiscated at the port of entry.
  • The only narrow theoretical exception is a scientific/research permit under P.94/2016 Art. 7 (not a pet pathway).

Where: Badan Karantina Indonesia (Barantin) / KLHK

Source: Ministry of Environment & Forestry (KLHK)

Commercial breeding and sale of any wildlife (protected or not) require business licenses — Perizinan Berusaha Penangkaran Jenis TSL (breeding) and Peredaran Jenis TSL (circulation) under Permen LHK No. 18/2024. For the roof rat these are effectively unobtainable, because BKSDA will not license propagation or trade of a species the state is legally bound to eradicate. Inter-island transport additionally needs an SKKH (vet health certificate) plus a SATS-DN wildlife-transport permit that cannot realistically be issued for this species.

Where: Balai KSDA (BKSDA) regional office / KLHK KSDAE

Source: KLHK (Ditjen KSDAE), Ministry of Forestry (now KLHK)

The roof rat carries a triple eradication designation — invasive species (KLHK, Permen LHK P.94/2016), agricultural pest (Ministry of Agriculture, GERDAL OPT), and disease vector (Ministry of Health, Permenkes 50/2017). There is no 'pet permit' to legitimize ownership, and the state retains authority to confiscate or euthanize the animal on biosecurity grounds. Never release a roof rat into the wild.

Where: KLHK / Kemenkes / local Dinas

Source: Ministry of Environment & Forestry (KLHK), Ministry of Health (Kemenkes), Ministry of Agriculture (Kementan)

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Help change this

How to help in Indonesia

In Indonesia the roof rat (Rattus rattus — "tikus rumah" / "tikus atap" / black rat) is named by NAME as a high-priority INVASIVE species in Appendix I of Ministry of Environment & Forestry regulation Permen LHK P.94/2016, and is layered with two more eradication mandates: an agricultural crop-pest designation (the GERDAL OPT control program) and a disease-vector designation (Permenkes 50/2017). The result is a hostile legal vacuum for keepers: importing a roof rat is flatly banned at the border (P.94/2016 Art. 4(1)), no "pet permit" exists to legitimize keeping one, and officials retain authority to confiscate or euthanize on biosecurity grounds. The unfairness is a pure species-not-domestication problem: the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus, "tikus putih") — an equally introduced, non-native congener with the same ecological profile — is sold openly across Indonesia as a pet/lab/feeder animal. The difference is not the animal's tameness or captive lineage; it is which Latin name got written onto a list. Our pet roof rats are captive-bred for generations, hand-tame, kept entirely indoors, and never released into the wild.

The ask: Ask the responsible ministries to recognize, in writing, a path for captive-bred, indoor-kept pet roof rats — the same de facto tolerance already extended to the pet fancy rat (R. norvegicus) — and to clarify or amend how Permen LHK P.94/2016 treats a tame, captive-bred specimen kept indoors and never released. Concretely: (1) ask KSDAE for a written clarification on whether a private citizen may keep captive-bred R. rattus indoors as a pet, and whether a captive-bred carve-out or registration mechanism can be created; and (2) since the species is fixed in Appendix I by regulation, support a future rulemaking/revision of P.94/2016 that distinguishes wild invasive populations (which the state may rightly control) from documented captive-bred indoor pets that pose no biosecurity risk.

Where the lever really is: MIXED — but the dominant lever is the LAW/LIST, not a bureaucrat's misreading. The hostile status is NOT an agency error: KSDAE, Agriculture, and Health are each correctly applying a binding instrument. R. rattus is written by name into Appendix I of Permen LHK P.94/2016 (entry 5), with an Art. 3(5) control/eradication mandate and an Art. 4(1) import ban; it is a crop pest under the GERDAL OPT program and a disease vector under Permenkes 50/2017. An official cannot waive a species off a regulatory list by email, and BKSDA legally cannot license breeding/transport (SATS-DN) of a species the state is bound to eradicate. So appealing to an agency to simply "allow it" will NOT work — that is asking a civil servant to ignore a regulation they are mandated to enforce. The real fix is regulatory: a revision of P.94/2016 (a ministerial regulation, amendable by KLHK, not requiring parliament) that carves out documented captive-bred, indoor-kept specimens, OR a formal de-listing/parity decision. THAT SAID, there is a genuine agency-clarification angle worth pursuing in parallel, because the keep/hobby-breed status is a true vacuum: no clause specifically criminalizes caging one tame roof rat indoors, and the fancy rat's open pet trade proves the state already tolerates a congeneric introduced rat as a pet. So the realistic play is two-pronged: (a) ask KSDAE for a WRITTEN CLARIFICATION/declaratory position on whether captive-bred indoor R. rattus may be kept, and press for parity with the fancy rat — useful even if it only confirms the vacuum; while (b) being honest that the durable fix is amending the regulation/list, which only KLHK (the rule-maker) can do. Indonesia has no fixed public-comment window for this, so the route is the official citizen-inquiry/aspiration channel (SP4N-LAPOR!) directed at KLHK, framed as a request to clarify-and-revise.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • SP4N-LAPOR! — National Public Aspiration & Complaint Portal (lapor.go.id) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Verified live, official 'no wrong door' federal portal jointly run by the Ministry of State Apparatus (PANRB), the Presidential Staff Office, and the Ombudsman. It routes a citizen inquiry or aspiration to the competent ministry (here: KLHK for the invasive-species rule; Kemenkes for the vector rule) and guarantees a tracked written response. The KSDAE site itself lists this as its public complaint channel. Best single channel for both the clarification ask (to KLHK) and the request to revise Permen LHK P.94/2016.
  • KLHK — Ditjen KSDAE (Directorate General of Conservation of Natural Resources & Ecosystems) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Verified live (June 2026). The federal authority that OWNS Permen LHK P.94/2016 and the invasive-species/wildlife-utilization rules — i.e. the only body that can issue a written clarification on keeping captive-bred R. rattus and the only rule-maker that can amend Appendix I to add a captive-bred carve-out. Address the clarify-and-revise request here (and via LAPOR! for a tracked reply). Submit in Bahasa Indonesia.
  • Badan Karantina Indonesia (Barantin) — National Quarantine Agency (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Verified live, official. The border-biosecurity authority enforcing the P.94/2016 Art. 4(1) import ban and domestic inter-area movement rules. Relevant only as a secondary touchpoint to confirm import/transport treatment of a captive-bred pet — NOT the body that can change the listing. Include only if your question is specifically about moving/importing an animal.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request to clarify and revise the treatment of captive-bred pet roof rats (Rattus rattus)

To the Directorate General of KSDAE, Ministry of Environment & Forestry,

I am writing as a private citizen and keeper of pet rats to ask for a written clarification, and ultimately a small revision of the rules. Rattus rattus is listed by name as an invasive species in Appendix I of Permen LHK P.94/2016. I fully support controlling wild invasive populations. However, the rats I am asking about are captive-bred for generations, hand-tame, kept entirely indoors in cages, and never released into the wild — they pose no biosecurity, crop, or disease risk.

The issue is one of species name, not of the animal itself: the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus, "tikus putih") is an equally introduced, non-native rat that is openly kept and sold as a pet across Indonesia. The same tolerance should reasonably extend to a tame, captive-bred roof rat.

I respectfully ask: (1) Please confirm in writing whether a private citizen may keep captive-bred R. rattus indoors as a pet, and whether any registration mechanism exists. (2) Please consider revising Permen LHK P.94/2016 to distinguish wild invasive populations from documented captive-bred, indoor-kept pets, creating a captive-bred carve-out.

Thank you for your consideration.

[Your name]
[Your city / contact]
id
Perihal: Permohonan klarifikasi dan revisi atas perlakuan terhadap tikus peliharaan hasil penangkaran (Rattus rattus)

Kepada Yth. Direktorat Jenderal KSDAE, Kementerian Lingkungan Hidup dan Kehutanan,

Saya menulis sebagai warga negara dan pemelihara tikus peliharaan untuk memohon klarifikasi tertulis, dan pada akhirnya sebuah revisi kecil atas peraturan. Rattus rattus tercantum secara eksplisit sebagai jenis invasif dalam Lampiran I Permen LHK P.94/2016. Saya sepenuhnya mendukung pengendalian populasi invasif di alam liar. Namun, tikus yang saya maksud adalah hasil penangkaran turun-temurun, jinak, dipelihara sepenuhnya di dalam rumah dalam kandang, dan tidak pernah dilepasliarkan — sehingga tidak menimbulkan risiko biosekuriti, pertanian, maupun penyakit.

Persoalannya terletak pada nama spesies, bukan pada hewannya: tikus putih (Rattus norvegicus) adalah tikus yang sama-sama bukan asli Indonesia, namun dipelihara dan diperjualbelikan secara terbuka sebagai hewan peliharaan di seluruh Indonesia. Toleransi yang sama sepatutnya juga berlaku bagi tikus atap hasil penangkaran yang jinak.

Dengan hormat saya memohon: (1) Mohon konfirmasi tertulis apakah warga sipil diperbolehkan memelihara R. rattus hasil penangkaran di dalam rumah sebagai hewan peliharaan, dan apakah ada mekanisme pendaftaran. (2) Mohon dipertimbangkan revisi Permen LHK P.94/2016 untuk membedakan populasi invasif liar dari hewan peliharaan hasil penangkaran yang dipelihara di dalam rumah, dengan menciptakan pengecualian bagi hasil penangkaran.

Atas perhatian Bapak/Ibu, saya ucapkan terima kasih.

[Nama Anda]
[Kota / kontak Anda]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Permen LHK P.94/2016 — Invasive Species (Jenis Invasif): R. rattus on Appendix I (entry 5); Art. 4(1) import ban; Art. 3(5) eradication/control mandate; Art. 7 research exemption — Ministry of Environment & Forestry (KLHK)
  • Permen LHK No. 18/2024 — Utilization of Plant & Wildlife Species (Pemanfaatan TSL): Art. 4 business licenses (Penangkaran / Peredaran) for all wildlife, protected or not — KLHK (Ditjen KSDAE)
  • Law No. 5/1990 — Conservation of Living Resources (Art. 21 prohibitions apply only to protected species) — Republic of Indonesia (via FAOLEX)
  • Permen LHK P.106/2018 — protected plant & animal species list (R. rattus absent → not protected) — KLHK / peraturan.go.id
  • Law No. 21/2019 — Animal, Fish & Plant Quarantine (SKKH / quarantine clearance for movement) — Republic of Indonesia (BPK)
  • Kepmenhut 447/Kpts-II/2003 — administration of capture & circulation of wild flora/fauna (SATS-DN domestic transport permit) — Ministry of Forestry (now KLHK)
  • Permenkes No. 50/2017 — environmental-health standards for vectors & disease-carrying animals (rats as leptospirosis/typhus vectors; mandated control) — Ministry of Health (Kemenkes)
  • GERDAL OPT — national rat-pest eradication program (rodenticides + barn-owl biocontrol); R. rattus classified as a plant-pest organism (OPT) — Ministry of Agriculture (Kementan)
  • Lapak Satwa — open listing of pet white rats (R. norvegicus): the de-facto-tolerance contrast (market practice, not a legal exemption) — lapaksatwa.co.id (recognized pet-trade platform; secondary)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, tikus rumah, tikus atap, tikus hitam, jenis invasif, roof rat, black rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Ireland? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Ireland

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. Ireland is now DR-verified, and it is favourable for mainland keepers. S.I. 374/2024 lists the roof rat (Rattus rattus) as an invasive alien species of national concern, but its First Schedule restricts that designation to 'Offshore islands only' — so on the Irish MAINLAND keeping and breeding pet roof rats is fully legal and unregulated by possession bans, while on the offshore islands (critical seabird breeding grounds) keeping/breeding/transport are prohibited. Commercial supply on the mainland triggers DAFM rules: you must register as a seller/supplier if you transfer six or more pet animals in a year (sale OR free), and rats may not be transferred under 4 weeks of age. Importing rodents follows national 'non-harmonised species' rules (advance DAFM notice/permit + a government-vet health certificate). The earlier S.I. 477/2011 grey area is superseded.

Confirmed by the agencies.
  • National Parks & Wildlife Service (NPWS) Wildlife Licensing Unit, Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, written reply June 2026: NPWS 'does not licence for such species' (roof rats, Rattus rattus) — i.e. it is not a species for which NPWS issues a keeping/wildlife licence — and indicated that animal-welfare questions fall to the Department of Agriculture (DAFM). This supports that keeping a pet roof rat on the Irish mainland is not gated by an NPWS wildlife permit; welfare, pet-sale registration, and import sit with DAFM. (The offshore-islands prohibition under S.I. 374/2024 is unaffected.)

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

On the Irish MAINLAND, keeping a pet roof rat is fully legal and unregulated by possession bans. S.I. 374/2024 lists Rattus rattus as an invasive alien species of 'national concern', but the First Schedule limits its geographical application to 'Offshore islands only' (Reg. 16), so the Reg. 17 keep/breed/transport prohibitions do NOT activate on the mainland. On offshore islands, keeping is prohibited. No domestication carve-out (the ban targets the species by binomial name, identical to R. norvegicus).

Sources: Irish Statute Book, Irish Statute Book, Invasive Species Ireland (NPWS / NBDC)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

Mainland: legal and unregulated by environmental law. Offshore islands: prohibited (S.I. 374/2024 Reg. 17(1)(c)). Commercial supply triggers DAFM registration (see Sell).

Sources: Irish Statute Book, National Parks & Wildlife Service

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

On the mainland, selling or even GIVING AWAY pet rats is legal but commercial law applies: supplying SIX or more pet animals in a calendar year (sale OR free supply) requires registration on the DAFM Register of Sellers and Suppliers of Pet Animals (S.I. 681/2019), which entails a private-vet premises inspection; rats may not be transferred under 4 weeks of age. Offshore islands: prohibited.

Sources: Irish Statute Book, Irish Statute Book, Irish Statute Book

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

Rodents are 'non-harmonised species' (outside the EU pet-passport system), so import follows Ireland's national rules: an EU-origin pet needs an Owner Declaration to DAFM at least one working day before arrival; a non-EU/GB pet needs an advance DAFM import permit (apply 1–2 months ahead) plus an official government-vet health certificate. Internal transport to an offshore island is an offence.

Sources: Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine, Irish Statute Book

Restrictions & responsibilities

MAINLAND: NPWS confirmed (June 2026) it does NOT licence roof rats, so keeping and breeding pet roof rats on the Irish mainland are legal and not gated by any NPWS wildlife licence. The only commercial layer is DAFM: supplying SIX or more pet animals in a calendar year (sale OR free) requires registration on the DAFM Register of Sellers and Suppliers of Pet Animals (S.I. 681/2019), with a private-vet premises inspection; rats may not be transferred under 4 weeks of age. OFFSHORE ISLANDS: keeping/breeding/transport of R. rattus are prohibited (S.I. 374/2024, 'Offshore islands only'). Never release — an escape is itself an offence.
  • Mainland: no NPWS licence needed to keep or breed (NPWS confirmed it does not licence the species)
  • If supplying >=6 pet animals per year (sale or free): register with DAFM (S.I. 681/2019) and meet the 4-week minimum transfer age
  • Offshore islands: do not keep, breed, or transport R. rattus (S.I. 374/2024)
  • Welfare/import questions: Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine (DAFM)

Where: DAFM (pet-sales registration; welfare; import). NPWS does not licence this species.

Source: Irish Statute Book, Irish Statute Book

Bringing a rat into Ireland from another EU state (including Northern Ireland) needs a DAFM import permit + a vet health certificate (within 48h) + TRACES notification. Non-EU import needs a DAFM permit applied for 1–2 months ahead. Never release a roof rat — an escape from confinement is itself an offence under S.I. 477/2011 Reg. 49.

Where: Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine (DAFM)

Source: Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • European Communities (Birds and Natural Habitats) Regulations 2011 (S.I. 477/2011) — Third Schedule + Regs 49–50 (R. rattus listed) — Irish Statute Book
  • Black rat (Rattus rattus) species account — Third Schedule listing under Regs 49 & 50; notes Reg 50 not yet enacted — Invasive Species Ireland (NPWS / NBDC)
  • European Union (Invasive Alien Species) Regulations 2024 (S.I. 374/2024) — national-concern schedule + market offence — Irish Statute Book
  • Animal Health and Welfare Act 2013 — general welfare duties — Irish Statute Book
  • Animal Health and Welfare (Sale or Supply of Pet Animals) Regulations 2019 (S.I. 681/2019) — DAFM registration ≥6/yr — Irish Statute Book
  • NPWS — Licences and Consents (Wildlife Licensing Unit) — National Parks & Wildlife Service
  • DAFM Pet Travel — rodent intra-EU / non-EU import (permit, health cert, TRACES) — Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine
  • Regulation (EU) 1143/2014 — Union list (coypu is the only listed rodent; R. rattus NOT listed) — EU / EUR-Lex

Search terms: Rattus rattus, black rat, roof rat, ship rat, francach dubh.

Last reviewed 2026-06-11. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Israel? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Israel

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. Israel's regulation of roof rats is a paradox: the species is freely keepable precisely because it is legally branded a 'pest.' Under the Wildlife Protection Law 5715-1955, Section 8 bars holding, transferring, and trading a 'wild animal' WITHOUT an INPA permit — but only for animals that are NOT pests. The Wildlife Protection Regulations 5736-1976 (Reg. 2) explicitly declare Rattus rattus a pest (מזיק), listed right beside Rattus norvegicus, so both rat species are entirely exempt from INPA keeping, transfer, and internal-trade permits — and there is no White-List issue for domestic keeping. (This overturns the preliminary White-List assumption.) The fancy rat is sold freely for this exact reason, not because of any special 'domesticated' status. The catch is at the other end: as a declared pest and invasive species, R. rattus is NOT on the INPA Mammal White List, so commercial import is barred — deliberately, to keep exotic rat lineages out — with only a narrow, contested veterinary 'accompanied pet' exemption for personal import. Commercial breeding/selling needs a municipal business license, and municipal sanitation bylaws treat any rat on a property as a nuisance subject to eradication, a theoretical exposure that coexists with the federal exemption.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

Keeping a roof rat needs NO INPA permit. The Wildlife Protection Law 5715-1955 s.8(3) bars holding a 'wild animal that is not a pest' without a permit; the Wildlife Protection Regulations 5736-1976 Reg. 2(2) expressly declare Rattus rattus a pest (מזיק) — alongside R. norvegicus at Reg. 2(1) — so it is carved out of the s.8 permit regime entirely, exactly like the freely-kept fancy rat. The one wrinkle is tiered government: municipal sanitation bylaws (under the Municipalities Ordinance) classify rats on a property as a 'nuisance' subject to a removal/eradication notice, drawing no distinction between a feral infestation and a caged pet — a theoretical exposure that does not displace the federal exemption.

Sources: State of Israel / Knesset (via INPA), Ministry of Environmental Protection / INPA, Ministry of Interior / Local Municipalities

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

Private hobby breeding of lawfully-held roof rats is unregulated and lawful: because INPA requires no holding permit for declared pests (Wildlife Protection Law 1955 s.8; 1976 Regs Reg. 2), it does not track or restrict their reproduction, and the Animal Protection (Welfare) Law 5754-1994 sets only general welfare standards, not a breeding ban. The status shifts to RESTRICTED only at commercial scale: a systematic breeding operation triggers a mandatory municipal business license under the Business Licensing Order 5773-2013 Item 3.2(a) ('breeding, keeping and treating of animals'), with veterinary/sanitation/fire inspections. There is no fixed numeric hobby-to-business threshold; it is judged qualitatively (scale, public access, income, nuisance).

Sources: State of Israel / Knesset (via INPA), Ministry of Environmental Protection / INPA, State of Israel (translated text), Ministry of Interior (secondary: licensing-practice summary)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

Private sale or gifting of captive-bred roof rats is lawful and needs no INPA permit: the Wildlife Protection Law 1955 s.8(1)-(2) require trade/transfer permits only for a 'wild animal that is not a pest', and R. rattus is a declared pest (1976 Regs Reg. 2(2)), so it is exempt — which is why both rat species are sold openly on Israeli platforms (e.g. Yad2, Facebook groups) without violating any wildlife-trafficking statute. The status is RESTRICTED only for commercial retail: a pet shop or systematic seller needs a municipal business license under the Business Licensing Order 5773-2013 Item 3.2, plus Animal Protection (Welfare) Law 1994 housing standards. Not CITES-listed.

Sources: State of Israel / Knesset (via INPA), Ministry of Environmental Protection / INPA, Ministry of Interior (secondary: licensing-practice summary)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

Internal transport of lawfully-held stock is unregulated beyond general welfare. International IMPORT is the heavily restricted edge: Israel runs a 'White List' (רשימה לבנה) admitting only listed species, and the 2018 INPA Mammal White List omits ALL Rattus species while listing other pet rodents (hamsters, chinchilla, degu, gerbil) — so commercial import of roof rats is effectively prohibited, a deliberate policy (per a 2023/2025 draft amendment) to bar non-native rat lineages. A narrow lawful pathway survives: the Ministry of Agriculture Veterinary Services 'accompanied pet' exemption permits importing up to two rodents with an origin Veterinary Health Certificate (issued ≤7 days pre-export), a 90-day-ownership / non-commercial declaration (Annex B/C to vs-airport@moag.gov.il ≥48h before arrival), and an inspection fee — though its application to a declared 'pest' is unsettled and INPA inspectors may still confiscate at the border. Under the assume-a-pathway lens this is legal_with_permit/restricted, not flat-prohibited. Never release.

Sources: Israel Nature & Parks Authority, Israel Nature & Parks Authority, Israel Ministry of Agriculture — Veterinary Services, Israel Ministry of Agriculture — Veterinary Services (via USDA APHIS), State of Israel / Knesset (via INPA)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Commercial-scale breeding or a retail pet shop selling rats needs a municipal Business License (רישיון עסק) under the Business Licensing Order 5773-2013 Item 3.2 ('breeding, keeping and treating of animals'). Private hobby breeding and one-off/low-volume private sales need NO license. There is no numeric hobby/business threshold — municipalities judge it qualitatively (scale, public foot traffic, income, odor/refuse nuisance).
  • Determine whether the operation is qualitatively 'commercial' (scale, public access, income, nuisance) — private hobby placement is exempt
  • If commercial: apply to the local municipality for a Business License under Item 3.2
  • Pass prior/periodic inspections by the municipal veterinarian, Ministry of Health, and Fire & Rescue Authority (ventilation, drainage, escape-proof enclosures, disease control)

Where: Local municipality business-licensing department (רישוי עסקים) · Fees: Set by the municipality

Source: Ministry of Interior (secondary: licensing-practice summary)

Importing a roof rat as a personal pet runs through the Ministry of Agriculture Veterinary Services 'accompanied pet' exemption (no advance import license for up to two rodents), but R. rattus's absence from the INPA Mammal White List means INPA may still veto entry. The standard small-rodent pathway (hamster, etc.) does NOT clearly extend to a species declared a 'pest', so pre-clearance between MoAg-VS and INPA is advisable. Commercial import is effectively barred.
  • Obtain an original Veterinary Health Certificate (in English) from a government vet in the origin country, issued ≤7 days before export
  • Hold the animal(s) for ≥90 days pre-flight; limit to 2 rodents; non-commercial only
  • Submit the Annex B/C declaration to Veterinary Services at Ben Gurion (vs-airport@moag.gov.il) ≥48 hours before arrival
  • Pre-clear the species with INPA (off the White List) to avoid confiscation; pay the arrival inspection fee

Forms: MoAg Veterinary Services pet-arrival declaration (Annex B / Annex C) · Where: Ministry of Agriculture Veterinary Services, Ben Gurion Airport (vs-airport@moag.gov.il); coordinate with INPA (import@npa.org.il) · Fees: Arrival inspection fee, historically ~55 NIS (subject to adjustment)

Source: Israel Ministry of Agriculture — Veterinary Services, Israel Ministry of Agriculture — Veterinary Services (via USDA APHIS), Israel Nature & Parks Authority, Israel Nature & Parks Authority

Municipal sanitation bylaws (under the Municipalities Ordinance; model bylaw 1972, and e.g. Haifa, Nof HaGalil, Lod) classify the presence of rats on a property as an actionable 'nuisance' subject to a removal/eradication notice — with no legal distinction between a feral infestation and a caged pet. A complaint can trigger an inspector's notice; non-compliance can mean fines and forced extermination billed to the owner. There is no way to 'register' a pet rat to opt out. Separately, releasing a roof rat is strictly prohibited (invasive-species/ecological-hazard ban) — never release.
  • Keep rats fully indoors in secure, sanitary enclosures; avoid odor/escape that could draw a neighbor complaint
  • Never release a roof rat — release of an invasive pest is a prosecutable offense

Where: Local municipality (sanitation / nuisance enforcement)

Source: Ministry of Interior / Local Municipalities

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Wildlife Protection Law 5715-1955 (חוק להגנת חיית הבר) — s.1 'wild animal' definition; s.8(1)-(3) holding/transfer/trade permits exempt 'pests' — State of Israel / Knesset (via INPA)
  • Wildlife Protection Regulations 5736-1976 (תקנות להגנת חיית הבר) — Reg. 2 designates Rattus norvegicus (2(1)) and Rattus rattus (2(2)) as 'pests' (מזיקים) — Ministry of Environmental Protection / INPA
  • Draft Amendment to Wildlife Protection Regulations, 5783-2023 — explains the deliberate intent: keep only endemic rats on the pest list so non-native rat species cannot enter freely under the pest exemption — Ministry of Environmental Protection / Gov.il (tazkirim)
  • INPA Mammal White List (Sept. 2018) — permitted mammals for import/trade; omits ALL Rattus species (lists hamster, chinchilla, degu, gerbil) — Israel Nature & Parks Authority
  • INPA — Import of Mammals ('species not on the White List are prohibited for import, commerce and possession'; import@npa.org.il) — Israel Nature & Parks Authority
  • Ministry of Agriculture — Import of Pets (Veterinary Services; accompanied-pet exemption ≤2 rodents, health certificate) — Israel Ministry of Agriculture — Veterinary Services
  • MoAg Veterinary Services — Pet-arrival declaration (Annex B/C) for notifying Ben Gurion ≥48h before arrival — Israel Ministry of Agriculture — Veterinary Services (via USDA APHIS)
  • Business Licensing Order (Businesses Requiring Licensing) 5773-2013 — Item 3.2(a) license for breeding/keeping/treating animals (commercial breeders + pet shops) — Ministry of Interior (secondary: licensing-practice summary)
  • Animal Protection (Welfare) Law 5754-1994 — general vertebrate welfare standards (food/water/space); no rodent breeding ban — State of Israel (translated text)
  • Model Municipal Bylaw (Sanitation & Removal of Nuisances) 1972 + city bylaws (Haifa, Nof HaGalil, Lod) — rats classed as an actionable 'nuisance' subject to eradication notice — Ministry of Interior / Local Municipalities
  • IUCN GISD — Rattus rattus ('100 worst' invasive; underpins Israel's deliberate import bar) — IUCN

Search terms: Rattus rattus, חולדה מצויה (chuldah metzuyah — common/house rat, the statutory designation for R. rattus), חולדת העליות (chuldat ha-aliyot — attic rat), חולדה שחורה (chuldah shechorah — black rat, literal), מזיק (mazik — 'pest', the operative legal classification).

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in India? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › India

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. India is permissive for the roof rat, with one commercial catch. R. rattus is NATIVE to the Indian subcontinent (its evolutionary cradle), so Indian law does NOT treat it as an invasive alien species. The Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act 2022 ABOLISHED the old Schedule V 'vermin' list (which had included rats), and R. rattus is on none of the protected schedules (I, II, IV) and not CITES-listed — so it carries no wildlife designation, and private keeping + non-commercial hobby breeding are UNREGULATED (only the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1960 welfare duties apply; the 2024 PARIVESH registration covers only CITES/Schedule-IV exotics, not native rats). Indian law draws NO distinction between the roof rat and the fancy rat — the Pet Shop Rules 2018 cover 'rodents of the rat or mice category' generically. The one real requirement is COMMERCIAL SALE: selling rats as a business (incl. online) needs registration with the State Animal Welfare Board under the PCA (Pet Shop) Rules 2018 (₹5,000, inspection, welfare standards). Internal transport is unregulated (anti-cruelty only); INTERNATIONAL IMPORT is heavily restricted (DGFT restricted-import licence + Sanitary Import Permit + vet certificate; cargo only, 6 airports). ⚠️ Local municipal sanitation bylaws (plague history) could theoretically limit keeping in dense housing.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

After the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act 2022 abolished Schedule V ('vermin', which had listed rats), R. rattus — a native species — is absent from Schedules I, II, and IV and is not CITES-listed, so it carries no wildlife designation and the WLPA's possession/registration prohibitions (Ch. V/VB) don't apply. The Living Animal Species (Reporting & Registration) Rules 2024 (PARIVESH 2.0) bind only CITES/Schedule-IV species, so a native rat owner is exempt. Possession is therefore governed only by the PCA Act 1960 §11 welfare duty (food/water/shelter, no abandonment). No permit to keep. 'Unregulated_unclear' (not 'legal') because legality is by statutory silence + a residual municipal-bylaw possibility, not an affirmative pet authorization.

Sources: Parliament of India (via PRS), Animal Welfare Board of India, MoEFCC (via PIB)

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

No federal statute requires a permit for private, non-commercial hobby breeding of non-scheduled small mammals. The Breeding of & Experiments on Animals (Control & Supervision) Rules 1998 (CPCSEA) govern only institutional/laboratory breeding and expressly exempt the pet trade; the PCA (Dog Breeding & Marketing) Rules 2017 cover dogs only — no analogous rodent-breeder rule exists. So hobby breeding of R. rattus falls through the gap (unregulated), bounded only by PCA Act §11 welfare. Ambiguity: there is no numerical 'hobby vs commercial' threshold — once offspring are sold for profit, the Pet Shop Rules (see sell_give) apply.

Sources: Animal Welfare Board of India, Parliament of India (via PRS)

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

COMMERCIAL sale requires registration. The PCA (Pet Shop) Rules 2018 define 'pet animal' to include 'rodents of the rat or mice category' (Rule 2(j)) — covering R. rattus and R. norvegicus identically — and Rule 3 bars operating a pet shop / trading in pet animals (incl. ONLINE: social media, e-commerce, classifieds) without a Certificate of Registration from the State Animal Welfare Board (Form I, ₹5,000, vet inspection, valid 5 yrs; caging/welfare standards + records). FREE, non-commercial gifting/rehoming is NOT a 'business' and doesn't trigger registration — but charging even a nominal 'rehoming fee' could be construed as commercial by a strict inspector.

Sources: Animal Welfare Board of India

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

INTERNAL (interstate/within India): unregulated beyond the Transport of Animals Rules 1978 / PCA Act anti-cruelty baseline (no transit permit/NOC, since R. rattus is non-scheduled). INTERNATIONAL IMPORT is heavily restricted: live rodents fall under ITC(HS) 01061900 ('Mammals: Other'), a 'Restricted' category — the DGFT pet-baggage route is for DOGS & CATS ONLY (Trade Notice 22/2022-23), so a pet rat must be imported as formal air cargo with (1) a DGFT restricted-import licence, (2) a Sanitary Import Permit (SIP) from DAHD via NSWS, (3) an official veterinary health certificate (DAHD SOP Annexure 12.1.1 for rodents), and (4) an Advance NOC from AQCS — entry only via 6 designated airports, with possible 30-day quarantine. Never release.

Sources: Directorate General of Foreign Trade, Department of Animal Husbandry & Dairying, Animal Welfare Board of India

Restrictions & responsibilities

To SELL roof rats as a business (including online), register as a pet shop with your State Animal Welfare Board under the PCA (Pet Shop) Rules 2018 (Form I, ₹5,000, vet inspection, 5-yr certificate; caging/welfare standards + records). Keeping, hobby breeding, and FREE rehoming need no registration. Internal transport is welfare-only.
  • For commercial sale: apply to your State Animal Welfare Board (Form I, ₹5,000) + pass the vet inspection
  • Free/non-commercial rehoming: nothing required

Where: State Animal Welfare Board (SAWB) · Fees: ₹5,000 (pet-shop registration)

Source: Animal Welfare Board of India

INTERNATIONAL IMPORT only: a pet roof rat must enter as air cargo with a DGFT restricted-import licence + a DAHD Sanitary Import Permit + a veterinary health certificate + an AQCS Advance NOC (6 designated airports; possible 30-day quarantine). The dog/cat pet-baggage route does NOT apply to rodents. Internal movement needs no permit. Never release.
  • Apply for the DGFT restricted-import licence (~2 months ahead)
  • Obtain a DAHD Sanitary Import Permit via NSWS
  • Get an origin-country veterinary health certificate (rodent SOP)
  • Submit to AQCS for an Advance NOC ≥7 days before arrival

Where: DGFT; DAHD (NSWS); AQCS

Source: Directorate General of Foreign Trade, Department of Animal Husbandry & Dairying

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Official sources

  • Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act 2022 — abolishes Schedule V ('vermin'); 4-schedule system; R. rattus on none of Sch. I/II/IV — Parliament of India (via PRS)
  • PCA (Pet Shop) Rules 2018 — 'rodents of the rat or mice category' = pet animal; State Board registration for sale/trade — Animal Welfare Board of India
  • Living Animal Species (Reporting & Registration) Rules 2024 — PARIVESH 2.0; applies only to CITES/Schedule-IV species (not native rats) — MoEFCC (via PIB)
  • DGFT Trade Notice 22/2022-23 — import of pets (baggage route = dogs & cats only; rodents = cargo, ITC(HS) 01061900 Restricted) — Directorate General of Foreign Trade
  • DAHD SOPs for Import of Live Animals (Sanitary Import Permit; Annexure 12.1.1 rodent veterinary health certificate) — Department of Animal Husbandry & Dairying

Search terms: Rattus rattus, chooha (चूहा), kala chooha (काला चूहा), roof rat, black rat, house rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Italy? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Italy

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.

Summary. Italy imposes no species-specific ban on keeping a captive-bred roof rat, but the picture is unsettled. The 1996 dangerous-animals decree (DM 19 April 1996, under Legge 150/1992) lists only porcupines among rodents, not Muridae, so R. rattus isn't a prohibited 'dangerous' species. Italy's 2022 exotic-animal law (D.Lgs 135/2022) targets wild-caught and dangerous/exotic species and was supposed to publish a 'lista negativa' of banned taxa by March 2023 — but as of 2026 that list is still unpublished, so the field is partly unresolved. R. rattus is NOT on the EU IAS Union list and not CITES-listed. In practice, keeping captive-bred rats is currently allowed (often with an informal ASL registration); hobby breeding registers with the local ASL under the EU Animal Health Law system; commercial sale needs ASL/SUAP authorization. The big caveat: if the lista negativa is eventually published and includes R. rattus, the status could flip overnight.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

No Italian law prohibits keeping captive-bred R. rattus: DM 19 April 1996 (the operative dangerous-species list) names only Hystricidae among rodents, and D.Lgs 135/2022's banning 'lista negativa' is still unpublished. Many local ASL (health authority) areas require an informal notification/registration for non-traditional companion animals. Status is 'currently permitted, often with ASL registration,' but not backed by an explicit authorizing provision — and could shift when the lista negativa publishes.

Sources: MASE (Ministero dell'Ambiente), Gazzetta Ufficiale

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Amateur hobby breeding of captive-bred R. rattus isn't expressly prohibited (it's not on any published negative list). Under the EU Animal Health Law (Reg. 2016/429, implemented by D.Lgs 134/2022), breeders of companion rodents register the activity with the local ASL (SINAC system); small amateur operations register directly at ASL without SUAP. No national licence for purely personal breeding. Risk: a future lista negativa including R. rattus would prohibit breeding.

Sources: Gazzetta Ufficiale, MASE (Ministero dell'Ambiente)

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Gratuitous transfer of captive-bred rats appears unimpeded for a hobbyist. Commercial sale requires ASL establishment authorization + a municipal SUAP/SCIA, a stamped entry/exit register, and per-animal seller self-certification (origin/age/health). No R. rattus-specific sale ban. Occasional hobby litters typically fall below the commercial-registration threshold (region-dependent).

Sources: Gazzetta Ufficiale

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Intra-EU non-commercial movement of pet rodents falls under Reg. (EU) 576/2013 Annex I Part B; Italy requires a health certificate from a licensed vet in the origin country, owner-accompanied, no change of ownership, max 5 animals. Commercial movement needs fuller animal-health certification. R. rattus isn't CITES-listed. Import from outside the EU needs third-country certification + likely Ministero della Salute authorization. Never release.

Sources: EU / EUR-Lex, Gazzetta Ufficiale

Restrictions & responsibilities

No national ban on captive-bred roof rats, but check with your local ASL (health authority): many require a notification/registration for non-traditional companion animals, and hobby breeders register with the ASL (SINAC). ⚠️ Watch the pending 'lista negativa' (D.Lgs 135/2022) — confirm with MASE/Ministero della Salute before acquiring, as R. rattus's future status is uncertain. Never release.
  • Check ASL notification requirement for keeping; register breeding with ASL (SINAC)
  • Confirm R. rattus is not (and won't be) on the lista negativa via Ministero della Salute / MASE

Where: Local ASL (Azienda Sanitaria Locale); Ministero della Salute DGSAF

Source: Gazzetta Ufficiale

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Italy
⏳ Time-sensitive: The "lista negativa" of banned species under D.Lgs 135/2022 has been overdue since 27 March 2023 and remains unpublished as of mid-2026; the government's correttivo (D.Lgs 220/2025) keeps the framework live and the decree could be issued at any time. There is no formally announced public-comment window, but the rule is actively being drafted now, so the window to influence its content is open and could close without notice — write before the decree is published.

In Italy, keeping a captive-bred roof rat (Rattus rattus, "ratto nero") is currently allowed: the only operative ban list — the dangerous-animals decree of 19 April 1996 under Law 150/1992 — lists only porcupines (Hystricidae) among rodents, not the mouse/rat family, and R. rattus is not on the EU invasive-species Union list or on CITES. Many local health authorities (ASL) ask keepers and hobby breeders to file an informal notification/registration. So the agency is not misreading the law; under the law as it stands today, your pet roof rat is permitted. The real risk is a law that has not been written yet. Italy's 2022 exotic-animal law (D.Lgs 135/2022) requires the government to publish a "lista negativa" — a binding list of species banned from being kept — but that list, due since March 2023, is still unpublished in 2026. Its final contents are unknown. The published intent targets primates, big cats, elephants and venomous species, not small companion rodents, but it is not final. If R. rattus were ever swept into that list, keeping and breeding could become illegal overnight. This is the moment to make the case, before the list is fixed.

The ask: Write to the two ministries that jointly draft the lista negativa (the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of the Environment / MASE) and ask them to confirm in writing that the captive-bred domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) — a small companion rodent, not a dangerous or wild-caught species — will NOT be included on the forthcoming lista negativa under D.Lgs 135/2022. Make the point that the relevant distinction is the species' captive-bred, domesticated, indoor-kept status, exactly like the familiar fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus), and not the wild form. Ask, plainly, that small companion rodents bred in captivity be kept off the ban list (or, if any threshold applies, that a clear path to keep them legally be preserved).

Where the lever really is: This is branch (b) with a twist: the lever is the LEGISLATURE/RULEMAKING side, not the front-line agency. Under the law AS IT EXISTS TODAY, the local ASL is applying it correctly — there is no species ban on R. rattus, so writing to an ASL to "clarify" or "permit" your rat will not change anything that needs changing, and any ASL registration they ask for is a legitimate notification, not a wrong. There is no agency misreading to fix. The actual exposure is a piece of secondary legislation that has not been enacted yet: the "lista negativa" mandated by D.Lgs 135/2022, drafted jointly by the Ministry of Health and MASE, overdue since March 2023 and still unpublished in 2026. Because that list is a ministerial decree (rulemaking) rather than an ASL decision, the correct touchpoint is the drafting ministries during the rulemaking window — to ensure captive-bred small companion rodents are not added — NOT a front-line health office. Appealing to a local ASL would be aimed at the wrong body entirely. The advocacy is preventive: shape the rule before it is finalized, because once R. rattus is on a statutory ban list, no agency could exempt it.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Ministero della Salute — Direzione Generale della Salute Animale (animal-health directorate; co-author of the D.Lgs 135/2022 implementing decrees, incl. the lista negativa) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    One of the two ministries that jointly draft and sign the lista negativa decree under D.Lgs 135/2022. The right body to ask that captive-bred small companion rodents (R. rattus) be kept off the ban list. Use the official contacts page; for a formal submission send to the institutional certified inbox (PEC) dgsa@postacert.sanita.it. Do not write to a named individual officer.
  • Ministero dell'Ambiente e della Sicurezza Energetica (MASE) — Ufficio Relazioni con il Pubblico (URP) (executive / agency) — urp@mase.gov.it
    The co-drafting ministry for the D.Lgs 135/2022 lista negativa and the authority that published the related positive list. The URP is the verified official intake channel; institutional PEC mase@pec.mase.gov.it for a formal submission. Writing to both ministries covers the two signatures the ban-list decree requires.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Direzione Generale della Salute Animale (Ministero della Salute) and to MASE,

I am writing about the forthcoming "lista negativa" of banned species under Legislative Decree 135/2022, which is still unpublished. I ask you to confirm that the captive-bred domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) will NOT be included on that list.

The roof rats kept by hobbyists are bred in captivity, tame, kept indoors as companion animals, and are never released into the wild. They are small companion rodents — like the familiar fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) — not dangerous or wild-caught species. The decree's stated aim targets dangerous and exotic taxa, and the only rodent on the 1996 dangerous-animals decree is the porcupine family.

I respectfully ask that captive-bred small companion rodents, including domesticated R. rattus, be excluded from the lista negativa, or that a clear legal path to keep them be preserved. Please confirm the current drafting status of the list and how the public may comment.

Thank you for your consideration.

[Your name]
[Your town/region, Italy]
Italiano
Alla Direzione Generale della Salute Animale (Ministero della Salute) e al MASE,

Scrivo in merito alla "lista negativa" delle specie di cui sarà vietata la detenzione, prevista dal D.Lgs 135/2022 e tuttora non pubblicata. Chiedo di confermare che il ratto nero domestico, allevato in cattività (Rattus rattus), NON sarà incluso in tale lista.

I ratti neri tenuti dagli appassionati sono allevati in cattività, docili, custoditi in casa come animali d'affezione e non vengono mai rilasciati in natura. Sono piccoli roditori da compagnia — come il comune ratto domestico (Rattus norvegicus) — e non specie pericolose o catturate in natura. La finalità dichiarata del decreto riguarda taxa pericolosi ed esotici, e l'unico roditore presente nel DM 19 aprile 1996 sugli animali pericolosi è la famiglia degli istrici (Hystricidae).

Chiedo rispettosamente che i piccoli roditori da compagnia allevati in cattività, incluso il R. rattus domestico, siano esclusi dalla lista negativa, oppure che sia preservato un chiaro percorso legale per detenerli. Vi prego di confermare lo stato di redazione della lista e le modalità con cui il pubblico può presentare osservazioni.

Vi ringrazio per l'attenzione.

[Your name]
[Comune/Regione, Italia]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • DM Ambiente 19 aprile 1996 — dangerous-animal list (Rodentia: only Hystricidae; Muridae not listed) — MASE (Ministero dell'Ambiente)
  • D.Lgs 5 agosto 2022 n. 135 — exotic-animal law (Art. 3; 'lista negativa' pending) + correttivo D.Lgs 220/2025 — Gazzetta Ufficiale
  • Regulation (EU) 576/2013 — non-commercial pet movement (Annex I Part B: rodents) — EU / EUR-Lex
  • ISPRA — Italian implementation of EU IAS Reg. 1143/2014 (R. rattus not on Union list) — ISPRA

Search terms: Rattus rattus, ratto nero, ratto dei tetti, sorcio nero.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Japan? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Japan

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. In Japan, keeping and hobby-breeding a captive-bred roof rat is legal and unregulated federally: the species is deliberately NOT a 'Specified Animal' (特定動物, hazardous) and NOT a 'Designated Invasive Alien Species' (特定外来生物) — a 2005 expert committee chose to exclude it because it's too long-established to regulate. Commercial activity (breeding for profit, retail sale, exhibition, or large-scale free rehoming) triggers registration as a First-Class (or Second-Class) Animal Handling Business with facility/welfare standards. The big restriction is IMPORT: bringing a roof rat into Japan is de-facto prohibited for the public — the Ministry of Health requires imported rodents to have lived since birth in a foreign-government-designated biosecure facility (homes/hobby breeders don't qualify). Never release one.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Private possession needs no federal permit: R. rattus is not a 'Specified Animal' (特定動物 — that list targets primates, big carnivores, large/venomous reptiles, not rodents), and it is not a 'Designated Invasive Alien Species' (特定外来生物). The 2005 Ministry of the Environment expert committee deliberately excluded it (long-established via maritime trade; eradication-vs-pet distinction). Domestic keeping is treated like keeping a fancy rat or guinea pig.

Sources: Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE), Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE), Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Private breeding without intent to profit/advertise/distribute commercially is entirely outside the commercial animal-handling law. (Commercial-scale breeding triggers First-Class Animal Handling Business registration — see sell_give.)

Sources: Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Selling for profit (or breeding to sell) requires registration as a First-Class Animal Handling Business (第一種動物取扱業) with the prefecture, plus facility/caging/disclosure standards and an Animal Handling Manager. Giving animals away free to 'a large number of unspecified people' on a continuing basis requires Second-Class (第二種) notification. Occasional free rehoming to friends/family is unregulated.

Sources: Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE), Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

DOMESTIC transport between prefectures is unregulated (subject only to carrier policies). IMPORT is de-facto prohibited for pets: under the Infectious Diseases Control Law's Animal Import Notification System, all live rodents need a health certificate from the EXPORTING government certifying the animal lived since birth in a government-designated disease-free facility — which homes and hobby breeders cannot obtain, so a pet roof rat cannot legally be imported. (R. rattus is not on the absolute-prohibition list, but the facility rule is an effective ban.) Export from Japan is legal with the destination country's health certificate (MAFF AQS). Never release.

Sources: Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW), Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Commercial selling/breeding (for profit) = First-Class Animal Handling Business registration (第一種動物取扱業) with the prefecture: facility floor plans, cleanable escape-resistant enclosures, space to 'stand/lie/move' naturally, an Animal Handling Manager, and written species/sex/origin disclosure at transfer. Large-scale non-commercial giveaway = Second-Class (第二種) notification (penalty up to ¥300,000 for failing to notify).
  • Register as a First-Class Animal Handling Business before any commercial sale/breeding
  • Or file a Second-Class notification for large-scale free rehoming

Where: Prefectural government (animal welfare center / public health dept)

Source: Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE), Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)

Importing a roof rat into Japan is effectively impossible for pet owners: imported rodents need an exporting-government health certificate proving the animal lived since birth in a government-DESIGNATED biosecure facility (homes/hobby breeders can't qualify). MHLW states such pets 'basically cannot be brought into Japan.'

Where: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (quarantine station at port of entry)

Source: Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW), Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Designated Invasive Alien Species list — Ministry of the Environment (R. rattus NOT listed) — Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)
  • List of Specified Animals (特定動物) — rodents excluded — Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)
  • MOE Expert Group minutes (July 2005) — rationale for excluding R. rattus (established; Watase/Blakiston lines) — Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)
  • Regulation of Animal Handling Business (動物取扱業の規制) — First-Class registration scope — Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)
  • Second-Class Animal Handling Business (第二種動物取扱業) — non-commercial large-scale transfer — Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)
  • Animal Import Notification System for rodents (designated-facility health certificate) — MHLW — Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW)
  • MHLW public warning — pet rodents 'basically cannot be brought into Japan' — Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, クマネズミ (kumanezumi), roof rat, black rat, ship rat.
