item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in South Korea? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › South Korea

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. South Korea has, as of December 14, 2025, become one of the most restrictive jurisdictions in the world for the pet roof rat — and earlier preliminary research here was wrong about why. The roof rat (Korean 곰쥐, R. rattus) is NOT an 'Alert Alien Species' (유입주의 생물); that label belongs to the Polynesian rat (R. exulans). Instead, Korea has flipped its entire exotic-animal regime from a 'negative list' (anything not banned is allowed) to a 'White List' (백색목록) positive list under the Wildlife Protection and Management Act: every mammal, bird, reptile and amphibian is now prohibited to import, breed, or sell by default unless the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment has expressly approved the species. Only 9 mammal species made the approved list — and the roof rat is not one of them. That makes R. rattus a 'Designated Managed Wild Animal' (지정관리 야생동물). The practical effect: importing one is banned outright (except for licensed academic research); breeding (증식) is prohibited; selling or even giving one away (거래/양도) is prohibited. People who already owned a roof rat before December 14, 2025 may keep that individual animal for the rest of its natural life ONLY IF they formally register it through the national WIMS portal by a hard deadline of June 13, 2026 — after which an unregistered animal becomes illegal contraband. There is no hobbyist exemption and no permit that reopens breeding or sale; the policy is deliberately designed to phase the species out of private hands by natural attrition.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

Keeping a roof rat is permitted ONLY under a transitional grandfather clause for animals already owned before the White List took effect (Dec 14, 2025). Such owners must file a possession declaration (보관 신고, Form 31-9) with their local mayor/county/district head through the national WIMS portal no later than June 13, 2026. A registered owner then receives a declaration certificate (신고확인증) and may keep that specific individual animal for the rest of its natural life. From June 14, 2026 onward, possessing an unregistered R. rattus is illegal harboring of contraband wildlife, subject to confiscation and penalties. No new acquisition is possible — the species is a 'Designated Managed Wild Animal' (지정관리 야생동물) because it is not on the 백색목록 White List.

Sources: National Law Information Center (법제처 국가법령정보센터), Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment (기후에너지환경부), Gimpo City Government (김포시청)

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

Breeding (증식) is unequivocally prohibited for both private citizens and commercial entities. The grandfather clause that allows continued possession of pre-existing animals expressly forbids breeding: municipal enforcement guidance states grandfathered Designated Managed Wild Animals 'may continue to be kept, but breeding and trading are not permitted' (증식·거래는 허용하지 않는다). The intent is biological containment — to eliminate the captive population over the lifespan of existing individuals. There are no hobbyist exemptions and no breeding permits available for a non-White-List species; even a Wild Animal Business Production License (생산업 허가) only applies to White-List species, so it cannot authorize breeding roof rats.

Sources: National Law Information Center (법제처 국가법령정보센터), Gimpo City Government (김포시청)

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

Commercial sale (판매) and private transfer or gifting (양도/양수) are prohibited under the same regime that bans breeding ('거래는 허용하지 않는다' — trading is not permitted). The grandfathered animal is legally tethered to the individual who filed the possession declaration. The 'transfer/acquisition' checkboxes on Form 31-9 exist for White-List animals or narrow state-approved exceptions (e.g., inheritance on the registered owner's death, or surrender to a licensed facility) — not for casual rehoming or sale of a roof rat between hobbyists. A Wild Animal Business Sales License does not help, because it covers only White-List species.

Sources: National Law Information Center (법제처 국가법령정보센터), Gimpo City Government (김포시청)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

Importation of R. rattus for the pet trade is banned outright — Designated Managed Wild Animals cannot be imported or brought into the country (Wildlife Act Art. 22-2), the only exemption being a rigorous permit for academic/scientific/state restoration purposes. A shipment intended for the pet trade would be denied entry or confiscated regardless of any origin health certificate. Internal transport of a legally grandfathered, WIMS-registered animal (e.g., to a veterinarian, or when the owner relocates) is generally tolerated as an inherent part of authorized possession, provided the animal is securely contained, never released, and the WIMS location data is updated on a permanent move — but the statute does not give explicit point-to-point transit rules, so confirm provincial-line movement with the Ministry.

Sources: National Law Information Center (법제처 국가법령정보센터), Animal and Plant Quarantine Agency

Restrictions & responsibilities

Since December 14, 2025, the roof rat is a 'Designated Managed Wild Animal' under Korea's White List positive-list system: importing, breeding, and selling/giving away the species are all prohibited. Only animals already owned before that date may be kept — and only if registered via the WIMS portal by June 13, 2026. After that deadline, an unregistered animal is illegal contraband subject to confiscation. There is no hobbyist exemption and no permit that reopens breeding or sale.
  • If you already own a roof rat (acquired before Dec 14, 2025): file the possession declaration (보관 신고, Form 31-9) via the WIMS portal https://wims.mcee.go.kr by June 13, 2026 to keep the animal lawfully for its natural life
  • Do NOT breed, sell, or give the animal away — these are prohibited even for grandfathered/registered animals
  • Do NOT import a roof rat — import for the pet trade is banned; a shipment would be confiscated regardless of health certificates
  • Update WIMS location data if you move; keep the animal securely contained and never release it

Forms: Form No. 31-9 — 지정관리 야생동물 (양도·양수·보관) 신고서 (Designated Managed Wild Animal Transfer/Acquisition/Possession Declaration) · Where: Local mayor / county governor / district head, filed through the national WIMS portal (야생동물종합관리시스템, https://wims.mcee.go.kr)

Source: National Law Information Center (법제처 국가법령정보센터), Gimpo City Government (김포시청)

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in South Korea. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in South Korea
⏳ Time-sensitive: TWO live deadlines. (1) Possession registration: owners of a roof rat acquired before Dec 14, 2025 MUST file the possession declaration (보관 신고, Form 31-9) via the WIMS portal (wims.mcee.go.kr) by June 13, 2026; after that an unregistered animal is illegal contraband. (2) The Ministry's "2026 White List revision" public-comment process (2026 백색목록 개정 국민 의견수렴) is currently open/announced on the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment website — submit any species-inclusion or humane-treatment comment through this window. Confirm the exact closing date on the Ministry notice before relying on it.

As of December 14, 2025, South Korea switched from a "negative list" (anything not banned is allowed) to a "White List" (백색목록 / positive list) under the Wildlife Protection and Management Act. Now every mammal, bird, reptile, and amphibian is banned to import, breed, or sell by default unless the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment has expressly approved the species. The approved White List names only 9 mammals — and the roof rat (곰쥐, Rattus rattus) is not one of them (neither is the fancy rat, R. norvegicus). That makes the roof rat a "Designated Managed Wild Animal" (지정관리 야생동물): importing it is banned, breeding (증식) is prohibited, and selling or even giving one away (거래·양도) is prohibited. There is no hobbyist exemption and no permit that reopens breeding or sale. The only people who may keep a roof rat are those who already owned one before Dec 14, 2025 AND who register that specific animal through the national WIMS portal (wims.mcee.go.kr) by the hard deadline of June 13, 2026; from June 14, 2026 an unregistered roof rat becomes illegal contraband. Korean law treats a captive-bred, hand-tamed roof rat as legally identical to a wild one — domestication carries no legal weight here, only the species name on the list does.

The ask: Two honest, separate asks. (1) IF YOU ALREADY OWN A ROOF RAT (acquired before Dec 14, 2025): register that individual animal through the WIMS portal (wims.mcee.go.kr, Form 31-9) before June 13, 2026 so you can lawfully keep it for the rest of its natural life — do not miss this deadline, and do not breed, sell, or give the animal away. (2) IF YOU WANT THE RULE CHANGED: the only real lever is the Ministry's annual White List revision and its public-comment process (2026 백색목록 개정 국민 의견수렴). Submit a comment asking the Ministry to evaluate documented, long-domesticated captive-bred R. rattus lineages for inclusion against the four safety criteria (climate suitability, reproductive rate, hybridization risk, disease risk), OR — more realistically achievable — ask for clear, humane rules for the grandfathered population (emergency/compassionate rehoming if an owner dies, and safe veterinary transport across provincial lines). Be honest with yourself: a high-reproduction, climate-suited rodent is a long shot for the White List, so the achievable win is humane treatment of the animals already here.

Where the lever really is: This is a LAW/LIST problem, not a bureaucracy-misreading problem. The agency is applying the law CORRECTLY: under the new positive-list ("White List") system effective Dec 14, 2025, every mammal is banned by default unless expressly listed, and the roof rat simply is not on the 9-mammal approved list (Ministry Notification No. 2025-55). There is nothing to "clarify" or "reinterpret" — the rule is unambiguous and the Ministry has no discretion to wave the species through on request. Therefore an appeal to the agency asking it to treat your tame, captive-bred roof rat as exempt will NOT work, because the agency is not making a mistake: it is doing exactly what the statute and the list require. The only lever that can actually change the outcome is changing the LIST itself — which happens through the Ministry's formal, recurring White List revision and its public-comment/opinion-submission process (and, behind that, the legislature that built the positive-list regime). So the correct target is the public-comment / rulemaking window for the White List, not a one-off plea to an inspector or a help-desk. Two practical notes specific to Korea: (a) there IS a live, recurring official comment process for the 2026 White List revision, so the door to petition is genuinely open even though success is unlikely for this species; and (b) for owners of existing animals, the immediate action is purely administrative compliance (WIMS registration by June 13, 2026), which is separate from advocacy and is not a request the agency can deny if filed correctly.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment (기후에너지환경부) — Biodiversity Division (생물다양성과), White List public-comment / 2026 revision process (public comment) — official contact page
    The agency that owns the White List and runs the annual revision and public-comment process (2026 백색목록 개정 국민 의견수렴). Because the law is being applied correctly, the ONLY way to change the outcome is to change the list through this channel. Watch the Ministry's notice board for the live comment notice and its submission instructions/deadline. Division phone: +82-44-201-7245 / -7248.
  • e-People (국민신문고) — official government petition and opinion portal (public comment) — official contact page
    Korea's single official portal for submitting policy suggestions, opinions, and requests for interpretation to any government agency, including the Ministry. Its 'Petition for Foreigners' page accepts submissions and replies in English and 15 other languages, so a non-Korean speaker can lodge a formal, on-record comment directed to the Ministry's Biodiversity Division. Use this to submit the White List inclusion request or the humane-treatment ask.
  • WIMS — Wildlife Information Management System (야생동물종합관리시스템) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    NOT an advocacy channel — this is the mandatory portal for the administrative step: existing owners file the possession declaration (Form 31-9) here by June 13, 2026 to lawfully keep their animal. Included because it is the time-critical action for anyone who already owns a roof rat.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Biodiversity Division, Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment / Public comment on the White List (백색목록) revision

I am writing about the status of the roof rat (곰쥐, Rattus rattus) under the White List system in effect since 14 December 2025. Because the species is not on the approved list, it is treated as a Designated Managed Wild Animal, and keeping, breeding, and transfer are effectively prohibited.

The animals I am concerned with are captive-bred, hand-tamed companion rats kept entirely indoors. They are never released into the wild, never sold into the wild trade, and are descended from long-domesticated lines — biologically and behaviorally distinct from wild-caught roof rats, much as domestic ferrets or fancy rats differ from their wild ancestors.

I respectfully ask the Ministry to (1) evaluate documented, captive-bred domesticated R. rattus lineages for inclusion on the White List against the four safety criteria, and (2) at minimum, adopt clear and humane rules for the already-registered grandfathered population — including compassionate rehoming when an owner dies or is incapacitated, and safe veterinary transport.

Thank you for considering this comment.

[Your name]
[Your city / country]
[Date]
한국어
기후에너지환경부 생물다양성과 귀중 / 백색목록(白色目錄) 개정 국민 의견 제출

2025년 12월 14일부터 시행된 백색목록 제도와 관련하여 곰쥐(Rattus rattus)의 분류에 대해 의견을 드립니다. 곰쥐는 백색목록에 포함되어 있지 않아 지정관리 야생동물로 취급되며, 사육·증식·양도가 사실상 금지되어 있습니다.

제가 말씀드리는 개체는 사람 손에서 번식하고 길들여져 실내에서만 기르는 반려 개체입니다. 자연에 방사하지 않으며, 야생 거래에 판매하지 않고, 오랫동안 가축화되어 온 혈통의 후손으로서 야생에서 포획된 곰쥐와는 생물학적·행동학적으로 구별됩니다. 이는 가축화된 페럿이나 애완용 시궁쥐가 그 야생 조상과 다른 것과 같습니다.

이에 정중히 요청드립니다. (1) 문서로 입증된 가축화된 사육 곰쥐 혈통을 네 가지 안전성 기준에 따라 백색목록 등재 대상으로 검토하여 주시고, (2) 최소한, 이미 신고된 경과조치(유예) 대상 개체에 대해 명확하고 인도적인 관리 기준을 마련하여 주시기 바랍니다. 여기에는 소유자의 사망이나 중대한 장애 시 인도적 양도, 그리고 동물병원 진료를 위한 안전한 이동이 포함됩니다.

의견을 검토하여 주셔서 감사합니다.

[이름]
[거주 도시 / 국가]
[날짜]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Wildlife Protection and Management Act (야생생물 보호 및 관리에 관한 법률), as amended/enforced Dec 14, 2025 — Designated Managed Wild Animal definition (Art. 2), possession reporting (Art. 22-4), import prohibition (Art. 22-2) — National Law Information Center (법제처 국가법령정보센터)
  • White List Designation Notification (백색목록 지정 고시), Ministry Notification No. 2025-55 — 888 approved species; only 9 mammals; R. rattus excluded — Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment (기후에너지환경부)
  • Wildlife Act Enforcement Rule (시행규칙) — administrative procedure and Form 31-9 for declaring grandfathered Designated Managed Wild Animals — National Law Information Center (법제처)
  • Municipal implementation guidance (Gimpo City) — confirms June 13, 2026 possession-declaration deadline and the absolute ban on breeding (증식) and trading (거래) of grandfathered animals; Wild Animal Business License thresholds — Gimpo City Government (김포시청)
  • APQA — pet/rodent import requirements (health certificate) — Animal and Plant Quarantine Agency

Search terms: Rattus rattus, 곰쥐, 지붕쥐, 지정관리 야생동물, 백색목록.

Last reviewed 2026-06-08. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Mexico? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Mexico

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. Mexico governs Rattus rattus entirely through federal wildlife law, not ordinary pet law. Both R. rattus and R. norvegicus are on the official invasive-species list (SEMARNAT Acuerdo, DOF 07/12/2016, 'muy alto' risk), which makes the roof rat 'vida silvestre exótica invasora' regardless of how tame or captive-bred it is — domestication is not a legal shield in Mexican jurisprudence. The Reglamento de la LGVS (RLGVS Art. 2) expressly excludes invasive species from the legal definition of 'mascota,' so the simple free pet authorization (trámite SEMARNAT-08-056) is foreclosed; the remaining lawful pathway to keep or breed one is to register the premises as a wildlife-management facility (PIMVS, Art. 78 Bis, trámite SEMARNAT-08-045) under a SEMARNAT-approved Plan de Manejo. Any transfer (sale or gift) requires documented legal provenance (Art. 51) and a recipient who also holds legal facilities; internal transport requires the provenance documents to travel with the animal. Cross-border IMPORT is categorically prohibited — LGVS Art. 27 Bis 1 bars importing any listed invasive species, and SEMARNAT cannot issue an import permit even if SENASICA's zoosanitary requirements are met. In practice R. norvegicus is sold openly despite identical listing (de-facto tolerance from its commercial ubiquity), an asymmetry R. rattus does not enjoy. Not CITES-listed.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

R. rattus is on the 2016 invasive-species Acuerdo (DOF 07/12/2016), so it is 'vida silvestre exótica invasora' regardless of domestication, and the simple pet authorization is foreclosed: RLGVS Art. 2 expressly excludes invasive species from the legal definition of 'mascota,' barring trámite SEMARNAT-08-056 for this species. The one lawful pathway to keep one is to register the premises as a wildlife-management facility (PIMVS) under LGVS Art. 78 Bis (trámite SEMARNAT-08-045) with a SEMARNAT-approved Plan de Manejo and a certified Responsable Técnico — a heavy, facility-grade authorization rather than an ordinary pet permit. A pathway therefore exists (not prohibited), but it eliminates ordinary hobbyist keeping; PROFEPA enforces (LGVS Art. 122).

Sources: Cámara de Diputados / DOF, DOF / SEMARNAT (via FAOLEX), Diario Oficial de la Federación / SEMARNAT, gob.mx / SEMARNAT, gob.mx / SEMARNAT

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

Because R. rattus cannot be a 'mascota,' any captive breeding must occur inside a registered PIMVS (LGVS Art. 78 Bis) operating under a SEMARNAT-approved Plan de Manejo that details containment, veterinary care, reproductive control, and contingency protocols. To then sell offspring, the PIMVS must also obtain an aprovechamiento (harvest/utilization) authorization (trámites SEMARNAT-08-032 / 08-034) setting a legal quota. There is no hobbyist or small-breeder exemption — one litter triggers the same PIMVS + Plan de Manejo obligation as a commercial farm — but the pathway exists, so breeding is legal with permit (the DR labels it 'Legal with a permit/license'). Breeding without a registered PIMVS is an LGVS violation (confiscation, closure, Art. 122 fines).

Sources: Cámara de Diputados / DOF, DOF / SEMARNAT (via FAOLEX), gob.mx / SEMARNAT, gob.mx / SEMARNAT

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

Any transfer of a listed exotic — sale or gift alike — is governed by the doctrine of legal provenance (Legal Procedencia, LGVS Art. 51): the transferor (who must operate a registered PIMVS) must hand the recipient documentation (factura/nota de remisión) citing the SEMARNAT aprovechamiento authorization number, and the recipient must themselves hold legal facilities (their own PIMVS) to lawfully receive an invasive exotic. This creates a closed chain of custody that confines lawful transfer to a network of registered facilities; transfer without provenance is treated as illicit-origin contraband and is heavily sanctioned by PROFEPA (Art. 122). A papered pathway exists, but the constraint runs through the entire chain → restricted. (In practice R. norvegicus changes hands openly without SEMARNAT docs — de-facto tolerance — but R. rattus draws scrutiny.)

Sources: Cámara de Diputados / DOF, DOF / SEMARNAT (via FAOLEX), PROFEPA

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

Internal movement of a lawfully-held R. rattus is restricted but lawful: there is no separate domestic-transport permit, but the original legal-provenance documentation (the PIMVS invoice/authorization letter) must accompany the animal at all times to survive a PROFEPA/highway inspection, and release into the wild is prohibited (LGVS Art. 27 Bis). Cross-border IMPORT, by contrast, is categorically PROHIBITED: LGVS Art. 27 Bis 1 forbids authorizing the import of any listed invasive species, so SEMARNAT/DGVS is statutorily stripped of authority to issue an import permit (trámite SEMARNAT-08-009) for R. rattus — even a captive-bred animal meeting every SENASICA zoosanitary requirement (health certificate, parasite treatment) cannot lawfully cross, because the environmental clearance cannot be granted. Not CITES-listed. Overall status restricted because a lawful internal-transport pathway exists; the import leg specifically has no lawful pathway (see notes).

Sources: Cámara de Diputados / DOF, SENASICA, gob.mx / SEMARNAT

Restrictions & responsibilities

Because R. rattus is invasive-listed, it cannot be kept under the ordinary pet authorization (RLGVS Art. 2 excludes invasive species from 'mascota'). The lawful pathway to keep or breed one is to register the premises as a PIMVS (Predio o Instalación que Maneja Vida Silvestre) under LGVS Art. 78 Bis, with a SEMARNAT-approved Plan de Manejo (containment engineering, veterinary/epidemiological protocols, reproductive control, contingency and final-disposition plans) and a certified Responsable Técnico. There is no hobbyist/small-breeder exemption — a single litter triggers the same obligation as a commercial facility. Never release (LGVS Art. 27 Bis).
  • File trámite SEMARNAT-08-045 (Conservación de vida silvestre fuera de su hábitat natural — PIMVS registration), form FF-SEMARNAT-020
  • Submit a technical Plan de Manejo prepared by a certified Responsable Técnico (containment, veterinary, reproductive, contingency, final-disposition)
  • To sell offspring, additionally obtain an aprovechamiento authorization (trámite SEMARNAT-08-032 / 08-034) setting a legal quota
  • Keep legal-provenance documentation for every specimen on site for PROFEPA inspection

Forms: SEMARNAT-08-045 — Conservación de la vida silvestre fuera de su hábitat natural (PIMVS; form FF-SEMARNAT-020), SEMARNAT-08-056 — Autorización de ejemplares exóticos como mascota (NOTE: foreclosed for invasive-listed species per RLGVS Art. 2) · Where: SEMARNAT — Dirección General de Vida Silvestre (DGVS), Espacio de Contacto Ciudadano, Av. Ejército Nacional 223, Col. Anáhuac, Miguel Hidalgo, C.P. 11320, Ciudad de México (or regional federal delegations) · Fees: PIMVS registration ~$686 MXN (indicative; varies per the annual Ley Federal de Derechos). SEMARNAT-08-056 would be free but is unavailable for this species.

Source: Cámara de Diputados / DOF, DOF / SEMARNAT (via FAOLEX), gob.mx / SEMARNAT, gob.mx / SEMARNAT

Transfer of a roof rat (sale or gift) requires documented legal provenance (LGVS Art. 51): a factura/nota de remisión citing the PIMVS aprovechamiento authorization number, plus a recipient who holds their own legal facilities. Internal transport requires that same provenance documentation to accompany the animal at all times; there is no separate domestic-transport permit. Moving or transferring without provenance is treated as illicit-origin trafficking (PROFEPA seizure + Art. 122 fines). Release is absolutely prohibited.
  • Obtain/keep the legal-provenance document (factura or PIMVS authorization letter citing the SEMARNAT authorization number)
  • Carry the provenance documentation with the animal during any internal transport
  • Transfer only to a recipient who holds their own PIMVS / legal facilities
  • Never release into the wild (LGVS Art. 27 Bis)

Where: SEMARNAT — Dirección General de Vida Silvestre (DGVS); enforcement by PROFEPA

Source: Cámara de Diputados / DOF, PROFEPA

IMPORT IS PROHIBITED. LGVS Art. 27 Bis 1 bars authorizing the importation of any species listed as invasive exotic; because R. rattus is on the 2016 list, SEMARNAT/DGVS cannot issue an import permit (trámite SEMARNAT-08-009) for it. Meeting SENASICA's zoosanitary requirements (health certificate, parasite treatment) does NOT cure this — the agricultural clearance and the environmental clearance are separate, and the missing environmental permit makes import legally impossible. An animal presented at the border will be rejected or confiscated. (R. rattus is not CITES-listed; domestic law applies the stricter absolute ban.)

Source: Cámara de Diputados / DOF, SENASICA, gob.mx / SEMARNAT

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Mexico

In Mexico, keeping a pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) is not handled under ordinary pet law at all — it is swept into federal wildlife law because the roof rat sits on Mexico's official invasive-species list (Acuerdo, DOF 7 December 2016), alongside the common fancy rat. Under the General Wildlife Law (LGVS) a listed species is 'vida silvestre exótica invasora' no matter how tame or how many generations it has been bred in captivity; Mexican law does not recognize a 'domesticated' roof rat as anything but wildlife. The trap is in the Reglamento (RLGVS, Article 2): it defines a 'pet' (mascota) but expressly EXCLUDES invasive exotic species from that definition. So the simple, free pet authorization that normally lets a citizen keep an exotic companion animal (trámite SEMARNAT-08-056) is legally unavailable for a roof rat. The only lawful way left to keep or breed one is to register your home as a formal wildlife-management facility — a PIMVS under Article 78 Bis (trámite SEMARNAT-08-045) — complete with a technical Management Plan (Plan de Manejo), containment engineering, and a certified technical expert: a regime designed for zoos, laboratories and commercial breeders, not pet owners. The contradiction is glaring next to the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus), which is on the very same 2016 invasive list yet is sold openly in chain pet stores and online with no SEMARNAT paperwork, purely because it has a long commercial history. The roof rat — equally domesticated, kept exactly the same way, captive-bred, tame, indoors, and never released — gets the full weight of the wildlife code. This is a species-not-domestication trap, not a finding that domesticated roof rats are dangerous.

The ask: Ask SEMARNAT's Dirección General de Vida Silvestre (DGVS) — with CONABIO's invasive-species program informing the science — to create a clear, written regulatory pathway for closed, captive-bred populations of Rattus rattus that does NOT require a full PIMVS. Concretely: amend or interpret RLGVS Article 2 so that domesticated, closed-colony (non-release) strains are not swept into the invasive 'mascota' exclusion, OR publish a declaratory criterion that such animals may obtain a SEMARNAT-08-056-type authorization with simple closed-colony conditions — treating R. rattus the same as the already-tolerated R. norvegicus. The point is proportionality: the listing exists to prevent release into the wild, and a fully captive-bred, indoor, closed colony poses zero release risk, so an authorization pathway (not a de-facto facility-only barrier) is the science-consistent reading. Where a true facility figure is genuinely needed for larger breeders, ask DGVS to confirm the lightest applicable trámite and whether a Plan de Manejo and Responsable Técnico can be scaled down for a small closed colony.

Where the lever really is: PRIMARY LEVER = THE FEDERAL AGENCY (SEMARNAT/DGVS), with CONABIO/CONANP input on the species listing — NOT the legislature, and NOT a state matter (wildlife regulation in Mexico is federal and centralized). The barrier is regulatory, and the agency owns it: the 'mascota' exclusion lives in RLGVS Article 2 (a SEMARNAT-issued regulation), the invasive listing is a SEMARNAT Acuerdo (DOF 07/12/2016) built on CONABIO risk assessments, and the PIMVS / Plan de Manejo machinery (Arts. 78 Bis, 51) is administered by DGVS. So the right move is to ask DGVS for a regulatory clarification or amendment carving out closed captive-bred strains, and to engage CONABIO on whether domesticated closed lines warrant the same risk treatment as feral populations. SECONDARY / WATCH = THE LEGISLATURE: there is a real legislative dimension but it does not change the conclusion. A 'listado positivo' / tighten-the-mascota-definition reform of the LGVS has circulated in the Cámara de Diputados (e.g., the 2024 iniciativa on a positive list of permitted species); such a bill could either entrench the invasive-species exclusion (bad) or be amended to preserve an authorization pathway for domesticated closed strains (good), so it is worth watching and a forward-looking touchpoint. But there is no live federal public-comment / rulemaking window open for this specific question right now, and the operative fix is an agency action, so DGVS (federal) is the main door. There is NO state-level lever to pursue.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • SEMARNAT — Dirección General de Vida Silvestre (DGVS), Espacio de Contacto Ciudadano (executive / agency) — contacto.ciudadano@semarnat.gob.mx
    The federal wildlife authority that interprets the LGVS/RLGVS, administers the pet authorization (SEMARNAT-08-056), the PIMVS registration (SEMARNAT-08-045), and the import permit (SEMARNAT-08-009), and that approves Management Plans. This is the office with the actual power to fix the RLGVS Art. 2 'mascota' exclusion or to publish a closed-colony criterion for R. rattus. Email verified as the official DGVS citizen-contact inbox; the linked page is the official SEMARNAT trámite sheet. Write in Spanish.
  • PROFEPA (Procuraduría Federal de Protección al Ambiente) (executive / agency) — denuncias@profepa.gob.mx
    The federal enforcement arm that inspects facilities, verifies legal provenance, confiscates specimens, and levies LGVS sanctions (Art. 122). Useful to ask the enforcement criterion for a private keeper of a closed captive-bred colony with no commercial intent, and what provenance documentation avoids seizure — and to put on record the asymmetry with the openly-tolerated R. norvegicus. Spanish required.
  • Cámara de Diputados — Comisión de Medio Ambiente y Recursos Naturales (legislature) — official contact page
    Secondary / watch touchpoint only. Because a 'listado positivo' / tighten-mascota reform of the LGVS has circulated in Congress, this committee is the official channel to (a) ask that any amendment of the LGVS/RLGVS 'mascota' rules expressly preserve an authorization pathway for domesticated closed strains, and (b) be alerted before a tightening bill advances. Use as a forward-looking channel — the operative fix today is the federal agency, not the legislature.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request for a regulatory pathway — keeping closed, captive-bred roof rats (Rattus rattus) as domestic animals

To the Dirección General de Vida Silvestre (SEMARNAT):

I am writing about roof rats (Rattus rattus) kept by private keepers as domestic companions. I understand that because R. rattus is on the invasive-species list (DOF 7 Dec 2016), it is treated as 'vida silvestre exótica invasora,' and that Article 2 of the Reglamento de la LGVS excludes invasive species from the definition of 'mascota' — so the SEMARNAT-08-056 pet authorization appears foreclosed, leaving only PIMVS registration (Art. 78 Bis) as a lawful route to keep one.

My concern is the species classification, not domestication: these animals are captive-bred over many generations, tame, kept strictly indoors, and never released — which is the exact risk the invasive listing addresses. A fully closed, captive-bred colony poses zero release risk. Notably, the fancy rat (R. norvegicus) is on the identical list yet is kept and sold openly with no wildlife paperwork; the roof rat should be treated consistently.

I respectfully request that the DGVS create a proportionate pathway for closed, captive-bred R. rattus — by interpreting or amending RLGVS Article 2 so domesticated closed strains are not caught by the invasive 'mascota' exclusion, or by publishing a written criterion allowing a SEMARNAT-08-056-type authorization under simple closed-colony conditions — rather than requiring every private keeper to register a full PIMVS. Please also confirm, if a facility figure is genuinely required for a small closed colony, the lightest applicable trámite and whether the Plan de Manejo and Responsable Técnico requirements can be scaled to a small non-commercial colony.

Thank you for your consideration.

[Your name]
[Your city / contact]
Español
Asunto: Solicitud de una vía regulatoria — tenencia de ratas de tejado (Rattus rattus) criadas en cautiverio cerrado como animales domésticos

A la Dirección General de Vida Silvestre (SEMARNAT):

Me dirijo a ustedes respecto de la tenencia de ratas de tejado (Rattus rattus) como animales de compañía por particulares. Entiendo que, al estar R. rattus en la Lista de Especies Exóticas Invasoras (DOF 07/12/2016), se le considera 'vida silvestre exótica invasora,' y que el artículo 2 del Reglamento de la LGVS excluye a las especies invasoras de la definición de 'mascota' — por lo que el trámite SEMARNAT-08-056 parecería estar vedado, quedando solo el registro como PIMVS (Art. 78 Bis) como vía legal para tenerla.

Mi inquietud es sobre la clasificación de la especie, no sobre la domesticación: estos ejemplares son criados en cautiverio durante muchas generaciones, mansos, mantenidos estrictamente en interiores y nunca liberados — precisamente el riesgo que la lista de invasoras busca evitar. Una colonia totalmente cerrada y criada en cautiverio no representa riesgo alguno de liberación. Cabe señalar que la rata 'fancy' (R. norvegicus) figura en la lista idéntica y, no obstante, se mantiene y vende abiertamente sin documentación de vida silvestre; la rata de tejado debería recibir un trato consistente.

Respetuosamente solicito que la DGVS establezca una vía proporcional para R. rattus criada en cautiverio cerrado — interpretando o reformando el artículo 2 del RLGVS para que las cepas domésticas cerradas no queden atrapadas en la exclusión de 'mascota' de las invasoras, o publicando un criterio por escrito que permita una autorización tipo SEMARNAT-08-056 bajo condiciones sencillas de colonia cerrada — en lugar de exigir a cada particular el registro de un PIMVS completo. Asimismo, en caso de que se requiera necesariamente una figura de instalación para una pequeña colonia cerrada, agradeceré confirmar el trámite más ligero aplicable y si los requisitos de Plan de Manejo y Responsable Técnico pueden ajustarse a una colonia pequeña y sin fines comerciales.

Agradezco de antemano su atención.

[Su nombre]
[Su ciudad / contacto]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Ley General de Vida Silvestre — Arts. 27, 27 Bis, 27 Bis 1, 51, 78 Bis, 122 — Cámara de Diputados / DOF
  • Reglamento de la LGVS — Art. 2 (definición de 'mascota' excluye especies exóticas invasoras); confinamiento + Plan de Manejo — DOF / SEMARNAT (via FAOLEX)
  • Acuerdo — Lista de Especies Exóticas Invasoras para México (DOF 07/12/2016; R. rattus + R. norvegicus, 'muy alto') — Diario Oficial de la Federación / SEMARNAT
  • Trámite SEMARNAT-08-056 — Autorización de ejemplares exóticos como mascota (gratuito; ~15 días) — foreclosed for invasive-listed species per RLGVS Art. 2 — gob.mx / SEMARNAT
  • Trámite SEMARNAT-08-045 — Conservación de la vida silvestre fuera de su hábitat natural (registro PIMVS; form FF-SEMARNAT-020) — gob.mx / SEMARNAT
  • Trámite SEMARNAT-08-032 — Autorización de aprovechamiento (harvest/utilization) de vida silvestre — gob.mx / SEMARNAT
  • Trámite SEMARNAT-08-009 — Autorización de importación de vida silvestre exótica (unavailable for invasive-listed R. rattus per LGVS Art. 27 Bis 1) — gob.mx / SEMARNAT
  • SENASICA — Módulo de Consulta de Requisitos para la Importación de Mercancías Zoosanitarias (MCRZI) — SENASICA
  • PROFEPA — enforcement of LGVS (Art. 122 sanctions; legal-provenance verification) — PROFEPA
  • CONABIO — ficha Rattus rattus (invasive risk 'muy alto') — CONABIO

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Malaysia? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Malaysia

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.

Summary. Malaysia (Peninsular) is permissive for the roof rat. R. rattus is NOT in the First Schedule (Protected) or Second Schedule (Totally Protected) of the Wildlife Conservation Act 2010 (Act 716) — which governs Peninsular Malaysia and only regulates scheduled species — so it's outside the PERHILITAN wildlife-permit regime. As an introduced pest, it sits in the same position as the fancy rat (R. norvegicus), which is openly bred and sold under the Animal Welfare Act 2015 (Act 772) + a DVS commercial-premises licence for sellers, with no wildlife-law interference. So keeping a captive-bred roof rat needs no wildlife permit (only Act 772 welfare standards); hobby breeding is free while commercial breeding/selling needs a DVS animal-business licence; and import runs through the DVS/MAQIS SPS permit system (health certificate + quarantine). Not CITES-listed. ⚠️ Sabah and Sarawak (East Malaysia) have their own separate wildlife laws — this covers Peninsular Malaysia.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

Act 716 s.9 requires a PERHILITAN licence only to keep PROTECTED/totally-protected wildlife; R. rattus is on neither schedule (classified as an unprotected pest, e.g., MyBIS), so no wildlife permit is needed for private keeping. The Animal Welfare Act 2015 (Act 772) imposes general welfare duties on any kept animal but doesn't bar keeping pet rats. The fancy rat is kept on the same basis. (Medium confidence: no explicit positive ruling on R. rattus specifically.)

Sources: Malaysia (via FAOLEX), Department of Veterinary Services (DVS) Malaysia, Malaysia Biodiversity Information System (Govt)

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

Act 716 captive-breeding permits (ss.9, 68) apply only to scheduled wildlife — not R. rattus. Private non-commercial hobby breeding has no specific permit. Commercial-scale breeding is an 'animal business' under Act 772, needing a DVS commercial-premises/pet licence (~RM100; vet inspection). Malaysian fancy-rat breeders operate openly without wildlife-law challenge.

Sources: Malaysia (via FAOLEX), Department of Veterinary Services (DVS) Malaysia

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

Selling live animals (incl. rats) as a business needs a DVS commercial-premises licence under Act 772; wildlife law doesn't apply (R. rattus unscheduled). Gratuitous transfer between private individuals has no added legal requirement. No prohibition on trading R. rattus found.

Sources: Department of Veterinary Services (DVS) Malaysia, DVS Malaysia

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

IMPORT into Peninsular Malaysia needs (1) prior DVS SPS approval, (2) a MAQIS import permit (E-Permit, 30-day validity), and (3) an origin-country veterinary health certificate (rodents need a health cert, no rabies vaccine). Not CITES-listed. DVS does a case-by-case risk assessment — approval isn't guaranteed; obtain before shipment. INTERNAL peninsular movement of non-protected pet rodents has no specific permit (disease-control powers aside); movement to/from Sabah or Sarawak crosses a separate veterinary frontier (DVS movement permit may apply). Never release.

Sources: DVS Malaysia, Malaysian Quarantine & Inspection Services (MAQIS), DVS Malaysia

Restrictions & responsibilities

Keeping a captive-bred roof rat in Peninsular Malaysia needs no wildlife permit (R. rattus is unscheduled) — only Act 772 welfare standards. Commercial breeding/selling needs a DVS animal-business/pet-shop licence; importing needs DVS SPS approval + a MAQIS E-Permit + a health certificate. Sabah/Sarawak have separate wildlife laws. Never release.
  • For commercial breeding/sale: obtain a DVS animal-business (pet-shop) licence
  • For import: DVS SPS approval, then MAQIS E-Permit, + origin health certificate

Where: DVS (animal business; import SPS); MAQIS (import E-Permit) · Fees: DVS animal-business licence ~RM100

Source: Department of Veterinary Services (DVS) Malaysia, Malaysian Quarantine & Inspection Services (MAQIS)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Wildlife Conservation Act 2010 (Act 716) — s.9 + Schedules 1–2 (R. rattus not listed); Peninsular Malaysia — Malaysia (via FAOLEX)
  • Animal Welfare Act 2015 (Act 772) — welfare duties + s.35 animal-business licence — Department of Veterinary Services (DVS) Malaysia
  • MyBIS — Rattus rattus species record (unprotected pest) — Malaysia Biodiversity Information System (Govt)
  • Animals Act 1953 (Act 647) + Animals Rules 1962 — animal import/movement — DVS Malaysia
  • MAQIS — live-animal import procedures (E-Permit) — Malaysian Quarantine & Inspection Services (MAQIS)
  • DVS — Import/Export Division (SPS approval) — DVS Malaysia
  • DVS animal-business / pet-shop licence framework — DVS Malaysia

Search terms: Rattus rattus, tikus rumah, tikus bumbung, roof rat, black rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in the Netherlands? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Netherlands

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.

Summary. Since 1 July 2024 the Netherlands keeps a 'positive list' (huis- en hobbydierenlijst) of mammals that may be kept, bred, or sold without a permit. The brown rat (Rattus norvegicus) is on it, but the black rat (Rattus rattus) is NOT, so keeping, breeding, importing, or trading black rats as pets is not permitted. A clear advocacy case to add the species.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Only the ~30 mammal species on the positive list (huis- en hobbydierenlijst, in force since 1 July 2024) may be kept; the brown rat is listed but the black rat is not, so keeping it is not permitted.

Sources: NVWA (Netherlands), LICG (NL info centre)

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Species not on the positive list may not be bred by private keepers.

Sources: NVWA (Netherlands)

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Species not on the positive list may not be bought, sold, or freely traded by private individuals.

Sources: NVWA (Netherlands)

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Species not on the positive list may not be imported by private keepers.

Sources: NVWA (Netherlands)

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Netherlands. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Netherlands

Since 1 July 2024 the Netherlands has used a "positive list" for mammals — the huis- en hobbydierenlijst. You may only keep, breed, buy or sell a mammal species if it is ON that list. The list was built by scientifically assessing more than 300 species. The brown/fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus forma domestica) IS on the list, so keeping domesticated brown rats is fully legal. The black rat / roof rat (Rattus rattus) is NOT on the list, so under the current rules a captive-bred, tame pet roof rat may not legally be kept, bred, or rehomed in the Netherlands. The barrier here is not an agency misreading the law — the law genuinely does not (yet) include this species. The legal framework is the Wet dieren and the Besluit houders van dieren, administered by RVO (Rijksdienst voor Ondernemend Nederland) with enforcement by the NVWA.

The ask: Ask RVO to assess the domesticated black rat / roof rat (Rattus rattus, kept-strain) for addition to the huis- en hobbydierenlijst, using the official assessment procedure. The Dutch positive-list system has a built-in legal pathway: any interested party can submit an assessment request ("beoordeling aanvragen") for an unlisted mammal species through Mijn RVO. The fancy brown rat is already on the list, which establishes that a domesticated Rattus species can meet the welfare criteria; the request is that the closely-related, equally domesticable roof rat be evaluated on the same six-factor framework (human health, nutrition, habitat, thermoregulation, social behaviour/reproduction, and domestication). First, contact RVO's helpdesk to confirm the exact steps and what scientific documentation is needed; then, if you are prepared to pursue it, file the formal assessment request.

Where the lever really is: This is branch (b): the LAW AS WRITTEN, specifically the species' ABSENCE from a statutory positive list. The Netherlands uses a "verboden tenzij" (forbidden-unless) positive-list scheme under the Wet dieren / Besluit houders van dieren: only the ~30 mammal species placed on the huis- en hobbydierenlijst (in force since 1 July 2024) may be kept, bred or traded. Rattus rattus is simply not on that list. RVO and the NVWA are applying the rule correctly when they say the roof rat may not be kept — so a complaint, an appeal, or a request that the agency "reinterpret" the rule will NOT work, because there is nothing being misread. The lever is to CHANGE WHAT IS ON THE LIST. Crucially, the Dutch system does not require a legislative bill or a one-off public-comment window for this: the regulation contains its own standing rulemaking/petition mechanism. Any belanghebbende (interested party) may file an official "beoordeling aanvragen" with RVO (via Mijn RVO, €500 per species, decision within 6 — extendable to 9 — months), supported by scientific sources on the assessment criteria, and the Adviescollege huis- en hobbydierenlijst evaluates the species for addition. That is the correct and only effective lever here, and it is administrative rulemaking, not agency reinterpretation. The strong tailwind for the Netherlands: the fancy brown rat (Rattus norvegicus forma domestica) is ALREADY on the list, which proves a domesticated Rattus line can satisfy the criteria — making the roof-rat case an evidence-driven extension rather than a novel claim.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • RVO (Rijksdienst voor Ondernemend Nederland) — general contact form / helpdesk for the huis- en hobbydierenlijst (executive / agency) — official contact page
    RVO administers the positive list and runs the assessment process. Use the helpdesk first to confirm exactly what an assessment request must contain and how an individual files it (DigiD via Mijn RVO). This is the right first touchpoint to understand the official pathway before committing the €500 application fee. Dutch-language form; RVO aims to reply within 3 working days. Phone: 088 042 47 47 (weekdays 08:30-17:00).
  • RVO — official species-assessment request portal ("diersoort laten beoordelen" / Mijn RVO) (public comment) — official contact page
    This is the statutory rulemaking lever: the official page describing how an interested party formally requests that a mammal species (here, Rattus rattus) be assessed for addition to the huis- en hobbydierenlijst. The actual request is submitted through Mijn RVO (https://mijn.rvo.nl/huisdierenlijst, DigiD login for individuals), costs €500 per species, and gets a decision within 6 months (extendable to 9). This — not an appeal to the agency — is what can actually change the list.
  • NVWA (Nederlandse Voedsel- en Warenautoriteit) — enforcement authority, for status confirmation (executive / agency) — official contact page
    The NVWA enforces which animals may be kept and is the right place to confirm in writing the current keeping status of Rattus rattus before you act. Useful as documentation, but note: the NVWA cannot add a species to the list — that is RVO's assessment process. Dutch-language web form.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request to assess the domesticated black rat (Rattus rattus) for the huis- en hobbydierenlijst

To the RVO team responsible for the huis- en hobbydierenlijst,

I am writing about a domesticated companion animal that is currently kept successfully elsewhere but cannot be kept in the Netherlands: the tame black rat / roof rat (Rattus rattus). I understand that since 1 July 2024 only mammal species on the huis- en hobbydierenlijst may be kept, and that Rattus rattus is not on it.

I would like to request that a domesticated, captive-bred line of Rattus rattus be assessed for addition to the list. These animals are bred in captivity, are tame and handleable, are kept indoors as pets, and are never released into the wild — exactly like the fancy brown rat (Rattus norvegicus forma domestica), which is already on the list. The relevant question is therefore the suitability of the kept, domesticated strain against your six assessment criteria, not the behaviour of wild populations.

Could you please confirm the exact steps for submitting an assessment request (beoordeling aanvragen) for this species, and what scientific documentation the Adviescollege expects? I am prepared to pursue the formal application.

Thank you for your time.

[Your name]
[Your contact details]
Nederlands
Onderwerp: Verzoek tot beoordeling van de gedomesticeerde zwarte rat (Rattus rattus) voor de huis- en hobbydierenlijst

Geacht RVO-team verantwoordelijk voor de huis- en hobbydierenlijst,

Ik schrijf u over een gedomesticeerd gezelschapsdier dat elders met succes wordt gehouden, maar in Nederland niet gehouden mag worden: de tamme zwarte rat / dakrat (Rattus rattus). Ik begrijp dat sinds 1 juli 2024 alleen zoogdiersoorten op de huis- en hobbydierenlijst gehouden mogen worden, en dat Rattus rattus daar niet op staat.

Graag verzoek ik om een gedomesticeerde, in gevangenschap gefokte lijn van Rattus rattus te laten beoordelen voor opname op de lijst. Deze dieren worden in gevangenschap gefokt, zijn tam en hanteerbaar, worden binnenshuis als huisdier gehouden en worden nooit in het wild losgelaten — precies zoals de tamme bruine rat (Rattus norvegicus forma domestica), die al op de lijst staat. De relevante vraag is dus de geschiktheid van de gehouden, gedomesticeerde lijn aan de hand van uw zes beoordelingscriteria, en niet het gedrag van wilde populaties.

Kunt u mij bevestigen wat de exacte stappen zijn om een beoordeling aan te vragen voor deze soort, en welke wetenschappelijke onderbouwing het Adviescollege verwacht? Ik ben bereid de formele aanvraag in te dienen.

Met vriendelijke groet,

[Uw naam]
[Uw contactgegevens]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Welke dieren mag ik als huisdier houden? — NVWA — NVWA (Netherlands)
  • Huis- en hobbydierenlijst (positieflijst) — LICG — LICG (NL info centre)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, black rat, roof rat, ship rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Norway? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Norway

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.

Summary. Norway is one of Europe's strictest exotic-pet regimes, but the roof rat is NOT a no-pathway ban — it's restricted, with a narrow dual-agency permit route. Two regimes overlap: (1) the Exotic Animal Regulation (FOR-2017-05-11-597) bans importing/selling/keeping exotic mammals, and its exempt 'companion' list names 'Domestisert rotte (Rattus norvegicus)' — the fancy rat is fully legal — but NOT R. rattus; (2) the Alien Organisms Regulation (FOR-2015-06-19-716) requires a Miljødirektoratet import permit for species on neither its prohibited (Annex I) nor free-import (Annex II) list. R. rattus is on neither annex, so it falls into the §6 DISCRETIONARY permit zone: a permit can be granted if import/keeping is unlikely to harm biodiversity — and because R. rattus is Red-Listed RE (Regionally Extinct) in Norway, the establishment risk from indoor captive-bred stock is near zero, which actually supports a permit rather than defeating it. A keeper would need BOTH Mattilsynet (exotic-classification/keeping) and Miljødirektoratet (import permit) to clear it; no private precedent is documented, but the legislative playbook to fix it is proven (see advocacy).

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Keeping R. rattus falls between two frameworks: FOR-2017-05-11-597 §2 bars keeping exotic mammals and R. rattus isn't on the exempt list (which names R. norvegicus); FOR-2015-06-19-716's indoor-keeping exemption (§8) applies to Annex II species, which R. rattus isn't. BUT it's not categorically banned — it sits in the §6 discretionary permit zone, and a reptile-style grandfather/keep-only authorization precedent exists. No active private pathway is published, and no 'possession = criminal' enforcement record was found → restricted, not flat-prohibited. Needs a Mattilsynet determination.

Sources: Landbruks- og matdepartementet / Mattilsynet (Lovdata), Klima- og miljødepartementet / Miljødirektoratet (Lovdata), Mattilsynet

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

FOR-2017-05-11-597 §2's bar on keeping exotic mammals encompasses breeding, and no captive-bred/domesticated-lineage exemption is written for R. rattus (the species-specific Appendix exemption covers only 19 reptiles). Lawful breeding would require first resolving the keeping/permit status above.

Sources: Landbruks- og matdepartementet / Mattilsynet (Lovdata), Mattilsynet

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

FOR-2017-05-11-597 §2 prohibits 'omsette' (trade/transfer, incl. gifting) of exotic mammals; R. rattus isn't carved out. No commercial or non-commercial transfer exemption exists for this species under current Norwegian law.

Sources: Landbruks- og matdepartementet / Mattilsynet (Lovdata)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Import requires a Miljødirektoratet §6 permit (R. rattus is on neither Annex I nor II) — discretionary, grantable where adverse-biodiversity impact is unlikely (the RE status helps). By contrast, R. norvegicus needs no alien-organism permit and travels non-commercially (≤5 animals + vet health cert + 48h Mattilsynet notice). Presenting R. rattus at the border without a prior §6 permit = illegal import. Never release.

Sources: Klima- og miljødepartementet / Miljødirektoratet (Lovdata), Mattilsynet

Restrictions & responsibilities

Norway bans 'exotic mammals,' and the fancy rat (R. norvegicus) is exempt but R. rattus is not — so a roof rat needs a Miljødirektoratet §6 alien-organisms import permit AND a Mattilsynet sign-off that it isn't barred as 'exotic.' The permit is discretionary (grantable where biodiversity risk is low — the species is regionally extinct in Norway, helping the case), but no private precedent is documented. Pursue BOTH agencies before acquiring; never release.
  • Apply to Miljødirektoratet for a §6 import permit (soknadssenter portal), arguing negligible establishment risk for indoor captive-bred stock (RE status)
  • Get a written Mattilsynet determination on the exotic-classification/keeping question

Forms: Miljødirektoratet — Tillatelse etter forskrift om fremmede organismer · Where: Miljødirektoratet (import permit); Mattilsynet (keeping/exotic classification)

Source: Klima- og miljødepartementet / Miljødirektoratet (Lovdata), Landbruks- og matdepartementet / Mattilsynet (Lovdata)

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Norway. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Norway

In Norway it is illegal to import, sell/give, or keep "exotic mammals" under the Exotic Animal Regulation (FOR-2017-05-11-597). The catch is in how the rule defines "exotic": it looks at the SPECIES, not at whether your individual animal is tame and captive-bred. The common fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is treated as an ordinary companion rodent and is fine to keep. But the roof rat (Rattus rattus) — even when it is a domesticated, captive-bred, indoor-only pet — is not on any companion-species exemption, so it falls outside the legal pet list. (On top of this, importing one requires a separate discretionary permit from the Environment Agency under the Alien Organisms Regulation, FOR-2015-06-19-716 §6, because R. rattus is on neither its prohibited nor its free-import annex.) The result: a tame pet rat is treated like wild exotic wildlife purely because of its species label.

The ask: Add the domesticated, captive-bred roof rat (Rattus rattus) to Norway's recognised companion-rodent framework — the same kind of exemption the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) already enjoys — so that tame, indoor-kept roof rats can be legally kept (and, ideally, transferred and bred) by responsible owners. This is exactly the mechanism Norway already used in 2017, when a long-standing ban was lifted and a positive list of 19 reptile species was created after civil-society advocacy. We are asking the Ministry of Agriculture and Food / Mattilsynet to open the same kind of review for domesticated roof rats.

Where the lever really is: This is branch (b): the problem is the LAW AS WRITTEN — the species is simply not on the companion-rodent exemption — not an agency misreading. Mattilsynet is applying FOR-2017-05-11-597 correctly: the regulation classifies "exotic" by species (is it a traditional Norwegian family pet?), not by whether your individual animal is domesticated, so R. norvegicus is exempt and R. rattus is not. Asking Mattilsynet to simply "allow" your tame roof rat will not work, because there is no discretion in the keeping ban for a species that isn't listed — the fix requires CHANGING the exemption list itself, which sits with the Ministry of Agriculture and Food (Landbruks- og matdepartementet) that owns the regulation, with Mattilsynet as the administering agency that initiates and advises on such amendments. So the lever is a regulatory/positive-list change (a petition to add domesticated R. rattus to the companion-species exemption), pursued through Mattilsynet/the Ministry — the proven 2017 reptile-reform pathway — NOT an appeal asking the agency to reinterpret a rule it is reading correctly. (The Environment Agency's §6 import-permit portal is a real, separate touchpoint for the import side and is included as a secondary channel, but it cannot fix the keeping/transfer status — only the listing change can.)

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Mattilsynet (Norwegian Food Safety Authority) — administers the Exotic Animal Regulation (executive / agency) — postmottak@mattilsynet.no
    Primary channel. Mattilsynet administers FOR-2017-05-11-597 and is the body that initiates and advises the Ministry of Agriculture and Food on amendments to the exotic-animal/companion-species lists. Ask it (a) to confirm in writing how captive-bred indoor R. rattus is classified, and (b) for the procedure to petition adding domesticated R. rattus to the companion-rodent exemption — the same route used for the 2017 reptile positive list. Official inbox and contact page both verified; English accepted.
  • Miljødirektoratet (Norwegian Environment Agency) — alien-organisms import permits (Søknadssenter) (executive / agency) — esshjelp@miljodir.no
    Secondary / import side. Because R. rattus is on neither annex of the Alien Organisms Regulation, an import would need a discretionary §6 permit here. Worth asking whether establishment risk is assessed as negligible for strictly indoor, captive-bred stock given that the species is Red-Listed RE (Regionally Extinct) in Norway. Note: this portal handles import only — it cannot change the keeping/transfer ban, which is the listing question for Mattilsynet/the Ministry. Portal and help-desk email verified.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request to add the domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) to Norway's companion-rodent exemption

Dear Norwegian Food Safety Authority,

I am writing about the Exotic Animal Regulation (FOR-2017-05-11-597). Under this rule the common fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is treated as an ordinary companion rodent, but the domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) is not — even though it is captive-bred, tame, kept strictly indoors, and never released.

The regulation classifies a species as "exotic," but the animals I am describing are domesticated pets, no more wild than a fancy rat. Roof rats are also Red-Listed RE (Regionally Extinct) in Norway, so indoor captive-bred animals pose no establishment risk.

I respectfully ask: please clarify in writing how captive-bred, indoor-kept R. rattus is classified, and tell me the procedure to petition adding domesticated R. rattus to the recognised companion-species exemption — the same kind of reform Norway adopted for reptiles in 2017.

Thank you for your consideration.

[Your name]
[Your town/region]
[Your email]
no
Emne: Anmodning om å føre opp den domestiserte svartrotta (Rattus rattus) på unntaket for kjæledyrgnagere i Norge

Til Mattilsynet,

Jeg skriver angående forskrift om forbud mot å innføre, omsette og holde eksotiske dyr (FOR-2017-05-11-597). Etter denne forskriften regnes den vanlige tamrotta (Rattus norvegicus) som en alminnelig kjæledyrgnager, mens den domestiserte svartrotta (Rattus rattus) ikke gjør det — selv om den er oppdrettet i fangenskap, tam, holdes utelukkende innendørs og aldri settes ut.

Forskriften klassifiserer en art som «eksotisk», men dyrene jeg beskriver er domestiserte kjæledyr, ikke mer ville enn en tamrotte. Svartrotta er dessuten rødlistet som RE (regionalt utdødd) i Norge, slik at innendørs oppdrettede dyr ikke utgjør noen etableringsrisiko.

Jeg ber høflig om: kan dere skriftlig avklare hvordan oppdrettet, innendørs holdt R. rattus klassifiseres, og opplyse om fremgangsmåten for å søke om å føre opp domestisert R. rattus på unntakslista for kjæledyrarter — tilsvarende reformen Norge gjennomførte for reptiler i 2017?

Takk for at dere vurderer dette.

[Ditt navn]
[Ditt sted/fylke]
[Din e-post]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • FOR-2017-05-11-597 — Exotic Animal Regulation (§2 bans exotic mammals; exempt list names R. norvegicus, not R. rattus; Annex = 19 reptiles) — Landbruks- og matdepartementet / Mattilsynet (Lovdata)
  • FOR-2015-06-19-716 — Alien Organisms Regulation (§§6–8 discretionary import permit; Annex I/II; R. rattus on neither) — Klima- og miljødepartementet / Miljødirektoratet (Lovdata)
  • Mattilsynet — Eksotiske pattedyr, reptiler og amfibier (permitted-rodent list: R. norvegicus exempt, R. rattus not) — Mattilsynet
  • Mattilsynet — permitted companion rodents (names 'Domestisert rotte: Rattus norvegicus') — Mattilsynet
  • Mattilsynet — Travelling to Norway with caged birds, rodents and rabbits (≤5, health cert, 48h notice) — Mattilsynet
  • Artsdatabanken — Rattus rattus, Red List 2021: RE (Regionally Extinct in Norway) — Artsdatabanken
  • Norsk Herpetologisk Forening — 2017 reptile positive-list reform (the advocacy playbook) — Norsk Herpetologisk Forening

Search terms: Rattus rattus, svartrotte, black rat, ship rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in New Zealand? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › New Zealand

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. New Zealand bars the ship rat (Rattus rattus) at the border and treats it as a top conservation pest, but the keeping picture is more nuanced than a flat ban. The Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) confirmed in writing (June 2026) that pet rats CANNOT be imported into New Zealand, and that there are NO registration or permit requirements under the Animal Welfare Act 1999 for keeping, breeding, or selling rats (only the Act's general welfare duties and codes of welfare apply). R. rattus is nonetheless central to the Predator Free 2050 programme and is managed as a pest under the Biosecurity Act 1993 and regional pest-management plans; whether private possession of a ship rat specifically (as opposed to the usual pet, the fancy rat R. norvegicus) is restricted under the Biosecurity Act / an unwanted-organism declaration is the open question MPI's welfare team did not resolve. Importing one is firmly prohibited; never release any rat.

Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), Animal Welfare Team, written reply June 2026: there are NO registration or permit requirements under the Animal Welfare Act 1999 for people keeping, breeding, or selling rats (only the Act's general welfare duties and codes of welfare apply; there is no pet-rat-specific code of welfare). MPI also confirmed that pet rats CANNOT be imported into New Zealand (per MPI's 'Bringing pets to NZ other than cats and dogs' guidance). Note: this welfare-team reply did not address whether the ship rat (Rattus rattus) specifically is restricted for private possession or breeding as a pest / 'unwanted organism' under the Biosecurity Act 1993 or regional pest-management plans.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-10

MPI confirmed (June 2026) there is no Animal Welfare Act 1999 registration or permit to keep rats, so keeping is not permit-gated at the welfare layer. However, R. rattus is a declared conservation pest central to Predator Free 2050 and is managed under the Biosecurity Act 1993 and regional pest-management plans; whether private possession of a ship rat specifically is restricted (for example as an 'unwanted organism') was not addressed by MPI's welfare team. Genuinely unsettled for R. rattus pending a Biosecurity-Act clarification (the fancy rat, R. norvegicus, is the species ordinarily kept as a pet).

Sources: New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office), NZ Department of Conservation, Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI)

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-10

MPI confirmed (June 2026) there are no Animal Welfare Act registration or permit requirements for breeding rats. As with keeping, the unresolved layer is the Biosecurity Act 1993 / pest-management status of breeding R. rattus specifically — propagating a declared pest may be restricted even though the welfare framework imposes no permit. Unsettled for R. rattus pending Biosecurity confirmation.

Sources: New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office), NZ Department of Conservation

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-10

MPI confirmed (June 2026) there are no Animal Welfare Act registration or permit requirements for selling rats. The open question is again the Biosecurity Act 1993: 'spreading' or trading a declared pest / unwanted organism can be restricted regardless of the welfare framework. Unsettled for R. rattus specifically pending Biosecurity confirmation.

Sources: New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office), NZ Department of Conservation

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

MPI confirmed in writing (June 2026) that pet rats CANNOT be imported into New Zealand — its 'Bringing pets to NZ (other than cats and dogs)' guidance lists rats among animals that may not be imported. Importation is therefore prohibited under NZ's strict biosecurity controls. Internal transport of any lawfully held animal is otherwise subject to the Animal Welfare (Transport within New Zealand) code of welfare. Never release.

Sources: Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), NZ Department of Conservation

Restrictions & responsibilities

Pet rats cannot be imported into New Zealand (MPI, June 2026) — there is no import pathway for a roof rat from any country. Internal transport of a lawfully held animal must meet the Animal Welfare (Transport within New Zealand) Code of Welfare. Never release any rat into the environment; R. rattus is a primary Predator Free 2050 eradication target.
  • Do not attempt to import a roof rat into New Zealand — it is not permitted
  • For any internal transport, meet the Animal Welfare (Transport within New Zealand) Code of Welfare

Where: Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) — Biosecurity / Animal Imports

Source: Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI)

Keepers of any animal owe the Animal Welfare Act 1999 duties (meet the animal's physical, health, and behavioural needs; provide treatment for sickness or injury); breaching a minimum standard in a code of welfare can support a prosecution. There is no code of welfare specific to pet rats, but the general duties apply. Never release a rat — release/spread of a pest is a serious biosecurity matter.

Source: New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office)

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Official sources

  • Animal Welfare Act 1999 — owner/keeper duties; codes of welfare (no registration/permit to keep/breed/sell rats — MPI, June 2026) — New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office)
  • Bringing pets to NZ (other than cats and dogs) — pet rats cannot be imported into New Zealand — Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI)
  • Rats — Department of Conservation (pests & threats; R. rattus a primary Predator Free 2050 target) — NZ Department of Conservation

Search terms: Rattus rattus, black rat, roof rat, ship rat, kiore (Pacific rat, distinct species).

Last reviewed 2026-06-10. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.
