item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Philippines? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Philippines

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. The Philippines is now DR-verified, and the picture is a permitted-but-burdensome 'wildlife' classification. Because feral Rattus rattus is everywhere, captive-bred pet roof rats fail the Wildlife Act's domestication test ('no genetically similar form in the wild') and default to 'exotic faunal species' under the DENR — unlike the fancy rat (R. norvegicus), which is exempt and managed as a domestic animal by the DA Bureau of Animal Industry. So keeping legally requires a DENR Certificate of Wildlife Registration (CWR), breeding requires a Wildlife Farm Permit (WFP), and selling/giving requires WFP-registered progeny plus paperwork (no hobbyist exemption). Transport/import layers DA-BAI and DENR permits on top. In practice, enforcement against hobbyists is negligible and a 'vermin' sanitation overlay (PD 856) adds ambiguity — but on the letter of the law, the permits are required.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-09

The Philippines treats Rattus rattus as an 'exotic faunal species' under the Wildlife Act (RA 9147): it fails the domestication test in the Joint IRR (Rule 1.1(nn)) — a domesticated species must have 'no genetically similar form in the wild', and feral R. rattus is ubiquitous — so captive-bred pet roof rats are not exempt (unlike fancy R. norvegicus). Keeping legally requires a DENR Certificate of Wildlife Registration (CWR) with proof of legal acquisition. In practice enforcement against hobbyists is negligible and a 'vermin' overlay (Sanitation Code, PD 856) muddies it, but the letter of the law requires the permit.

Sources: Republic of the Philippines (LawPhil), DENR-BMB, Republic of the Philippines (Supreme Court E-Library)

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

Breeding R. rattus for sale/trade requires a Wildlife Farm Permit (WFP) from DENR (DAO 2004-55/62): a management/breeding plan, a biosecurity facility, LGU clearance and scaled fees. No hobbyist breeding exemption exists for exotic wildlife.

Sources: Republic of the Philippines (LawPhil), DENR, DENR-BMB

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-09

Only WFP-registered progenies may be commercially traded (RA 9147 s.27). There is NO small-breeder/hobbyist exemption — even a free transfer technically requires a notarized deed of donation and a new CWR for the recipient, or the animal becomes 'illegal wildlife'. Enforcement against small hobbyist trades is historically negligible, but it is strictly illegal without the permit.

Sources: Republic of the Philippines (LawPhil), DENR

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

Importing requires a DA-BAI SPSIC + DENR clearance; internal transport requires a DA-BAI Local Shipping Permit + Veterinary Health Certificate + a DENR Local Transport Permit. Never release a roof rat.

Sources: Bureau of Animal Industry (DA), BAI-NVQSD, Republic of the Philippines (LawPhil)

Restrictions & responsibilities

On a plain reading of RA 9147, a captive roof rat is an 'exotic species' needing DENR-BMB registration (a CWR to keep/hobby-breed; a Wildlife Farm Permit to sell commercially). In practice rats are also 'vermin' (PD 856) and pet rats are sold openly with no recorded enforcement — a grey zone. Get a DENR-BMB determination before relying on either reading. Import: BAI SPSIC + DENR exotic-species clearance. Never release.
  • Ask DENR-BMB whether commensal R. rattus needs a CWR or is exempt as 'vermin'
  • For commercial breeding/sale: apply for a Wildlife Farm Permit (WFP)
  • For import: BAI SPSIC + DENR exotic-species clearance

Where: DENR-BMB (CWR/WFP); BAI (import/transport)

Source: DENR-BMB, DENR

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Philippines
⏳ Time-sensitive: House Bill 7232, the "Revised Wildlife Resources Conservation and Protection Act," was filed 21 January 2026 in the 20th Congress and is moving through the House; it expressly covers exotic species bred or cultured in captivity. While this rewrite of the Wildlife Act is pending in committee, there is a live window to ask that captive-bred, domesticated companion rodents be recognized as domestic animals (or given a light registration tier) rather than full exotic wildlife. Confirm the bill's current committee stage on congress.gov.ph before writing, since status can change.

In the Philippines, the pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) is treated as "exotic wildlife," not as a companion animal — even when it is captive-bred, tame, and kept indoors. This happens because of how the law defines a "domesticated" species. Under the rules that carry out the Wildlife Resources Conservation and Protection Act (RA 9147), an animal only counts as "domesticated" if it has "no genetically similar form in the wild." Since feral black/roof rats live everywhere in the country, the domesticated pet line gets caught by that test and defaults to DENR's exotic-wildlife system. The practical result: to legally keep one you need a DENR Certificate of Wildlife Registration (CWR); to breed or pass animals to others you need a Wildlife Farm Permit (WFP) and registered progeny — there is no hobbyist exemption. Meanwhile the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus), which is just as non-native, is exempt and is handled as an ordinary pet by the Bureau of Animal Industry. So two domesticated pet rodents, kept the same way, are regulated completely differently — purely because of an ancestry-based wording, not because of anything about the animals or how they are kept. (In practice there is also a "vermin" overlay under the Sanitation Code, PD 856, and enforcement against hobbyists is essentially nil — but on the letter of the law the permits are required.)

The ask: Treat the multi-generation, captive-bred, domesticated pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) the same way the law already treats the domesticated fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus): as a domestic companion animal managed by the Bureau of Animal Industry — or, short of that, create a clear, lightweight registration tier for captive-bred companion R. rattus that does not require a full Wildlife Farm Permit to keep one or to give offspring to another keeper. The fix should turn on whether the animal is actually domesticated and captive-bred, not solely on whether a wild population exists somewhere. Captive-bred pet roof rats are tame, raised indoors, never taken from the wild, and never released.

Where the lever really is: Hybrid, but the controlling lever is the LAW / the implementing rule — NOT a simple agency clarification. The "domesticated species = no genetically similar form in the wild" test sits in the Joint Implementing Rules and Regulations (Rule 1.1(nn)) under RA 9147. DENR-BMB is applying that test CORRECTLY when it classifies feral-ubiquitous R. rattus as exotic wildlife — so writing to BMB to "just exempt" the species, by itself, will not (and legally cannot) overturn a definition the agency is faithfully following. The durable fix is to change the definition or carve out captive-bred companion rodents, which happens in one of two places: (1) the STATUTE — and there is a live, time-sensitive vehicle, House Bill 7232, the "Revised Wildlife Resources Conservation and Protection Act" (filed 21 Jan 2026, 20th Congress), which expressly governs exotic species bred or cultured in captivity; this is the moment to ask that captive-bred domesticated rodents be recognized as companion animals; or (2) the IRR / a formal DENR species-determination or rulemaking — which BMB CAN do administratively (a positive determination plus a light CWR tier), so a clarification/declaratory request to BMB is still worthwhile as a parallel track. Bottom line: lead with the legislature on HB 7232 (the change that actually amends the rule), and use BMB only for the administrative carve-out it genuinely has power to grant — do not expect BMB to waive a definition it is correctly applying.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • House of Representatives of the Philippines — Find/Contact Your Representative (House Members directory) (legislature) — official contact page
    Primary lever. The definition that catches domesticated R. rattus lives in the law/IRR, so durable change runs through Congress. Use this official directory to find your district representative (and the Committee on Natural Resources) and ask, while House Bill 7232 — the Revised Wildlife Act — is pending, that captive-bred domesticated companion rodents be recognized as domestic animals or given a light registration tier.
  • DENR — Biodiversity Management Bureau (BMB), Wildlife Resources Division (official contact page) (executive / agency) — wrd@bmb.gov.ph
    Parallel administrative track. BMB cannot waive the statutory domestication test, but it CAN issue a formal species-determination/clarification and has rulemaking authority over the CWR/WFP regime. Ask it to (a) confirm the classification in writing and (b) consider a positive determination or a light hobbyist CWR tier for captive-bred companion R. rattus. wrd@bmb.gov.ph (Wildlife Resources Division) and bmb@bmb.gov.ph (general inbox) are the verified official addresses; the contact form is the safest channel.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Recognize captive-bred pet roof rats (Rattus rattus) as domestic companion animals

Dear [Office of Representative / DENR-BMB Wildlife Resources Division],

I am writing as a Filipino keeper of domesticated pet rats to ask for fairer treatment of the captive-bred pet roof rat (Rattus rattus).

Under the rules implementing RA 9147, an animal is only "domesticated" if it has no genetically similar form in the wild. Because feral roof rats live everywhere, our tame, captive-bred pet line is pushed into the exotic-wildlife system (a Certificate of Wildlife Registration to keep, a Wildlife Farm Permit to breed or rehome), while the equally non-native fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is treated as an ordinary companion animal under the Bureau of Animal Industry.

This is a difference in wording, not in the animals. Our roof rats are captive-bred over many generations, tame, raised indoors, never taken from the wild, and never released.

I respectfully ask that captive-bred, domesticated R. rattus be recognized as a domestic companion animal like the fancy rat — or, short of that, that a clear, lightweight registration tier be created for keeping one and for passing offspring to another keeper, without a full Wildlife Farm Permit. The test should be whether the animal is genuinely domesticated and captive-bred.

[For the legislator:] I would be grateful if you would raise this as House Bill 7232 (Revised Wildlife Resources Conservation and Protection Act) is considered.
[For DENR-BMB:] I would also welcome a written determination of how this species is currently classified.

Thank you for your consideration.

Respectfully,
[Your name]
[Your city/province]
[Your email / contact]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • RA 9147 — Wildlife Resources Conservation and Protection Act (2001): Secs. 5 (exotic species), 6 (possession), 27 (illegal acts) — Republic of the Philippines (LawPhil)
  • DENR DAO 2004-62 — registration of threatened/non-threatened/exotic faunal species (CWR; fees) — DENR-BMB
  • DENR DAO 2004-55 — RA 9147 implementing guidelines (Wildlife Farm Permit; sale rules) — DENR
  • PD 856 — Code on Sanitation, Ch. XVI Vermin Control (rats classified vermin) — Republic of the Philippines (Supreme Court E-Library)
  • BAI — Pet Import (Sanitary & Phytosanitary Import Clearance; rodent viral screening) — Bureau of Animal Industry (DA)
  • BAI — One-Time Local Shipping Permit for live animals (internal transport) + AO 19 — BAI-NVQSD

Search terms: Rattus rattus, daga, black rat, roof rat, ship rat.

Last reviewed 2026-06-09. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Poland? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Poland

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.

Summary. Poland is permissive for the roof rat. Rattus rattus is NOT on the EU invasive-species Union list (Reg. 1143/2014) and NOT on Poland's national IAS list (Council of Ministers Regulation of 9 Dec 2022, Dz.U. 2022 poz. 2649), so the blanket keep/breed/sell/transport prohibitions of the 2021 Alien Species Act (Ustawa o gatunkach obcych) do not apply. It's also not on the CITES appendices (so no registry duty) and not on Poland's dangerous-animals list (so no RDOŚ permit). That leaves only the general Animal Welfare Act's standard care duties. So a hobbyist may keep, breed, give away and transport captive-bred roof rats. One caveat: ecologists do classify R. rattus as an alien synanthropic species present in Polish seaports/the Odra corridor, and the IAS framework is designed to add species when evidence supports it — so a future national-list addition can't be excluded. We've queued a GDOŚ confirmation inquiry.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

R. rattus is on neither the EU Union list nor Poland's national IAS list (Dz.U. 2022 poz. 2649), so the Art. 7 keeping prohibition of the 2021 Alien Species Act doesn't apply. Not on CITES (so no Art. 64 registry duty) and not on the dangerous-animals list (Dz.U. 2011 nr 173 poz. 1037, so no RDOŚ permit). Only the Animal Welfare Act's general care duties apply.

Sources: ISAP / Sejm RP, ISAP / Sejm RP, ISAP / Sejm RP

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

No permit/registration exists for breeding captive R. rattus: the Animal Welfare Act licenses only dog/cat breeding, and the Alien Species Act's prohibitions apply only to listed IAS (R. rattus isn't listed). Hobby rat breeders operate without state registration (voluntary club affiliation only). Confidence not maximal because R. rattus's ecological 'alien' status leaves a future listing possible.

Sources: ISAP / Sejm RP, ISAP / Sejm RP

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Sale/gift of captive-bred R. rattus is unprohibited: the Alien Species Act bans 'introduction to trade' only for listed IAS (R. rattus not listed), and no CITES restriction applies. General consumer/animal-welfare standards apply to sales. No authoritative Polish ruling specifically on R. rattus sale was found → medium confidence.

Sources: ISAP / Sejm RP

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Internal transport is unrestricted. Intra-EU non-commercial movement of pet rodents (EU Reg. 576/2013) needs no certificate/passport if owner-accompanied. Commercial cross-border movement of rodents needs an intra-EU health certificate (Comm. Impl. Reg. 2021/403). No IAS bar applies (R. rattus unlisted). Never release.

Sources: EU / EUR-Lex, ISAP / Sejm RP

Restrictions & responsibilities

Keeping a captive-bred roof rat is legal in Poland (not on the EU or national invasive list), subject to standard Animal Welfare Act care. ⚠️ Watch GDOŚ: R. rattus could be added to the national IAS list in a future revision, which would flip its status. Never release a roof rat.

Source: ISAP / Sejm RP

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Poland

Good news first: in Poland, keeping, breeding, giving away and transporting captive-bred roof rats (Rattus rattus, "szczur śniady") is currently legal. The roof rat is NOT on the EU Union list of invasive alien species (Reg. 1143/2014), NOT on Poland's national invasive-species list (Council of Ministers Regulation of 9 Dec 2022, Dz.U. 2022 poz. 2649), NOT on CITES, and NOT on the dangerous-animals list. That means the keep/breed/sell/transport bans of the 2021 Alien Species Act (Ustawa o gatunkach obcych) do not apply, and only the general Animal Welfare Act care duties do. The catch: this is a watch-item, not a settled freedom. Polish ecologists (IOP Kraków) record R. rattus as an alien synanthropic species present in Polish seaports and the Odra corridor, and it sits on the IUCN "100 worst invasives" list. The national invasive-species framework is built to ADD species as evidence accumulates, through GDOŚ-run analyses and consultations. If R. rattus were ever added to the national list, keeping and breeding would flip overnight to prohibited-without-permit — sweeping up tame, captive-bred pets alongside any feral concern. The job now is to make sure that, if listing is ever proposed, the distinction between domesticated captive stock and wild/feral populations is on the record before a rule is written.

The ask: Ask GDOŚ to (1) confirm in writing that Rattus rattus is not currently on, and is not actively proposed for, Poland's national invasive-alien-species list, and what the status of any such process is; (2) confirm that a private person running a closed, non-commercial hobby colony of captive-bred roof rats has no registration or permit duty under the Alien Species Act, and that giving away or selling captive-bred animals to private individuals needs no permit; and (3) note for the record — for any future listing assessment — that responsible keepers want domesticated, captive-bred indoor stock treated as a distinct category from feral/wild populations, with a captive-keeping exemption or grandfathering for existing tame animals rather than a blanket ban. Then monitor GDOŚ consultations so you can comment IF and WHEN a listing is ever proposed.

Where the lever really is: This is branch (b)-adjacent but with a critical twist: there is NO current law restricting roof rats, so there is nothing an agency is misreading and nothing yet to repeal. The lever is NOT a clarification fight and NOT a present rulemaking comment — it is WATCH-AND-PREPARE. The binding instrument is a Council of Ministers regulation (a list) issued under the Alien Species Act; a species lands on it only after GDOŚ commissions a scientific risk analysis and runs public consultations. So if the status ever changes, the real decision is legislative/executive (the regulation + the Sejm-passed Act behind it), and appealing to GDOŚ to "exempt my pets" once a species is correctly listed would not work — a listing decision rides on ecological risk, not on individual keeping. The productive moves NOW are: (1) get GDOŚ's written confirmation of the current non-listed status and the absence of any permit duty (a declaratory/informational request the agency CAN answer, because it administers the list), and (2) put the captive-bred-vs-feral distinction on record and subscribe to GDOŚ's IAS consultation channel so that IF a national-listing proposal ever opens a comment window, keepers can argue for a captive-keeping carve-out at the rulemaking stage — the only stage where it can actually be built in. In short: lever = the AGENCY for confirmation today, and the FUTURE PUBLIC-COMMENT/rulemaking window for any listing proposal; there is no live bill to fight right now.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Generalna Dyrekcja Ochrony Środowiska (GDOŚ) — General Directorate for Environmental Protection (executive / agency) — kancelaria@gdos.gov.pl
    Administers Poland's invasive-alien-species framework (the national list under the Alien Species Act) and runs the species risk-analysis and public consultations. The right body to (a) confirm in writing that Rattus rattus is not listed and not actively proposed, and (b) confirm there is no permit/registration duty for a closed captive hobby colony. Official inbox verified live on the GDOŚ gov.pl contact page: kancelaria@gdos.gov.pl.
  • GDOŚ — Invasive Alien Species (IGO) consultations / project pages (public comment) — official contact page
    GDOŚ publishes its analyzed-species lists and any open public consultations on invasive species here. This is the channel to monitor so that IF a national listing of Rattus rattus is ever proposed, keepers can submit comments during the official window arguing for a captive-bred/domesticated carve-out. No roof-rat consultation is open now — this is for ongoing watch.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To: General Directorate for Environmental Protection (GDOŚ)
Subject: Status of Rattus rattus (szczur śniady) under the invasive alien species framework and keeping of captive-bred animals

Dear Sir or Madam,

I keep tame, captive-bred roof rats (Rattus rattus) as pets. They are bred in human care, kept indoors their whole lives, and are never released into the wild.

I understand that Rattus rattus is not on the EU Union list, nor on Poland's national list of invasive alien species (Dz.U. 2022 poz. 2649), and that the keeping/breeding prohibitions of the Act on Alien Species (Dz.U. 2021 poz. 1718) therefore do not apply. I would be grateful for written confirmation of three points:
1) Is Rattus rattus currently on, or actively proposed for, Poland's national invasive-species list, and what is the status of any such process?
2) Does a private person running a closed, non-commercial hobby colony of captive-bred roof rats have any registration or permit duty under the Act on Alien Species?
3) Does giving away or selling captive-bred roof rats to private individuals require any permit or registration?

Finally, should listing ever be assessed, I ask that domesticated, captive-bred indoor animals be considered a distinct category from feral populations, and that any future rule allow continued keeping of existing tame animals rather than a blanket ban.

Thank you for your time.
[Your name]
[Your contact details]
Polski
Do: Generalna Dyrekcja Ochrony Środowiska (GDOŚ)
Dotyczy: Status Rattus rattus (szczura śniadego) na gruncie przepisów o inwazyjnych gatunkach obcych oraz utrzymywanie zwierząt pochodzących z hodowli zamkniętej

Szanowni Państwo,

Utrzymuję jako zwierzęta domowe oswojone szczury śniade (Rattus rattus) pochodzące z hodowli. Zwierzęta te rodzą się i są wychowywane pod opieką człowieka, przebywają wyłącznie w pomieszczeniach zamkniętych i nigdy nie są wypuszczane do środowiska.

Z posiadanych przeze mnie informacji wynika, że Rattus rattus nie figuruje na liście unijnej ani na krajowej liście inwazyjnych gatunków obcych (Dz.U. 2022 poz. 2649), wobec czego zakazy utrzymywania i hodowli wynikające z Ustawy o gatunkach obcych (Dz.U. 2021 poz. 1718) nie mają zastosowania. Będę wdzięczny/wdzięczna za pisemne potwierdzenie trzech kwestii:
1) Czy Rattus rattus jest obecnie umieszczony na krajowej liście inwazyjnych gatunków obcych lub jest aktywnie rozważany do umieszczenia na niej, i jaki jest status tego procesu?
2) Czy osoba prywatna prowadząca zamkniętą, niekomercyjną hodowlę hobbystyczną szczurów śniadych pochodzenia hodowlanego podlega jakimkolwiek obowiązkom rejestracyjnym lub zezwoleniowym na gruncie Ustawy o gatunkach obcych?
3) Czy nieodpłatne przekazanie lub sprzedaż osobom prywatnym szczurów śniadych z hodowli zamkniętej wymaga zezwolenia lub rejestracji?

Na koniec, gdyby kiedykolwiek rozważano umieszczenie tego gatunku na liście, proszę o potraktowanie zwierząt udomowionych, pochodzących z hodowli i utrzymywanych w pomieszczeniach zamkniętych jako odrębnej kategorii względem populacji dziko żyjących, oraz o to, by ewentualne przyszłe przepisy dopuszczały dalsze utrzymywanie już posiadanych oswojonych zwierząt, a nie wprowadzały całkowitego zakazu.

Dziękuję za poświęcony czas.
[Imię i nazwisko]
[Dane kontaktowe]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Ustawa z 11 sierpnia 2021 o gatunkach obcych (Dz.U. 2021 poz. 1718) — Art. 7 (IAS prohibitions apply only to listed species) — ISAP / Sejm RP
  • Rozporządzenie RM z 9 grudnia 2022 (Dz.U. 2022 poz. 2649) — national + Union IAS lists (R. rattus NOT listed) — ISAP / Sejm RP
  • Rozporządzenie MŚ z 3 sierpnia 2011 (Dz.U. 2011 nr 173 poz. 1037) — dangerous animals list (R. rattus not listed) — ISAP / Sejm RP
  • Regulation (EU) 576/2013 — non-commercial movement of pet rodents (no certificate, owner-accompanied) — EU / EUR-Lex
  • IOP Kraków — Rattus rattus alien-species record (alien synanthropic; not regulatorily listed) — Instytut Ochrony Przyrody PAN

Search terms: Rattus rattus, szczur śniady, szczur czarny.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Portugal? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Portugal

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.

Summary. Portugal is legal-with-permit for the roof rat on the MAINLAND, and prohibited only on the ISLANDS — the earlier 'prohibited' reading was wrong. The key is an easy-to-miss detail: in Decreto-Lei 92/2019, the national invasive list (LNEI) entry 'Rattus spp.' carries an ASTERISK, meaning it is classified invasive ONLY in the Autonomous Region of Madeira, not on continental Portugal. So on the mainland the roof rat is an ordinary non-native species that ICNF (the conservation institute) licenses under Article 5 — a captive-keeping/breeding license (valid 3 years, annual stock registry, escape-proof containment) that issues a breeder's-license number against which the animals are registered. That is exactly how mainland breeders lawfully keep and breed 'all kinds of Rattus.' The genuine prohibition is on the islands: Madeira (DLR 17/2023/M) and the Azores (DLR 15/2012/A) list Rattus as invasive and bar captive keeping/breeding, with no keeper derogation found. Once licensed, mainland keepers can transfer animals with a declaração de cedência bearing the license number.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

On mainland Portugal, 'Rattus spp.' in LNEI Annex II is asterisked = invasive only in Madeira, so the Art. 16 prohibition does NOT apply on the continent. Rattus is an exotic species keepable under an ICNF Art. 5 license (detenção/criação), granted to private persons who demonstrate escape-proof containment; the license number serves as the animals' registration. (ISLANDS: prohibited — Madeira DLR 17/2023/M; Azores DLR 15/2012/A.)

Sources: Diário da República / Governo de Portugal, ICNF, ICNF, Região Autónoma da Madeira / DRE, Região Autónoma dos Açores / DRE

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Breeding (criação em cativeiro) is explicitly a licensed activity under DL 92/2019 Art. 5 — the ICNF license covers 'detenção, cultivo ou criação' of exotic species for commercial/scientific/educational purposes, valid 3 years (renewable) with an annual stock census to ICNF. A mainland breeder licensed to breed Rattus operating under an ICNF breeder-license number is the direct case. (ISLANDS: prohibited.)

Sources: Diário da República / Governo de Portugal, ICNF, ICNF

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Transfer/sale of specimens of a licensed exotic species is part of the Art. 5 framework: each transfer is accompanied by a declaração de cedência bearing the breeder's license number, which the recipient retains. Transfers to other licensed keepers, labs, or facilities are the standard case; transfer to an unlicensed private buyer who then registers appears permissible but should be confirmed with ICNF. (ISLANDS: prohibited.)

Sources: Diário da República / Governo de Portugal, ICNF

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Intra-mainland transport of licensed specimens is permitted with documentation identifying the license holder + species. ⚠️ Cross-territory movement (mainland↔islands) is separately controlled by DGAV and would likely be barred to Madeira/Azores, where Rattus is listed invasive with no derogation. Intra-EU movement of pet rodents otherwise follows Reg. 576/2013. Never release.

Sources: Diário da República / Governo de Portugal, DGAV, Região Autónoma da Madeira / DRE

Restrictions & responsibilities

On mainland Portugal, get an ICNF Art. 5 exotic-species license (detenção/criação) BEFORE keeping/breeding a roof rat: apply via ICNF's unified form, show escape-proof containment, then file an annual stock census; the license (valid 3 yrs) gives you a breeder/registration number that goes on transfer declarations. ⚠️ In MADEIRA and the AZORES, Rattus is a prohibited invasive species — do not keep/breed/import there. Never release.
  • Apply for an ICNF Art. 5 license (Divisão de Aplicação de Normativos) via the unified form, with a containment plan
  • Submit the annual stock registry to ICNF
  • Use a declaração de cedência (with the license number) for any transfer

Forms: ICNF — Licenciamento de Espécies Exóticas (formulário único) · Where: ICNF — Divisão de Aplicação de Normativos (DAN) · Fees: Set by Portaria; confirm current fee with ICNF (initially uncharged pending the implementing Portaria)

Source: ICNF, ICNF

ISLAND BAN: In the Autonomous Regions of Madeira (DLR 17/2023/M) and the Azores (DLR 15/2012/A), Rattus is listed as an invasive species and keeping/breeding/transporting it is prohibited, with no keeper derogation identified. The mainland license pathway does not extend to the islands.

Where: IFCN (Madeira); SRRN (Azores)

Source: Região Autónoma da Madeira / DRE, Região Autónoma dos Açores / DRE

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Portugal

On mainland (continental) Portugal, the domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) is NOT actually banned — but a one-character detail in the law makes it look that way, and that ambiguity is the real barrier. Portugal's invasive-species law, Decreto-Lei 92/2019, lists "Rattus spp." on the National List of Invasive Species (LNEI), but the entry carries an asterisk (*). The law's own legend states that asterisked species are "classified as invasive ONLY in the Autonomous Region of Madeira." That means the Article 16 prohibition applies to Rattus on Madeira (and, separately, the Azores have their own ban) — but NOT on the mainland, where the roof rat is simply a non-native exotic species that ICNF (the national conservation institute) can license under Article 5 (a hold/breed license, valid 3 years, with escape-proof containment and an annual stock census). The problem is that this asterisk is easy to miss and under-communicated: the conservation community itself flags it as an anomaly "to be corrected in a future revision," and front-line ICNF officers may read "Rattus spp." as a flat genus-wide ban and wrongly refuse keepers. On top of that, the Article 5 license was designed for commercial breeders and researchers, not hobbyists, so even keepers who clear the misreading face a process built for someone else. On the islands of Madeira and the Azores, the ban is real and written into regional law — that is a different, legislative problem, and a keeper there should not expect the agency to override it.

The ask: For mainland keepers: ask ICNF, in writing, to confirm the plain meaning of its own law — that because the LNEI "Rattus spp." entry is asterisked (Madeira-only), the Article 16 prohibition does NOT apply on continental Portugal, and the roof rat is therefore an exotic species licensable under Article 5. Ask for a written clarification or circular stating this, and for a clear, proportionate licensing pathway suited to a private companion-animal keeper (containment criteria for small rodents, the current form, the decision time, and the fee). These rats are captive-bred, tame, kept indoors in escape-proof enclosures, and never released. We are not asking the agency to change a law — we are asking it to apply, and communicate, the law it already has.

Where the lever really is: PRIMARY LEVER = THE AGENCY (ICNF), via written clarification + a fit-for-purpose licensing pathway. On the MAINLAND this is squarely a bureaucracy-misreading / under-application problem, not a bad-law problem. The statute is actually favorable: the LNEI "Rattus spp." entry is asterisked, and DL 92/2019's own legend defines the asterisk as "invasive ONLY in the Autonomous Region of Madeira." So the Article 16 ban does not reach the mainland, where Article 5 licensing governs exotic species. The barrier is that the asterisk is obscure (the conservation sector itself calls it an anomaly "to be corrected in a future revision"), so officers may apply a flat genus-wide ban that the law does not require — exactly the kind of error a declaratory/written clarification from ICNF fixes. Asking ICNF to issue that clarification is asking it to apply its own law correctly; it is the right and sufficient lever for mainland keepers, and no legislative change is needed. SECONDARY / DIFFERENT BRANCH — the ISLANDS: in Madeira (DLR 17/2023/M) and the Azores (DLR 15/2012/A), Rattus is listed invasive by regional statute with no keeper derogation found. That is the law as written, correctly applied, and appealing to the regional agency will NOT change it — relief there would require the regional legislature or an EU Reg. 1143/2014 derogation mechanism (e.g., for sterilized/contained companion animals). This kit's targets are aimed at the mainland (the agency branch), where the realistic win lives; island keepers are flagged that their fight is legislative, not administrative.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • ICNF — Espécies Exóticas (exotic-species licensing inbox) (executive / agency) — exoticas@icnf.pt
    The national conservation institute that grants Article 5 exotic-species licenses and administers the LNEI. This is the office that can confirm in writing that the asterisked 'Rattus spp.' entry is Madeira-only, so the mainland roof rat is licensable, not prohibited. exoticas@icnf.pt is the verified official inbox for exotic-species licensing forms and queries; the linked page is the official licensing procedure.
  • ICNF — general inquiries (geral@icnf.pt) (executive / agency) — geral@icnf.pt
    ICNF's verified general inbox and contact page (HQ: Av. Dr. Alfredo Magalhães Ramalho 1, 1495-165 Algés; tel. +351 213 507 900). Use as a backstop to route a formal written request for clarification to the responsible division (Divisão de Aplicação de Normativos) if the exotic-species inbox does not respond.
  • ICNF — Formulários de Espécies Exóticas (official application form) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Where the unified Article 5 licensing form and guidance notes are published. A mainland keeper who wants to actually apply (not just seek clarification) submits the completed form here / to exoticas@icnf.pt. Included so the kit shows the concrete next step, not only the advocacy ask.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request for written clarification — keeping Rattus rattus on mainland Portugal under DL 92/2019

To the ICNF Exotic Species team,

I am writing about keeping domesticated roof rats (Rattus rattus) as companion animals on mainland Portugal, and I would be grateful for a written clarification.

In the National List of Invasive Species (Annex II, DL 92/2019), the entry "Rattus spp." carries an asterisk, and the legend states that asterisked species are classified as invasive only in the Autonomous Region of Madeira. On that reading, the Article 16 prohibition does not apply on continental Portugal, and Rattus rattus is an exotic species that may be kept and bred under an Article 5 license.

Please confirm: (1) that on the mainland Rattus rattus is treated under Article 5 (license), not the Article 16 prohibition; and (2) the current form, the containment criteria for small rodents, the decision time, and the fee for a private keeper.

These animals are captive-bred, tame, kept permanently indoors in escape-proof enclosures, and are never released into the wild. We seek only to keep them lawfully and responsibly.

Thank you for your time.

[Your name]
[Your contact details] [Your town/district]
Português
Assunto: Pedido de esclarecimento por escrito — detenção de Rattus rattus em Portugal continental ao abrigo do DL 92/2019

À equipa de Espécies Exóticas do ICNF,

Venho expor a detenção de ratos-pretos domesticados (Rattus rattus) como animais de companhia em Portugal continental e solicitar, com agradecimento, um esclarecimento por escrito.

Na Lista Nacional de Espécies Invasoras (Anexo II do DL 92/2019), a entrada "Rattus spp." tem um asterisco, e a legenda indica que as espécies assinaladas com asterisco são classificadas como invasoras apenas na Região Autónoma da Madeira. Nessa leitura, a proibição do artigo 16.º não se aplica no continente, sendo o Rattus rattus uma espécie exótica passível de detenção e criação ao abrigo de uma licença do artigo 5.º.

Agradeço que confirmem: (1) que, no continente, o Rattus rattus é tratado ao abrigo do artigo 5.º (licença) e não da proibição do artigo 16.º; e (2) o formulário em vigor, os critérios de confinamento para pequenos roedores, o prazo de decisão e a taxa aplicável a um detentor particular.

Estes animais são criados em cativeiro, dóceis, mantidos permanentemente em interior, em alojamentos à prova de fuga, e nunca são libertados na natureza. Pretendemos apenas detê-los de forma lícita e responsável.

Grato(a) pela atenção dispensada.

[O seu nome]
[Os seus contactos] [A sua localidade/distrito]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Decreto-Lei 92/2019 — Arts. 5 (licença), 16 (proibição, p/ territórios onde listada), 21 (autorização excecional); Anexo II (LNEI; 'Rattus spp.' com asterisco = só Madeira) — Diário da República / Governo de Portugal
  • ICNF — Lista Nacional de Espécies Invasoras (LNEI) com legenda do asterisco (Madeira-only para Rattus spp.) — ICNF
  • ICNF — Licenciamento de Espécies Exóticas (procedimento Art. 5/21) — ICNF
  • ICNF — Formulários Espécies Exóticas (formulário único; normas orientadoras) — ICNF
  • Decreto Legislativo Regional 17/2023/M (Madeira) — regime de espécies exóticas invasoras (Rattus proibido) — Região Autónoma da Madeira / DRE
  • Decreto Legislativo Regional 15/2012/A (Açores) — conservação da natureza; Rattus invasor, detenção proibida — Região Autónoma dos Açores / DRE
  • DGAV — Trânsito de animais entre o Continente e as Regiões Autónomas — DGAV
  • CITES — Portugal national authorities (ICNF/DAN contacts: P. Carmo, J. Loureiro) — CITES Secretariat

Search terms: Rattus rattus, ratazana-preta, rato-preto, rato-do-telhado.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Romania? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Romania

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.

Summary. Romania has no statute that names the roof rat, and in practice it's treated like the fancy rat (R. norvegicus), which is openly kept and sold as a companion animal with no special permit. R. rattus is NOT on the OUG 57/2007 protected-species annexes (4A/4B), NOT on the EU invasive-species Union list (Reg. 1143/2014), and NOT on Romania's ~20-species national IAS list (2023) — so none of those bar it. The one genuine ambiguity is classification: Legea 205/2004 (Art. 9) requires county DSVSA authorization to keep a 'wild animal,' but companion/domestic animals need only standard welfare compliance. Authorities implicitly treat captive-bred rats as companion animals (sold freely on OLX/Hobby-Zoo under 'rozătoare'), so most likely no permit is needed; only if an authority deemed a captive R. rattus a 'wild animal' would a DSVSA authorization apply. A one-question check to ANSVSA/the Ministry of Environment settles it.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

No Romanian law defines R. rattus as protected (not in OUG 57/2007 Annex 4A/4B) or invasive (not on the EU or national IAS list), so no prohibition applies; the fancy rat is kept freely as a companion animal with no permit. The unresolved point: Legea 205/2004 Art. 9 requires DSVSA authorization to keep a 'wild animal,' and it's unconfirmed whether authorities would class a captive-bred R. rattus as 'wild' or 'companion' (police guidance on 'wild animals' targets primates/big cats/raptors/venomous reptiles, not commensal rodents). Practically treated as a pet → likely no permit.

Sources: Portal Legislativ (Romania), Portal Legislativ, Romanian Police

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-07

Hobby-scale breeding of standard domesticated rodents needs no licence; commercial breeding registers the unit with the county DSVSA (ANSVSA framework). Scientific/feeder breeding facilities need Legea 43/2014 authorization. If R. rattus were classed as a 'wild animal,' Legea 205/2004 Art. 9 authorization would apply. No blanket breeding ban; the barrier is classification ambiguity, not a prohibition.

Sources: Portal Legislativ (Romania), ANSVSA

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-07

Rodents (inc. rats) are sold openly on Romanian pet-trade platforms; commercial sale requires a DSVSA-registered pet-shop/breeder unit, while private gifting/adoption is subject only to general welfare law (Legea 205/2004). No specific prohibition on selling/giving R. rattus. Commercial wild-caught native fauna is barred, but captive-bred animals from registered operations are treated differently. Same classification dependency.

Sources: Portal Legislativ (Romania), ANSVSA

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Intra-EU non-commercial movement of pet rodents (Reg. (EU) 576/2013 Annex I Part B; national rules apply pending EU Part-B harmonisation) needs owner documentation; commercial movement needs a veterinary health certificate. R. rattus isn't on the EU IAS list, so no IAS import bar. Internal transport of a lawfully-held companion animal is unrestricted (if classed 'wild,' an ANSVSA movement doc may apply). Third-country import needs border vet inspection + health cert + TRACES. Never release.

Sources: EU / EUR-Lex, ANSVSA, EU / EUR-Lex

Restrictions & responsibilities

Romania most likely treats a captive-bred roof rat like the fancy rat — a companion animal needing no permit — but it hasn't been confirmed whether authorities might class it as a 'wild animal' (which would need a county DSVSA authorization under Legea 205/2004 Art. 9). It's on no protected or invasive list. Confirm the classification with ANSVSA/the Ministry of Environment before acquiring. Never release a roof rat.
  • Ask ANSVSA whether captive-bred R. rattus is a companion animal (no permit) or a 'wild animal' (DSVSA authorization)

Where: ANSVSA / county DSVSA; Ministry of Environment

Source: Portal Legislativ (Romania)

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Help change this

How to help in Romania

In Romania there is no law that bans keeping the roof rat (Rattus rattus, "șobolanul negru") as a pet. It is not on the protected-species annexes of OUG 57/2007, not on the EU invasive-species Union list (Reg. 1143/2014), and not on Romania's national IAS list. The fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is kept and sold freely as a companion animal with no permit. The single open question is classification: Legea 205/2004 (Art. 9) requires a county DSVSA authorization to keep a "wild animal," but companion/domestic animals only need standard welfare compliance. Captive-bred, tame roof rats are sold openly on Romanian pet platforms as "rozătoare," which strongly suggests they are treated as companion animals needing no permit — but no authority has put that classification in writing. So the problem is not a ban; it is an unwritten ambiguity that leaves keepers unsure whether a captive-bred roof rat is a "companion animal" (no permit) or a "wild animal" (DSVSA authorization).

The ask: Ask the Ministry of Environment, Waters and Forests for a short written clarification: is a captive-bred, tame Rattus rattus kept indoors as a hobby classified as a companion animal (same regime as the fancy rat, Rattus norvegicus — no special permit), or as a "wild animal" requiring a county DSVSA authorization under Legea 205/2004 Art. 9? Also confirm it is not on the OUG 57/2007 protected annexes or the national IAS list, and what (if any) documentation applies to intra-EU transport. The goal is a written answer that keepers can rely on — not a change to any law.

Where the lever really is: This is branch (a): the lever is the AGENCY, not the legislature. There is no statute or list that names or bans Rattus rattus in Romania — nothing to repeal and no positive list to be added to. The only obstacle is administrative ambiguity: it is unconfirmed whether officials would read a captive-bred roof rat as a "companion animal" (no permit) or a "wild animal" under Legea 205/2004 Art. 9 (DSVSA authorization). That is exactly the kind of question an agency can settle with a written interpretation — there is no defective law for a legislature to fix. Importantly, ANSVSA (the veterinary authority) has already replied that roof-rat legality falls OUTSIDE its competence and formally redirected the matter to the Ministry of Environment, Waters and Forests. So the correct and verified touchpoint is the Ministry of Environment, via its Law-544/2001 public-information channel and/or its petition form, requesting a written classification. A legislative or public-comment approach would be the wrong tool here: there is no bill, no list, and no rulemaking window — the species simply has not been addressed in writing, and a clarifying letter to the right ministry is the lever.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Ministry of Environment, Waters and Forests (Ministerul Mediului, Apelor și Pădurilor) — petition form (executive / agency) — official contact page
    The verified competent authority. ANSVSA stated roof-rat legality is outside its competence and redirected the question here. The official petition form is the cleanest written channel for a citizen to request a classification clarification and receive a logged reply.
  • Ministry of Environment, Waters and Forests — Law 544/2001 public-information request (executive / agency) — solicitari544@mmediu.ro
    The Ministry's official public-information (Law 544/2001) inbox, the exact address ANSVSA provided when redirecting. Use this to request a written statement on whether captive-bred R. rattus is a companion animal or a 'wild animal' under Legea 205/2004 Art. 9, and whether it appears on any protected or invasive list.
  • Ministry of Environment, Waters and Forests — petitions inbox (executive / agency) — petitii@mmediu.ro
    The Ministry's official petitions email (verified on the ministry's own contact page) — an alternate written channel if the public-information route does not produce a substantive classification answer.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request for written classification — keeping captive-bred roof rats (Rattus rattus) as pets

Dear Ministry of Environment, Waters and Forests,

I am writing to request a written clarification about the legal status of keeping the roof rat (Rattus rattus, șobolanul negru) as a companion animal in Romania. ANSVSA has indicated this question falls within your competence.

The animals in question are captive-bred, tame, kept indoors for their whole lives, and never released into the wild — exactly like the commonly kept fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus). As far as I can determine, R. rattus is not listed on the protected-species annexes of OUG 57/2007, nor on the EU invasive-species Union list, nor on Romania's national IAS list.

My questions are: (1) Is a captive-bred, tame Rattus rattus kept as a hobby treated as a companion animal under the same regime as the fancy rat (no special permit), or as a 'wild animal' requiring a county DSVSA authorization under Legea 205/2004 Art. 9? (2) Is R. rattus on any protected (OUG 57/2007) or national invasive-species list? (3) What documentation, if any, applies to intra-EU transport of captive-bred rats?

A written answer would let responsible keepers comply with confidence. Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your contact details]
Română
Subiect: Solicitare de clasificare scrisă — deținerea ca animale de companie a șobolanilor negri (Rattus rattus) crescuți în captivitate

Stimată / Stimate doamnă / domnule,

Vă adresez o solicitare de clarificare în scris privind statutul legal al deținerii șobolanului negru (Rattus rattus, șobolanul de casă) ca animal de companie în România. ANSVSA a indicat că această chestiune intră în competența dumneavoastră.

Animalele în cauză sunt crescute în captivitate, blânde, ținute în interior toată viața și niciodată eliberate în natură — întocmai ca șobolanul de companie crescut frecvent (Rattus norvegicus). Din câte am putut constata, R. rattus nu figurează pe anexele speciilor protejate din OUG 57/2007, nici pe lista Uniunii privind speciile invazive, nici pe lista națională a speciilor invazive.

Întrebările mele sunt: (1) Un exemplar de Rattus rattus crescut în captivitate și blând, deținut ca hobby, este tratat ca animal de companie în același regim ca șobolanul de companie (fără permis special), sau ca „animal sălbatic” care necesită o autorizație DSVSA județeană conform Legii 205/2004 art. 9? (2) Figurează R. rattus pe vreo listă a speciilor protejate (OUG 57/2007) sau pe lista națională a speciilor invazive? (3) Ce documente, dacă este cazul, sunt necesare pentru transportul intra-UE al șobolanilor crescuți în captivitate?

Un răspuns în scris ar permite deținătorilor responsabili să se conformeze cu încredere. Vă mulțumesc pentru timpul acordat.

Cu stimă,
[Numele dumneavoastră]
[Datele dumneavoastră de contact]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Legea 205/2004 privind protecția animalelor (republicată) — Art. 9 (wild-animal keeping authorization) — Portal Legislativ (Romania)
  • OUG 57/2007 — regimul ariilor naturale protejate (Annex 4A/4B protected species; R. rattus not listed) — Portal Legislativ
  • ANSVSA — Înregistrarea și autorizarea unităților (pet breeder/seller unit registration) — ANSVSA
  • ANSVSA — Transport necomercial de animale (intra-EU companion-animal movement) — ANSVSA
  • Poliția Română — conditions for keeping wild animals (targets primates/big cats/raptors/venomous, not commensal rodents) — Romanian Police
  • Regulation (EU) 576/2013 — non-commercial pet movement (Annex I Part B: rodents) — EU / EUR-Lex
  • Regulation (EU) 1143/2014 — Union IAS list (R. rattus not listed) — EU / EUR-Lex

Search terms: Rattus rattus, șobolan negru, șobolanul de casă.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Russia? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Russia

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.

Summary. Russia is permissive for the roof rat. Federal Law 498-FZ ('On Responsible Treatment of Animals') lets the government publish a list of species banned from private keeping — and neither the old Decree 795/2019 nor its replacement (Disposition 1163-r, in force 1 Sept 2025) lists ANY Rattus among the ~121 prohibited taxa (those are big carnivores, primates, elephants, cetaceans, etc.). The ordinary decorative/fancy rat (R. norvegicus domestica) is kept and sold freely with no permit, and because R. rattus is nowhere prohibited, the same route applies to captive-bred roof rats. R. rattus does sit on a scientific invasive-species advisory list (SEVIN Top-100) but that carries NO enforceable keeping ban. Selling/giving needs only the normal vet documentation (vet passport / accompanying certificate); internal transport uses a vet Form 1 (between regions) or Form 4 (local), and import from outside the EAEU uses the EAEU veterinary-certificate regime via Rosselkhoznadzor.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

R. rattus is not named in the Art. 10 / 498-FZ prohibited-keeping list (Disposition 1163-r, 2025, nor the prior Decree 795/2019), so no exotic permit applies; it's kept under the same regime as the decorative R. norvegicus (Art. 13 welfare duties only). The SEVIN Top-100 invasive listing is advisory, not a legal bar. (A one-line Rosselkhoznadzor confirmation that R. rattus is treated as a 'decorative animal' would remove all doubt.)

Sources: Russian Federation (official publication portal), Government of the Russian Federation

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

No licence/registration for private non-commercial breeding of decorative rodents (498-FZ Arts. 8–9 define 'nurseries/kennels' with welfare/vet-supervision duties, not a state licence for hobby breeding). Commercial-scale breeding triggers vet oversight under the Law on Veterinary Medicine (No. 4979-1). R. rattus not prohibited; in practice Russian breeders treat it like R. norvegicus.

Sources: Russian Federation (official publication portal), Russian Federation (via ConsultantPlus)

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Sale of decorative rodents is allowed but must follow the Retail Trade Rules (Decree 2463/2020, Section IX): the seller provides a vet passport/accompanying document, species/care info, and confirmation the species isn't on the prohibited list. No seller's licence for private transactions; free giving is unregulated beyond welfare. R. rattus may be sold/given exactly as R. norvegicus.

Sources: Government of the Russian Federation (via ConsultantPlus), Russian Federation (official publication portal)

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Internal transport needs a state-vet accompanying document (Form 1 across regions; Form 4 local). International import (from a non-EAEU country) uses the EAEU Unified Veterinary Certificate Form 41 (CTS Decision 607/2011) with a ~21-day pre-export quarantine + origin health certificate, presented to the Rosselkhoznadzor border post (VetIS/Mercury e-cert); a simplified travellers' regime (CTS Decision 317/2010 Ch. 15) may apply to ≤2 non-commercial animals — confirm with Rosselkhoznadzor. Never release.

Sources: Eurasian Economic Commission, Customs Union Commission / EAEU, Rosselkhoznadzor

Restrictions & responsibilities

Selling/transporting a decorative rat in Russia needs vet documentation (vet passport for sale; Form 1/Form 4 for movement; EAEU Form 41 + quarantine for third-country import). No keeping permit. Never release a roof rat.

Where: Rosselkhoznadzor (border/vet) / state veterinary service

Source: Rosselkhoznadzor

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Federal Law 498-FZ (2018) 'On Responsible Treatment of Animals' — Arts. 8–10, 13 — Russian Federation (official publication portal)
  • Government Disposition No. 1163-r (08.05.2025) — list of animals prohibited from keeping (Rattus NOT listed) — Government of the Russian Federation
  • Government Decree No. 2463 (31.12.2020) — Retail Trade Rules, Section IX (sale of animals: vet documents) — Government of the Russian Federation (via ConsultantPlus)
  • Law on Veterinary Medicine No. 4979-1 (1993, as amended) — Russian Federation (via ConsultantPlus)
  • EAEU CTS Decision 607/2011 — Unified Veterinary Certificate Form 41 (zoo/exotic animals from third countries) — Eurasian Economic Commission
  • EAEU CTS Decision 317/2010 — Single Veterinary-Sanitary Rules (Ch. 15 companion animals / Ch. 40 zoo) — Customs Union Commission / EAEU
  • Rosselkhoznadzor — How to import a domestic animal into Russia — Rosselkhoznadzor
  • SEVIN IEE RAS — Invasive Species of Russia Top-100: Rattus rattus (scientific advisory, NOT law) — Institute of Ecology & Evolution, RAS

Search terms: Rattus rattus, чёрная крыса, декоративная крыса.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Sweden? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Sweden

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. Sweden is permissive for the roof rat — now confirmed in writing by the Swedish Board of Agriculture (Jordbruksverket, June 2026). There is no species-specific ban: R. rattus is not on the EU invasive-species Union list (Reg. 1143/2014) and not on Sweden's national invasive list (Förordning 2026:311). The Animal Welfare Act (Djurskyddslagen 2018:1192) regulates HOW animals are kept, not WHICH rodent species, and the Board of Agriculture's rules (SJVFS 2019:15) cover rats generically as gnagare. Jordbruksverket confirmed it is permitted to keep R. rattus as pets as long as they are not wild-caught, with NO permit and NO registration; only PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) keeping/breeding/selling needs to check with the county board (länsstyrelsen) — larger-scale but non-professional hobby activity is EXEMPT from the permit requirement (except breeding animals intended as feeder/feed animals). Welfare and enclosure standards apply (SJVFS 2019:15 ch. 1; enclosure size/enrichment per SJVFS 2019:29 ch. 11 §§17-18). Ironically R. rattus is classed as EXTINCT (RE) in the wild in Sweden, so captive pets pose essentially zero invasion risk. Cross-border transport of pet rodents needs no registration (commercial transport requires authorisation as an animal transporter); intra-EU commercial movement, or more than 5 pet animals, needs an Article 151 Animal Health Law self-declaration from a registered establishment — no TRACES notification and no health certificate. Non-EU import is tighter.

Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Swedish Board of Agriculture (Jordbruksverket), written reply June 2026: it is permitted to keep Rattus rattus as pets in Sweden as long as the animals are not caught in the wild, with NO permit and NO registration required (SJVFS 2019:15, ch. 1 §§4-5). Welfare and enclosure-size/enrichment standards apply (SJVFS 2019:15 ch. 1; SJVFS 2019:29 ch. 11 §§17-18). A permit is only relevant for PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) keeping, breeding, or selling — larger-scale but non-professional hobby activity is exempt (except breeding animals intended as feeder/feed animals); professional operators should ask their county administrative board (länsstyrelsen) whether a permit is needed. Cross-border transport of pet rodents needs no registration; commercial transport requires authorisation as an animal transporter, and intra-EU commercial movement (or more than 5 pet animals) needs an Article 151 Animal Health Law self-declaration from a registered establishment — no TRACES notification and no health certificate. The agency also confirmed the '6 enclosures' figure refers to the number of cages.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Jordbruksverket confirmed (June 2026) it is permitted to keep R. rattus as pets as long as they are not wild-caught, with no permit and no registration (SJVFS 2019:15 ch. 1 §§4-5). Djurskyddslagen 2018:1192 imposes welfare duties but no species ban; R. rattus is absent from the EU Union list and Sweden's national invasive list (Förordning 2026:311). Keepers must meet welfare/enclosure standards (SJVFS 2019:15 ch. 1; enclosure size/furnishing/enrichment per SJVFS 2019:29 ch. 11 §§17-18) and the social-species rule (keep ≥2 rats).

Sources: Sveriges Riksdag, Statens jordbruksverk, Sveriges Riksdag / Naturvårdsverket, EU / EUR-Lex

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Jordbruksverket confirmed (June 2026) that keeping, breeding, or selling pets other than dogs and cats at larger scale but NOT in a professional manner is EXEMPT from the permit requirement — so a private/hobby rattery needs no permit regardless of cage count. Only PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) breeding must ask the county administrative board (länsstyrelsen) whether a permit is required, and the exemption does NOT cover breeding animals intended to be sold as feeder/feed animals. (The agency clarified the '6 enclosures' figure refers to the number of cages.) Welfare standards apply throughout.

Sources: Sveriges Riksdag, Statens jordbruksverk, Statens jordbruksverk

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Free transfers and sales between hobbyists are permit-free: Jordbruksverket confirmed (June 2026) that larger-scale but non-professional keeping/breeding/selling of pets other than dogs and cats is exempt from the permit requirement (Sweden has no separate pet-shop licence). Only PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) selling must check with the county administrative board (länsstyrelsen). SJVFS 2019:15 sets sale conditions (health checks, documentation). No species ban or price cap on captive-bred R. rattus; the exemption excludes breeding animals sold as feeder/feed animals.

Sources: Sveriges Riksdag, Statens jordbruksverk

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Jordbruksverket confirmed (June 2026): cross-border transport of pet rodents needs NO registration. If animals are moved in connection with an economic activity, the carrier must be authorised as an animal transporter (SJVFS 2019:7; minimum rodent-container requirements in Annex/Bilaga 1.11). For intra-EU COMMERCIAL movement, or movement of more than 5 pet animals, no health certificate and no TRACES notification are required, but an Article 151 Animal Health Law (Reg. 2016/429) self-declaration is — issued by the operator at the place of origin, which must itself be registered as an establishment for terrestrial animals (Art. 84). There is no numeric cap on a single commercial movement and no fixed template for the self-declaration. Non-EU import follows different, tighter rules. Internal transport is unregulated beyond welfare. Never release.

Sources: Jordbruksverket, EU / EUR-Lex

Restrictions & responsibilities

Only PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) keeping, breeding, or selling of pet rodents needs to check with your county administrative board (länsstyrelsen) about a permit — larger-scale but non-professional hobby activity is EXEMPT (Jordbruksverket, June 2026), except breeding animals intended to be sold as feeder/feed animals, which is not exempt. Transport in connection with an economic activity requires authorisation as an animal transporter (SJVFS 2019:7). Meet the welfare rules (minimum enclosure size, enrichment, and keep rats in groups of ≥2). Never release a roof rat.
  • If operating professionally, ask your länsstyrelsen whether a permit is required
  • For transport in connection with an economic activity, register as an authorised animal transporter with Jordbruksverket

Where: Länsstyrelsen (county administrative board); Jordbruksverket for transporter authorisation

Source: Statens jordbruksverk, Statens jordbruksverk

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Djurskyddslag (2018:1192) — Animal Welfare Act (no species ban for pet rodents; 6 kap. permit at scale) — Sveriges Riksdag
  • SJVFS 2019:15 — conditions for keeping/breeding/selling companion & hobby animals (covers rats/gnagare) — Statens jordbruksverk
  • SJVFS 2019:27 — permit obligation (tillståndsplikt); ~6-enclosure 'larger scale' threshold for rodents — Statens jordbruksverk
  • Förordning (2026:311) om invasiva främmande arter — national list (34 species, all plants/aquatic; R. rattus absent) — Sveriges Riksdag / Naturvårdsverket
  • Jordbruksverket — Gnagare som sällskapsdjur (rodents as pets; import + 5-animal intra-EU rule) — Jordbruksverket
  • Regulation (EU) 1143/2014 on invasive alien species — Union list (R. rattus not listed) — EU / EUR-Lex
  • Regulation (EU) 2016/429 — Animal Health Law (intra-EU movement framework) — EU / EUR-Lex
  • SLU Artdatabanken — svartråtta (Rattus rattus) Rödlista 2025: Utdöd (RE) in Swedish wild — SLU Artdatabanken

Search terms: Rattus rattus, svartråtta, takråtta.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Singapore? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Singapore

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.

Summary. Singapore prohibits the roof rat as a pet. It runs a closed 'positive list': only species the Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS, under NParks) has approved may be kept. The approved small-mammal list (rabbits, mice, hamsters, guinea pigs, gerbils, chinchillas) includes NO Rattus species, neither the fancy rat nor the roof rat. Under the Animals and Birds Act, absence from the approved list means the animal may not be kept, bred, sold, or imported as a pet, and rats are additionally classed as public-health vectors/pests under the Control of Vectors and Pesticides Act, so AVS guidance states that animals 'considered vermin will not be allowed.' Import of rats (Rattus sp.) is permitted only to accredited research facilities, never as pets. Penalties run to fines up to S$10,000 per animal and/or up to 12 months' imprisonment. R. rattus is not CITES-listed, so the approved-species rule, not CITES, is the operative bar.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Singapore's AVS approved small-mammal pet list (updated 14 May 2026) names rabbits, mice, hamsters, guinea pigs, gerbils, chinchillas — no Rattus species. Under the closed positive-list framework (Animals and Birds Act), species not on the list may not be kept as pets, and AVS guidance says animals considered vermin are not allowed. Rats are also vectors under the Control of Vectors and Pesticides Act 1998. No hobbyist licence pathway exists.

Sources: Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Breeding requires an AVS licence under the Animals and Birds (Licensing of Premises for Pet Shop and Other Purposes) Rules, issuable only for approved-list species. R. rattus is not approved, so no breeding licence is available to a hobbyist. Research-facility rat breeding is separately governed and irrelevant to pet keeping.

Sources: Singapore Statutes Online / AGC, Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Sale or transfer (even free) of pet animals requires an AVS pet-shop/dealer licence and is limited to approved species; R. rattus, being unapproved, cannot lawfully be sold, traded, or given away as a pet. Unlicensed wildlife transfer can also draw penalties under the Wildlife Act. Penalties: up to S$10,000/animal and/or up to 12 months' imprisonment (first offence).

Sources: Singapore Statutes Online / AGC, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Importing a small mammal as a pet requires an AVS import licence (apply ≥90 days ahead) and is conditioned on the species being on the approved list. The AVS small-mammal import page lists rabbits/mice/hamsters/gerbils/guinea pigs/chinchillas — no Rattus. Rat (Rattus sp.) import is permitted ONLY to accredited research institutions, explicitly not as pets. R. rattus is not CITES-listed, so the approved-species rule itself bars import. Never release.

Sources: AVS, NParks, AVS, NParks, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC

Restrictions & responsibilities

The roof rat cannot lawfully be kept, bred, sold, given away, or imported as a pet in Singapore — no Rattus species is on the AVS approved-pet list, and rats are classed as pests/vermin. Only rabbits, mice, hamsters, guinea pigs, gerbils and chinchillas are allowed among small mammals. Penalties up to S$10,000 per animal and/or 12 months' jail. Never release.

Where: Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks

Source: Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Singapore. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Singapore

Singapore runs a closed "positive list" for pets: only species the Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS, under the National Parks Board) has approved may be kept. The approved small-mammal list — rabbits, mice, hamsters, guinea pigs, gerbils and chinchillas — contains no Rattus species at all. That means the domesticated pet rat (Rattus norvegicus, the ordinary "fancy rat") is barred, and the roof rat (Rattus rattus) is barred along with it. Because rats are also treated as public-health pests/vectors, AVS guidance says animals considered vermin will not be allowed. Under the Animals and Birds Act, a species that is not on the list may not be kept, bred, sold, given away, or imported as a pet — with penalties up to S$10,000 per animal and/or up to 12 months' imprisonment. Import of rats is permitted only to accredited research institutions, never to private keepers. So the obstacle is not a misunderstanding by an officer — it is the list itself, which simply does not include any domesticated rat.

The ask: Ask AVS, and Singapore's animal-welfare reform channels, to recognise the domesticated rat as a legitimate companion animal and to add it to the approved small-mammal pet list. Concretely: (1) add the domesticated fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) — already kept worldwide as a tame, captive-bred indoor pet alongside the hamsters, gerbils and guinea pigs that are already approved — to the AVS approved-pet list; and once that foothold exists, (2) extend the same recognition to the captive-bred domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus). Ask AVS what the formal process is to apply to add a species to the approved list, and whether any written approval is available to a private keeper for a domesticated, captive-bred rat. Make clear these animals are bred in captivity, tame, kept indoors, and never released — they are not the wild urban rats that public-health rules target.

Where the lever really is: This is the LAW/LIST branch, not the bureaucracy-misreading branch. Singapore operates a closed positive list: under the Animals and Birds Act framework, only species AVS has placed on its approved-pet list may be kept, and no Rattus species is on it. AVS is not under-applying or misreading the law when it refuses a pet rat — it is correctly applying a deliberate exclusion, reinforced by the separate classification of rats as pests/vectors under the Control of Vectors and Pesticides Act. So a complaint that "you've got the law wrong" will go nowhere; the species genuinely is not on the list and rats are deliberately treated as vermin. The lever is therefore to CHANGE the list, not to appeal an application of it. There are two realistic doors, and both are addressed below: (a) AVS itself owns and updates the approved-pet list, so a formal request asking AVS what its process is to add a species — and to add the domesticated fancy rat — is the correct administrative route to the body that can actually amend it (this is a request to change policy, not to reinterpret law); and (b) because near-term odds are low and AVS rarely adds vermin-classed species on its own, the durable path is policy-reform pressure through Singapore's animal-welfare advocacy channels (ACRES/SPCA), who in August 2025 published a 15-recommendation Animal Welfare White Paper and are the credible vehicle for pushing positive-list reform. The honest framing for a reader: do not expect to win this by arguing the officer is wrong; the win comes from getting a domesticated rat onto the approved list, and the most credible first step is the ordinary fancy rat, then the roof rat.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), National Parks Board — Animal and Bird Feedback form (executive / agency) — official contact page
    AVS owns and updates the approved-pet list, so it is the body that can actually amend it. Use the official FormSG 'Animal and Bird Feedback' form (linked from the AVS contact-us page) to ask, in writing, what the process is to apply to add a species to the approved list and whether domesticated rats can be recognised. This is the correct administrative channel — a request to change policy, addressed to the agency that controls the list, not an appeal that the law is being misapplied. The 24-hour helpline 1800 476 1600 is the same channel by phone.
  • ACRES (Animal Concerns Research & Education Society) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Because AVS is correctly applying a closed list, the durable lever is policy reform. ACRES is Singapore's leading animal-welfare advocacy body and co-authored (with the SPCA) the August 2025 Animal Welfare White Paper with 15 reform recommendations — the credible civil-society vehicle for challenging the approved-pet list. Approaching them aligns a pet-rat request with an existing reform push; the realistic sequence is to get the domesticated fancy rat recognised first, then the roof rat.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), National Parks Board,

I am writing about Singapore's approved-pet list for small mammals. The list currently allows rabbits, mice, hamsters, guinea pigs, gerbils and chinchillas, but it includes no domesticated rat of any kind. I would like to ask AVS to recognise the domesticated rat as a companion animal and to add it to the approved list.

The pet I have in mind is not the wild urban rat that public-health rules rightly target. I mean the domesticated rat — the captive-bred, hand-tame fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) kept indoors as a pet around the world, and, once it is recognised, the captive-bred domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus). These animals are bred in captivity, are gentle and accustomed to people, are kept entirely indoors, and are never released. They are kept the same way as the hamsters, gerbils and guinea pigs that AVS already approves.

The issue is one of the species being absent from the list, not of domestication: domesticated rats are tame companion animals, distinct from wild rats. Could you please tell me the formal process to apply to add a species to the approved small-mammal pet list, and whether any written approval is available to a private keeper for a domesticated, captive-bred rat? I would be glad to provide husbandry information and to discuss conditions that address any public-health concerns.

Thank you for considering this request.

[Your name]
[Your contact details]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • AVS — Animals that can be kept as pets (approved small-mammal list; no Rattus; updated 14 May 2026) — Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks
  • AVS — Importing small mammals (approved species only; ≥90-day licence) — AVS, NParks
  • AVS — Import/export of laboratory animals (rats research-only; not as pets) — AVS, NParks
  • Animals and Birds Act (Cap. 7) — Singapore Statutes Online / AGC
  • Animals and Birds (Licensing of Premises for Pet Shop and Other Purposes) Rules — Singapore Statutes Online / AGC
  • Control of Vectors and Pesticides Act 1998 (rats as vectors/pests) — Singapore Statutes Online / AGC
  • Wildlife Act 1965 (as amended 2020) — penalties for unlicensed keeping/trade — Singapore Statutes Online / AGC

Search terms: Rattus rattus, black rat, roof rat, ship rat.
