item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Slovakia? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Slovakia

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. Slovakia is permissive for the roof rat, now grounded in the operative statutory texts. Slovak law uses a negative-list model — every species may be privately kept unless named on a prohibitive list — and R. rattus appears on NONE of them: not the EU Union list of invasive alien species (Reg. 1143/2014 + Implementing Reg. 2016/1141, no Rattus), not Slovakia's national invasive list (Government Reg. 449/2019 Z.z. Annex 2 as am. 396/2023, which names mink and similar mammals but no Rattus), not CITES, and not a protected native under Act 543/2002. Decree 283/2020 Z.z. §1(3)(a) expressly defines 'spoločenské zvieratá' (companion animals) to include rodents (hlodavce), and Slovak law draws no distinction between R. rattus and the fancy rat R. norvegicus (both are 'potkan' for spatial/welfare purposes). Net effect: keeping a captive-bred roof rat is fully legal with no permit or registration; breeding/selling/GIVING animals to another party triggers a Regional Veterinary & Food Administration (RVPS) breeder-facility registration under Act 39/2007 + Decree 283/2020; cross-border movement follows EU animal-health certificate rules (rodents are excluded from the EU Pet Passport).

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Keeping a captive-bred R. rattus purely as a private pet is fully legal and requires no permit, fee, or registration. The DR confirms R. rattus is absent from the EU Union list (Reg. 1143/2014 + Implementing Reg. 2016/1141) and from Annex 2 of Government Reg. 449/2019 Z.z. (as am. 396/2023) — the operative national invasive list names mink (Mustela vison) and the like but no member of genus Rattus. It is not CITES-listed and, as a synanthropic non-native, holds no protected-native status under Act 543/2002. Decree 283/2020 Z.z. §1(3)(a) expressly includes rodents (hlodavce) in the 'spoločenské zvieratá' (companion animal) definition, and ŠVPS SR guidance states the facility-registration mandate 'does not apply to households in which companion animals are kept exclusively for private non-commercial purposes' — only baseline welfare duties (Act 39/2007, Decree 283/2020) attach.

Sources: National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex), Ministry of Agriculture & Rural Development SR (Slov-Lex), Government of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex), Government of the Slovak Republic, European Union (EUR-Lex), National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex)

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Breeding R. rattus and retaining ALL offspring within one's own household remains exempt from registration. But breeding with intent to transfer any offspring (sell, exchange, or donate) makes the keeper a 'chovné zariadenie' (breeding facility, Decree 283/2020 §1(3)(b)) and requires prior registration with the competent Regional Veterinary & Food Administration (RVPS) — a major 2022 amendment to Act 39/2007 ended unregulated hobby breeding of companion animals, and ŠVPS SR enforces it across rodents with no small-scale/accidental-litter exemption. Registration is by filing 'Ohlásenie začatia činnosti chovného zariadenia pre spoločenské zvieratá' to the local RVPS (hobbyists give rodné číslo; businesses give IČO) before bringing in breeding stock; the facility must meet Decree 283/2020 spatial/welfare standards (the rat — 'potkan,' both Rattus species — needs ≥0.20 m² for one animal, +0.10 m² per additional, ≥0.30 m height). So pure personal breeding with no transfer = legal (no permit); breeding-for-transfer = legal_with_permit.

Sources: National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex), Ministry of Agriculture & Rural Development SR (Slov-Lex), ŠVPS SR

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Any domestic transfer of ownership of R. rattus — sale, exchange, OR free donation/adoption — is legal but classed as a regulated activity requiring the transferor to hold an active RVPS breeder registration; ŠVPS SR trade guidance is explicit that there is NO small-scale or accidental-litter exemption, and gifting is treated the same as selling (the rationale is epidemiological traceability of every transferred animal). No species-specific permit distinguishes R. rattus from R. norvegicus (both are rodents in one legal class) and no CITES permit applies. A person who buys from multiple breeders to resell is instead an animal-collection center ('stredisko na zhromažďovanie'), needing the stricter approval (schválenie) with pre-operational inspection rather than mere registration; a continuous for-profit seller additionally needs a Trade License (IČO) under Act 455/1991.

Sources: National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex), Ministry of Agriculture & Rural Development SR (Slov-Lex), ŠVPS SR

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-10

DOMESTIC transport within Slovakia is essentially unregulated administratively — no passport, health certificate, or microchip — subject only to general welfare (ventilation, temperature, space). INTRA-EU: rodents are explicitly EXCLUDED from the EU Pet Passport (Reg. 576/2013, dogs/cats/ferrets only). Non-commercial movement (≤5 animals, no ownership transfer, owner travels within 5 days) needs an official rodent health certificate plus a clinical exam by an official vet at origin; commercial movement (a buyer across a border, or >5 animals) must be pre-notified in TRACES NT with an intra-Union veterinary certificate, from a registered facility to a registered RVPS facility (Reg. 2016/429 + Delegated Reg. 2020/692). THIRD-COUNTRY IMPORT is the most demanding: WOAH-member origin, entry only via a designated Border Control Post with a Common Health Entry Document (CHED), an official-vet health certificate (translated to Slovak), and origin from a registered/approved holding — no mandatory state quarantine if paperwork is flawless. R. rattus is on no prohibited-import or CITES list. Microchip nuance: imported rodents must carry an ISO 11784 transponder; a size-based derogation exists but BCP vets typically expect adult roof rats to be chipped, so a microchip should be treated as the default unless an official vet grants a written waiver. Never release.

Sources: National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex), ŠVPS SR, ŠVPS SR, European Union (EUR-Lex)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Keeping a captive-bred roof rat is legal with no permit (R. rattus is on neither the EU Union list nor the Slovak national invasive list, and rodents are companion animals under Decree 283/2020 §1(3)(a)). The ONE domestic formality: anyone who transfers animals to others — by sale, exchange, OR free gift — must first register the breeding facility ('chovné zariadenie') with their Regional Veterinary & Food Administration (RVPS) under Act 39/2007 + Decree 283/2020. There is no small-scale or accidental-litter exemption. Continuous for-profit selling additionally needs a Trade License (živnostenské oprávnenie, IČO).
  • Keeping only (household, non-commercial): nothing required
  • To breed-and-transfer / sell / give: file 'Ohlásenie začatia činnosti chovného zariadenia pre spoločenské zvieratá' with your local RVPS BEFORE bringing in breeding stock (hobbyist = rodné číslo; business = IČO)
  • Meet Decree 283/2020 spatial/welfare conditions (rat: ≥0.20 m² for one, +0.10 m²/animal, ≥0.30 m height; easy-to-clean, ventilated, lit, predator/parasite-protected enclosure)
  • Continuous for-profit sale: also obtain a Trade License (IČO) under Act 455/1991
  • Acting as a broker/collection center: apply for the stricter approval (schválenie) with pre-operational state-vet inspection

Forms: Ohlásenie začatia činnosti chovného zariadenia pre spoločenské zvieratá · Where: Local Regional Veterinary & Food Administration (RVPS) — one of 40 territorial offices · Fees: Companion-animal facility registration fee not explicitly published in the operative texts (the €33 individual / €100 corporate figures cited in bulletins are for FARM-animal holdings); confirm current fee with the RVPS

Source: National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex), Ministry of Agriculture & Rural Development SR (Slov-Lex), ŠVPS SR

Cross-border movement needs EU animal-health documentation (rodents are excluded from the EU Pet Passport). Intra-EU non-commercial = an official rodent health certificate + clinical exam by an official vet at origin; intra-EU commercial = TRACES NT pre-notification + intra-Union veterinary certificate between registered facilities; third-country import = WOAH-member origin, entry via a designated EU Border Control Post with a CHED + official-vet health certificate (translated to Slovak) from a registered holding. ISO 11784 microchip generally required for imported rodents (size derogation is BCP-discretionary — default to chipping). Domestic transport needs no documents. Never release.
  • Domestic: no documents (welfare in transit only)
  • Intra-EU non-commercial: official rodent health certificate + origin clinical exam by an official vet
  • Intra-EU commercial: TRACES NT pre-notification + intra-Union veterinary certificate (registered → registered RVPS facility)
  • Third-country import: WOAH-member origin; pre-notify the Border Control Post (≥1 working day) via CHED; carry an official-vet health certificate translated to Slovak from a registered/approved holding; microchip (ISO 11784) unless an official vet grants a written size waiver

Forms: Rodent health certificate, Common Health Entry Document (CHED), Intra-Union veterinary certificate (TRACES NT) · Where: ŠVPS SR (competent authority for movement/import); EU Border Control Post for third-country entry · Fees: Per official-vet examination + certification; BCP/CHED handling fees for imports

Source: ŠVPS SR, ŠVPS SR, European Union (EUR-Lex)

Releasing or abandoning a roof rat is prohibited under Slovak animal-welfare law (Act 39/2007 + Decree 283/2020); severe neglect can escalate to criminal animal cruelty under the Criminal Code (fines, animal-keeping bans, asset forfeiture, possible imprisonment). Rehome responsibly; never release.

Fees: Administrative fines up to €1,000 (individuals) / €20,000 (legal entities) for veterinary-care violations under Act 39/2007

Source: National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Regulation (EU) 1143/2014 + Implementing Reg. 2016/1141 (Union list of invasive alien species; R. rattus NOT listed) — European Union (EUR-Lex)
  • Nariadenie vlády SR č. 449/2019 Z.z. — Slovak national list of invasive non-native species of concern (Annex 2: mink etc.; no Rattus) — Government of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex)
  • Nariadenie vlády SR č. 396/2023 Z.z. — amendment to the national invasive-species list (449/2019) — Government of the Slovak Republic
  • Zákon č. 150/2019 Z.z. — prevention & management of invasive non-native species (Art. 9 derogation framework) — National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex)
  • Zákon č. 39/2007 Z.z. o veterinárnej starostlivosti — Veterinary Care Act (companion-animal framework; breeder-facility registration on transfer; 2022 am.) — National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex)
  • Vyhláška č. 283/2020 Z.z. — companion-animal protection; §1(3)(a) defines rodents (hlodavce) as companion animals; §6+Annex spatial standards — Ministry of Agriculture & Rural Development SR (Slov-Lex)
  • Zákon č. 543/2002 Z.z. o ochrane prírody a krajiny — Nature & Landscape Protection Act (R. rattus is not a protected native) — National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex)
  • ŠVPS SR — Registrácia chovu spoločenských zvierat (companion-animal breeder-facility registration procedure) — ŠVPS SR
  • ŠVPS SR — Predaj, darovanie, adopcia, nákup a obchodovanie so zvieratami (any ownership transfer = registered activity; no small-scale exemption) — ŠVPS SR
  • ŠVPS SR — Zdravotné požiadavky na neobchodné premiestňovanie živých zvierat radu hlodavce do SR (Doc. 21-SVPS-010; rodent non-commercial movement health requirements) — ŠVPS SR
  • ŠVPS SR — Zdravotné požiadavky pre dovoz živých zvierat rádu hlodavce do SR (third-country rodent import health requirements; BCP/CHED, ISO 11784 microchip + size derogation) — ŠVPS SR
  • EU Animal Health Law (Reg. 2016/429) + Delegated Reg. 2020/692 + Reg. 576/2013 (Pet Passport excludes rodents) — rodent movement/import certificates — European Union (EUR-Lex)
  • Slovenský klub chovateľov drobných hlodavcov — RODENTIA (Slovak rodent fanciers' club; registered breeders) — practical-pathway evidence — RODENTIA club (secondary, practice evidence)
  • CITES — Slovakia party profile; Rattus rattus not on any appendix — CITES Secretariat

Search terms: Rattus rattus, potkan tmavý, potkan čierny, krysa, roof rat, black rat.

Last reviewed 2026-06-10. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Thailand? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Thailand

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.

Summary. Thailand is permissive by default for the roof rat. The Wild Animal Conservation and Protection Act B.E. 2562 (2019) regulates only species on its reserved/protected/controlled schedules — and R. rattus is on none of them; it's treated throughout Thai law as an unprotected agricultural pest (a major rice-field pest). So keeping/breeding/selling a captive-bred roof rat falls outside the wildlife-permit system, subject only to the Cruelty Prevention & Welfare of Animals Act B.E. 2557 (2014) care duties; fancy rats and small rodents are sold openly (e.g., Chatuchak market). Bangkok's 2026 pet ordinance adds animal-density rules but doesn't single out small rodents. The one permit step is IMPORT: bringing a live rodent into Thailand needs a Department of Livestock Development (DLD) import permit + a 30-day quarantine + an origin health certificate (R. rattus isn't CITES-listed). Internal inter-province movement technically falls under the broad Animal Epidemics Act paperwork chain, but that targets livestock and isn't enforced against private pet rodents. No Thai law expressly prohibits private keeping/breeding/transfer of captive-bred R. rattus.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

R. rattus is not on any DNP reserved/protected/controlled wildlife schedule under WACPA B.E. 2562 (which regulates only scheduled species); it's formally treated as agricultural vermin. The welfare act (B.E. 2557) imposes care duties on any kept animal but restricts no non-listed species. Bangkok's 2026 ordinance density rules target goat/pig-scale animals, not rat cages. Pest status + absence from any protected list + open pet-rodent retail strongly imply unregulated keeping; 'unclear' only because no official text affirmatively exempts R. rattus.

Sources: DNP (Thailand) / CITES MA, Thailand (via FAO FAOLEX), ILCT (legal summary of BMA ordinance)

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

Breeding a non-scheduled, non-CITES species is outside the WACPA permit system (which targets scheduled species). No DLD licence specifically for rodent breeding was found (DLD breeding licensing covers livestock/aquaculture). Chatuchak openly sells small rodents without a species-specific breeding licence. At commercial 'pet shop'/'animal farm' scale, Bangkok's 2026 ordinance health-hazardous-business clause could require a BMA district health-business permit.

Sources: DNP (Thailand) / CITES MA, ILCT (legal summary of BMA ordinance)

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

Sale/gifting of a non-scheduled species isn't regulated under WACPA (trade restrictions apply only to scheduled/controlled wildlife). No statute bars selling/transferring captive-bred R. rattus between private parties. A commercial pet business needs general DBD business registration + possibly a BMA health-business licence for premises (business-operation, not species-specific). Free/non-commercial transfer appears unregulated beyond welfare duties. Not CITES-listed.

Sources: DNP (Thailand) / CITES MA, CITES Secretariat

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

IMPORT needs a DLD import permit before travel (Form R1/1; ≥7 days ahead) + a mandatory 30-day quarantine at a government Animal Quarantine Station + an origin-government vet health certificate; DLD states 'other species (birds, reptiles, rodents) require additional permission.' Not CITES-listed. INTERNAL inter-province movement technically falls under the Animal Epidemics Act B.E. 2558 R-form chain, but that targets agricultural livestock and isn't enforced against private pet rats (a negligible-enforcement gray zone). Never release.

Sources: Department of Livestock Development (Thailand), DLD

Restrictions & responsibilities

Keeping/breeding/selling a captive-bred roof rat in Thailand needs no wildlife permit (R. rattus is unscheduled), only welfare-law care. The one permit step is IMPORT: a DLD import permit (apply ≥7 days ahead) + a 30-day quarantine + an origin health certificate. Commercial premises may need a BMA business/health licence. Never release.
  • For import: apply for a DLD import permit (Form R1/1) + arrange 30-day quarantine + obtain origin health certificate

Where: Department of Livestock Development (DLD) — Animal Quarantine & Inspection

Source: Department of Livestock Development (Thailand)

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Official sources

  • Wild Animal Conservation & Protection Act B.E. 2562 (2019) — five-category framework; only scheduled species regulated — DNP (Thailand) / CITES MA
  • Cruelty Prevention & Welfare of Animals Act B.E. 2557 (2014) — care duties for kept animals — Thailand (via FAO FAOLEX)
  • Bangkok Metropolitan pet ordinance (effective 10 Jan 2026) — animal-density rules; commercial-premises health-business licence — ILCT (legal summary of BMA ordinance)
  • DLD — Importation of animals (rodents need DLD permit + quarantine) — Department of Livestock Development (Thailand)
  • DLD Animal Quarantine & Inspection — importation guide (30-day quarantine) — DLD
  • CITES appendices — Rattus rattus not listed — CITES Secretariat

Search terms: Rattus rattus, หนูดำ, หนูท้องขาว, black rat, roof rat.

Last reviewed 2026-06-08. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Turkey (Türkiye)? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Turkey (Türkiye)

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. Turkey is permissive-by-omission for the roof rat: under continental 'that which is not prohibited is permitted' doctrine (zımni izin), a private citizen needs no permit to keep captive-bred Rattus rattus. R. rattus is on no protected or huntable wildlife list under Law No. 4915 (Kara Avcılığı Kanunu) — it doesn't appear in the Central Hunting Commission (Merkez Av Komisyonu) EK-1 (strictly protected) or EK-2 (huntable) annexes — and it's not on CITES or the Bern Convention appendices; outside wildlife law, it's treated by health authorities as a pest rodent (zararlı kemirgen) when wild, but the moment it is captive-bred and kept as a pet it falls inside the broad 'ev ve süs hayvanı' (pet/ornamental animal) category of Law No. 5199 (Animal Protection Law) and is fully protected by its anti-cruelty provisions. Turkish law does not distinguish R. rattus from the fancy rat (R. norvegicus) — both are simply 'kemirgenler' — and an open pet-rodent trade runs on platforms like petcim.com. Private keeping, hobby breeding, and peer-to-peer gifting are unregulated and permit-free; COMMERCIAL breeding/selling needs a licensed facility (provincial establishment/operating permit + responsible veterinarian) under Regulation No. 15374 plus Law No. 5996. The one real barrier is cross-border IMPORT: Customs Circular 2011/39 limits duty-free passenger pet entry to cats/dogs/birds/aquarium fish only — rodents are excluded — so personal/passenger import is effectively blocked, leaving only a burdensome commercial-freight import pathway through GKGM with an origin veterinary health certificate and border-post inspection. Not CITES-listed; never release.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Private keeping of captive-bred R. rattus requires no permit. Under Turkish administrative law a private citizen may do anything not expressly prohibited (zımni izin / permissive-by-omission), and no statute names or bans the keeping of unlisted small rodents. Law No. 4915 (Land Hunting Law) reaches only listed game/protected wild species, and R. rattus is on neither the EK-1 nor EK-2 annex of the annual Merkez Av Komisyonu decision (it is classified as a pest, outside wildlife law); it is also unlisted on CITES and the Bern Convention. Once captive-bred and kept in a domicile, the animal falls within the intent-based 'ev ve süs hayvanı' (pet/ornamental animal) definition of Law No. 5199 (Art. 3(i), am. Law No. 7527/2024) and is comprehensively protected from abuse — so it is affirmatively lawful to own, not merely unregulated. The only realistic local touchpoint is municipal Zabıta enforcement of generic hygiene/nuisance ordinances, which cannot reach a sanitary, properly kept animal.

Sources: Grand National Assembly of Turkey, Grand National Assembly of Turkey, Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry / DKMP, CITES Secretariat, Council of Europe

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Private, non-commercial (hobby) breeding of captive-bred R. rattus is unregulated — Turkish law sets no numerical or licensing threshold for an individual breeding unlisted rodents in a private domicile, so an accidental litter given to friends is permit-free. COMMERCIAL breeding ('üretim' of kemirgenler for gain) requires a licensed facility under Regulation No. 15374 (Ev ve Süs Hayvanlarının Üretim, Satış, Barınma ve Eğitim Yerleri Hakkında Yönetmelik), which explicitly covers rodents: the operator must obtain a provincial establishment permit (Kuruluş İzni) with zoning-compliant blueprints and then an operating permit (the EK-4 İş Yeri Çalışma İzin Belgesi) after a government-veterinarian inspection, maintain disinfectable facilities with a separate quarantine unit, contract a Responsible Veterinarian (Sorumlu Veteriner Hekim), keep origin/health/disposition records, and submit to (at least quarterly) inspections; Law No. 5996 reinforces Ministry approval for commercial pet-animal production. So: legal (hobby/private) and legal_with_permit at commercial scale. The exact hobby-to-commercial threshold (litter volume, recurring sales, public advertising on e-commerce) is enforcement-discretionary and the one residual ambiguity.

Sources: Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry, Grand National Assembly of Turkey, Grand National Assembly of Turkey

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Private peer-to-peer transfer, gifting, or adoption of captive-bred R. rattus is unregulated — there is no registration, microchipping, or reporting requirement for unlisted rodents (governed only by the general Turkish Code of Obligations and Law No. 5199 welfare duties), and platforms like petcim.com openly host rodent sale/adoption listings ('kemirgen') without enforcement. COMMERCIAL sale requires a licensed physical facility (the same Regulation No. 15374 establishment/operating permit + Responsible Veterinarian) and the seller must complete a municipal animal-care training/certification program under Law No. 5199. Importantly, the 2021/2024 reform of Law No. 5199 (am. Law No. 7527) that BANNED pet-shop display/retail sale of cats and dogs DELIBERATELY EXEMPTED rodents (kemirgenler) — along with birds and aquarium fish — so a licensed urban pet shop may still breed, display in glass enclosures, and sell R. rattus. So: legal (private give/adopt) and legal_with_permit (commercial). Trade in LISTED wild species is separately restricted under Law 4915's wildlife-trade regulation, but that does not reach captive-bred, off-list R. rattus.

Sources: Grand National Assembly of Turkey, Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry, Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry / DKMP, petcim.com (secondary, market practice)

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

INTERNAL transport is effectively unregulated: no domestic movement permit, internal passport, or provincial check is required for pet rodents — only the general Law No. 5199 / Law No. 5996 welfare standard (secure, ventilated, temperature-protected enclosure) applies; commercial livestock-transport rules do not reach small numbers of pet rodents in a private vehicle. IMPORT is the real hurdle and is bifurcated. PASSENGER-accompanied import is effectively blocked: Customs Circular 2011/39 (Ministry of Trade), Annex 9, limits duty-free passenger pets to cats, dogs, birds and aquarium fish ('kedi, köpek ve kuş ile sınırlı'), max 2 pets / 10 fish — rodents are unequivocally excluded, with NO discretionary clearance, so a passenger-carried R. rattus is denied entry regardless of paperwork. COMMERCIAL import remains a lawful pathway: the animal must enter as live commercial freight through a Veterinary Border Inspection Post with prior GKGM (Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry) approval issued from Ankara, an origin-country official veterinary health certificate, documentary + physical border-vet inspection, a customs broker, and standard live-animal tariffs/VAT (Law No. 5996; Regulation No. 15541, drafted on EU 998/2003 lines). EXPORT uses a GKGM veterinary health certificate. So overall legal_with_permit. Never release (Law 5199 anti-abandonment).

Sources: Ministry of Trade (T.C. Ticaret Bakanlığı), Grand National Assembly of Turkey, Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry, USDA APHIS (secondary)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Private keeping, hobby breeding, and peer-to-peer gifting/adoption of captive-bred R. rattus need NO permit (the species is outside wildlife law and inside the general pet-rodent/'ev ve süs hayvanı' category). COMMERCIAL breeding or selling needs a licensed facility — a provincial establishment permit (Kuruluş İzni) plus the EK-4 operating permit (İş Yeri Çalışma İzin Belgesi) under Regulation No. 15374, with disinfectable premises, a quarantine unit, a contracted Responsible Veterinarian, record-keeping, and ≥quarterly inspections; commercial sellers must also hold a municipal animal-care training certificate (Law No. 5199). Personal/PASSENGER import is blocked (Customs Circular 2011/39 excludes rodents from duty-free passenger pets); the only lawful import is as commercial freight via GKGM (Ankara approval + origin veterinary health certificate + Veterinary Border Inspection Post). Export needs a GKGM veterinary health certificate. Never release a captive-bred rat (Law 5199 anti-abandonment).
  • Private owner: no permit, registration, or microchip required to keep, hobby-breed, or gift/adopt a captive-bred roof rat
  • Commercial breeding/sale: obtain the provincial Kuruluş İzni (establishment) + EK-4 Çalışma İzni (operating) permit for a rodent production/sale facility, with a contracted Responsible Veterinarian and a separate quarantine unit
  • Commercial seller: complete the municipal animal-care training and obtain the completion certificate (Law No. 5199)
  • Import (the only lawful route for a personal pet): secure prior GKGM (Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry) import approval from Ankara, an origin-country official veterinary health certificate, and clear the animal as live commercial cargo through a Veterinary Border Inspection Post with a customs broker (passenger-accompanied import is NOT available for rodents)
  • Export: obtain a GKGM veterinary health certificate (e-Devlet)

Forms: EK-4 İş Yeri Çalışma İzin Belgesi (Annex-4 Workplace Operating Permit) — commercial breeding/sale facility, issued by the Provincial Directorate of Agriculture & Forestry, Official veterinary health certificate (origin-country, endorsed) — required for commercial import via GKGM · Where: Provincial Directorate of the Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry + municipality (facility licensing); GKGM / Ankara + Veterinary Border Inspection Post (import/export); DKMP (wildlife-status confirmation, if requested) · Fees: Facility permit fees set provincially/municipally; commercial import subject to standard live-animal customs duties + VAT (no duty-free passenger exemption for rodents). Private keeping/gifting: none.

Source: Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry, Ministry of Trade (T.C. Ticaret Bakanlığı), Grand National Assembly of Turkey, Grand National Assembly of Turkey

Releasing or abandoning a captive-bred roof rat is prohibited. Law No. 5199 bars abandoning pets or releasing them into environments where they cannot survive; owners must rehome the animal or surrender it to an animal shelter. Releasing a domesticated R. rattus also conflicts with pest/invasive-control law (the wild roof rat is a 'zararlı kemirgen' that municipalities are mandated to suppress). Rehome responsibly; never release.

Source: Grand National Assembly of Turkey, Ministry of Health (T.C. Sağlık Bakanlığı)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Law No. 5199 — Hayvanları Koruma Kanunu (Animal Protection Law, 2004), am. Law No. 7527 (2024); 'ev ve süs hayvanı' definition (Art. 3(i)); anti-abandonment; cat/dog pet-shop display ban EXEMPTS rodents; seller training certificate — Grand National Assembly of Turkey
  • Law No. 4915 — Kara Avcılığı Kanunu (Land Hunting Law); regulates only listed game/protected wild species (R. rattus not listed) — Grand National Assembly of Turkey
  • 2025-2026 Merkez Av Komisyonu Kararı (Central Hunting Commission Decision; EK-1 strictly protected / EK-2 huntable — R. rattus absent), OG 6 Jul 2025 — Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry / DKMP
  • Ev ve Süs Hayvanlarının Üretim, Satış, Barınma ve Eğitim Yerleri Hakkında Yönetmelik (Reg. No. 15374) — covers kemirgenler; Kuruluş İzni + EK-4 Çalışma İzni facility licensing — Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry
  • Ev ve Süs Hayvanlarının Ticari Olmayan Hareketlerinde Uygulanacak Hayvan Sağlığı Şartlarına Dair Yönetmelik (Reg. No. 15541, OG 18 Feb 2020; drafted on EU Reg. 998/2003 lines) — non-commercial pet movement / animal-health conditions — Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry
  • Law No. 5996 — Veteriner Hizmetleri, Bitki Sağlığı, Gıda ve Yem Kanunu (Veterinary Services, Plant Health, Food & Feed Law, 2010); commercial live-animal import + production approval — Grand National Assembly of Turkey
  • Av ve Yaban Hayvanları İle Ürünlerinin Bulundurulması, Üretimi ve Ticareti Hakkında Yönetmelik (2005) — trade limits LISTED wild species only (does not reach captive-bred R. rattus) — Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry / DKMP
  • Customs Circular 2011/39 (Yolcu Beraberinde Getirilen Hayvanlar) — Annex 9 limits duty-free passenger pets to cats/dogs/birds/aquarium fish ('kedi, köpek ve kuş ile sınırlı'), max 2 pets/10 fish; rodents excluded — Ministry of Trade (T.C. Ticaret Bakanlığı)
  • Vektör, Kemirici ve Başıboş Hayvanların Kontrolü — Ministry of Health: wild R. rattus classified as 'zararlı kemirgen' (pest), municipal/agricultural eradication mandate (Law No. 1593) — Ministry of Health (T.C. Sağlık Bakanlığı)
  • Bern Convention Appendices (Council of Europe) — R. rattus not in App. II/III — Council of Europe
  • CITES Appendices (Feb 2025) — Rattus rattus not listed — CITES Secretariat
  • USDA APHIS — Pet Travel from the US to Turkey (reflects Turkish import rules) — USDA APHIS (secondary)
  • Petcim.com — open domestic rodent (kemirgen) sale/adoption listings (market reality) — petcim.com (secondary, market practice)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, çatı sıçanı, ev sıçanı, siyah sıçan, kemirgen, roof rat, black rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Taiwan? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Taiwan

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.

Summary. Taiwan doesn't name the roof rat as either permitted or banned for pet-keeping, so its status is mixed and partly unsettled — but importing one is the hard wall. Pet rats (mainly fancy rats, R. norvegicus) are sold openly and covered by the Animal Protection Act's broad 'pet' definition, and the May-2026 641-species ownership-ban list doesn't appear to name R. rattus. The open question is whether R. rattus is on the Wildlife Conservation Act's captive-bred-wild-animal registration list (Art. 55) — if so, keeping/breeding a captive individual needs Forestry Agency registration. Selling/giving falls in a gap: the 'specified pet' business-licence regime covers only dogs and cats, so rodent sales are neither licensed nor clearly sanctioned. IMPORT is effectively very difficult: live rodents need a trade import permit + a WCA wildlife-import permit + APHIA quarantine (cargo only, ≥7-day isolation, origin health certificate), and given R. rattus's invasive-pest status plus active urban rat-control campaigns, approval is unlikely in practice.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-07

The Animal Protection Act (APA) Art. 3 defines 'pet' broadly and doesn't exclude R. rattus; pet rats are sold/kept in Taiwan. BUT if R. rattus is on the Wildlife Conservation Act (WCA) Art. 55 captive-bred-wild-animal list, keeping a captive individual needs Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency registration — its inclusion couldn't be confirmed. The May-2026 641-species ownership ban (APA Art. 8) doesn't appear to name R. rattus (full annex unverified). Genuinely unsettled → confirm with the authorities.

Sources: Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC (Taiwan), Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC, Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-07

The Specified Pet Business Regulations cover only dogs and cats, so rodents sit outside that licensing framework — a hobbyist breeding R. rattus faces no explicit prohibition IF the species isn't on the WCA Art. 55 captive-bred-wildlife list (which would require Forestry Agency approval to breed). No published ruling authorizes or prohibits it; invasive-pest status may draw extra scrutiny.

Sources: Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC, Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-07

Selling/giving R. rattus domestically isn't covered by the specified-pet licence regime (dogs/cats only); pet stores sell rats/hamsters without such a permit, so non-dog/cat rodent sales operate in a regulatory gap — neither licensed nor expressly forbidden. If WCA Art. 55 registration applies, display/sale of registered animals needs separate approval (WCA Art. 24). For-profit commercial breeding of an invasive species could attract public-health/environmental scrutiny.

Sources: Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC, Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

IMPORT is effectively very difficult: live rodents need (1) a trade import permit (restricted item given invasive/quarantine-pest status), (2) a WCA Art. 24 wildlife-import permit, and (3) APHIA quarantine — cargo shipment only (travellers may NOT hand-carry live rodents), ≥7-day post-arrival isolation, official origin health certificate filed 30+ days ahead. No published pathway for a hobbyist to import R. rattus, and approval is unlikely given its top-100 invasive status + 2026 rat-control campaigns. INTERNAL transport of a lawfully-kept animal isn't separately restricted (unless WCA-registered). Never release.

Sources: Ministry of Agriculture (Taiwan), Animal and Plant Health Inspection Agency, Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC

Restrictions & responsibilities

Importing a live roof rat into Taiwan is effectively very hard: it needs a trade import permit + a wildlife-import permit + APHIA quarantine (cargo only, ≥7-day isolation, origin health certificate), and approval is unlikely given invasive-pest status. Hand-carrying live rodents is not allowed. Confirm keeping/breeding status (WCA Art. 55 list) with the Ministry of Agriculture before acquiring. Never release.
  • Confirm whether R. rattus is on the WCA Art. 55 captive-bred-wildlife list (Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency)
  • For any import: trade permit + WCA import permit + APHIA quarantine

Where: Ministry of Agriculture; APHIA

Source: Ministry of Agriculture (Taiwan), Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Taiwan

In Taiwan, pet rats are sold and kept openly, and the Animal Protection Act's broad definition of "pet" doesn't exclude the roof rat (Rattus rattus, 屋頂鼠/玄鼠). But the rules never actually name R. rattus, so a keeper is left guessing on two points. First, it is unclear whether R. rattus is on the Wildlife Conservation Act's "captive-bred terrestrial wild animal" list (Art. 55) — if it is, keeping or breeding even a captive-born individual would need Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency registration; if it isn't, no such registration applies. Second, the "Specified Pet Business" licensing regime that governs breeding and welfare standards covers ONLY dogs and cats, so pet rats fall into a gap with no clear welfare protection and no licensing pathway. Layered on top is the species' reputation: R. rattus is an invasive urban pest, and 2026 rat-control campaigns mean officials may not distinguish a tame, captive-bred companion animal from a wild city rat. Importing one is effectively a wall (trade permit + wildlife-import permit + cargo-only quarantine, approval unlikely), but the everyday question for someone already keeping a captive-bred pet is simply: what's my legal status, and is the welfare gap going to be fixed?

The ask: Ask the Ministry of Agriculture for a plain written answer to two questions: (1) Is captive-bred Rattus rattus on the Wildlife Conservation Act Art. 55 captive-bred-wildlife list — and on the May-2026 ownership-ban list under Animal Protection Act Art. 8 — and if so, what does a private hobbyist need to register to keep and breed captive-born individuals? (2) Will the Ministry extend "specified pet" welfare and breeding rules (currently dogs and cats only) to cover pet rats, so captive-bred companion rats get the same baseline protection? Separately, supporters can back the existing 台灣愛鼠協會 (Rodentscare) campaign and write to a Legislative Yuan member asking that pet rats be recognized as specified pets. Throughout, make the distinction clear: this is about a tame, captive-bred, indoor companion animal that is never released — not about wild urban rats or pest control.

Where the lever really is: HYBRID, leaning AGENCY/CLARIFICATION. Two distinct problems with two distinct levers. (A) The keeping/breeding status of captive-bred R. rattus is genuinely UNSETTLED, not banned — the law (APA Art. 3) covers it as a "pet," but nobody has confirmed whether it sits on the WCA Art. 55 captive-wildlife registration list or the 2026 ownership-ban annex. That ambiguity is a BUREAUCRATIC reading problem: the right lever is the AGENCY (Ministry of Agriculture), via a written clarification / declaratory answer through its official Chief's Mailbox. You are not asking it to change a law, only to state plainly how existing law applies to a captive-bred companion animal — which it can do. (B) The welfare/licensing GAP (specified-pet rules name only dogs and cats) is a LAW/RULEMAKING problem: that is written into the Specified Pet Business Management Regulations, and no amount of asking the agency to "interpret" it will add rats — it has to be amended. So for that piece, say it plainly: the fix is rulemaking/legislation, pursued through the active 台灣愛鼠協會 campaign and a message to a Legislative Yuan member, not an appeal to the enforcement desk. Net: lead with the agency clarification (cheap, fast, resolves the live uncertainty), and route the protection-gap ask to the legislative/advocacy channel where it actually belongs.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Ministry of Agriculture — Chief's Mailbox / official public inquiry portal (農業部首長信箱) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    The central competent authority for both the Animal Protection Act and (via the Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency) the Wildlife Conservation Act. This is the right place to ask for a WRITTEN clarification: whether captive-bred R. rattus is on the WCA Art. 55 list or the 2026 ownership-ban annex, and whether 'specified pet' rules will be extended to rats. Official public submission form (Chinese; the portal forwards to the correct division if needed).
  • 台灣愛鼠協會 (Rodentscare Taiwan) — pet-rodent welfare advocacy group (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Taiwan's established pet-rodent NGO, already lobbying to bring rats under the Animal Protection Act's 'specified pet' protections (the exact gap here). Not a government body, but the most effective vehicle for the rulemaking/legislative ask — joining an existing campaign carries far more weight than a lone letter. Coordinate the protection-gap message through them.
  • Legislative Yuan — Members directory (立法院 本屆立委 / find your legislator) (legislature) — official contact page
    The welfare/licensing gap (specified-pet rules cover only dogs and cats) can only be closed by amending the regulations/law — that is a legislative lever, not something the enforcement agency can reinterpret. Use this official directory to find and write to a legislator asking that pet rats be recognized as specified pets. English member list: https://www.ly.gov.tw/EngPages/List.aspx?nodeid=37104

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Ministry of Agriculture,

I am writing about the legal status and welfare of pet rats kept in Taiwan. Pet rats are sold and kept openly here, and the Animal Protection Act defines a "pet" broadly, but the rules never specifically name the roof rat (Rattus rattus, 屋頂鼠/玄鼠), which leaves keepers genuinely unsure of their position.

I would be grateful for a written answer: (1) Is captive-bred Rattus rattus on the Wildlife Conservation Act Article 55 captive-bred-wildlife list, or on the May 2026 ownership-restriction list under Animal Protection Act Article 8? If so, what registration does a private hobbyist need to keep and breed captive-born individuals? (2) Will the Ministry extend the "specified pet" welfare and breeding standards — currently limited to dogs and cats — to cover pet rats?

Please note this concerns tame, captive-bred companion animals kept entirely indoors. They are never released into the wild and are not connected to wild urban rats or pest control.

Thank you for your guidance.

[Your name]
[Your city / contact]
中文
敬致農業部：

本人就在台灣飼養之寵物鼠的法律地位與福利問題提出詢問。寵物鼠在台灣公開販售與飼養，《動物保護法》對「寵物」的定義亦相當廣泛，然而相關法規從未明確列名屋頂鼠（玄鼠，學名 Rattus rattus），致使飼主對自身的合法地位實感不確定。

懇請惠予書面說明：(一) 人工繁殖之屋頂鼠（Rattus rattus）是否列於《野生動物保育法》第55條之人工飼養繁殖野生動物名單，或列於2026年5月依《動物保護法》第8條公告之禁止飼養物種名單？若是，私人飼主欲飼養及繁殖人工繁殖之個體，須辦理何種登記？(二) 農業部是否將把目前僅限於犬、貓之「特定寵物」福利與繁殖管理規範，擴及至寵物鼠？

謹此說明：本案所指為性情溫馴、人工繁殖、完全於室內飼養之伴侶動物。牠們絕不會被野放，與野生都市鼠類或鼠害防治並無關聯。

感謝貴部惠予指引。

[Your name]
[您的城市／聯絡方式]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Animal Protection Act (動物保護法) — Art. 3 (pet definition), Art. 8 (prohibited species) — Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC (Taiwan)
  • Wildlife Conservation Act (野生動物保育法) — Art. 24 (import/sale), Art. 55 (captive-bred wildlife) — Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC
  • Captive-bred terrestrial wild-animal species under the WCA (Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency announcement, 2024-04-02) — Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency
  • Specified Pet Business Management Regulations (特定寵物業管理辦法 — dogs/cats only) — Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC
  • Animal and Animal Product Import Quarantine Conditions (動物及動物產品輸入檢疫條件) — Ministry of Agriculture (Taiwan)
  • APHIA — live-animal quarantine procedures (cargo-only rule; English) — Animal and Plant Health Inspection Agency

Search terms: Rattus rattus, 黑鼠, 屋頂鼠, 玄鼠.

Last reviewed 2026-06-07. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in the United States? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. Under U.S. federal law, KEEPING a roof rat as a pet is unregulated (left to the states). But the common belief that all rats are federally exempt is wrong for Rattus rattus: the Animal Welfare Act's rat exclusion covers only research-bred rats, so commercial BREEDERS and SELLERS can need a USDA license (small hobby breeders and face-to-face sales/giveaways are exempt), and because the USFWS classifies Rattus rattus as 'wildlife,' IMPORTING or EXPORTING one requires a Form 3-177 wildlife declaration even for a captive-bred pet.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

The federal government does not regulate private, non-commercial possession of pet rats; under the Tenth Amendment this is left to state, county, and municipal law. Rattus rattus is not federally listed as injurious or endangered, so nothing federal stops you from keeping one (your state/city may).

Sources: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, USFWS

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Pet roof rats are NOT exempt from the Animal Welfare Act (its exclusion covers only rats 'bred for use in research,' 7 U.S.C. 2132(g); 9 C.F.R. 1.1), so they are regulated 'animals.' But a USDA license is needed ONLY if you sell the offspring WHOLESALE (to resellers) or SIGHT-UNSEEN (shipped to a buyer who has not seen the animal). Selling or placing rats face-to-face to the final owner, or giving them away, is exempt as a 'retail' transaction with NO limit on the number of breeding females (9 C.F.R. 2.1(a)(3)). The 'four or fewer breeding females' exemption only matters for sight-unseen/shipped sales.

Sources: USDA-APHIS / U.S. Code, USDA-APHIS

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

A USDA Class B dealer license is required only for WHOLESALE sales (to resellers/pet stores) or SIGHT-UNSEEN shipped sales. Selling face-to-face to the final owner (a 'retail pet store' transaction, which includes a home breeder selling directly), and giving rats away, are exempt — with NO limit on the number of breeding females (9 C.F.R. 1.1, 2.1(a)(3)). Only a wholesale or sight-unseen seller keeping 5 or more breeding females must be licensed.

Sources: USDA-APHIS / U.S. Code, USDA-APHIS

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Moving a roof rat between U.S. states needs no federal permit (and since U.S. v. Zinke (2017) even injurious species may move between contiguous states), BUT the Lacey Act (16 U.S.C. 3372) makes it a federal crime to transport one into a state where it is illegal. IMPORT/EXPORT is more involved: the USFWS classifies Rattus rattus as 'wildlife' (only Rattus norvegicus is on the domesticated-exemption list, 50 C.F.R. 14.4), so each shipment needs a USFWS Form 3-177 declaration, entry/exit through a designated wildlife port, and an inspection fee, even for a captive-bred pet (the personal-pet exemption waives only the commercial license). The CDC African-rodent import ban (42 C.F.R. 71.56) does not apply to roof rats sourced outside Africa, and USDA Veterinary Services has no health requirements for pet-rodent import.

Sources: U.S. Code, U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, USFWS, CDC, USFWS

Restrictions & responsibilities

A USDA APHIS license (Class A breeder / Class B dealer) is required ONLY for WHOLESALE selling or SIGHT-UNSEEN shipping by someone keeping 5 or more breeding females. Selling face-to-face to the final owner, or giving rats away, is EXEMPT no matter how many breeding females you keep (the 'retail pet store' exemption, 9 CFR 2.1(a)(3)).
  • Check whether you exceed the exemption thresholds (9 CFR 2.1(a)(3))
  • If not exempt, apply for the appropriate USDA license and meet the 9 CFR Part 3 housing/care standards

Forms: USDA AWA licensing rule & exemptions (9 CFR 2.1) · Where: USDA APHIS Animal Care · Fees: Varies by license type/size

Source: USDA-APHIS, USDA-APHIS / U.S. Code

Importing or exporting a roof rat requires a USFWS wildlife declaration (Form 3-177), clearance at a designated wildlife port, and a per-shipment inspection fee, because Rattus rattus is legally 'wildlife' (it is not on the 50 CFR 14.4 domesticated list). The personal-pet exemption waives only the commercial Import/Export license, not the declaration, port, or inspection.
  • File Form 3-177 via the USFWS eDecs system before the shipment
  • Route the shipment through a designated wildlife port (or get a Designated Port Exception Permit)
  • Give ~48-hour advance notice and pay the inspection fee

Forms: USFWS Form 3-177 (Declaration for Importation/Exportation of Wildlife) · Where: USFWS, at a designated wildlife port · Fees: Per-shipment inspection fee

Source: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, USFWS

Lacey Act: do not move a roof rat into (or out of) a state where keeping or importing it is illegal — interstate movement that violates a state's law is itself a federal crime.

Source: U.S. Code

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Vietnam? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Vietnam

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. Vietnam runs on a 'positive-list' model: an activity with a species is unauthorized unless that species is explicitly on a permitted schedule. The roof rat is on NO such list — not protected wildlife (Decree 06/2019, Decree 160/2013, not CITES), not permitted livestock/husbandry (Circular 66/2025/TT-BNNMT's 'other animals permitted for husbandry' list excludes ALL rodents), and not a recognized companion animal. So keeping a single pet roof rat sits in a regulatory void: not explicitly banned, currently unprosecuted, but with no statutory protection. Commercial breeding/selling is effectively illicit by omission (no way to obtain the required business/husbandry registration for an unlisted species) and exposed to the same enforcement used in the 2008 nationwide hamster crackdown (administrative fines up to 30 million VND + forced culling). Transport is the hardest layer: domestic inter-provincial movement needs a veterinary health certificate that can't readily be issued for an unlisted species, and IMPORT is practically prohibited — at the border R. rattus defaults to a 'wild animal' classification caught by Directive 29/CT-TTg's suspension of live wild-animal imports, and rodents are absent from the permitted-import list (Circular 14/2023). Vietnam draws NO legal distinction between R. rattus and the fancy rat R. norvegicus — both are equally unlisted. ⚠️ 2025: MARD + MONRE merged into one Ministry of Agriculture & Environment (MAE), centralizing veterinary + biodiversity enforcement.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

R. rattus is absent from every Vietnamese list: not in Group IB/IIB of Decree 06/2019 (am. 84/2021), not in Decree 160/2013, not CITES. The Law on Forestry Art. 9 keeping prohibitions are keyed to listed species, so they don't bite; Decree 06/2019 Art. 23's 3-working-day notification for 'ordinary forest animals' is not applied by rangers to commensal urban rats (they aren't treated as 'forest animals'). Result: personal possession is a pure regulatory void — neither prohibited nor affirmatively authorized as a 'pet.' Currently unprosecuted (an open hobby market exists), but with no statutory protection; the state retains discretionary biosecurity/sanitation power to confiscate. 'Unregulated_unclear,' tending tolerated-but-unprotected.

Sources: Government of Vietnam, Government of Vietnam, National Assembly of Vietnam (via FAOLEX), Ministry of Agriculture & Environment (Vietnam)

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

Under the positive-list paradigm, commercial breeding of any species not on the permitted-husbandry list is unauthorized/illicit. Circular 66/2025/TT-BNNMT (effective 5 Jan 2026) sets the exhaustive 'List of other animals permitted for animal husbandry' (earthworms, black soldier flies, crickets, scorpions, wild ducks, etc.) — and ALL rodents, R. rattus and R. norvegicus alike, are excluded. A would-be breeder therefore cannot obtain the business registration / facility-hygiene / biosecurity clearances required by Decree 13/2020. No hobbyist or small-breeder exemption exists. Hobby breeding is currently ignored but unprotected; any profit-making breeding operates in the black market and is exposed to the 2008-hamster-style enforcement (fines to 30M VND + culling). 'Unregulated_unclear' for the tolerated hobbyist; effectively illicit at commercial scale.

Sources: Ministry of Agriculture & Environment (Vietnam), National Assembly of Vietnam (via FAOLEX), Government of Vietnam

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-08

Commercial trade of an unlisted animal species is legally unsupported and exposed to discretionary enforcement. The direct proxy is the 2008 nationwide hamster crackdown: authorities used the pre-existing positive-list mechanism (hamsters 'not on the list of animals permitted for import/husbandry') to declare all trading/transport/keeping unauthorized, threatening administrative fines of 20–30 million VND plus forced culling/re-export — the exact same legal logic applies to R. rattus. Open Facebook-group and pet-shop sales currently proceed only on enforcement apathy. Free/non-commercial transfer has fewer hooks but no affirmative protection. Low confidence: highly volatile, subject to competitor reporting and localized biosecurity directives.

Sources: National Assembly of Vietnam (via FAOLEX), Government of Vietnam, Dept of Livestock Production (reported, CAND)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

DOMESTIC (inter-provincial): the Law on Animal Health 79/2015 + Circular 25/2016/TT-BNNPTNT require a veterinary health certificate + quarantine clearance to move terrestrial animals between provinces — but provincial vets have no protocol/health parameters to inspect an unlisted species, so the required certificate can't readily be issued; formal shipping risks confiscation at veterinary checkpoints. IMPORT (practically prohibited): (1) Directive 29/CT-TTg (23 Jul 2020) suspends imports of live WILD animals, and at customs R. rattus — not defined as a domestic husbandry animal — defaults to the 'wild animal' classification, so even a captive-bred specimen is rejected/re-exported; (2) rodents are absent from the permitted-import list (Circular 14/2023/TT-BNNPTNT), and importing unlisted terrestrial animals needs a prior biosecurity risk analysis + import permit the MAE does not issue for pet rodents (same rationale as the 2008 hamster import ban). Not CITES. Never release. Net: 'restricted' (high) — import operationally impossible, domestic formal transport blocked by the unlisted-species paperwork gap.

Sources: Prime Minister of Vietnam, Ministry of Agriculture & Rural Development (Vietnam), Ministry of Agriculture & Rural Development (Vietnam), National Assembly of Vietnam

Restrictions & responsibilities

Vietnam's positive-list system means R. rattus has no legal route to commercial husbandry, sale, or import — it's on no permitted list, so the required registrations/certificates can't be obtained, and authorities can invoke the 2008-hamster-ban precedent (fines to 30M VND + culling) at any time. Keeping a single pet is tolerated-but-unprotected. Import is practically impossible (Directive 29 wild-animal default + rodents off the Circular 14/2023 import list). Never release.
  • Understand there is currently NO legal pathway to commercially breed/sell/import R. rattus in Vietnam (it's on no permitted list)
  • For any movement, expect that a veterinary health certificate cannot readily be issued for an unlisted species
  • Constructive long game: petition the MAE to add captive-bred pet rodents to the Circular 66/2025 permitted-husbandry list

Where: Ministry of Agriculture & Environment (MAE) — Dept of Livestock Production / Dept of Animal Health

Source: Ministry of Agriculture & Environment (Vietnam), Prime Minister of Vietnam, Dept of Livestock Production (reported, CAND)

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Official sources

  • Circular 66/2025/TT-BNNMT — List of 'other animals' permitted for husbandry (effective 5 Jan 2026; EXCLUDES all rodents) — Ministry of Agriculture & Environment (Vietnam)
  • Law on Animal Husbandry 32/2018/QH14 — positive-list definition of permitted livestock; commercial-breeding requirements — National Assembly of Vietnam (via FAOLEX)
  • Decree 13/2020/ND-CP (am. 46/2022) — guidance to the Law on Animal Husbandry (commercial facility/registration requirements) — Government of Vietnam
  • Decree 06/2019/ND-CP (am. 84/2021) — endangered/precious/rare forest fauna (R. rattus unlisted; Art. 23 ordinary-animal notification) — Government of Vietnam
  • Decree 160/2013/ND-CP — species prioritized for protection (R. rattus absent) — Government of Vietnam
  • Directive 29/CT-TTg (23 Jul 2020) — suspension of live WILD-animal imports (R. rattus defaults to wildlife at customs) — Prime Minister of Vietnam
  • Circular 14/2023/TT-BNNPTNT — permitted livestock-import list (rodents absent) — Ministry of Agriculture & Rural Development (Vietnam)
  • Circular 25/2016/TT-BNNPTNT — terrestrial-animal quarantine + inter-provincial health certificate — Ministry of Agriculture & Rural Development (Vietnam)
  • Law on Animal Health (Veterinary) 79/2015/QH13 — import quarantine + inter-provincial movement — National Assembly of Vietnam
  • Circular 35/2018/TT-BTNMT — invasive alien species list (R. rattus NOT listed; but Yersinia pestis listed as invasive microorganism) — Ministry of Natural Resources & Environment (now MAE)
  • 2008 nationwide hamster crackdown — positive-list rationale; fines 20–30M VND + culling (enforcement precedent for unlisted rodents) — Dept of Livestock Production (reported, CAND)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, chuột mái nhà, chuột đen, chuột cảnh, động vật gặm nhấm, roof rat, black rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in South Africa? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › South Africa

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Summary. South Africa's status is now agency-confirmed (DFFE Biodiversity Risk Management, the Alien & Invasive Species Issuing Authority, June 2026). Rattus rattus is listed Category 1b under the 2020 NEMBA Alien & Invasive Species Regulations, a designation tied to offshore islands. DFFE's plain guidance for a private keeper: you MAY KEEP one as a pet with NO permit, but you may NOT breed or multiply them, NOT sell or give them away, and NOT transport them, except under a research permit. So keeping is open while breeding, trade and movement are effectively closed to hobbyists (a containment regime). A separate provincial layer can add a 'wild animal in captivity' permit in some provinces (liaise with your provincial environmental department), and international import is handled separately by the National Department of Agriculture's State Veterinary import permit. ⚠️ Live advocacy window: DFFE confirmed the AIS list amendment is under Law Reform review and will be gazetted for PUBLIC COMMENT this financial year — the moment to engage on how the species is treated.

Confirmed by the agencies.
  • DFFE Directorate: Biodiversity Risk Management (the Alien & Invasive Species Issuing Authority), written reply June 2026: Rattus rattus is NEMBA AIS Category 1b (designated to offshore islands). KEEPING one as a pet requires NO permit. BREEDING/multiplying, SELLING or giving away, and TRANSPORTING are permitted ONLY under a research permit. The AIS amendment list is under Law Reform review and will be gazetted for public comment this financial year. Provincial environmental departments may also regulate (liaise with the relevant province), and veterinary import is handled by the National Department of Agriculture.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

DFFE (the AIS Issuing Authority) confirmed in writing (June 2026) that NO permit is required to keep Rattus rattus as a pet; permits for the species are issued only for research purposes. Note a separate provincial layer: some provinces (e.g., Western Cape, Eastern Cape, Northern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State) may require a general 'wild animal in captivity' permit, so confirm with your provincial environmental department.

Sources: DFFE, DFFE / South African Government, Absolute Exotics SA (secondary)

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

DFFE confirmed (June 2026): you cannot breed or multiply Rattus rattus unless it is for research purposes. There is no hobbyist/companion breeding permit; the only permits available for the species are research permits. This makes captive propagation by a private keeper effectively prohibited.

Sources: DFFE / South African Government

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

DFFE confirmed (June 2026) that selling or giving away Rattus rattus is not permitted ('No'); as with breeding, the only permits issued for the species are for research. Note the practical contrast: the fancy rat (R. norvegicus) carries the same island Cat 1b listing yet is openly traded — a species-not-domestication inconsistency to raise in the public-comment process.

Sources: DFFE / South African Government, African Journal of Ecology (Wiley)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

DFFE confirmed (June 2026) that you may transport Rattus rattus only for research purposes, so there is no ordinary pet-transport pathway. Inter-provincial movement also implicates provincial transport permits, and international import is handled separately by the National Department of Agriculture (State Veterinary import permit + health protocol). Never release a roof rat.

Sources: DFFE / South African Government, Absolute Exotics SA (secondary), National Dept of Agriculture (DALRRD)

Restrictions & responsibilities

DFFE (the AIS Issuing Authority) has confirmed that, for a privately kept Rattus rattus, you may keep one as a pet without a permit, but you may NOT breed/multiply or sell/give them away except under a research permit. There is no companion/hobbyist breeding or sales permit for the species. Never release a roof rat.
  • If your purpose is genuine research, apply to DFFE Biodiversity Risk Management for a research permit
  • Otherwise: keeping is allowed, but do not breed, sell, or give the animal away

Where: DFFE Biodiversity Risk Management (AIS Issuing Authority)

Source: DFFE / South African Government

No NATIONAL permit is needed to keep a roof rat as a pet (DFFE confirmed). But some provinces (Western Cape, Eastern Cape, Northern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State) may require a general 'wild animal in captivity' permit; the other four do not. Confirm with your provincial environmental department.
  • Check your provincial conservation authority (e.g., CapeNature in the Western Cape) on whether a captivity permit is required

Where: Provincial environmental department / conservation authority

Source: Absolute Exotics SA (secondary)

Transport of Rattus rattus is permitted only for research purposes (DFFE). International import is separately handled by the National Department of Agriculture's State Veterinary Import Permit (apply before shipment) + health certificate. Inter-provincial movement also implicates provincial transport permits.

Where: DFFE (research transport); National Dept of Agriculture / DALRRD (import); provincial authority (inter-provincial)

Source: National Dept of Agriculture (DALRRD), Absolute Exotics SA (secondary)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in South Africa
⏳ Time-sensitive: Act when the NEMBA Alien & Invasive Species amendment is gazetted for public comment (expected 2026 per DFFE).

South Africa’s environment department (DFFE) confirmed (June 2026) that an amendment to the NEMBA Alien and Invasive Species lists is in Law-Reform review and will be gazetted for public comment.

The ask: When the amended AIS list is gazetted for comment, submit a comment asking that domesticated R. rattus kept as pets be handled distinctly from wild invasive populations — for example a keeping/permit pathway rather than a blanket prohibition.

Where the lever really is: This is executive rulemaking with a built-in public-comment step — so the lever is the gazette comment window (and a letter to DFFE’s biodiversity directorate), not Parliament.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Dept. of Forestry, Fisheries & the Environment (DFFE) — Biodiversity / AIS (public comment) — AISpermits@dffe.gov.za
    DFFE runs the AIS listing and its comment process; the official comment address is published with the gazette notice.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment (DFFE), Biodiversity,

I am commenting on the amendment to the NEMBA Alien and Invasive Species lists.

I ask that domesticated roof rats (Rattus rattus) kept as pets be handled distinctly from wild invasive populations. Captive-bred pet roof rats are tame, kept indoors in secure cages, and never released. Rather than a blanket prohibition, a keeping or permit pathway would meet the conservation aim without penalising responsible pet owners.

Please consider this distinction in the amended list.

Sincerely,
[Your name]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • NEMBA Alien & Invasive Species Lists (GG 43726, GN 1003, 18 Sep 2020) — R. rattus Category 1b — DFFE
  • NEMBA Alien & Invasive Species Regulations (GG 43735, GN 1020, 2020) — s.71 restricted activities — DFFE / South African Government
  • Genetic diversity of rodent species sold in South African pet shops (Afr. J. Ecol. 2022) — fancy rat openly traded — African Journal of Ecology (Wiley)
  • Province-by-province exotic-pet permit overview (some provinces require captivity permits) — Absolute Exotics SA (secondary)
  • Traveling with an exotic pet in South Africa — inter-provincial transport permit — Absolute Exotics SA (secondary)
  • DALRRD — South African Veterinary Import Permit application process — National Dept of Agriculture (DALRRD)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, black rat, roof rat, house rat, swartrot, dakrot.
