item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Alberta? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Canada › Alberta

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Alberta-specific rules; Canada’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Alberta is silent. See Canada.

Summary. Alberta is the strictest jurisdiction in Canada — and one of the strictest anywhere. Under the Agricultural Pests Act and the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation, the ENTIRE genus Rattus is a declared pest, and the law prohibits the import, purchase, sale, transport, and possession of any live rat. There is NO exemption for 'fancy', tame, or captive-bred rats. The only legal route is a special Ministerial permit reserved for accredited research institutions, zoos, or approved labs. A pet roof rat in Alberta may be seized and destroyed, and the keeper fined. Alberta has defended its 'rat-free' status since 1950.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

The Agricultural Pests Act declares the whole genus Rattus a pest, and possession of a live rat by a private citizen is unlawful — Alberta enforces a zero-tolerance 'rat-free' policy. There is explicitly no exemption for fancy, tame, or domesticated rats; a single caged pet is treated as an unacceptable escape risk. Wild sightings are reported to the 310-RATS line and eradicated.

Sources: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Breeding requires possession, which is prohibited, and the statute separately forbids the purchase, sale, or distribution of a declared pest. There is no legal hobby or commercial breeding of rats in Alberta.

Sources: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling, giving, or otherwise distributing a live rat is expressly prohibited as dealing in a declared pest. No pet-trade layer exists for rats in Alberta.

Sources: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Transporting a live rat into or within Alberta is prohibited except under a highly restricted Ministerial permit (research institutions, zoos, approved labs only). Whether a non-resident may drive a securely caged pet rat continuously THROUGH Alberta without stopping is not clearly addressed in the published rules — we have asked the province to clarify. Treat any presence of a rat in Alberta as prohibited unless you hold a permit.

Sources: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

Restrictions & responsibilities

The only lawful way to possess, breed, or transport a rat in Alberta is a special permit issued by the Minister of Agriculture, available only to accredited research institutions, major zoos, or government-approved laboratories — not to private pet keepers.
  • Pet keeping is not permitted — there is no pet-owner permit

Where: Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation (Ministerial permit)

Source: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

If you move to Alberta, you cannot bring a pet rat with you. Rehome it responsibly before relocating; do not transport it into the province. Rat sightings are reported to 310-RATS (310-7287) and acted on.

Source: Government of Alberta

Alberta's only legal route to hold any Rattus is a Ministerial Form-6 permit (AR 184/2001 s.11) limited to research facilities, zoos, and inspectors — no private/hobby pathway. Even the fancy rat (R. norvegicus) is prohibited for private keeping.

Forms: AR 184/2001 Form 6 — Ministerial permit to keep rats (research/zoo/inspector only) · Where: Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation — Inspection and Investigation Section

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Alberta. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Alberta

Alberta is one of the only places on Earth with a true, total ban on keeping any pet rat. Under the Agricultural Pests Act (RSA 2000, c. A-8) and the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation (AR 184/2001), the ENTIRE genus Rattus — every rat species, including the ordinary tame "fancy" pet rat (Rattus norvegicus) and the roof rat (Rattus rattus) — is a declared agricultural pest. The Government of Alberta states plainly: "It is illegal to own pet rats in Alberta." Possession, import, purchase, sale, transport, and breeding of any live rat are all prohibited. The only permit (a Ministerial permit under AR 184/2001) is reserved for accredited research institutions, zoos, and government labs — there is no private or hobby pathway, not even for a single captive-bred, tame rat kept indoors in a cage. Penalties can reach $5,000 per animal, and a pet rat found in the province can be seized and destroyed. This ban is the backbone of Alberta's 75-year "rat-free" status, and it makes no distinction between a wild invasive rat and a domesticated companion animal that has never lived outdoors.

The ask: Ask the Legislative Assembly (your MLA) to amend the Agricultural Pests Act / Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation to create a narrow, well-defined exemption for domesticated, captive-bred pet rats kept indoors under reasonable conditions (for example: spayed/neutered or single-sex housing, secure escape-proof caging, microchipping or registration, and a ban on outdoor release) — distinct from Alberta's wild-rat eradication program, which would continue unchanged. Be clear and honest about what this is NOT: do not ask the rat-control program or Alberta Agriculture to "make an exception," because that office is correctly applying a law it cannot rewrite. The change has to come from the Legislature.

Where the lever really is: This is branch (b): the problem is the LAW AS WRITTEN, not a bureaucracy misreading it. The Agricultural Pests Act and AR 184/2001 declare the whole genus Rattus a pest at the statutory/regulatory level, and the rat-control agency is correctly and deliberately applying that prohibition — the Government of Alberta's own website confirms "It is illegal to own pet rats in Alberta." There is no exemption list a tame or captive-bred rat could be added to, and the sole permit category is statutorily confined to research/zoo/lab operators. Therefore appealing to the agency (rats@gov.ab.ca / 310-FARM) will NOT change anything — that line exists to report and eradicate rats, and the staff there have no authority to legalize pet keeping. The only lever that can change this is the Legislature: amending the Act or the Regulation to carve out a domesticated-pet-rat exemption. Practically, that means writing to your MLA (and, where relevant, the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation in their legislative/policy capacity). The single narrow thing the agency CAN properly answer is a factual clarification (e.g., whether a non-resident may transit a securely caged pet rat through the province) — included only as a secondary, agency-appropriate touchpoint, not as the reform lever.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Legislative Assembly of Alberta — Members of the Legislative Assembly directory (Find Your MLA / Member Contact list) (legislature) — official contact page
    The total ban is set in statute (Agricultural Pests Act) and regulation (AR 184/2001). Only the Legislature can amend it, so your own MLA is the correct first touchpoint. This official directory lists all 87 MLAs by name and constituency with individual contact pages and a downloadable contact list, letting you reach the representative who can raise or sponsor a change.
  • Legislative Assembly of Alberta — Find Your MLA by riding (Elections Alberta MLA search) (legislature) — official contact page
    Use this official Elections Alberta tool to identify exactly which MLA represents your address/riding before you write, so your letter reaches your own representative (constituent letters carry the most weight).
  • Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation — Rat Control Program inbox (factual clarification ONLY, not policy change) (executive / agency) — rats@gov.ab.ca
    Included only for a narrow factual question this office can legitimately answer — e.g., whether a non-resident may transit a securely caged pet Rattus through Alberta. Do NOT use this channel to request legalization: the rat-control program is correctly enforcing the statute and cannot amend it. (Phone: 310-FARM in Alberta / 403-742-7901 outside.)

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Please amend the Agricultural Pests Act to allow domesticated pet rats

Dear [MLA name / Member for [constituency]],

I am a constituent writing about Alberta's total ban on keeping pet rats. Under the Agricultural Pests Act and the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation (AR 184/2001), the entire genus Rattus is a declared pest, so even a tame, captive-bred pet rat kept indoors is illegal.

I fully support Alberta's program against wild, invasive rats. But the current law makes no distinction between a wild rat and a domesticated companion animal that is captive-bred, hand-tame, housed in a secure escape-proof cage, kept entirely indoors, and never released. These animals pose no threat to the rat-free program.

Because this is set in statute and regulation, only the Legislature can fix it — the rat-control office is simply applying the law. I respectfully ask you to support amending the Act/Regulation to create a narrow exemption for domesticated pet rats kept under reasonable conditions (secure caging, no outdoor release, single-sex or altered housing), while Alberta's wild-rat eradication continues unchanged.

Thank you for considering this. I would welcome your reply.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your address / constituency]
[Your email]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Agricultural Pests Act (RSA 2000, c. A-8) — declares the genus Rattus a pest — Government of Alberta
  • Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation (AR 184/2001) — Government of Alberta
  • Rat prevention and control / rat-free Alberta — Government of Alberta

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

Last reviewed 2026-06-06. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in British Columbia? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Canada › British Columbia

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the British Columbia-specific rules; Canada’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where British Columbia is silent. See Canada.

Summary. In British Columbia, keeping a tame, captive-bred roof rat is legal. BC's Wildlife Act protects native and some designated non-native 'wildlife', but the Designation and Exemption Regulation (B.C. Reg. 168/90), section 8(h), exempts a non-native animal that 'is tame and kept in captivity for the use of man'. Rattus rattus is not a Controlled Alien Species (that list is for dangerous exotics like big cats and venomous snakes), so a captive-bred pet roof rat qualifies for the exemption and needs no provincial permit to keep, breed, or sell. Feral roof rats (e.g., on Haida Gwaii) are managed as invasive wildlife — never release one.

Confirmed by the agencies.
  • FrontCounter BC, Provincial Contact Centre, B.C. Ministry of Water, Land and Resource Stewardship (written reply June 2026): 'Rattus rattus is not designated as wildlife under the Wildlife Act. A provincial wildlife permit would not be required.' Keeping a roof rat therefore needs no provincial wildlife permit in British Columbia. (Releasing one remains prohibited — feral roof rats are managed as invasive wildlife; never release.)

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

FrontCounter BC (B.C. Ministry of Water, Land & Resource Stewardship) confirmed in writing (June 2026) that Rattus rattus is not designated as wildlife under the Wildlife Act, so no provincial wildlife permit is required to keep one. This matches the regulation: section 8(h) of the Designation and Exemption Regulation (B.C. Reg. 168/90) exempts a non-native animal that is tame and kept in captivity for human use, and R. rattus is not a Controlled Alien Species — so a captive-bred, tame roof rat needs no provincial captive-wildlife permit.

Sources: Province of British Columbia, Province of British Columbia

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

As an exempt tame species not listed as a Controlled Alien Species, breeding is legal without a provincial permit — subject to municipal bylaws, business licensing, and BC's animal-welfare law.

Sources: Province of British Columbia

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling or giving a tame, exempt roof rat is legal at the provincial level, subject to municipal pet-shop/business licensing and consumer-protection rules. No provincial dealer permit is required.

Sources: Province of British Columbia

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Moving a tame, securely-contained roof rat within BC is not restricted by provincial wildlife authorities, provided it is not released into the wild. Interprovincial transport follows the destination province's rules (you cannot bring one into Alberta).

Sources: Province of British Columbia

Restrictions & responsibilities

Releasing a roof rat into the wild is strictly prohibited under BC's ecological-protection rules — feral R. rattus are managed and eradicated as invasive wildlife (e.g., on the Haida Gwaii archipelago). Keep pets securely contained and rehome responsibly; never release.

Source: Province of British Columbia

Commercial breeding or selling is governed by municipal business licensing and zoning plus BC's Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act care standards — check your municipality.
  • Check municipal business-licensing/zoning if breeding or selling commercially

Where: Your municipality · Fees: Set locally

Source: Province of British Columbia

  • Wildlife Act — Designation and Exemption Regulation (B.C. Reg. 168/90), s. 8(h) tame-captive exemption — Province of British Columbia

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Ontario? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Canada › Ontario

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Ontario-specific rules; Canada’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Ontario is silent. See Canada.

Summary. Ontario does not regulate roof rats at the provincial level — they are legal by default. Rattus rattus is not listed as prohibited or restricted under the Invasive Species Act, and as a non-native species it falls outside the Fish and Wildlife Conservation Act (which covers native 'game' and 'specially protected' wildlife). So keeping, breeding, selling, and transporting roof rats is unregulated by the province. The real rules are MUNICIPAL: city bylaws on exotic/pet animals, breeder/pet-shop licensing, animal limits, and the Provincial Animal Welfare Services Act (PAWS) care standards.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Rattus rattus is not listed under the Invasive Species Act (unlike wild pigs or nutria) and is not native 'game' or 'specially protected' wildlife under the Fish and Wildlife Conservation Act, 1997 — so it is outside the Ministry of Natural Resources' regulatory scope. No provincial permit is needed to keep one. Your municipality may regulate exotic pets or cap animal numbers.

Sources: Government of Ontario, Government of Ontario

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

The province has no jurisdiction over rat breeding. Breeding is governed by municipal bylaws, animal-control rules, and the Provincial Animal Welfare Services Act (PAWS) care standards. Operating commercially in a residential zone often needs a municipal kennel/pet-shop licence.

Sources: Government of Ontario

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling or giving roof rats is unregulated provincially. A retail storefront needs the municipality's pet-shop / commercial-establishment licence; private face-to-face placement and giveaways do not.

Sources: Government of Ontario, Government of Ontario

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

No provincial permit is required to move roof rats within or across Ontario's borders. Interprovincial transport is subject to the destination province's rules (you cannot bring one into Alberta).

Sources: Government of Ontario

Restrictions & responsibilities

The binding layer in Ontario is municipal: many cities license commercial breeders/pet shops, cap the number of animals per dwelling, or regulate 'exotic' pets. Check your city's animal bylaw. The Provincial Animal Welfare Services Act (PAWS) sets enforceable minimum care standards everywhere.
  • Check your municipality's animal/exotic-pet bylaw and any breeder/pet-shop licensing
  • Meet PAWS minimum care standards

Where: Your municipality; Animal Welfare Services (PAWS) · Fees: Set locally

Source: Government of Ontario

Never release a roof rat outdoors — it is a non-native species and release is both ecologically harmful and an animal-welfare concern. Rehome responsibly.

Source: Government of Ontario

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Quebec? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Canada › Quebec

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Quebec-specific rules; Canada’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Quebec is silent. See Canada.

Summary. In Quebec, keeping, breeding, and selling a roof rat is legal and largely unregulated at the provincial level: Rattus rattus is not a Schedule 1 prohibited species under the Règlement sur les animaux en captivité, so no captivity permit is needed for ordinary hobbyists. The one catch is IMPORT: section 13 requires anyone bringing an animal into Quebec to file a prior written import notice — and while the regulation explicitly exempts the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) and the house mouse from that notice, it does NOT name Rattus rattus. So importing a roof rat into Quebec appears to require a notice the fancy rat is spared. Captive facilities must also meet the regulation's housing standards.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Neither Rattus rattus nor Rattus norvegicus is listed in Schedule 1 (prohibited/restricted species) of the Règlement sur les animaux en captivité, so keeping a roof rat as a pet needs no provincial captivity permit for normal hobbyist numbers.

Sources: Gouvernement du Québec, Gouvernement du Québec

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Breeding is legal without a wildlife permit, but facilities must meet the regulation's housing standards (enclosures free of injury hazards, allowing the animal to avoid its own waste, kept dry and clean). Commercial operations also need ordinary business licensing.

Sources: Gouvernement du Québec, Gouvernement du Québec

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling or giving roof rats is legal at the provincial level; commercial sale requires ordinary business licensing and compliance with the captive-animal housing standards. No species-specific dealer permit is required.

Sources: Gouvernement du Québec

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Section 13 of the Règlement sur les animaux en captivité requires a prior written import NOTICE to the Ministry (MELCCFP) — stating the species' scientific name, origin, planned import date, and place of captivity — before bringing an animal into Quebec. The regulation explicitly EXEMPTS the Norway rat (rat surmulot, R. norvegicus) and house mouse (Mus musculus) from this notice when imported by an individual for personal purposes, but it does NOT list Rattus rattus. On the face of the text, importing a roof rat into Quebec requires filing that notice. We have asked the Ministry to confirm. (This is a notice/declaration, not a discretionary permit.)

Sources: Gouvernement du Québec, Gouvernement du Québec

Restrictions & responsibilities

Before importing a roof rat into Quebec, file the section 13 import notice with MELCCFP (scientific name, origin, date, place of captivity). The fancy rat (R. norvegicus) and house mouse are exempt from this notice; R. rattus is not named, so file the notice unless the Ministry confirms otherwise.
  • Send the written import notice to MELCCFP before the animal arrives
  • Include the binomial name, origin, planned date, and place of captivity

Where: Ministère de l'Environnement, de la Lutte contre les changements climatiques, de la Faune et des Parcs (MELCCFP)

Source: Gouvernement du Québec, Gouvernement du Québec

Housing standards apply to anyone keeping animals in captivity: enclosures must prevent injury and aggression, let the animal avoid contact with its feces, and be kept dry and clean. These matter most for breeders and larger setups.

Source: Gouvernement du Québec

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Quebec

In Quebec, keeping, breeding, and giving or selling a pet roof rat (Rattus rattus, the "rat noir" / "rat des toits") is legal and needs no provincial captivity permit — the species is not on the prohibited list (Annexe I) of the Règlement sur les animaux en captivité (C-61.1, r. 5.1). There is one snag, and it is narrow. Section 13 of that regulation requires a person to file a prior written import notice with the Ministry (MELCCFP) before bringing certain captive animals into Quebec. The regulation explicitly EXEMPTS the fancy/Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus, "rat surmulot") and the house mouse (Mus musculus) from that notice when an individual imports them for personal purposes — but it does NOT name Rattus rattus. So on the face of the text, a tame domestic roof rat is treated more strictly than its near-identical cousin the fancy rat. This looks like a drafting oversight (roof rats are simply rarer in the pet trade), not a deliberate choice to single them out.

The ask: Ask the Ministry (MELCCFP) to do one of two simple things: (1) confirm in writing that the section 13 import-notice exemption already granted to the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) and house mouse is understood to extend in practice to the domestic roof rat (Rattus rattus) kept as a pet; or, better, (2) add Rattus rattus to the same section 13 exemption so the regulation treats the two domestic rat species the same. This is a one-line, common-sense fix that closes a paperwork gap — it does not ask Quebec to legalize anything new, because keeping roof rats is already legal.

Where the lever really is: This is branch (a): the BUREAUCRACY / drafting gap, and the correct lever is the AGENCY (MELCCFP) — either a written clarification or a one-species addition to the existing section 13 exemption. It is NOT a "law as written" prohibition. Concretely for Quebec: keeping/breeding/selling roof rats is already legal because Rattus rattus is absent from the prohibited-species schedule. The only friction is that section 13's import-notice exemption names Rattus norvegicus and Mus musculus but omits Rattus rattus. That omission is exactly the kind of thing an agency can fix or interpret — it is not the legislature having deliberately banned or listed the species. The Ministry administers C-61.1, r. 5.1 and can issue a written interpretation of the exemption's scope, and regulation amendments here are made by government/ministerial rulemaking rather than by a statute of the National Assembly. So the productive move is to write the agency, not to lobby an MNA. (If the Ministry were ever to respond that the omission is deliberate and it must apply the notice as written, the fallback would be a rulemaking/prepublication window — but there is no open window now, and there is no statutory list of the National Assembly to repeal here, so the legislature is not the lever.)

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Ministère de l'Environnement, de la Lutte contre les changements climatiques, de la Faune et des Parcs (MELCCFP) — official information-request form (Secteur de la faune et des parcs) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Official online intake for written questions to the Ministry; has a wildlife-and-parks routing category, so it lands the section 13 exemption question with the unit that administers the captive-animals regulation. Best first channel because it creates a tracked written record.
  • MELCCFP — Wildlife customer service (Service à la clientèle, secteur de la faune) (executive / agency) — renseignements.faune@environnement.gouv.qc.ca
    Verified official wildlife inquiry inbox (also listed on the quebec.ca general-contact page, phone 1-877-346-6763). Use it to email the same clarification/exemption request directly to the faune team.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Section 13 import notice — exemption for the domestic roof rat (Rattus rattus)

To the Wildlife sector, MELCCFP,

I am writing about a small but real inconsistency in the Regulation respecting animals in captivity (C-61.1, r. 5.1). Keeping a domestic roof rat (Rattus rattus) as a pet is legal in Quebec — the species is not on the prohibited schedule. However, section 13's exemption from the prior import notice names the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) and the house mouse, but does not name Rattus rattus, even though the two are kept identically as pets.

These are captive-bred, tame animals, kept indoors as companions, never taken from or released into the wild. The point is the species, not whether it is domesticated — the roof rat is simply the less common cousin of the familiar fancy rat.

Could you please (1) confirm in writing whether the section 13 exemption is understood to apply in practice to a domestic Rattus rattus imported by an individual for personal purposes, or (2) add Rattus rattus to that same exemption? This is a one-line fix that treats the two domestic rat species consistently.

Thank you for your time.

[Your name]
[Your municipality / region]
[Your email]
Français
Objet: Avis d'importation de l'article 13 — dispense pour le rat noir domestique (Rattus rattus)

Au secteur de la faune, MELCCFP,

Je vous écris au sujet d'une incohérence mineure mais réelle dans le Règlement sur les animaux en captivité (C-61.1, r. 5.1). Garder un rat noir domestique (Rattus rattus) comme animal de compagnie est légal au Québec — l'espèce ne figure pas à l'annexe des espèces prohibées. Or, la dispense d'avis d'importation prévue à l'article 13 nomme le rat surmulot (Rattus norvegicus) et la souris commune, mais ne nomme pas le Rattus rattus, alors que les deux sont gardés de façon identique comme animaux de compagnie.

Il s'agit d'animaux nés en captivité, apprivoisés, gardés à l'intérieur comme compagnons, jamais prélevés dans la nature ni relâchés. L'enjeu tient à l'espèce, et non à la domestication: le rat noir est simplement le cousin moins répandu du rat surmulot bien connu.

Pourriez-vous (1) confirmer par écrit si la dispense de l'article 13 s'applique en pratique au Rattus rattus domestique importé par un particulier à des fins personnelles, ou (2) ajouter le Rattus rattus à cette même dispense ? Il s'agit d'une correction d'une seule ligne qui traiterait de façon cohérente les deux espèces de rats domestiques.

Je vous remercie de votre attention.

[Votre nom]
[Votre municipalité / région]
[Votre courriel]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Regulation respecting animals in captivity (C-61.1, r. 5.1) — English (s.13 import notice; R. norvegicus exemption) — Gouvernement du Québec
  • Règlement sur les animaux en captivité (C-61.1, r. 5.1) — français — Gouvernement du Québec

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Saskatchewan? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Canada › Saskatchewan

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Saskatchewan-specific rules; Canada’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Saskatchewan is silent. See Canada.

Summary. Saskatchewan is the clearest 'yes' in Canada. The province runs an aggressive feral-rat eradication program (landowners must destroy wild rats), yet it ALSO explicitly lists the Black Rat (Rattus rattus) on its official Captive Wildlife allowed list. Because the species is named on the allowed list, residents may keep, breed, and sell captive R. rattus as pets with NO captive-wildlife licence and no provincial registration. Large-scale breeding can still trigger municipal zoning or business-licensing rules.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

The Black Rat (Rattus rattus) is explicitly named on Saskatchewan's Captive Wildlife allowed list (under The Wildlife Act, 1998 and the Captive Wildlife Regulations, 2021), which exempts listed species from the captive-wildlife licence requirement. So a resident may keep a captive-bred roof rat as a pet with no provincial licence — even though feral rats must be destroyed under the province's pest-control duty.

Sources: Government of Saskatchewan, Government of Saskatchewan / SVMA

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Because the species is on the allowed list, small-scale keeping and breeding are unregulated by wildlife law. A large commercial operation may meet a municipal 'commercial wildlife farm' / kennel definition or local business-licensing and zoning rules, so check your municipality if breeding at scale.

Sources: Government of Saskatchewan, Government of Saskatchewan / SVMA

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling or giving an allowed-list captive species is permitted; only large-scale commercial sale brings municipal pet-shop/business licensing into play. No provincial dealer licence is required for an allowed species.

Sources: Government of Saskatchewan

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Transport of a captive R. rattus within and into Saskatchewan is legal for an allowed-list species. Interprovincial transport is legal but subject to the destination province's rules — note you cannot transport one into (or, unresolved, through) Alberta.

Sources: Government of Saskatchewan

Restrictions & responsibilities

Feral rats are a different matter: under the Pest Control Act / pest declarations, every landowner and occupant has an affirmative duty to destroy and prevent the spread of wild rats. This applies to feral animals, not to your securely-caged, captive-bred pet — but never release a pet rat.

Source: Government of Saskatchewan

Operating a large-scale breeding or sales facility may require a municipal business licence and must comply with zoning and provincial animal-welfare standards, even though the species itself needs no wildlife licence.
  • Check your municipality's business-licensing and zoning rules if breeding/selling at scale

Where: Your municipality · Fees: Set locally

Source: Government of Saskatchewan / SVMA

  • Saskatchewan Pests Declaration / Pest Control Act — feral-rat eradication duty — Government of Saskatchewan

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Alaska? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Alaska

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the Alaska-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Alaska is silent. See United States.

Summary. Alaska is the most restrictive state in the nation for the roof rat — it's flatly PROHIBITED. Alaska uses a 'clean list' (whitelist): only species on 5 AAC 92.029 may be kept without a permit, and the Dept of Fish & Game is barred from issuing a permit for anything not on it. The ONLY rat on the list is the albino lab Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus var. albinus); Rattus rattus appears nowhere. On top of that, 5 AAC 92.141 makes it unlawful to harbor or transport live Muridae rodents (which includes the roof rat) — Alaska runs active 'rat-free' eradication programs. Anchorage adds a city-wide ban on the entire genus Rattus. Keeping/breeding/selling/importing are all prohibited (a class A misdemeanor, up to $25,000).

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Alaska's clean list (5 AAC 92.029) permits only listed species; the only rat on it is 'White rat Rattus norvegicus Var. albinus.' R. rattus is absent, and ADF&G is legally precluded from issuing a possession permit for an unlisted species. Independently, 5 AAC 92.141 prohibits harboring live Muridae rodents (defined to include true rats — 5 AAC 92.990(49)). ADF&G guidance states only albino rats are legal pets. Prohibited.

Sources: Alaska Board of Game / ADF&G (via Cornell LII), Alaska Dept of Fish & Game, Municipality of Anchorage / ADF&G

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Breeding presupposes lawful possession, which is barred; no permit pathway exists for unlisted species. The Municipality of Anchorage separately bans breeding any member of the genus Rattus without a Health Director research permit (AMC 16.90.030).

Sources: Alaska Board of Game / ADF&G (via Cornell LII), Municipality of Anchorage / ADF&G

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

The clean-list framework bars buying/selling/trading unlisted species, and giving one away facilitates unlawful possession by the recipient. Anchorage additionally bans import/buy/sell of any Rattus (AMC 16.90.030).

Sources: Alaska Board of Game / ADF&G (via Cornell LII), Municipality of Anchorage / ADF&G

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

5 AAC 92.141 makes it unlawful to enter Alaska (or operate any conveyance) while harboring live Muridae rodents — the roof rat is named in ADF&G guidance as covered. Import is also barred by the clean list (unlisted species can't be imported; no permit can issue). Class A misdemeanor (up to 1 yr / $25,000). Never release.

Sources: Alaska Dept of Fish & Game, Alaska Board of Game / ADF&G (via Cornell LII)

Restrictions & responsibilities

The roof rat is prohibited statewide in Alaska (clean-list exclusion + Muridae harboring ban), and Anchorage bans the whole genus Rattus. Do NOT bring one to Alaska — only the albino lab Norway rat is legal (and even that needs a permit in Anchorage). Violations are a class A misdemeanor (up to 1 year / $25,000). Never release.

Where: Alaska Dept of Fish & Game — Wildlife Permits

Source: Alaska Board of Game / ADF&G (via Cornell LII), Alaska Dept of Fish & Game

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Alaska. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Alaska
⏳ Time-sensitive: No proposal window is open right now — the Board of Game's site currently shows it is not accepting proposals (the 2026/2027 cycle deadline of May 1, 2026 has passed and covered only certain regions). The next realistic opportunity to file a statewide clean-list proposal is the upcoming statewide cycle, with proposals expected to be due around May 1, 2027. Watch the Board of Game site for the official "Call for Proposals" announcement (usually issued by January) and the online submission portal that opens with it. In the meantime, you can ask to join the Board's notification list so you are alerted the moment the window opens.

Alaska is the strictest state in the country for the pet roof rat (Rattus rattus). Alaska runs a "clean list" (a whitelist): under regulation 5 AAC 92.029, only the species on that list may be kept, and the only rat on it is the albino lab Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus var. albinus). The roof rat is not on the list at all. By law, the Department of Fish & Game is FORBIDDEN from issuing a possession permit for any species the list leaves off — so there is no permit you can apply for. On top of that, a separate rule (5 AAC 92.141) bans harboring or transporting live Muridae rodents (which includes the roof rat), and the Municipality of Anchorage bans the entire genus Rattus. The result: keeping, breeding, selling, giving away, importing, or transporting a pet roof rat in Alaska is prohibited and is a class A misdemeanor (up to one year and/or $25,000). This is not a case of the agency misreading the law — the agency is applying it exactly as written. The list itself is the obstacle.

The ask: The fix is to get captive-bred Rattus rattus ADDED to the clean list (5 AAC 92.029) — exactly as the domesticated albino Norway rat already is. That is a regulation change, and the body with the power to make it is the Alaska Board of Game, through its public proposal-and-comment process. The realistic path is to file (or support) a Board of Game proposal in the next statewide cycle asking the Board to add the captive-bred, domesticated roof rat to the list as a permitted pet, documenting that it meets the same safety criteria the albino Norway rat already satisfies. Asking ADF&G directly will NOT work — by statute they cannot permit an unlisted species, so the request has to go to the Board that controls the list.

Where the lever really is: This is squarely branch (b): the obstacle is the LAW/LIST AS WRITTEN, not an agency misreading. The Department of Fish & Game is applying 5 AAC 92.029 correctly — the regulation states in plain terms that if a species is not on the list, ADF&G is forbidden from issuing a possession permit for it. The roof rat simply is not on the list. So a letter, appeal, or permit request to ADF&G will go nowhere, because there is no discretion to grant: the agency is barred by the regulation itself. The only thing that changes this is amending the list, and the list is controlled by the Alaska Board of Game through its public rulemaking (proposal-and-comment) process. The key precedent is that the domesticated albino Norway rat IS on the list — proving the mechanism already exists to list a tame, captive-bred true rat, so the ask is "extend the same treatment to captive-bred Rattus rattus," not "carve out an exception." Therefore the lever is the LEGISLATIVE/RULEMAKING channel (Board of Game proposal + public comment), not an administrative appeal. (Note: even if listed statewide, Anchorage's separate genus-Rattus ban would still need a municipal fix — but the statewide list is the threshold issue and the right first target.)

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Alaska Board of Game — Proposal & Public Comment process (Boards Support Section) (public comment) — official contact page
    The Board of Game controls the 5 AAC 92.029 clean list and is the ONLY body that can add the roof rat to it. Its public proposal-and-comment process is the correct lever. Submit a proposal (or comment) through the official Board of Game portal when the Call for Proposals opens; until then, ask the Boards Support Section to add you to the notification list so you catch the next window.
  • Alaska Board of Game — regulatory proposal portal (boardofgame.adfg.alaska.gov) (public comment) — official contact page
    This is where the official proposal forms and the online submission option are posted once a Call for Proposals is issued, and where proposal books are opened for public comment. This is the channel through which a clean-list amendment for captive-bred Rattus rattus would actually be filed and commented on.
  • ADF&G Wildlife Permits / Possession program (executive / agency) — dfg.dwc.permits@alaska.gov
    Use this ONLY to request a written confirmation of the current status and to be pointed to the Board process — not as a place to win the change. By regulation this office cannot permit an unlisted species, so it cannot grant possession; a note here is useful to get the official statement in writing and to confirm the listing route, which strengthens a future Board proposal.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Alaska Board of Game / Boards Support Section,

I am writing about Alaska's clean list of animals that may be kept as pets, 5 AAC 92.029. I am asking the Board to add the captive-bred, domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) to that list as a permitted pet.

The domesticated albino Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus var. albinus) is already on the list. The pet roof rat is the same kind of animal: captive-bred for generations, hand-tame, kept entirely indoors as a companion, and never released to the wild. The distinction in the regulation is by species, not by whether the animal is domesticated — yet a tame, captive-bred roof rat poses no more risk than the listed lab rat.

Because the Department cannot issue a permit for a species the list leaves off, the only path is to amend the list, which is the Board's authority. I respectfully request that captive-bred Rattus rattus be added to 5 AAC 92.029, subject to the same indoor-only, no-release conditions, and I ask to be notified when the next Call for Proposals opens so I may submit a formal proposal.

Thank you for your consideration.

[Your name]
[Your city/region, Alaska]
[Your email / phone]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • 5 AAC 92.029 — Permit for Possessing Live Game (clean list; only 'White rat Rattus norvegicus Var. albinus') — Alaska Board of Game / ADF&G (via Cornell LII)
  • 5 AAC 92.141 + 92.990(49) — Muridae rodent transport/harboring prohibition (incl. roof rat) — Alaska Dept of Fish & Game
  • Anchorage Municipal Code 16.90.030 — genus Rattus banned except research permit — Municipality of Anchorage / ADF&G

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Alabama? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Alabama

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Alabama-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Alabama is silent. See United States.

Summary. Alabama doesn't name Rattus rattus anywhere, and the whole question turns on one classification: is your captive-bred roof rat a 'domestic animal' or a 'wild rodent'? State health rules (ADPH r. 420-4-4-.01(6)) define a 'domestic animal' as one bred through human association to the point of genetic changes in temperament/color/conformation — so a pedigreed, captive-bred, color-mutation roof rat can qualify, and if it does, keeping/breeding/selling are unregulated at the state level. If it's instead treated as a 'wild rodent,' the wildlife rule (Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.26) is harsh: it bans importing a wild rodent from out of state AND bans transporting one within the state at all (even an Alabama-born animal) except by a licensed game-breeder. There's no R. rattus-specific safe harbor, so the practical risk is an officer disagreeing that your animal is 'domestic.' Importing a domestic pet rat needs an electronic health certificate (eCVI); a 'semi-wild' classification adds a 10-day State-Veterinarian notice. Get a written ADCNR classification before importing or selling.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

No Alabama statute names Rattus rattus, and there is no state pet-rodent permit. Legality turns on classification: ADPH r. 420-4-4-.01(6) defines a 'domestic animal' as one bred through human association to a degree producing genetic changes (temperament/color/conformation) distinguishing it from wild animals of its species; 'wildlife' (r. 420-4-4-.01(12)) is everything else. A pedigreed, captive-bred, color-mutation roof rat can meet the 'domestic' test → keeping is unregulated, no permit. But if an officer deems it a 'wild rodent,' ADCNR r. 220-2-.26 bars possession of one imported from out of state (in-state-trapped wild rodents fall to unprotected-nongame rules but then can't be transported — see transport). No species-specific exemption names R. rattus, so the owner carries the evidentiary burden of domestication.

Sources: Alabama Dept of Conservation & Natural Resources, Alabama Dept of Public Health

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

Alabama has NO statewide commercial pet-breeder or small-rodent breeder license; if the animal is 'domestic,' non-commercial and hobby breeding are unregulated by the state. Commercial breeding is governed at the LOCAL/municipal level (e.g., the City of Gadsden's Commercial Breeder Permit + business license) — check your city/county. If the rat is instead classed as a 'wild rodent,' breeding it for transport/sale requires an ADCNR Game Breeder license (Code of Ala. §9-11-30; ~$250/yr non-cervid; facility inspections). Federally, USDA AWA exempts face-to-face/retail and small hobby sellers; the >4-breeding-female wholesale/sight-unseen threshold is the federal commercial demarcation (no Alabama state threshold).

Sources: City of Gadsden, Alabama, Alabama Legislature, Alabama Dept of Conservation & Natural Resources

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

Alabama has no state-level pet-dealer/pet-shop licensing act for domestic small animals; selling a 'domestic' pet rat needs only a standard retail revenue/business license for a storefront (Ala. Dept of Revenue 'Pet Shop' code), and private/free transfer is unregulated. BUT 220-2-.26 expressly prohibits the sale of a 'wild rodent' — so if the animal is classed wild, sale/transfer is banned. Everything again hinges on the domestic-vs-wild classification.

Sources: Alabama Dept of Conservation & Natural Resources, Alabama Dept of Revenue

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

INTRASTATE: ADCNR r. 220-2-.26(1) bans transporting a 'wild rodent' anywhere within Alabama — explicitly 'whether such member originated within or without the state' — EXCEPT by a properly licensed game-breeder. So if the animal is classed 'wild,' even a vet trip is unlawful; only the 'domestic animal' classification (or a game-breeder license) makes intrastate transport legal/unregulated. IMPORT (legal_with_permit): a domestic pet rat entering Alabama needs an electronic Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (eCVI via Global Vet Link or AgView; paper APHIS Form 7001 prohibited since 2019; valid 30 days). A 'semi-wild' classification additionally triggers a 10-day advance notice to the State Veterinarian (r. 80-3-6-.23); a 'wild rodent' classification = import banned. EXPORT: unregulated by Alabama (meet the destination state's rules; USFWS Form 3-177 for international, since the federal government treats R. rattus as wildlife). Never release. Net: 'restricted' because the binding intrastate ban + the import paperwork both turn on a classification the state hasn't settled for R. rattus.

Sources: Alabama Dept of Conservation & Natural Resources, Alabama Dept of Agriculture & Industries, Alabama Dept of Agriculture & Industries

Restrictions & responsibilities

Everything turns on whether your roof rat is a 'domestic animal' (ADPH genetic-change test, r. 420-4-4-.01(6)) or a 'wild rodent' (ADCNR r. 220-2-.26). If 'domestic': keeping/breeding/selling are state-unregulated and intrastate transport is legal; import needs an eCVI. If 'wild': import, sale, and ALL intrastate transport are barred except via a game-breeder license. Get a written ADCNR classification before importing or selling, and keep pedigree/photos documenting captive breeding + color mutations.
  • Ask ADCNR (WFF) in writing whether a pedigreed, captive-bred R. rattus is a 'domestic animal' or a restricted 'wild rodent' under 220-2-.26
  • For import: obtain an electronic CVI (Global Vet Link or AgView) from a USDA-accredited vet (valid 30 days); ask ADAI whether the 10-day State-Vet pre-report (80-3-6-.23) applies
  • For commercial breeding/sale: check your city/county for a local commercial-breeder permit + business license
  • Keep documentation (pedigree, photos of domestic color mutations) to support the 'domestic animal' classification

Where: Alabama DCNR (Wildlife & Freshwater Fisheries — classification); Alabama Dept of Agriculture & Industries (State Veterinarian — eCVI/import); local animal control (commercial breeding) · Fees: Game Breeder license ~$250/yr (only if 'wild')

Source: Alabama Dept of Conservation & Natural Resources, Alabama Dept of Public Health, Alabama Dept of Agriculture & Industries

Never release a roof rat — releasing any captive-raised/non-indigenous mammal into the wild in Alabama is illegal without express written ADCNR Commissioner permission, and it's ecologically harmful. Rehome responsibly.

Source: Alabama Dept of Conservation & Natural Resources

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Help change this

How to help in Alabama

Alabama law never mentions the roof rat (Rattus rattus) by name. There is no pet-rodent permit, no statewide ban, and no list that puts the species on or off limits. Instead, everything hinges on one classification question: is your captive-bred, tame pet roof rat a "domestic animal" or a "wild rodent"? Alabama's public-health rule (Ala. Admin. Code r. 420-4-4-.01(6)) defines a "domestic animal" as one bred through human association to the point of genetic changes in temperament, color, or conformation that distinguish it from wild animals of the same species. A pedigreed, captive-bred, color-mutation roof rat that has never lived in the wild fits that test. If it is "domestic," keeping, breeding, and giving it away are unregulated by the state, and you can take it to the vet freely. But Alabama's wildlife rule (Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.26) is harsh toward any "wild rodent": it bans importing one from out of state, bans selling one, and bans ALL transport within the state — even an Alabama-born animal, even a trip to the vet — except by a licensed game breeder. Because no Alabama rule names R. rattus as an exempt domestic pet, every owner carries the burden of proving their tame animal is "domestic," and a single officer could decide to treat the whole species as a restricted "wild rodent." That uncertainty is the problem.

The ask: Ask the Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources (Wildlife and Freshwater Fisheries Division) for a written interpretation confirming that a pedigreed, captive-bred Rattus rattus exhibiting domestication traits (genetic docility and domestic color mutations) is a "domestic animal" under ADPH Rule 420-4-4-.01(6) — and therefore exempt from the possession, sale, and intrastate-transport bans of r. 220-2-.26 — rather than a restricted "wild rodent." Even better, ask the agency to recognize pedigreed captive-bred Rattus as a category of domestic animal so individual owners no longer carry that burden case by case (New Jersey's genus-level exemption for Rattus is the model to cite). Separately, ask the Alabama Department of Agriculture and Industries (State Veterinarian) to confirm in writing that importing a captive-bred pet roof rat requires only a standard electronic Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (eCVI), not the 10-day "semi-wild animal" pre-report under r. 80-3-6-.23.

Where the lever really is: This is branch (a): a BUREAUCRATIC CLASSIFICATION problem, and the lever is the AGENCY — not the legislature. Here is why, concretely for Alabama. No statute and no administrative list names Rattus rattus. The restriction does not come from the species being placed on a prohibited list by the legislature; it comes entirely from how an agency might READ a generic, undefined phrase ("wild rodent" in r. 220-2-.26) against a separate definition of "domestic animal" (r. 420-4-4-.01(6)) that a captive-bred pet roof rat can already satisfy. The law as written actually contains the exemption we want — the "domestic animal" carve-out — so we are not asking anyone to change a law. We are asking the agency to apply the existing definition correctly and to say so in writing. That makes the correct tool a written agency interpretation / declaratory ruling from ADCNR Wildlife and Freshwater Fisheries (the body that administers r. 220-2-.26), optionally backed by ADPH (which owns the "domestic animal" definition) and ADAI's State Veterinarian (for the import question). A legislative campaign would be the wrong tool here: there is no bad statute to repeal and no species on a statutory list to remove. Conversely, the honest caveat in the other direction: if ADCNR responds that it categorically treats R. rattus as a "wild rodent" regardless of captive-breeding history, then it would be applying r. 220-2-.26 in a way the rule's text arguably permits, and at that point the durable fix shifts to a rulemaking petition (asking ADCNR to amend 220-2-.26 to add a captive-bred-Rattus exemption) rather than a one-off appeal — because you cannot argue an agency out of a reading the rule lets it hold; you have to change the rule. Start with the clarification request; escalate to a rulemaking petition only if the agency confirms a categorical "wild rodent" reading.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources — Wildlife and Freshwater Fisheries Division (official Contact Us page) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    ADCNR Wildlife and Freshwater Fisheries administers r. 220-2-.26, the rule that defines and restricts a 'wild rodent.' This is the agency that can issue the written classification we need (domestic vs. wild). The official contact page routes to the Wildlife Section and to enforcement/permits — the right institutional doors for an interpretation request. Start here.
  • Alabama DCNR — Wildlife Section official inbox (executive / agency) — DCNR.Wildlife@dcnr.alabama.gov
    Verified official, role-based Wildlife Section mailbox (not an individual's personal address) listed on the DCNR Contact Us page. Use it to send the written request for a classification interpretation of captive-bred Rattus rattus under r. 220-2-.26 and ADPH r. 420-4-4-.01(6).
  • Alabama Department of Agriculture and Industries — Animal Industries Division / State Veterinarian (official contact) (executive / agency) — ask-me@agi.alabama.gov
    ADAI's Office of the State Veterinarian governs animal import into Alabama (eCVI) and the 10-day 'semi-wild animal' pre-report (r. 80-3-6-.23). Ask here, in writing, whether a captive-bred pet roof rat is treated as a standard domestic pet (eCVI only) or as a semi-wild animal. The contact form and ask-me inbox are the verified official channels.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request for written classification — captive-bred domestic roof rat (Rattus rattus)

To the Wildlife and Freshwater Fisheries Division:

I am writing to request a written interpretation of how Alabama classifies a pedigreed, captive-bred pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) kept as a household companion. My concern is the difference between a "domestic animal" under ADPH Rule 420-4-4-.01(6) and a restricted "wild rodent" under Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.26.

These animals are captive-bred over many generations, tame, kept indoors only, and never released. They show the genetic changes in temperament and color that the "domestic animal" definition describes — much like the fancy rat sold in pet stores. The issue is not whether a wild-caught rat is wild; it is that a domesticated, captive-bred animal should be recognized as domestic.

Would you please confirm in writing that such an animal is a "domestic animal" — and therefore exempt from the possession, sale, and intrastate-transport provisions of r. 220-2-.26 — so an owner needs no game-breeder license simply to keep one or take it to a veterinarian? If feasible, I would also welcome the Division recognizing pedigreed, captive-bred Rattus as a domestic category, as some other states have done, so owners are not left to prove this animal by animal.

Thank you for your time and guidance.

[Your name]
[Your city, Alabama]
[Your email / phone]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.26 — Restrictions on possession, sale, importation & transport of certain animals ('wild rodent' clause; intrastate transport ban; game-breeder exception; Lacey Act incorporation) — Alabama Dept of Conservation & Natural Resources
  • Ala. Admin. Code r. 420-4-4-.01(6),(12) — ADPH definitions of 'Domestic animal' (genetic-change test) vs 'Wildlife' — Alabama Dept of Public Health
  • ADAI Import Requirements — mandatory electronic CVI (Global Vet Link / AgView); paper Form 7001 prohibited since 2019; 30-day validity — Alabama Dept of Agriculture & Industries
  • Ala. Admin. Code r. 80-3-6-.23 — Wild/semi-wild captive animals imported into Alabama (10-day State-Vet pre-report) — Alabama Dept of Agriculture & Industries
  • Code of Ala. 1975 §9-11-30 — Game Breeder License (required only if the animal is classed 'wild') — Alabama Legislature
  • City of Gadsden — Commercial Breeder Permit & Business License (example of LOCAL commercial-breeding regulation) — City of Gadsden, Alabama
  • Alabama Dept of Revenue — retail/'Pet Shop' license codes (storefront sale) — Alabama Dept of Revenue
  • ADPH Rabies Control & Bite Manual — rodent bites almost never require PEP; no rabies vaccine/quarantine mandate for pet rats — Alabama Dept of Public Health

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat, wild rodent, domestic animal.

Last reviewed 2026-06-08. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Arkansas? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Arkansas

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the Arkansas-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Arkansas is silent. See United States.

Summary. Arkansas uses a positive-list captive-wildlife system, and the roof rat falls through it. The Game & Fish Commission lists species as Unrestricted (R1.01), Permit-Required (R1.02), or Prohibited (R1.03) — and any species on NONE of the lists is 'prohibited by default until evaluated.' The fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is explicitly on the Unrestricted list and exempt from the possession/breeder/import rules; Rattus rattus is not on any list. So under a strict reading, keeping/breeding/selling/importing a roof rat is prohibited-by-default pending an AGFC species evaluation — another 'species-not-domestication' trap. There's a clear path: petition AGFC to add captive-bred R. rattus to the Unrestricted list (it poses no different risk than the fancy rat). We've queued that inquiry.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

AGFC's captive-wildlife framework (Code R1.00) classifies species as Unrestricted/Permit-Required/Prohibited and makes any UNLISTED species prohibited by default until evaluated. R. norvegicus is on the Unrestricted list (R1.01) and exempt from Code 09.02; Rattus rattus is on none of the lists, so a strict reading makes private possession prohibited-by-default pending an AGFC determination. (Genuine ambiguity: no enforcement names R. rattus and some sources treat 'rats' as unregulated pocket pets — but that rests on the R. norvegicus exemption.)

Sources: Arkansas Game & Fish Commission, Arkansas Game & Fish Commission, Arkansas Game & Fish Commission

Breeding   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

The Wildlife Breeder/Dealer Permit (Code 09.07) is available only for species on the Permit-Required list (R1.02); R. rattus isn't on it, and unlisted species are prohibited by default — so there is currently no breeding-permit pathway for the roof rat under the AGFC framework (unless AGFC determines it's outside their jurisdiction).

Sources: Arkansas Game & Fish Commission, Arkansas Game & Fish Commission

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Sale/transfer of captive wildlife runs through the same AGFC framework; R. norvegicus is exempt from Code 09.07/09.10 by name, R. rattus is not. As an unlisted (prohibited-by-default) species, commercial sale has no permit pathway; gifting falls under the same possession framework. Resolve the possession classification with AGFC first.

Sources: Arkansas Game & Fish Commission, Arkansas Game & Fish Commission

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Importing wildlife needs an AGFC Wildlife Importation Permit (Code 09.10) unless the species is Unrestricted (R1.01) — R. rattus isn't, creating a circular bar. Separately, the Dept of Agriculture (ALPC Rule 125.00) requires an entry permit + CVI for 'zoo, wild, and/or exotic animals' (rodents not explicitly named). In-state transport of a lawfully-held animal isn't separately restricted, but the possession question controls. Never release a roof rat.

Sources: Arkansas Game & Fish Commission, Arkansas Dept of Agriculture

Restrictions & responsibilities

Because R. rattus is unlisted on AGFC's captive-wildlife lists (only the fancy rat is Unrestricted), it is prohibited-by-default until AGFC evaluates it. Request a species determination from AGFC (captivewildlife@agfc.ar.gov) BEFORE acquiring one, and consider petitioning to add captive-bred R. rattus to the Unrestricted list. Never release one.
  • Email AGFC captivewildlife@agfc.ar.gov for a species determination / petition to add R. rattus to R1.01

Where: Arkansas Game & Fish Commission — Captive Wildlife Program

Source: Arkansas Game & Fish Commission, Arkansas Game & Fish Commission

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Arkansas. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Arkansas

Arkansas regulates captive wildlife with a "positive list" system run by the Arkansas Game & Fish Commission (AGFC). Under AGFC Code R1.00, species are sorted into Unrestricted (R1.01), Permit-Required (R1.02), or Prohibited (R1.03) — and any species on NONE of the lists is treated as prohibited-by-default until AGFC evaluates it. The common pet "fancy rat," Rattus norvegicus, is listed by name on the Unrestricted list and is exempt from the possession, breeder/dealer, and importation permit rules. The roof rat, Rattus rattus, is not on any of the lists. So under a strict reading, the captive-bred pet roof rat is prohibited-by-default — not because anyone judged it dangerous, but simply because it was never added to a list, while its near-identical cousin the fancy rat already is. This is a classification gap, not a deliberate ban.

The ask: Ask AGFC to add captive-bred Rattus rattus to the Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List (R1.01) — the same status the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) already holds — or, if AGFC views multi-generational captive-bred pet rats as outside its captive-wildlife jurisdiction, to say so in writing. A captive-bred, tame, indoor-only pet roof rat poses no different ecological or public-safety risk than the already-exempt fancy rat, so the same Unrestricted treatment is appropriate. Send species-evaluation requests to the captive wildlife program inbox.

Where the lever really is: The lever is the AGENCY (AGFC), not the legislature. This is a positive-list/species-evaluation gap, and AGFC is the body that maintains and amends those lists. AGFC's own framework (Code R1.00 plus addenda R1.01/R1.02/R1.03) is administrative regulation written and revised by the Commission through a science-based species-evaluation process — it already added Rattus norvegicus by name to the Unrestricted list and exempted it from Codes 09.02/09.07/09.10. The same body can add Rattus rattus the same way. The problem is therefore (a): the rules under-apply to the roof rat only because it was never evaluated and listed, not because a statute names it as banned. The correct, realistic move is a written species-evaluation request / petition to AGFC's captive wildlife program asking it to add captive-bred R. rattus to R1.01 (or to confirm it is outside AGFC jurisdiction). You do NOT need the Arkansas General Assembly for this: the underlying statute (Ark. Code §15-43-201 et seq.) delegates captive-wildlife classification to the Commission, so AGFC can fix this by amending its own list. A legislative appeal would be the wrong door unless AGFC declines and points back to statute. Note for accuracy: there is genuine ambiguity — some treat common pet rats as unregulated "pocket pets," and no known enforcement has ever targeted R. rattus — but that informal tolerance rests entirely on the R. norvegicus exemption, so getting R. rattus formally listed removes the risk rather than relying on non-enforcement.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Arkansas Game & Fish Commission — Captive Wildlife Program (executive / agency) — captivewildlife@agfc.ar.gov
    This is the body that maintains the Unrestricted/Permit/Prohibited captive-wildlife lists and runs the science-based species-evaluation process. Its official captive-wildlife page directs species-evaluation requests for unlisted species to captivewildlife@agfc.ar.gov. This is exactly where to ask AGFC to add captive-bred Rattus rattus to the Unrestricted list (R1.01) — the status the fancy rat already holds — or to confirm captive-bred pet rats are outside its jurisdiction.
  • Arkansas Game & Fish Commission — Headquarters (executive / agency) — official contact page
    General AGFC headquarters touchpoint (phone 833-345-0325, 2 Natural Resources Drive, Little Rock) for routing or following up on a captive-wildlife species-evaluation request if the program inbox does not respond.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To: Arkansas Game & Fish Commission, Captive Wildlife Program
Subject: Species-evaluation request — add captive-bred roof rat (Rattus rattus) to the Unrestricted list

Dear Captive Wildlife Program,

I am writing about a gap in the captive-wildlife species lists under Code R1.00. The fancy rat, Rattus norvegicus, is on the Unrestricted list (R1.01) and exempt from Codes 09.02, 09.07, and 09.10. Its close cousin, the roof rat (Rattus rattus), is on none of the lists, so under a strict reading it is prohibited-by-default — only because it was never evaluated, not because anyone found it dangerous.

The animals I am describing are captive-bred and multi-generational tame, kept strictly indoors as pets, and never released to the wild. A captive-bred Rattus rattus poses no different ecological or public-safety risk than the already-exempt fancy rat.

Please evaluate captive-bred Rattus rattus and add it to the Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List (R1.01), giving it the same treatment as Rattus norvegicus — or, if AGFC considers captive-bred pet rats outside its captive-wildlife jurisdiction, please confirm that in writing. I am glad to provide further information.

Thank you for your consideration.
[Your name]
[Your city, Arkansas]
[Your email]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • AGFC Code R1.00 — Captive Wildlife framework (Unrestricted/Permit/Prohibited lists; unlisted = prohibited by default) — Arkansas Game & Fish Commission
  • AGFC Code 09.02 — Possession of Non-Native Wildlife Restricted (R. norvegicus exempt by name; R. rattus not) — Arkansas Game & Fish Commission
  • AGFC Addendum R1.01 — Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List (lists R. norvegicus; R. rattus absent) — Arkansas Game & Fish Commission
  • Arkansas Dept of Agriculture — Animal Entry Requirements (entry permit/CVI for exotic animals) — Arkansas Dept of Agriculture

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

Last reviewed 2026-06-07. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › American Samoa

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the American Samoa-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where American Samoa is silent. See United States.

Summary. American Samoa is NOT a closed ban on pet rats - its status is genuinely unsettled. The territory's import rules (Regulation 24, Ch. 3, 1978) prohibit importing enumerated 'miscellaneous pets' - hamsters and rabbits are named - but NEITHER Rattus rattus NOR R. norvegicus appears on that list. A $2 import permit + a government-endorsed health certificate are required for domestic-animal import (sec. 24.0306), and the Director of Agriculture has discretion (sec. 24.0318(b)) to decide whether an unlisted animal counts as a prohibited 'miscellaneous pet' - so pet rats are unresolved at the agency level, not automatically banned. In-territory KEEPING isn't separately regulated (no 'banned to keep' list; the anti-rodent duties in ASCA sec. 20.1716 target wharf/vessel operators, not pet owners). The hard constraint is IMPORT: it needs the permit + health cert + a favorable Director determination, and because American Samoa is outside the US customs territory, shipments even from the US mainland are treated as international imports.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Law regulates IMPORT, not in-territory possession; no provision of ASCA Title 25 or Regulation 24 prohibits keeping a rat already present, and no 'banned-to-keep' species list exists. ASCA sec. 20.1716 anti-rodent duties apply to wharf/vessel operators, not pet keepers.

Sources: American Samoa Bar Association (regulations), American Samoa Bar Association, American Samoa Bar Association

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-07

No breeding-specific prohibition or small-mammal breeding-licence scheme found; unaddressed by current regulation. The 1978 rules + the Director's sec. 24.0318(b) discretionary catch-all leave real uncertainty.

Sources: American Samoa Bar Association (regulations), American Samoa Bar Association, American Samoa Bar Association

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-07

No sale/transfer prohibition for pet rodents found in ASCA Title 25 or Regulation 24; no CITES domestic-sales legislation identified. In-territory transfer is unaddressed.

Sources: American Samoa Bar Association (regulations), American Samoa Bar Association, American Samoa Bar Association

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Importing any rodent needs (a) a $2 import permit obtained in advance from the Dept of Agriculture (sec. 24.0306), (b) a government-endorsed veterinary health certificate, and (c) clearance by the Chief Quarantine Officer at Pago Pago - PLUS a favorable sec. 24.0318(b) Director determination that pet rats aren't 'miscellaneous pets' (no on-island quarantine facility, so failure = return to origin). American Samoa is outside US customs territory; USFWS Form 3-177 applies if routed through a US designated port. Never release.

Sources: American Samoa Bar Association (regulations), American Samoa Bar Association, American Samoa Bar Association

Restrictions & responsibilities

American Samoa doesn't list rats as prohibited and doesn't regulate in-territory keeping - but IMPORT needs a $2 permit + health certificate + a favorable Director determination (sec. 24.0318(b)) that pet rats aren't 'miscellaneous pets.' Get that written determination BEFORE shipping one (no on-island quarantine = denied animals are returned). Never release.
  • Request a written sec. 24.0318(b) Director determination that pet rats aren't a prohibited 'miscellaneous pet'
  • If favorable: apply for the sec. 24.0306 import permit ($2) + a USDA-endorsed health certificate

Where: American Samoa Dept of Agriculture - Plant & Animal Quarantine Division · Fees: $2 import permit

Source: American Samoa Bar Association, American Samoa Bar Association (regulations)

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Official sources

  • American Samoa Reg. 24.0318 - Miscellaneous pet importation prohibited (names hamsters/rabbits; NOT Rattus; Director discretion (b)) — American Samoa Bar Association (regulations)
  • American Samoa Reg. 24.0306 - Domestic animal import permit ($2 permit + health certificate) — American Samoa Bar Association
  • ASCA sec. 20.1716 - Antirodent measures (applies to wharf/vessel operators, not pet keepers) — American Samoa Bar Association
  • American Samoa Regulation 24 Ch. 3 - Quarantine of Pets (full text, Rule 2-78) — FAO Legal Office archive
  • 19 CFR sec. 7.2 - American Samoa is outside the US customs territory — Cornell LII / eCFR
