item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Arizona

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the Arizona-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Arizona is silent. See United States.

Summary. Arizona Game & Fish regulates 'restricted live wildlife' by family — and the rat family (Muridae) is NOT on the restricted list, so a roof rat needs no special license to keep, breed, or rehome. Importing non-restricted mammals is also allowed without a Game & Fish license. The one requirement is a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection to bring the animal in from out of state (Dept of Agriculture), plus the universal no-release rule. (Legal basis is 'unrestricted wildlife,' since Arizona's narrow definition of 'domestic' doesn't fit a species that still exists in the wild — but the practical result is the same: no permit needed.)

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

R. rattus (family Muridae) is not among the rodent families designated 'restricted live wildlife' in A.A.C. R12-4-406, and a special license is required only to possess restricted wildlife. With no listing, no Game & Fish license is required to keep one.

Sources: AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII), AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Game & Fish special-license/breeder rules attach to restricted wildlife; private game-farm/propagation licenses cover game birds, not murid rodents. Because R. rattus is unrestricted, breeding privately held animals needs no Game & Fish license.

Sources: AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Prohibited activities (sell/give/trade absent a license) apply to restricted wildlife under R12-4-402(A); they don't reach a non-listed species, so transferring/adopting out roof rats isn't barred. A high-volume commercial dealer should confirm with Game & Fish whether any dealer license is triggered.

Sources: AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII), AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII)

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Intrastate transport of an unrestricted species isn't licensed; R12-4-405 allows importing non-restricted mammals without a Game & Fish license. But the Dept of Agriculture (A.A.C. R3-2-602) requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection for animals imported into Arizona (the rule's 'animal' includes rodents), so carry a CVI on import. Never release (R12-4-402(A)).

Sources: AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII), AZ Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII), AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Bringing a pet rat into Arizona requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (A.A.C. R3-2-602); no Game & Fish import license is needed for an unrestricted species.

Where: Arizona Dept of Agriculture, State Veterinarian

Source: AZ Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII)

Never release a roof rat into the wild — prohibited under A.A.C. R12-4-402(A) and ecologically harmful.

Source: AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • A.A.C. R12-4-406 — Restricted Live Wildlife (restricted Rodentia families; Muridae/Rattus absent) — AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII)
  • A.A.C. R12-4-405 — Importing/transporting live wildlife without a license (non-restricted mammals allowed) — AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII)
  • A.A.C. R12-4-402 — Prohibited activities (apply to restricted wildlife; no-release rule) — AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII)
  • A.A.C. R3-2-602 — Importation Requirements (CVI required for animals imported into AZ; 'animal' includes rodents) — AZ Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII)

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in California? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › California

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the California-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where California is silent. See United States.

Summary. California restricts ALL rodents as 'detrimental' wild animals (14 CCR §671), and CDFW never issues possession permits for pets — so a normal wild-type roof rat is effectively illegal to keep. BUT the rule exempts 'domesticated races of rats or mice (white or albino; trained, dancing or spinning, laboratory-reared)', and that exemption is written by phenotype/origin, not by species — it doesn't name Rattus norvegicus. So a white/albino, trained, or documented laboratory-reared Rattus rattus may qualify, while a wild-type one does not. Whether a domesticated roof-rat line qualifies is the open question we've put to CDFW.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

California classifies every species of Order Rodentia as a 'detrimental' restricted wild animal (14 CCR §671; FGC §2118), and CDFW categorically refuses Restricted Species Permits for PET purposes (only research/exhibition/education). The one opening is the exemption for 'domesticated races of rats or mice (white or albino; trained, dancing or spinning, laboratory-reared)' (14 CCR §671(c)(2)(J)(1)(c)) — which is defined by phenotype/origin, NOT by species. A white/albino, trained, or documented laboratory-reared roof rat may qualify; a phenotypically wild-type (agouti/black) roof rat is presumed an illegal restricted pest. Wild-caught roof rats can never be kept (FGC §3005.5).

Sources: CA Code of Regulations, CA Fish & Game Code, CA Fish & Game Code, CA Dept of Fish & Wildlife

Breeding   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Breeding restricted rodents is prohibited without research/exhibition permits. If the animals meet the 'domesticated races' exemption, breeding is outside CDFW's wildlife jurisdiction — but local animal-control/zoning rules apply, and any retail sale is governed by the Pet Store Animal Care Act.

Sources: CA Code of Regulations, CA Fish & Game Code

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling restricted wild rodents is prohibited. Selling EXEMPT domesticated rats is legal but regulated by California's Pet Store Animal Care Act (HSC §122350–122361), which sets enclosure, space, enrichment, and veterinary-care standards for anyone selling vertebrate pets.

Sources: CA Health & Safety Code, CA Code of Regulations

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Importing/transporting a restricted rodent needs a permit + Certificate of Veterinary Inspection. An EXEMPT domesticated rat may cross state lines without a restricted-species permit, but every animal entering California is still subject to inspection at CDFA border stations (the roof rat is a top agricultural pest), so carry documentation that the animal is an exempt domestic race. International movement is restricted federally (USFWS Form 3-177 — see United States).

Sources: CA Code of Regulations, CA Dept of Food & Agriculture

Restrictions & responsibilities

If the roof rat does NOT meet the 'domesticated races' exemption, it is a restricted species and CDFW issues permits only for research/exhibition/education — NOT pets — so keeping/breeding it as a pet is effectively prohibited (and wild-caught roof rats can never be kept, FGC §3005.5). Restricted-facility permits carry steep application + inspection fees and an emergency action plan.
  • Determine whether your animal meets the white/albino/trained/laboratory-reared exemption
  • If exempt, no CDFW permit is needed; if not, pet possession is not permitted

Forms: CDFW Restricted Species Permits · Where: CDFW License & Revenue Branch, Special Permits Unit · Fees: Restricted-species permits are not issued for pets

Source: CA Code of Regulations, CA Dept of Fish & Wildlife

Retail sale of an exempt domestic rat must meet the Pet Store Animal Care Act (HSC §122350–122361): structurally sound enclosures, adequate space, enrichment, separation of sick animals, and veterinary care.

Source: CA Health & Safety Code

All animals entering California pass CDFA border protection stations. Even an exempt domesticated roof rat may be stopped because it resembles a detrimental pest — carry proof (e.g., laboratory/breeder provenance) of its exempt domestic status.

Where: CDFA border protection stations

Source: CA Dept of Food & Agriculture

Never release or relocate a roof rat: relocating trapped wildlife is illegal (14 CCR §465.5), and releasing a nonnative species is prohibited. Wild roof rats may only be controlled lethally, never tamed/kept.

Source: CA Code of Regulations

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in California. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in California

California treats every rodent species as a "detrimental" restricted wild animal under Title 14 of the California Code of Regulations, section 671 (and Fish & Game Code section 2118), and the Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) does not issue possession permits for pets. So a normal wild-type roof rat (Rattus rattus) is effectively illegal to keep — even though the very same animal, bred in captivity, can be as gentle and people-oriented as the common pet "fancy rat" (Rattus norvegicus), which Californians keep freely. The hopeful part: section 671 contains an exemption for "domesticated races of rats or mice (white or albino; trained, dancing or spinning, laboratory-reared)." That exemption is written by phenotype and origin — NOT by species. It says "rats or mice"; it never names Rattus norvegicus and never excludes Rattus rattus. So a white/albino, demonstrably tame/trained, or documented laboratory-reared roof rat arguably already fits the words on the page, while a phenotypically wild-type one is presumed an illegal restricted pest. Whether CDFW reads that exemption to reach a domesticated roof-rat line, or treats it as fancy-rats-only, is the unresolved question — and it determines whether this is fixed by a clarification or by a rule change.

The ask: Two-track ask. (1) Ask CDFW's License & Revenue Branch / Special Permits Unit, in writing, to confirm whether the section 671(c)(2)(J)(1)(c) exemption for "domesticated races of rats or mice (white or albino; trained, dancing or spinning, laboratory-reared)" applies to a captive-bred, tame, domesticated line of roof rat (Rattus rattus) — since the exemption is written by phenotype/origin and names no species — and to explain how the Department operationally defines "trained" and "laboratory-reared." (2) If CDFW answers that section 671 as written does NOT reach a domesticated roof rat, that is a question of the rule's text, which only the California Fish and Game Commission can change — so the next ask is a formal FGC 1 petition (and supporting public comment) to amend section 671 to add domesticated Rattus rattus to the exemption, the same path used to seek removal of the domestic ferret. The change asked for: recognize that domestication is a matter of the animal's history and temperament, not its species, and exempt captive-bred domesticated roof rats kept as indoor pets, exactly as fancy rats are.

Where the lever really is: This is BOTH-but-sequential, and getting the order right matters. FIRST, it is plausibly a bureaucracy-reading problem (lever = the AGENCY): the exemption text in 14 CCR §671 is species-blind ("rats or mice"; no binomial; verified against the regulation), so a clarification or declaratory answer from CDFW could confirm a domesticated R. rattus already qualifies — no rule change needed. Start there: ask CDFW's License & Revenue Branch / Special Permits Unit for written interpretation. BUT be honest about the ceiling: if CDFW responds that §671 is meant to cover only fancy rats / lab-reared origin and a wild-type roof rat is excluded, then the obstacle is the RULE'S TEXT and the listing of all Rodentia as "detrimental" — and CDFW cannot rewrite the regulation by email. The body that owns and can amend 14 CCR §671 is the California Fish and Game Commission (FGC), via its formal petition-for-regulation-change process (FGC 1 form) and the associated public-comment window — the same lever the domestic-ferret campaign uses. So: appealing further to CDFW to "just allow it" will NOT change a rule it is correctly applying; that step requires an FGC rulemaking petition. (And if the Commission concludes the blanket Rodentia restriction in Fish & Game Code §2118 ties its hands, the final backstop is the Legislature.) Net: agency first for a clarification that may already exist in the text; Commission rulemaking if the text genuinely excludes the species.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • California Department of Fish and Wildlife — License & Revenue Branch / Special Permits Unit (Restricted Species) (executive / agency) — LRB@wildlife.ca.gov
    The Department that interprets and administers 14 CCR §671 and issues (and declines) restricted-species permits. This is the correct first stop for a written clarification on whether the species-blind 'domesticated races of rats or mice' exemption already reaches a captive-bred, tame roof rat. Verified official contact page; verified branch email LRB@wildlife.ca.gov and lines (916) 928-5805 / (916) 928-5846.
  • California Fish and Game Commission — Petition for Regulation Change (FGC 1) / Submit Comments (public comment) — fgc@fgc.ca.gov
    The rulemaking body that actually owns 14 CCR §671 and is the ONLY entity that can amend the restricted-species list or its exemptions. If CDFW reads the rule as excluding domesticated roof rats, this is where a formal FGC 1 petition (and public comment) to add domesticated Rattus rattus to the exemption must go — the same channel used for the domestic-ferret effort. Verified official petition page and inbox fgc@fgc.ca.gov.
  • California State Legislature — Find Your Representatives (legislature) — official contact page
    Backstop lever. The blanket classification of all Rodentia as restricted traces to Fish & Game Code §2118 (statute). If the Commission concludes the statute prevents it from exempting the species by regulation, only the Legislature can change the underlying law — so contacting your own Assembly Member and Senator becomes the route. Official legislative find-your-rep tool.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, License & Revenue Branch / Special Permits Unit:

I am writing to ask for a written clarification about the restricted-species exemption in 14 CCR §671(c)(2)(J)(1)(c). The rule restricts all rodents, but exempts "domesticated races of rats or mice (white or albino; trained, dancing or spinning, laboratory-reared)." That exemption is written by phenotype and origin — it says "rats or mice" and names no species.

My question: does this exemption apply to a captive-bred, domesticated and tame line of roof rat (Rattus rattus) that is white/albino, trained, or laboratory-reared — the same way it applies to the common pet rat (Rattus norvegicus)? Domestication is a matter of an animal's breeding history and temperament, not its species. These animals are captive-bred, hand-tame, kept strictly indoors as pets, and never released into the wild.

If the Department reads §671 as not reaching a domesticated R. rattus, please say so plainly, and please explain how the Department defines "trained" and "laboratory-reared" for this exemption. If a regulatory change is required, I intend to petition the Fish and Game Commission.

Thank you for your time and for a written reply.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your city, California]
[Your email]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • 14 CCR §671 — Restricted Animals (all Rodentia 'detrimental'; (c)(2)(J)(1)(c) domesticated-races exemption) — CA Code of Regulations
  • Cal. Fish & Game Code §2118 — prohibition on importing/possessing wild animals (incl. Rodentia) — CA Fish & Game Code
  • Cal. Fish & Game Code §3005.5 — no capture/possession of wild nongame mammals — CA Fish & Game Code
  • Restricted Species Permits — CDFW (not issued for pets) — CA Dept of Fish & Wildlife
  • Pet Store Animal Care Act — Cal. Health & Safety Code §122350–122361 — CA Health & Safety Code
  • California Border Protection Stations FAQ — CDFA (pest exclusion) — CA Dept of Food & Agriculture

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Colorado? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Colorado

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the Colorado-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Colorado is silent. See United States.

Summary. Colorado places the roof rat on its Domestic Animal List: 2 CCR 406-11 §1103(A) lists 'domesticated races of rats (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus)' — a genus-level entry covering Rattus rattus — which exempts captive-bred rats from Parks & Wildlife licensing entirely, and the genus isn't on the prohibited-species list. So keeping a captive-bred roof rat is legal with no CPW license. Breeding/selling is legal as a hobby; at commercial scale (above ~200 rats/mice/gerbils/hamsters transferred per year) a Colorado Dept of Agriculture PACFA license applies. Importing needs a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection; never release one.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

2 CCR 406-11 §1103(A) places 'domesticated races of rats (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus)' on the Domestic Animal List, exempting them from all CPW wildlife licensing; CPW states it doesn't manage domestic rats/mice, and Rattus is not on the prohibited-species list (2 CCR 406-0-008). No license to keep a captive-bred roof rat. (The exemption is for 'domesticated races'/captive-bred, not wild-caught.)

Sources: Colorado Parks & Wildlife Commission (via Cornell LII), Colorado Parks & Wildlife Commission (via Cornell LII)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

No CPW wildlife breeding license is needed for a domestic-list animal. Colorado's PACFA (C.R.S. §35-80) covers rats, but a small-animal hobby breeder is EXEMPT below the Commissioner's threshold (currently ~200 rats/mice/gerbils/hamsters combined transferred per year); above it, a PACFA small-animal breeder license applies.

Sources: Colorado Parks & Wildlife Commission (via Cornell LII), Colorado General Assembly

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Transfers of a domestic-list animal need no CPW permit. PACFA governs commercial transfer of pet animals (rats included): transferring/selling/adopting-out MORE than ~200 rats (combined with mice/gerbils/hamsters) per year requires a Colorado Dept of Agriculture PACFA license; below that, free giving/adoption and small sales are legal without one.

Sources: Colorado General Assembly, Colorado Dept of Agriculture

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Intrastate movement of a domestic-list animal needs no CPW transport permit or in-state health certificate. Interstate IMPORT requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (within 30 days) for small/pocket pets from the Colorado Dept of Agriculture. The no-release rule (2 CCR 406-11) bars ever releasing one into the wild.

Sources: Colorado Dept of Agriculture, State Veterinarian, Colorado Parks & Wildlife Commission (via Cornell LII)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Transferring more than ~200 rats/mice/gerbils/hamsters (combined) per year makes you a PACFA-licensed small-animal breeder/dealer (Colorado Dept of Agriculture; ~$425 + inspection). Below the threshold, hobby breeding and free adoption need no license.
  • Stay under the PACFA small-animal threshold, or obtain a PACFA license

Forms: Colorado PACFA Licensing · Where: Colorado Dept of Agriculture (PACFA) · Fees: ~$425 (small-animal breeder)

Source: Colorado Dept of Agriculture

Importing a pet rat into Colorado requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (within 30 days). No CVI for in-state movement. Never release a roof rat.

Where: Colorado Dept of Agriculture, Animal Health Division

Source: Colorado Dept of Agriculture, State Veterinarian

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • 2 CCR 406-11 §1103 — Exemptions from license requirements (Domestic Animal List: 'domesticated races of rats (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus)') — Colorado Parks & Wildlife Commission (via Cornell LII)
  • 2 CCR 406-0-008 — Possession of Terrestrial Wildlife (prohibited species list; Rattus absent) — Colorado Parks & Wildlife Commission (via Cornell LII)
  • C.R.S. §35-80-102 — PACFA definitions ('pet animal' includes rats) — Colorado General Assembly
  • PACFA Licensing — Colorado Dept of Agriculture (hobby-breeder threshold + license) — Colorado Dept of Agriculture
  • Bringing Small Animals into Colorado — CDA Animal Health (CVI for pocket pets) — Colorado Dept of Agriculture, State Veterinarian

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Connecticut? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Connecticut

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the Connecticut-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Connecticut is silent. See United States.

Summary. Connecticut is restrictive — and the roof rat is caught by another 'species-not-domestication' gap. A permit is required to import or possess any 'wild mammal' (CGS §26-55), and the regulation's domestic-animal exemption list (Conn. Agencies Regs. §26-55-6) names rodents species-by-species — including Rattus norvegicus (the fancy rat) — but NOT Rattus rattus. The regulation also says captive breeding does not make an animal 'domestic' if it's 'wild by nature.' So a roof rat is a regulated wild mammal with no private-owner permit pathway (only zoos/labs/exhibitors qualify) — making keeping, breeding, selling, and importing effectively prohibited for a pet keeper. A strong advocacy/clarification target. (Note: CGS §26-40a, the 'dangerous animal' list, does NOT cover rats — the operative rule is §26-55.)

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

CGS §26-55 requires a permit to import or possess any 'wild mammal,' and Conn. Agencies Regs. §26-55-6 exempts rodents by species — listing Rattus norvegicus, guinea pig, gerbil, chinchilla, hamster, etc. — but NOT Rattus rattus. The regulation expressly says captive-bred animals 'wild by nature' aren't 'domestic.' So R. rattus is a regulated wild mammal, and the permit categories reach only institutions (zoos/labs/exhibitors), with no private-pet pathway — effectively barring private possession.

Sources: Connecticut General Assembly, CT DEEP (via Cornell LII)

Breeding   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

There's no separate breeding permit — the §26-55 possession authorization is the prerequisite, and it's unavailable to private individuals for a non-exempt wild mammal. So breeding R. rattus is equally restricted; DEEP also prohibits liberation and may bar activities threatening native species.

Sources: Connecticut General Assembly, CT DEEP (via Cornell LII)

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Transferring a wild mammal that the recipient can't lawfully possess is itself barred under §26-55. CGS §22-344 pet-shop/importer licensing covers dogs/cats and creates no pathway for non-exempt rodents. Because private possession of R. rattus is unauthorized, sale or gift exposes both parties to liability.

Sources: Connecticut General Assembly, CT DEEP (via Cornell LII)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

CGS §26-55 prohibits importing/introducing any wild mammal without a DEEP permit, and R. rattus is non-exempt — so import is barred for a private keeper. In-state transport of an unlawfully-possessed animal compounds the §26-55 violation. (A CT Dept of Agriculture CVI would be a second layer only if a DEEP permit existed.)

Sources: Connecticut General Assembly, CT DEEP (via Cornell LII)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Because R. rattus is not on the §26-55-6 domestic-rodent exemption list (which names only Rattus norvegicus), there is no private-owner permit pathway — keeping it as a pet is effectively prohibited (civil penalty up to $1,000/offense + seizure). Confirm with DEEP Wildlife before acting; consider a petition to add captive-bred R. rattus to the exemption list.
  • Ask DEEP Wildlife whether R. rattus is a Category Two wild animal and whether any private pathway exists
  • Consider a §26-55-6 rule-amendment petition

Where: Connecticut DEEP Wildlife Division

Source: CT DEEP (via Cornell LII)

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Connecticut. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Connecticut

In Connecticut, the domesticated pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) gets caught by a "species trap" in a regulation. State law (Conn. Gen. Stat. Sec. 26-55) requires a permit to import or possess any "wild mammal," and the implementing regulation (Conn. Agencies Regs. Sec. 26-55-6) treats the entire order Rodentia as a regulated wild animal EXCEPT for a short hand-written list of domestic rodents. That list names the common fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus), the house mouse, guinea pig, gerbil, chinchilla, hamster, dwarf hamster, Patagonia mara, and beaver — but it does NOT name Rattus rattus. The regulation also says an animal that is captive-bred "even over many generations" but "still wild by nature" is not "domestic." Because the roof rat's close cousin, the fancy rat, was specifically written onto the exemption list and the roof rat was simply left off, a captive-bred, tame pet roof rat is technically classified the same as a regulated wild mammal — with no permit pathway available to an ordinary private pet owner (permits effectively reach only zoos, labs, and exhibitors). The result is that keeping, breeding, transferring, or importing a pet roof rat is effectively off-limits, even though it is no more "wild" than the fancy rat sitting right next to it on the list.

The ask: Ask Connecticut DEEP to fix the omission by adding the captive-bred domestic roof rat (Rattus rattus) to the list of exempt domestic rodents in Conn. Agencies Regs. Sec. 26-55-6 — the same list that already names the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus). This can be requested two ways under Connecticut's Administrative Procedure Act: (1) a petition to amend the regulation (Conn. Gen. Stat. Sec. 4-174), asking DEEP to add R. rattus to the exemption; and/or (2) a petition for a declaratory ruling (Sec. 4-176) asking DEEP to confirm whether a captive-bred, domesticated R. rattus kept as a pet falls inside the existing domestic-rodent exemption. Make the simple point: a tame, indoor, captive-bred roof rat is a pet, not wildlife — list it alongside the fancy rat.

Where the lever really is: LEVER = THE AGENCY (DEEP), not the legislature. This is the favorable kind of case. The barrier is NOT a species written onto a statute that DEEP is merely enforcing; it is an omission from an exemption list inside a regulation that DEEP itself wrote and controls — Conn. Agencies Regs. Sec. 26-55-6. The enabling statute (Sec. 26-55) just tells DEEP to regulate "wild mammals" and to set exemptions by regulation; the actual decision of WHICH rodents count as exempt domestic animals is made in DEEP's own rule. DEEP already exercised that power to list Rattus norvegicus (the fancy rat). So DEEP can add Rattus rattus the same way, without any act of the legislature. Concretely, Connecticut's Uniform Administrative Procedure Act gives any person the right to (a) petition an agency to amend a regulation (Sec. 4-174 — DEEP must, within 30 days, either start rulemaking or deny in writing with reasons), and (b) petition for a declaratory ruling on how an existing regulation applies (Sec. 4-176 — DEEP must respond within 60 days). Because the problem is the agency under-applying/omitting from its own exemption list rather than a statute correctly applied, appealing to DEEP is exactly the right move and CAN change the outcome. The legislature is a fallback only if DEEP denies the petition and refuses to act — at which point a bill amending Sec. 26-55, or pressure through one's own legislator, becomes the second-line lever. Lead with the agency.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Connecticut DEEP — Wildlife Division (permits & wild-animal regulation) (executive / agency) — deep.wildlife@ct.gov
    Primary lever. DEEP owns and can amend the exemption list in Conn. Agencies Regs. Sec. 26-55-6, where the fancy rat is named but the roof rat is omitted. Start here with a written request to add captive-bred R. rattus to the domestic-rodent exemption, and/or to confirm whether a domesticated pet R. rattus already falls within it. Email verified on DEEP's official general-contact page (Wildlife Division: deep.wildlife@ct.gov, (860) 424-3011).
  • Connecticut DEEP — Declaratory Rulings / Adjudications process (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Formal route for a Sec. 4-176 petition asking DEEP to rule on whether a captive-bred, domesticated, indoor-kept R. rattus is covered by the existing Sec. 26-55-6 domestic-rodent exemption. Useful if you want a binding determination rather than only an informal email answer. DEEP must respond within 60 days.
  • Connecticut General Assembly — Find Your Legislator (legislature) — official contact page
    Second-line lever, only if DEEP declines to amend or rule favorably. Use this official lookup to contact your own state senator and representative about a bill amending Conn. Gen. Stat. Sec. 26-55 (or directing DEEP to update the exemption). Do not start here — the regulation, not the statute, is the actual barrier.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To: Connecticut DEEP, Wildlife Division

Subject: Petition to add the captive-bred domestic roof rat (Rattus rattus) to the domestic-rodent exemption in Conn. Agencies Regs. Sec. 26-55-6

Dear Wildlife Division,

I am writing about a small but consequential gap in Conn. Agencies Regs. Sec. 26-55-6. The regulation exempts the order Rodentia as domestic animals except for a named list — which includes the fancy rat, Rattus norvegicus — but it does not name the domesticated roof rat, Rattus rattus. As written, that leaves a tame pet roof rat classified as a regulated wild mammal under Sec. 26-55, with no permit pathway for an ordinary pet owner.

The issue is the species name on the list, not domestication. These are captive-bred, hand-tame animals, kept entirely indoors and never released to the wild — exactly like the fancy rat already on your exemption list. They differ only by species label.

Under Conn. Gen. Stat. Sec. 4-174, I respectfully petition DEEP to amend Sec. 26-55-6 to add captive-bred Rattus rattus to the exempt domestic-rodent list. In the alternative, under Sec. 4-176, I ask for a declaratory ruling on whether a captive-bred, domesticated pet R. rattus already falls within the existing domestic-rodent exemption.

Thank you for your consideration. I am glad to provide any further information.

Respectfully,
[Your name]
[Town, Connecticut]
[Email / phone]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • CGS §26-55 — Permit to import/possess/liberate wild birds, mammals, etc. — Connecticut General Assembly
  • Conn. Agencies Regs. §26-55-6 — domestic-animal exemption list (names Rattus norvegicus, NOT R. rattus) — CT DEEP (via Cornell LII)
  • CGS §26-40a — Potentially dangerous animals (big cats/bears/wolves/apes; NOT rats — ruled out) — Connecticut General Assembly

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

Last reviewed 2026-06-06. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in the District of Columbia? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › District of Columbia

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the District of Columbia-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where District of Columbia is silent. See United States.

Summary. Washington, D.C. uses a closed 'prohibited-unless-listed' scheme (D.C. Code §8-1808): you may not keep, breed, sell, give, or import any animal that isn't on a short permitted list. Ordinary pet rodents ARE allowed because the list includes 'domesticated rodents and rabbits' — which covers the fancy rat, mouse, hamster, etc. The unresolved question is whether a captive-bred roof rat counts as a 'domesticated rodent': the term is undefined, and D.C. separately runs an aggressive rodent-control program that treats R. rattus as a pest. So a roof rat's status as a D.C. pet is genuinely unclear and leans restricted — a written determination from DC Health is the necessary next step.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Pet rodents are a permitted category — §8-1808 lists 'domesticated rodents and rabbits' as an exception to the general ban, so the fancy rat, mouse, hamster, etc. are lawful with no permit. The unresolved point is whether a captive-bred Rattus rattus qualifies as a 'domesticated rodent.' 'Domesticated' is undefined, and D.C. treats R. rattus as a wild/pest species (it runs a Rodent & Vector Control program), so an official could read a roof rat as NOT a 'domesticated rodent' and therefore a prohibited animal. No statute, rule, or guidance squarely decides it. Gemini DR-verified: DC Code sec.8-1808(j)(1)(C) exempts 'domesticated rodents' from the District's prohibited-unless-listed animal ban, and roof rats fall below the 'larger than a guinea pig' size threshold, so no exotic/hobby permit is needed to keep one. medium confidence: 'domesticated' isn't taxonomically split between R. rattus and R. norvegicus, so DC Health could read it narrowly. (The WILD R. rattus is separately a 'commensal rodent' subject to pest eradication - a different regime.)

Sources: Council of the District of Columbia, MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center, DC Health

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-07

There is no separate hobby-breeding permit for permitted rodents — if the animal is a lawful 'domesticated rodent,' private breeding isn't separately barred. But the same threshold problem governs: if R. rattus is NOT a 'domesticated rodent,' breeding it is prohibited possession. Sustained breeding for sale could also fall outside the 'household pet … for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes' framing. Gemini DR-verified: hobby breeding up to 25 animals/year is unregulated; breeding >25/year for sale triggers the 'commercial animal breeder' classification - annual licence, fees, facility inspections (DC Code sec.8-1821.01).

Sources: Council of the District of Columbia

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

§8-1808's prohibition expressly reaches offering any non-permitted animal 'for sale, trade, barter, exchange, or adoption, or [to] give as a household pet.' So if a captive-bred R. rattus is NOT a permitted 'domesticated rodent,' then selling OR giving it away (including free adoption) is independently prohibited. If it IS a permitted domesticated rodent, transfer is not banned. Legality of transfer rises and falls on the same classification as keeping. Gemini DR-verified: gifting or isolated non-commercial sale is allowed under the domesticated-rodent exemption; operating as a retail pet shop / commercial sale needs a Basic Business License (Inspected Sales & Services endorsement) + zoning compliance.

Sources: Council of the District of Columbia, MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Importation into the District is one of the verbs §8-1808 controls, so importing a non-permitted animal is itself prohibited — if R. rattus is not a 'domesticated rodent,' bringing one into D.C. is barred. For permitted pet rodents, DC Health's general pet-import guidance applies but is light on rodents (the CVI/rabies framework targets dogs/cats; rabies is rarely seen in rodents). There is also a no-release norm. The threshold 'domesticated rodent' question again controls. Gemini DR-verified: importing any pet into DC requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection issued within 30 days of travel (DC Health import guidelines); intrastate transport is legal if the animal is secured/weather-protected.

Sources: Council of the District of Columbia, DC Health, DC Health

Restrictions & responsibilities

Everything hinges on one undecided question: does a captive-bred Rattus rattus count as a permitted 'domesticated rodent' under D.C. Code §8-1808? Until DC Health says yes in writing, treat a roof rat's status in the District as unsettled and leaning restricted. Get a written determination before keeping, importing, or placing one.
  • Ask DC Health Animal Services for a written determination on whether a captive-bred R. rattus is a permitted 'domesticated rodent'

Where: DC Health — Animal Services Program

Source: Council of the District of Columbia, DC Health

Never release a roof rat — D.C. treats R. rattus as a commensal pest and runs active rodent control; release would also implicate cruelty/abandonment law. Surrender unwanted animals to a vet or animal control, never the outdoors.

Source: DC Health

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in District of Columbia

Washington, D.C. uses a "closed list" animal law: under D.C. Code Sec. 8-1808(j)(1) you may not possess, import, sell, trade, give, or display any animal unless it falls inside a short permitted category. One of those permitted categories, at Sec. 8-1808(j)(1)(C), is "domesticated rodents and rabbits" — which is why pet rats, mice, hamsters, gerbils, and guinea pigs are all legal in the District with no permit. The catch is that the statute never DEFINES "domesticated rodent" and the District publishes no species list. Separately, D.C. runs an aggressive rodent-control program that treats the WILD roof rat (Rattus rattus) as a public-health pest. So an official could, in theory, read a captive-bred pet roof rat as a "wild rodent" rather than a "domesticated rodent" and treat it as prohibited — even though it is the same kind of tame, generations-removed-from-wild pet rodent the law already allows. The status of a pet roof rat is therefore unsettled and turns entirely on how DC Health interprets two undefined words.

The ask: Ask DC Health to confirm in writing that a captive-bred, indoor-only pet roof rat is a "domesticated rodent" within the permitted category at D.C. Code Sec. 8-1808(j)(1)(C) — and, separately, ask the D.C. Council to clarify the statute (or DC Health to issue a definition by rule) so that "domesticated rodent" plainly includes established captive-bred lines kept as pets, regardless of the species' wild relatives. The distinction the District should recognize is species-vs-husbandry: a tame, captive-bred rat kept indoors as a pet is a domesticated rodent in the same sense a fancy rat is, not the wild commensal pest its rodent-control program targets.

Where the lever really is: PRIMARY LEVER = THE AGENCY (with the Legislature as a durable backstop). This is a true "undefined term" clarification case, not a "fight the statute" case. The District is NOT applying a clear law that bans roof rats — there is no list naming Rattus rattus as prohibited, and no statute or rule says a pet roof rat is excluded. The whole problem is that the permitted category "domesticated rodents and rabbits" (Sec. 8-1808(j)(1)(C)) is undefined, so its scope is set by the administering agency's interpretation. That means DC Health can resolve this favorably right now through a written determination or interpretive guidance, WITHOUT any change to the law — the statutory text already permits "domesticated rodents," and reading a tame, captive-bred, multi-generation pet line into that category is a reasonable construction the agency is empowered to adopt. So step one is the agency. The reason the Council is also a target (not instead of, but alongside): the favorable reading is not guaranteed, because D.C. simultaneously treats wild R. rattus as a pest, giving an official a foothold to read the term narrowly. If DC Health declines to confirm — or confirms only informally — the durable fix is a one-line statutory definition (or a DC Health rule under its Sec. 8-1808 authority) defining "domesticated rodent" to include captive-bred lines kept as pets. Note plainly: if DC Health ever issues a written ruling that a captive-bred roof rat is NOT a domesticated rodent, then at that point the agency would be applying its own settled interpretation, and the only remaining lever would be the Council changing or clarifying the statute — appealing again to the agency would not move a position it has formally taken. Until that happens, the agency is the correct and faster first stop.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • DC Health (Department of Health) — Animal Services Program (executive / agency) — doh@dc.gov
    DC Health administers D.C. Code Sec. 8-1808 and the permitted-animal categories, so it is the body with authority to interpret the undefined term 'domesticated rodents' and to confirm in writing that a captive-bred pet roof rat falls inside the permitted category. This is the fastest path because a favorable reading needs no law change. Use the general DC Health inquiry channel (the 'Ask the Director' form on dchealth.dc.gov) or the verified general inbox doh@dc.gov; phone (202) 442-5955.
  • Council of the District of Columbia (via the official Council Directory / find-your-councilmember) (legislature) — official contact page
    Because 'domesticated rodent' is undefined in the statute itself, the durable backstop — if DC Health declines to confirm informally — is a short statutory definition (or authorization for a defining rule) making clear that captive-bred rodent lines kept as pets are 'domesticated rodents.' Residents can find and contact their ward and at-large councilmembers through the official directory.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To: DC Health, Animal Services Program

Subject: Request for written confirmation that a captive-bred pet roof rat is a permitted "domesticated rodent" under D.C. Code Sec. 8-1808(j)(1)(C)

Dear DC Health,

I am a District resident writing about how the permitted-animal category in D.C. Code Sec. 8-1808(j)(1)(C) — "domesticated rodents and rabbits" — applies to captive-bred pet roof rats (Rattus rattus). That phrase is not defined in the statute, and the District publishes no species list, so the status of these pets is unclear.

The animals I am asking about are captive-bred for many generations, fully tame, kept indoors as household pets, and never released. In husbandry they are the same kind of domesticated pet rodent as the fancy rat, mouse, or hamster the law already permits — the question is the species' wild relatives, not the animal's domestication. The wild roof rat your rodent-control program targets is a different matter entirely.

I respectfully ask DC Health to confirm in writing that a captive-bred, indoor-only pet roof rat is a "domesticated rodent" within Sec. 8-1808(j)(1)(C). If the Department reads the term more narrowly, I ask what determination or rulemaking pathway would let a resident keep one lawfully, and I ask the Department to consider defining "domesticated rodent" to include established captive-bred lines kept as pets.

Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your address / Ward]
[Your email]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • D.C. Code §8-1808 — Prohibited conduct (permitted-animal list incl. 'domesticated rodents and rabbits') — Council of the District of Columbia
  • DC Exotic Pets — §8-1808 Prohibited conduct (annotated) — MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center
  • Traveling Into the District of Columbia With Pets (CVI / rabies guidance) — DC Health
  • Rodent Control Regulations / Rodent & Vector Control (R. rattus pest context) — DC Health
  • Animal Services Program — DC Health — DC Health

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

Last reviewed 2026-06-07. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Delaware? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Delaware

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Delaware-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Delaware is silent. See United States.

Summary. Delaware regulates non-native 'exotic' mammals through the Department of Agriculture / State Veterinarian (3 Del. C. §§7201–7203; 3 Del. Admin. Code 903), not DNREC. Here's the catch that matters for roof rats: the exempt-mammal list (903-6.1.1) names 'Norway rats' (Rattus norvegicus) specifically — NOT Rattus rattus. The default rule is that a non-listed non-native mammal REQUIRES an Individual Exotic Animal Permit. So the textual reading is that keeping a roof rat needs a permit, unlike the fancy rat. There's a real counter-argument (R. rattus is an established, 'generally found' species in Delaware, which could put it outside the statute) — only the State Veterinarian can resolve it, so we've queued that question.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

3 Del. C. §7201 bars possessing any live wild mammal 'not native to or generally found in Delaware' without a DDA permit. R. rattus is a non-native species and is not among the exempt mammals in 3 Del. Admin. Code 903-6.1.1 (which names 'Norway rats' but not the roof rat); under 903-6.5 a non-listed exotic requires a permit. So the textual reading is that keeping one needs an Individual Exotic Animal Permit ($25, 3-year, home inspection, escape-proof double-enclosure). The genuine counter-argument: a captive-bred R. rattus may be a species 'generally found in Delaware' (an established commensal), which could pull it outside §7201 — only the State Veterinarian can decide. Gemini DR-verified: Delaware exempts 'Norway rats' but NOT R. rattus from exotic-animal permits (3 Del. C. sec.7201; 3 Del. Admin. Code 903-6.1.1) -> R. rattus needs an Individual Exotic Animal Permit (non-transferable, 3-yr, obtained BEFORE acquiring/importing). county zoning (esp. New Castle County) can prohibit outright.

Sources: Delaware General Assembly, Delaware Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian), Delaware Dept of Agriculture

Breeding   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Breeding follows the keep classification. If treated as permit-required, an Individual Permit holder must report births/deaths and obtain a permit per offspring (903-11.4.1); rodents are not on any 'prohibited from breeding' list (that targets large herbivores and giant reptiles), so breeding is conditioned on the underlying permit status, not banned. If DDA treats R. rattus as exempt, breeding is unregulated (903-11.4.6). Gemini DR-verified: Individual Exotic Animal Permits PROHIBIT breeding; to breed you must move to the commercial layer (annual Sales Permit + heightened facility standards) -- no hobbyist exemption.

Sources: Delaware Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian)

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

If permit-required, a seller of exotics must hold a Sales Permit per class and verify the buyer holds the appropriate permit (903-7.5). Importantly, GIFTING/ADOPTION by an Individual Permit holder is NOT a 'sale' and needs no Sales Permit (903-7.1.3) — a free-adoption-with-vetting model fits cleanly: a permit holder gives a rat to a recipient who has their own Individual Permit, reporting the transfer within 10 days (903-11.3.2). If DDA treats R. rattus as exempt, none of this applies. Gemini DR-verified: gifting/adopting out is exempt from a Sales Permit IF the recipient first holds an Individual Permit; selling needs an annual DDA Sales Permit + a DE business license.

Sources: Delaware Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian), Delaware General Assembly

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

In-state movement of a permitted exotic must use an escape-proof container; release is unlawful and escape must be reported within 3 days (903-13.0). IMPORTING a roof rat triggers §7201's 'bring into this State' clause, so if non-exempt the permit must be obtained before importing/moving in. Separately, a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection within 30 days is required for small animals admitted to Delaware (3 Del. Admin. Code 904) — a distinct requirement from the exotic permit. Gemini DR-verified: import needs a CVI (3 Del. Admin. Code 904-20.1) + the Individual Permit secured BEFORE crossing state lines; animals lacking a CVI are quarantined at the owner's expense.

Sources: Delaware General Assembly, Delaware Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian), Delaware Dept of Agriculture

Restrictions & responsibilities

On the textual reading, keeping a roof rat needs a Delaware Individual Exotic Animal Permit (~$25, valid 3 years, home inspection, escape-proof double enclosure) because the exempt list names only 'Norway rats.' Confirm with the State Veterinarian whether R. rattus is exempt (as 'generally found in Delaware' or equivalent to the Norway rat) before relying on this.
  • Ask the DDA State Veterinarian whether R. rattus is exempt or permit-required
  • If permit-required: apply for an Individual Exotic Animal Permit

Forms: Delaware Exotic Animals (DDA) · Where: Delaware Dept of Agriculture — Poultry & Animal Health (State Veterinarian) · Fees: ~$25 / 3 years (Individual Permit)

Source: Delaware Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian), Delaware Dept of Agriculture

A Certificate of Veterinary Inspection within 30 days is required to bring a small animal into Delaware (3 Del. Admin. Code 904), separate from any exotic permit.
  • Get a CVI within 30 days before importing

Where: Delaware Dept of Agriculture

Source: Delaware Dept of Agriculture

County codes add a layer (Kent and Sussex ordinances reach 'nondomesticated mammals'; New Castle County via its Dept of Land Use). Check your county/town. And never release a roof rat — it is itself an established invasive.

Where: Your county

Source: Delaware Dept of Agriculture

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Delaware

In Delaware, "exotic" (non-native) mammals are regulated by the Department of Agriculture / State Veterinarian (3 Del. C. ch. 72; 3 Del. Admin. Code 903), and any non-native mammal that is NOT on the Department's exempt list needs an Individual Exotic Animal Permit ($25, valid 3 years, home inspection, escape-proof enclosure). Here is the trap for roof rats. The binding regulation's exempt list (903-6.1.1) names "Norway rats" — that is the species Rattus norvegicus, the ordinary fancy rat — but it does NOT name the roof rat (Rattus rattus). So a near-identical domestic pet may be swept into the exotic-permit system simply because the rule names one rat species and not its cousin. Confusingly, the Department's own public webpage simplifies that list to just "Rats," which suggests the agency may already mean to cover pet rats generally. That gap between the codified species name and the plain-English webpage is exactly what needs to be cleared up: a keeper reading the website thinks "rats are exempt," while the regulation as written names only the Norway rat.

The ask: Ask the State Veterinarian's office, in writing, to confirm that captive-bred Rattus rattus (roof/black rat) kept as a tame indoor pet is covered by the existing "Rats" exemption shown on the Department's exotic-animals webpage — i.e., that it is exempt just like the listed Norway rat and the other small pet rodents (hamsters, gerbils, mice, guinea pigs). If the Department cannot read the current exemption that broadly, ask it to add "Rattus rattus" to the exempt mammal list (903-6.1.1) through the rulemaking process the regulation already provides at 903-4.3, on the ground that the domestic roof rat is the same kind of small, captive-bred, tame pet rodent the list is meant to cover. Either path — a written clarification or a formal addition — fixes the gap.

Where the lever really is: This is an AGENCY lever, not a legislative one. The Delaware statute (3 Del. C. §7201) does not single out the roof rat or put it on any banned list; it simply says non-native mammals need a permit unless exempted, and it delegates the exempt list to the Department of Agriculture's regulation (903). The whole problem lives in that regulation's exempt list — it names "Norway rats" (Rattus norvegicus) but is silent on the roof rat (Rattus rattus) — and crucially, the very same regulation (903-4.3) hands the State Veterinarian the power to add or delete species from that list "when suggested by the public through the rule making process." So the body that created the gap is the body that can close it. Two things make this even cleaner in Delaware: (1) the Department's own published exotic-animals webpage already lists "Rats" generically as exempt, which gives the agency an easy, no-rulemaking way to confirm in writing that pet roof rats are covered; and (2) if a written read isn't enough, the formal §4.3 petition is a documented, built-in channel for the durable fix. Because the statute itself never names the roof rat, going to the Legislature is unnecessary here — the General Assembly already delegated the list to the agency, and the agency can fix it under powers the rule expressly grants. The correct levers are therefore (a) a written clarification/declaratory read from the State Veterinarian and (b) a 903-4.3 rulemaking petition to add Rattus rattus to the exempt list.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Delaware Department of Agriculture — Poultry & Animal Health Section (State Veterinarian's office) (executive / agency) — deanimalhealth@delaware.gov
    This is the office that administers the exotic-animal permit program and maintains the exempt list. It is the right place to ask for a written clarification that captive-bred Rattus rattus is covered by the exempt 'Rats' entry, and it is the office that processes a 903-4.3 petition to add the species. Use the official contact-us page or the general section inbox — do not address an individual staff member by name.
  • Delaware Department of Agriculture — Exotic Animals program page (permit guidance & exempt-list reference) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    This is the Department's own public exotic-animals page; it lists 'Rats' as exempt and explains the permit/exemption framework. Cite it in your letter as the basis for asking the State Veterinarian to confirm in writing that pet roof rats fall under that exempt entry.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Delaware State Veterinarian, Poultry & Animal Health Section:

I am writing about how Delaware's exotic-animal exemption applies to the domestic roof rat (Rattus rattus). Your Department's exotic-animals webpage lists "Rats" among the exempt small pet rodents, but the regulation's exempt list (3 Del. Admin. Code 903-6.1.1) names only "Norway rats" (Rattus norvegicus). I am asking the Department to confirm in writing that a captive-bred, tame Rattus rattus kept as a pet is covered by that "Rats" exemption — the same as the listed Norway rat and other small pet rodents like hamsters and gerbils.

This is a species-naming gap, not a difference in the animal. These rats are captive-bred for generations, hand-tame, kept indoors in escape-proof enclosures, and never released — they are pets, no different in keeping from the fancy rat.

If the current exemption cannot be read to cover them, I respectfully ask the Department to add "Rattus rattus" to the exempt mammal list through the rulemaking process provided at 903-4.3. I am glad to supply documentation in support.

Thank you for your consideration.

[Your name]
[Your Delaware town/county]
[Your email]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Del. Code Title 3, ch. 72 §§7201–7203 — Possession of Mammals or Reptiles Exotic to Delaware — Delaware General Assembly
  • 3 Del. Admin. Code 903 — Exotic Animal Regulations (6.1.1 exempt list names 'Norway rats'; 6.5 non-listed = permit) — Delaware Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian)
  • Delaware Dept of Agriculture — Exotic Animals (permit guidance: 'if the animal is not on the list, it requires a permit') — Delaware Dept of Agriculture
  • 3 Del. Admin. Code 904 — Health Requirements Governing the Admission of Animals (import CVI within 30 days) — Delaware Dept of Agriculture

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Florida? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Florida

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Florida-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Florida is silent. See United States.

Summary. Florida is permissive to keep a pet roof rat — with one paid-sale catch, now confirmed directly by FWC. FWC decides 'domestic vs. wild' by SPECIES, not by how tame an individual is, so roof/black rats count as 'wild rats' even when captive-bred for generations. The upshot (FWC Captive Wildlife, written reply 2026-06-08): KEEPING one as a pet needs NO license, and GIVING one away (any transfer with no money) needs NO license — all rats are exempt from personal-possession licensing. But SELLING one (any transfer for money) requires a Class III 'Exhibition or Public Sale' (ESC) license. Importing a roof rat into Florida needs a free 45-day FWC Wildlife Importation Permit plus a veterinary health certificate. Never release a nonnative.

Confirmed by the agencies.
  • FWC Captive Wildlife Office (written reply, 2026-06-08): FWC determines whether an animal is domestic or wild by the SPECIES, not by an individual's tameness — so black/roof rats are treated as wild rats even when captive-bred. KEEPING one as a pet requires NO license (all rats, wild or domestic, are exempt from personal-possession licensing), and GIVING one away with no money changing hands requires NO license. SELLING one (any transfer for payment) requires a Class III 'Exhibition or Public Sale' (ESC) license.
  • FDACS Division of Animal Industry (written guidance, 2020): importing animals into Florida requires a veterinary health certificate (OCVI) issued within 30 days; reportable diseases must be reported.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

FWC confirmed in writing (2026-06-08) that ALL rats — wild or domestic — are exempt from personal-possession licensing, so keeping a captive-bred roof rat as a pet needs no FWC license. (Consistent with F.A.C. 68A-6.003(14)(d), which exempts 'Rats and mice' for personal use, and with roof rats not being on FWC's Prohibited Nonnative Species list.)

Sources: Florida Administrative Code, FL FWC

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

Breeding for personal use — keeping the offspring as your own pets or giving them away free — requires no FWC license (all rats are exempt from personal-possession licensing). There is no separate FWC 'breeding permit.' Note: the moment you SELL offspring (transfer for money), the selling rule below applies (a Class III ESC license).

Sources: Florida Administrative Code

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

RESOLVED by FWC's written reply (2026-06-08): because FWC treats roof rats as WILDLIFE by species (not by tameness), SELLING one — any transfer where money changes hands — requires a Class III 'Exhibition or Public Sale' (ESC) license. GIVING one away with no payment requires NO license (all rats are exempt from personal-possession licensing). This supersedes the brief 2020 verbal 'no license to sell' guidance, which didn't account for the species-based doctrine.

Sources: FL FWC, Florida Administrative Code, Florida Administrative Code

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Moving an exempt personal pet within Florida needs no permit. IMPORTING a roof rat into Florida (it is non-native wildlife) requires a FREE FWC Wildlife Importation Permit (CWL), valid 45 days (applicant must be 16+); and FDACS requires a veterinary health certificate (OCVI) for animals entering the state. It is illegal to release any nonnative species.

Sources: FL FWC, FDACS, FL FWC

Restrictions & responsibilities

To SELL roof rats (any transfer for money), you need a Class III 'License to Possess Wildlife for Exhibition or Public Sale' (ESC), $50/yr — confirmed required by FWC (2026-06-08) because roof rats are wildlife by species. GIVING them away free needs no license. No experience hours, but a disaster plan + inventory/source recordkeeping are required for the ESC.
  • If you'll sell for money: apply for the Class III Exhibition/Public Sale (ESC) license and file a disaster plan
  • If only giving away free: nothing required

Forms: FWC — Sale of Wildlife · Where: FWC Captive Wildlife Office · Fees: $50/yr (Class III ESC) to sell; $0 to give away

Source: FL FWC, Florida Administrative Code

To bring a roof rat INTO Florida, get a free FWC Wildlife Importation Permit (CWL), valid 45 days (applicant must be 16+), plus a veterinary health certificate (OCVI) issued within 30 days. Applies to private and commercial moves alike.
  • Apply for the FWC Wildlife Importation Permit (CWL) before crossing into Florida
  • Carry a veterinary health certificate (OCVI) issued within 30 days

Forms: FWC — Importation of Wildlife · Where: FWC Captive Wildlife Office · Fees: No cost (CWL); veterinary fee for the OCVI

Source: FL FWC, FDACS

It is illegal to release any nonnative species, including roof rats, into the wild in Florida. Keep them contained and rehome responsibly; never release. Local city/county ordinances may also limit exotic-pet keeping or large breeding operations.

Where: Your county animal services / municipal code enforcement

Source: FL FWC

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Fla. Admin. Code 68A-6.003 — Permit Requirements & Exceptions ((14)(d) 'Rats and mice' personal use; (12) dealer) — Florida Administrative Code
  • Fla. Admin. Code 68A-6.004 — Possession of Class I/II/III Wildlife (Class III ESC sale license) — Florida Administrative Code
  • Class III Wildlife — FWC — FL FWC
  • Sale of Wildlife — FWC (Class III Exhibition/Public Sale license) — FL FWC
  • Importation of Wildlife — FWC (free CWL, 45-day) — FL FWC
  • Prohibited Nonnative Species List — FWC (black rat not listed) — FL FWC
  • Regulations for Nonnative Species — FWC (no-release) — FL FWC
  • Official Certificates of Veterinary Inspection — FDACS — FDACS

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Georgia? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Georgia

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Georgia-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Georgia is silent. See United States.

Summary. Despite Georgia's reputation for strict exotic-pet laws, the roof rat is explicitly carved out: the state's Wild Animal license rule (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 391-4-8-.05) lists the rodent order as 'all species except … Rattus rattus …,' naming the roof rat among the species that need NO Wild Animal License. So you can legally keep, breed, and give away a captive-bred roof rat with no DNR license, and pet rodents are exempt from Georgia's import veterinary-certificate (CVI) rule. The only caveat is commercial scale: selling more than 30 self-raised animals a year (or running a business) requires a Georgia Dept of Agriculture pet-dealer license.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Georgia's Wild Animal license requirement (O.C.G.A. §27-5-5) applies only to species the Board of Natural Resources lists by rule. Rule 391-4-8-.05's Order Rodentia entry reads 'All species except … Rattus rattus …,' naming the roof/black rat among the species that do NOT require a Wild Animal License. So no DNR license or permit is needed to keep one as a pet. Gemini DR-verified: R. rattus is named in the Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 391-4-8-.05 wildlife-license exemption (alongside R. norvegicus) -> treated as a standard pet by the GDA, not regulated wildlife.

Sources: Georgia DNR / Secretary of State, Georgia General Assembly, Georgia DNR Law Enforcement Division

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

There is no separate breeding permit for an exempt rodent — if keeping is unlicensed, hobby breeding is likewise unregulated by DNR (R. rattus is off the regulated wild-animal list). The only breeding-adjacent touchpoint is the Dept of Agriculture pet-dealer threshold, which governs commercial selling, not breeding itself. Gemini DR-verified: hobby breeding is free only up to the GDA Pet Dealer threshold - selling/exchanging/adopting-out >1 litter OR >30 adults per 12 months requires a GDA Pet Dealer License (40-13-13-.07); 'giving away' counts as 'offers for adoption.'

Sources: Georgia DNR / Secretary of State, Georgia General Assembly (Animal Protection Act)

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

DNR places no sale restriction on R. rattus (it is exempt from the wild-animal list). But the Georgia Animal Protection Act defines 'pet' to include 'rodent,' so selling above the statutory threshold makes you a 'pet dealer' needing a Dept of Agriculture license: the exemption covers a person who 'sells only animals that he or she has produced and raised, not to exceed 30 animals a year' and isn't otherwise a licensed business. Casual sale/giving below that threshold needs no license. Gemini DR-verified: a GDA Pet Dealer License is required above the >1-litter / >30-adult hobbyist exemption; rodents are exempt from outgoing sales-record keeping.

Sources: Georgia General Assembly (Animal Protection Act), Georgia Dept of Agriculture

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Georgia's import Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) requirement covers 'all pets except fish and rodents,' so rodents — including R. rattus — are exempt from the import CVI. No state import permit or health certificate is required for a pet roof rat. (Federal USFWS Form 3-177 still applies to international movement — see United States.) Gemini DR-verified: rodents are exempt from the CVI requirement for pets entering Georgia (40-13-2-.19(4)); intrastate unrestricted. (Federal: international import = USFWS Form 3-177 + CDC African-rodent embargo.)

Sources: Georgia Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Selling more than 30 self-raised animals per year, or operating as a business, makes you a 'pet dealer' under the Georgia Animal Protection Act and requires a Dept of Agriculture pet-dealer license. Private, low-volume placement and giveaways are exempt.
  • Stay under 30 self-raised animals/year to remain exempt, or apply for a GA Dept of Agriculture pet-dealer license

Forms: Georgia Pet Dealer Licenses · Where: Georgia Dept of Agriculture (Companion Animal/Equine Division) · Fees: Set by the Department

Source: Georgia General Assembly (Animal Protection Act), Georgia Dept of Agriculture

Never release a roof rat — it is a non-native species; rehome responsibly.

Source: Georgia DNR Law Enforcement Division

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 391-4-8-.05 — Wild Animals, License Required (Order Rodentia exemption naming Rattus rattus) — Georgia DNR / Secretary of State
  • O.C.G.A. §27-5-5 — Wild animals for which a license or permit is required — Georgia General Assembly
  • Bringing Animals into Georgia — import CVI rule ('all pets except fish and rodents') — Georgia Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian)
  • O.C.G.A. §4-11-2 — Definitions ('pet dealer,' 30-animal exemption, 'pet' includes rodent) — Georgia General Assembly (Animal Protection Act)
  • Pet Dealer Licenses — Georgia Dept of Agriculture
  • Guide to Legal Pets — Georgia DNR Law Enforcement Division

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.
