item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Guam? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Guam

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the Guam-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Guam is silent. See United States.

Summary. On Guam, keeping a captive-bred roof rat as a pet is effectively prohibited. The binding layer is import: under Guam's animal-import rules (9 GAR Title 9, ch. 1) every animal needs Territorial Veterinarian clearance to enter, and the Dept of Agriculture's official Species Listing for Importation expressly BANS 'mice and rodents for breeding or pet sale' (accepting rodents only as research / brown-tree-snake-control mice). With no lawful way to import or commercially handle pet rodents, breeding and sale are barred outright, and there's no lawful source for a pet roof rat. (Bare possession isn't separately criminalized — that narrow point is unclear — but the practical reality is prohibition.) Never release one.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

No statute names Rattus for possession and no general exotic-pet possession ban was found, so bare possession isn't separately criminalized (that narrow point is unclear). BUT the only lawful way to OBTAIN a captive-bred pet roof rat is import, and DOAG's Species Listing for Importation bans 'mice and rodents for breeding or pet sale' — so there is no lawful pathway to acquire/keep one. A wild-caught island rat would be a captive 'wild or feral animal' (9 GAR §1100) subject to the no-release rule.

Sources: Guam Dept of Agriculture (Animal Health/Animal Control), Compiler of Laws, Judiciary of Guam

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

DOAG's Species Listing for Importation specifically bans 'mice and rodents FOR BREEDING or pet sale' by name — breeding-purpose rodents are the express target. Stock can't be lawfully imported, so a roof-rat breeding colony has no lawful basis.

Sources: Guam Dept of Agriculture (Animal Health/Animal Control)

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

The same DOAG listing bans rodents 'for breeding or PET SALE.' Commercial distribution is the exact disallowed purpose, and there can be no legal supply chain since import of stock is barred; non-commercial give-away faces the same wall.

Sources: Guam Dept of Agriculture (Animal Health/Animal Control)

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Import is the binding layer and it's closed: 9 GAR §1102 subjects ALL animals to Territorial-Veterinarian inspection and §1103(d) bars entry until passed/permitted; DOAG's Species Listing places 'mice and rodents for breeding or pet sale' in the BANNED column. The mainland permit-exemption (§1101(b)) applies only if the animal complies with all rules — the species ban is such a rule. Releasing/turning loose is independently barred (§1103(c)).

Sources: Compiler of Laws, Judiciary of Guam, Guam Dept of Agriculture (Animal Health/Animal Control)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Guam's Dept of Agriculture import list bans rodents for breeding or pet sale, and all animal imports need Territorial Veterinarian clearance — so there's no lawful way to bring in or keep a captive-bred pet roof rat. Do not attempt to import one; never release any animal (9 GAR §1103(c)).
  • Ask the DOAG Territorial Veterinarian whether any individual entry permit/variance exists

Where: Guam Dept of Agriculture, Animal Health / Territorial Veterinarian

Source: Guam Dept of Agriculture (Animal Health/Animal Control), Compiler of Laws, Judiciary of Guam

Guam prohibits importing/keeping/breeding/selling rats (DOAG closed import list, Mar 2023) -- even the fancy rat (R. norvegicus); the only exception is institutional mice for brown-tree-snake research. No private-keeper permit pathway. Never release (R. rattus is an established invasive pest here).

Where: Guam DOAG -- Animal Health Division (Quarantine)

Source: Guam Department of Agriculture

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Guam. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Guam

On Guam, you cannot legally obtain or keep a captive-bred pet roof rat (Rattus rattus). The block is the import layer: the Guam Department of Agriculture (DOAG) runs a closed, positive Species Listing for Importation, and that list places "mice and rodents for breeding or pet sale" in the BANNED column. The only rodents allowed in are mice imported by institutions for brown-tree-snake control and research. Every animal entering Guam also needs Territorial Veterinarian clearance (9 GAR Title 9, ch. 1), and a banned species cannot pass that clearance. There is no published private-keeper permit pathway — even the common fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is barred — so there is no lawful way to bring in, breed, sell, give away, or therefore keep a pet roof rat. Bare possession is not separately named in any statute (that narrow point is unclear), but in practice the import ban makes keeping one impossible. Guam also has a real, established invasive-rodent and brown-tree-snake crisis, so any change faces a high bar. Never release any animal.

The ask: Ask DOAG, in writing, to (1) confirm whether a single captive-bred, altered (non-breeding), microchipped, health-certified domestic rat kept solely as an indoor pet really falls under "mice and rodents for breeding or pet sale," and (2) consider amending the Species Listing for Importation — or granting an individual entry permit/variance under 9 GAR §1101/§1111 — to allow such an animal under strict conditions (sterilized so it cannot breed, permanently indoors, microchipped, with a no-release/biosecurity agreement), the same way altered pet rabbits and other small companion mammals are handled. Make clear this is about one tame, captive-bred companion animal that is biologically incapable of establishing a wild population, not about the invasive island rats.

Where the lever really is: This is branch (b)-as-a-regulation, not a misread. The prohibition is NOT a bureaucrat misapplying an unclear rule — DOAG is correctly applying its own Species Listing for Importation, which deliberately bans "mice and rodents for breeding or pet sale." So a complaint that "the agency got the law wrong" will go nowhere; the agency is reading it exactly as written. BUT — unlike a legislative statute naming the species — this ban lives in an administrative POSITIVE LIST that DOAG itself owns, adopts, and can amend (regulatory authority 9 GAR Title 9, ch. 1, under 5 GCA §60108). That makes the realistic lever a rulemaking/list-amendment petition (or an individual entry-permit/variance request) directed AT DOAG — asking the agency to change its own list, not asking it to reinterpret a statute. This is why the primary target is DOAG and the secondary target is a Guam senator: senators have oversight of DOAG and, given Guam's genuine invasive-rodent and brown-tree-snake sensitivities, political backing may be needed to move a list amendment. Do not frame this as "you are applying the law wrong"; frame it as "please amend the list / grant a conditioned variance." Set expectations realistically: Guam is the hardest US jurisdiction for this ask because R. rattus is an established invasive pest there, so the strongest version of the request is a narrowly conditioned individual variance (sterilized, indoor-only, microchipped, no-release) rather than a broad delisting.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Guam Department of Agriculture — Animal Health Section (Territorial Veterinarian / Quarantine) (executive / agency) — quarantine@doag.guam.gov
    DOAG owns and can amend the Species Listing for Importation that contains the ban, and the Territorial Veterinarian issues entry permits/variances under 9 GAR §1101/§1111. This is the only office that can change the list or grant a conditioned variance — the correct primary target for a positive-list ask. Email verified as the current official quarantine inbox; the same page hosts an official feedback form.
  • Guam Legislature — Senators Directory (contact your senator), 38th Guam Legislature (legislature) — official contact page
    Senators have oversight of DOAG. Because Guam's invasive-rodent and brown-tree-snake sensitivities make a list amendment politically charged, a senator's backing can help move DOAG to consider a narrowly conditioned variance or rule change. Secondary channel; use the official directory and contact your own senator — no individual is named here.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request to confirm status of — and consider a conditioned pathway for — a single captive-bred pet domestic rat

Dear Guam Department of Agriculture, Animal Health Section,

I am writing about the Species Listing for Importation, which places "mice and rodents for breeding or pet sale" in the banned column. I would like to keep one captive-bred, tame domestic rat solely as an indoor companion animal — not for breeding, and not for sale or any commercial purpose.

These animals are bred in captivity over many generations, are hand-tame, live their whole lives indoors in a cage, and are never released. A single sterilized, indoor-only animal cannot establish a wild population and poses no greater biosecurity risk than the small companion mammals Guam already permits.

Could you please confirm in writing (1) whether such a single pet animal truly falls under "mice and rodents for breeding or pet sale," and (2) whether the Department would consider amending the Species Listing, or granting an individual entry permit or variance under 9 GAR §1101/§1111, for one altered (non-breeding), microchipped, health-certified pet kept permanently indoors under a no-release agreement?

I fully respect Guam's invasive-species and brown-tree-snake concerns and am asking only about one tame, captive-bred companion that cannot breed. I would welcome any conditions that would make such a pathway possible.

Thank you for your time and for the work you do to protect Guam.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your village/contact]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • DOAG Species Listing for Importation (Mammals — Banned: 'mice and rodents for breeding or pet sale') — Guam Dept of Agriculture (Animal Health/Animal Control)
  • 9 GAR Title 9, Div. 1, Ch. 1 — Importing Animals (§§1100-1113; Territorial Vet clearance; no-release) — Compiler of Laws, Judiciary of Guam
  • Guam CQA/DOAG Pet Import Requirements (other vertebrates 'generally prohibited entry') — Guam Customs & Quarantine Agency / DOAG
  • Guam DOAG Species Listing for Importation (Mar 9, 2023) -- mice/rodents prohibited for breeding/pet sale; only BTS-research exception — Guam Department of Agriculture

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Hawaii? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Hawaii

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the Hawaii-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Hawaii is silent. See United States.

Summary. Hawaii is legal-with-permit for domesticated rats — not the flat ban earlier research suggested. Hawaii runs four animal lists under HAR Chapter 4-71: Prohibited, Restricted (research/exhibition), Restricted (private/commercial), and Conditionally Approved. Domesticated rats sit on the CONDITIONALLY APPROVED list (HAR §4-71-6.5), which means they can be imported and kept WITH a prior HDOA Plant Quarantine import permit (Form PQ-7), entering only through Honolulu and inspected at the Airport Animal Quarantine Facility — a standard administrative permit available to private keepers, not a research-only carve-out. The one genuine open question is species precision: the list covers 'domesticated rats' (clearly the fancy rat, R. norvegicus), and whether it extends by name to a domesticated/fancy R. rattus needs written HDOA confirmation (if not, R. rattus would fall to the default-prohibited bucket and need a case-by-case permit). Wild/feral Rattus remains an invasive pest under separate public-health law — a different regime from the import-permit system.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Domesticated rats are on Hawaii's Conditionally Approved list (HAR §4-71-6.5 / AR-71C), NOT the Prohibited list — so they may be kept under a valid HDOA Plant Quarantine import permit (HRS §150A-6.2). Possession without a permit for a listed animal is unlawful; an animal on no list is prohibited by default. Confidence is medium because whether the 'domesticated rats' entry covers R. rattus by name (vs only R. norvegicus) needs HDOA confirmation.

Sources: Hawaii Dept of Agriculture & Biosecurity, Hawaii State Legislature, HDOA Plant Quarantine Branch

Breeding   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

No express breeding prohibition in the public HAR 4-71 text, but each imported animal must be permitted, and the Board may attach permit conditions on reproduction, facility type, and disposition of offspring (HRS §150A-6.2 allows time/place/use/special-precaution conditions). Establishing a breeding colony should be cleared with HDOA first.

Sources: Hawaii Dept of Agriculture & Biosecurity, Hawaii State Legislature

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

HAR 4-71 is import-focused (the permit controls the introduction event); no provision specifically regulates intra-state sale/transfer of conditionally-approved animals already lawfully held. Whether a Hawaii recipient needs their own permit/documentation isn't specified publicly and likely turns on permit conditions — confirm with HDOA before transferring.

Sources: Hawaii Dept of Agriculture & Biosecurity

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Importing requires an HDOA Plant Quarantine permit (Form PQ-7) obtained in advance; rats/mice/guinea pigs/chinchillas enter ONLY through Honolulu International Airport and are submitted by the carrier to the Airport Animal Quarantine Holding Facility for inspection. No state law regulates transport OUT of Hawaii (airlines set their own policies). The permit is the gatekeeping mechanism. Never release.

Sources: HDOA Plant Quarantine Branch, Hawaii Dept of Agriculture & Biosecurity

Restrictions & responsibilities

To bring/keep a domesticated rat in Hawaii, get an HDOA Plant Quarantine import permit (Form PQ-7) BEFORE importing; the animal enters only via Honolulu and is inspected at the Airport Animal Quarantine Facility. ⚠️ Confirm in writing that the Conditionally Approved 'domesticated rats' entry covers R. rattus specifically before relying on it. Never release a roof rat (feral Rattus is an invasive pest).
  • Apply for an HDOA Plant Quarantine import permit (Form PQ-7) via the online portal or by mail, in advance
  • Confirm with HDOA whether domesticated R. rattus is covered by the Conditionally Approved list or needs a case-by-case 150A-6.2 permit

Forms: HDOA Plant Quarantine — Application for Permit to Import (Form PQ-7) · Where: Hawaii Dept of Agriculture & Biosecurity — Plant Quarantine Branch · Fees: Import permit fee (confirm current schedule with HDOA)

Source: HDOA Plant Quarantine Branch, Hawaii State Legislature

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Hawaii

Good news first: keeping a pet rat in Hawaii is NOT flatly banned. Hawaii regulates animal imports through lists under Hawaii Administrative Rules (HAR) Chapter 4-71, and "domesticated rats" sit on the Conditionally Approved Animals list (HAR §4-71-6.5) — meaning they can be lawfully imported and kept WITH a prior Hawaii Department of Agriculture & Biosecurity (HDOA) Plant Quarantine import permit (Form PQ-7). Animals enter only through Honolulu and are inspected at the Airport Animal Quarantine Facility. The catch is a species-precision gap. The Conditionally Approved entry is for "domesticated rats," and HDOA's own supporting materials describe that as the laboratory/fancy Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus) — bred for generations under controlled conditions and unlikely to establish in the wild. A domesticated, captive-bred fancy roof rat (Rattus rattus) shares that same tame, indoor-only, never-released profile, but it is not named on the list, and the wild roof rat is exactly the invasive pest Hawaii fights. So an applicant for a domesticated R. rattus risks falling through a gap: not clearly covered by the "domesticated rats" entry, and an unlisted animal is prohibited by default. This is a bureaucratic reading/coverage question, not a flat statutory ban — the permitting pathway already exists and HDOA controls the list.

The ask: Ask HDOA, in writing, to clarify and (if needed) close the gap: (1) Confirm whether the HAR §4-71-6.5 Conditionally Approved "domesticated rats" entry already covers a domesticated/fancy Rattus rattus lineage, or only Rattus norvegicus. (2) If it does not currently cover domesticated R. rattus, add the domesticated/captive-bred R. rattus lineage to the Conditionally Approved entry, OR confirm that a private keeper may obtain a case-by-case import permit for domesticated R. rattus under HRS §150A-6.2. (3) State the standard permit conditions, fee, and processing time for a few pet rats. Request a written determination you can rely on before importing.

Where the lever really is: Branch = (a) AGENCY, with a narrow rulemaking fallback — NOT a fight with the legislature. Here is the concrete reasoning. The statute (HRS §150A-6.2) does NOT ban rats; it delegates to the Board of Agriculture the power to maintain the prohibited/restricted/conditionally-approved lists and to issue permits with conditions. The substantive species lists live in administrative rule (HAR Chapter 4-71) and in the published Conditionally Approved list (AR-71C) — instruments HDOA owns. "Domesticated rats" are ALREADY on the Conditionally Approved (keep-with-permit) list, so there is no statute correctly banning pet rats that the agency is merely enforcing. The only live problem is whether HDOA reads "domesticated rats" to include a domesticated/fancy Rattus rattus or only Rattus norvegicus. That is a classic agency interpretation/coverage gap — fixable by the agency without the legislature: a written determination (declaratory clarification) that the entry covers domesticated R. rattus, or a case-by-case HRS §150A-6.2 permit, or, if HDOA insists the entry is genus-specific, a routine update to the Conditionally Approved list to name the domesticated R. rattus lineage. Because the lever is the agency's own list and permit power, appealing to HDOA is exactly the right move — this is the opposite of trying to get an agency to ignore a statute it is correctly applying. The legislature is NOT the first stop. Escalation to a HAR Chapter 4-71 amendment (which has a public-comment/rulemaking window) only becomes relevant IF HDOA both refuses to read the existing entry to cover domesticated R. rattus and declines a case-by-case permit. Start with the written agency inquiry; keep the rulemaking-comment route in reserve.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Hawaii Department of Agriculture & Biosecurity — Plant Quarantine Branch (Import Permits / Form PQ-7) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    This is the office that maintains the Conditionally Approved Animals list and issues the import permits. It is the correct first stop to get a written determination on whether domesticated Rattus rattus is covered, and to apply for a permit (Form PQ-7). Verified live: it links the PQ-7 application and explains the conditionally-approved permit process.
  • Hawaii Department of Agriculture & Biosecurity — Plant Quarantine Branch Office Contacts (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Official contacts page for the Plant Quarantine Branch (Oahu main office phone 808-832-0566; airport 808-837-8413). Use it to direct a written species-coverage inquiry to the branch that controls the list. Listed because the branch's published page does not post a dedicated permit-inquiry email, so an official page/phone is the verified channel rather than an unconfirmed inbox.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To: Hawaii Department of Agriculture & Biosecurity, Plant Quarantine Branch

Re: Coverage of the Conditionally Approved "domesticated rats" entry for a domesticated Rattus rattus

I am a Hawaii resident seeking to keep a domesticated, captive-bred pet rat as an indoor companion animal, fully in compliance with state import rules. I understand "domesticated rats" are on the Conditionally Approved Animals list (HAR §4-71-6.5) and may be imported with a Plant Quarantine permit (Form PQ-7).

My question concerns species precision. The animals I keep are domesticated, captive-bred, hand-tame Rattus rattus — multi-generation pet lineages kept strictly indoors in enclosures and never released, indistinguishable in behavior and risk from the fancy Norway rat already covered. They are not wild-caught and pose no establishment risk.

Please confirm in writing: (1) Does the Conditionally Approved "domesticated rats" entry include a domesticated/fancy Rattus rattus lineage, or only Rattus norvegicus? (2) If it does not, may a private keeper obtain a permit for domesticated R. rattus under the same Conditionally Approved pathway or a case-by-case permit under HRS §150A-6.2 — or could the domesticated R. rattus lineage be added to the Conditionally Approved entry? (3) What permit conditions, fee, and processing time apply?

Thank you for a written determination I can rely on before importing.

[Your name]
[Your city, Hawaii]
[Your email / phone]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • HAR §4-71-6.5 — List of Conditionally Approved Animals (AR-71C; domesticated rats listed, NOT prohibited) — Hawaii Dept of Agriculture & Biosecurity
  • HRS §150A-6.2 — Animal import (Board maintains lists + issues permits; may set conditions) — Hawaii State Legislature
  • HDOA — Importing Animals to Hawai'i + Application for Permits (Form PQ-7; Honolulu entry; AAQHF inspection) — HDOA Plant Quarantine Branch
  • HAR §4-71-6 — List of Prohibited Animals (AR-71P; domesticated rats NOT on it) — HDOA

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat, 'iole.

item.dc:creator: admin

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Iowa

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the Iowa-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Iowa is silent. See United States.

Summary. Iowa is one of the cleaner states for the roof rat. The Dangerous Wild Animals law (Iowa Code ch. 717F) is a closed list — big cats, bears, wolves, primates, crocodilians, venomous snakes — that includes NO rodents, and DNR jurisdiction (ch. 481A) covers native wildlife and wild releases, not an indoor captive-bred pet. So keeping, breeding, and selling/giving are legal at the state level. Two administrative touchpoints: a pet-shop/dealer license (IDALS) only kicks in above $500/yr OR 6+ animals/yr in sales, and importing needs a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (Iowa's prohibited-rodent import list — the monkeypox seven — does NOT include Rattus). Never release one.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Iowa Code §717F.1 defines 'dangerous wild animal' as a closed list of enumerated families/orders (Canidae, Felidae, Ursidae, Rhinocerotidae, Proboscidea, Primates, Crocodilia, venomous snakes/lizards) — order Rodentia is absent. DNR (ch. 481A) regulates native wildlife and wild introductions, not a captive-bred indoor pet rodent. No state possession permit applies.

Sources: Iowa Legislature, Iowa Legislature / Iowa DNR

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

ch. 717F doesn't cover rodents and §481A.47 governs only wild introductions, not closed-colony captive breeding. IDALS Animal Welfare rules (IAC 21 ch. 67) require a pet-shop/dealer license only above the thresholds ($500/yr OR 6+ animals/yr); hobby breeding below that is unregulated.

Sources: Iowa Legislature, Iowa Dept of Agriculture & Land Stewardship

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

No Iowa law prohibits selling/giving captive-bred rodents not on the ch. 717F list. Commercial sale above $500/yr OR 6+ animals/yr makes you a 'pet shop' needing an IDALS license (IAC 21-67); free adoption and small sales are exempt.

Sources: Iowa Dept of Agriculture & Land Stewardship

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Intrastate transport is unregulated. IMPORT requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection under IAC 21-65; Iowa's prohibited-rodent import list (prairie dogs, Gambian rats, dormice, etc. — the 2003 monkeypox seven) does NOT include Rattus rattus. Confirm the pet-rodent CVI application with IDALS. Never release a roof rat.

Sources: Iowa Dept of Agriculture & Land Stewardship (via Cornell LII), Iowa Legislature

Restrictions & responsibilities

An IDALS pet-shop/dealer license is required only if you sell/breed above the thresholds ($500/yr OR 6+ animals/yr); below that, hobby breeding and free adoption need no license.
  • Stay under the IAC 21-67 thresholds, or obtain an IDALS pet-shop license

Where: Iowa Dept of Agriculture & Land Stewardship (Animal Welfare)

Source: Iowa Dept of Agriculture & Land Stewardship

Importing a pet rat into Iowa requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (IAC 21-65). Rattus is not on Iowa's prohibited-import rodent list. No CVI for in-state movement; never release.

Where: IDALS Animal Industry Bureau

Source: Iowa Dept of Agriculture & Land Stewardship (via Cornell LII)

  • Iowa Code §481A.47 — Importing/introducing fish & game (native wildlife / wild introduction) — Iowa Legislature / Iowa DNR
  • IAC 21 ch. 65 (21-65.3) — Animal & Livestock Importation (CVI; prohibited-rodent list excludes Rattus) — Iowa Dept of Agriculture & Land Stewardship (via Cornell LII)
  • IAC 21 ch. 67 — Animal Welfare (pet-shop/dealer license; $500 / 6-animal thresholds) — Iowa Dept of Agriculture & Land Stewardship

Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the Idaho-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Idaho is silent. See United States.

Summary. Idaho is currently legal for the roof rat — but it's the state to watch. R. rattus is not on Idaho's 'deleterious exotic animal' list (IDAPA 02.04.27), which is the rule that bans high-risk exotics, so keeping, breeding, and selling/giving a captive-bred roof rat is legal with no Dept of Agriculture possession permit. Importing animals into Idaho requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (and the deleterious-animal import ban doesn't reach R. rattus). ⚠️ Advocacy watch: in the 2026 session, Idaho's Senate passed S1271 — the 'Rodents of Unusual Size Act' — which would have explicitly banned possessing roof rats (and several other rodents); it DIED in the House (failed 32–38). It can return in 2027, so Idaho keepers should monitor the legislature and be ready to testify.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Idaho prohibits possession of 'deleterious exotic animals' listed in IDAPA 02.04.27 (admin rule under Idaho Code §25-3900 et seq.); Rattus rattus is NOT on that list, so no Dept of Agriculture possession permit is required to keep a captive-bred roof rat. (Idaho Fish & Game governs native wildlife, not pet rodents.) Currently legal — but see the 2026 S1271 advocacy watch.

Sources: Idaho State Dept of Agriculture, Idaho Legislature

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Because R. rattus isn't a deleterious exotic animal, no ISDA possession/propagation permit applies, and Idaho has no separate breeder-license regime for pet rodents (federal USDA/AWA may apply at commercial scale). Hobby breeding is legal.

Sources: Idaho State Dept of Agriculture

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

No Idaho law restricts selling or giving away a non-deleterious pet rodent, and there's no state pet-dealer license reaching private rodent sales/rehoming. Sale and free rehoming of captive-bred R. rattus are legal at the state level.

Sources: Idaho State Dept of Agriculture

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Importing animals into Idaho generally requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (IDAPA 02.04.21); the deleterious-exotic import ban doesn't reach R. rattus. Whether a CVI is enforced for owner-traveled pet rodents is unclear (small-pet leniency is common) — confirm with the State Vet before crossing. Intrastate transport is unregulated. Never release a roof rat.

Sources: Idaho State Dept of Agriculture, Idaho State Dept of Agriculture

Restrictions & responsibilities

Importing into Idaho may require a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (IDAPA 02.04.21); confirm whether owner-traveled pet rodents are exempt. No paperwork for in-state movement. Never release a roof rat.
  • Confirm pet-rodent import requirements with the ID State Veterinarian

Where: Idaho State Dept of Agriculture, Animal Industries

Source: Idaho State Dept of Agriculture

⚠️ Legislative watch: 2026 Senate Bill S1271 ('Rodents of Unusual Size Act') would have banned possessing roof rats — it passed the Senate but failed the House (32–38). It could return in 2027. Idaho keepers should monitor the legislature and be ready to testify (captive-bred pet ≠ wild pest). Check local ordinances too.
  • Monitor the Idaho Legislature for a re-introduced rodent-ban bill (successor to S1271)

Source: Idaho Legislature

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Idaho
⏳ Time-sensitive: Watch for a 2027 successor to Senate Bill S1271 — and act when it is introduced, before the committee hearing.

Keeping a domesticated roof rat is currently legal in Idaho. But in 2026, Senate Bill S1271 (the “Rodents of Unusual Size Act”) would have added roof rats to the state’s prohibited list; it passed the Senate and failed only narrowly in the House (32–38), so a successor bill could return.

The ask: Ask your Idaho state legislators to oppose any future bill that bans privately kept, captive-bred roof rats, and to distinguish domesticated pet Rattus rattus from wild pest populations.

Where the lever really is: This is a law-as-written question, not a bureaucratic one. The threat is a future statute, so the people who matter are your elected Senator and Representative (and testifying when a bill is in committee). Writing a state agency will not stop a bill.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Find & write your Idaho State Senator and Representative (legislature) — official contact page
    They cast the votes on any ban — S1271 was decided here, 32–38 in the House.
  • House & Senate committees that hear these bills (legislature) — official contact page
    Bills are heard in committee first; signing up to testify there is high-leverage.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Dear Senator / Representative [name],

I am a constituent in [town]. I'm writing to ask you to oppose any bill that would ban privately kept, captive-bred roof rats (Rattus rattus) as pets, such as the 2026 "Rodents of Unusual Size Act" (S1271).

Domesticated, captive-bred roof rats are not the wild pests the bill is aimed at. They are kept in cages indoors, never released, and are no more an agricultural threat than the fancy pet rats Idahoans already keep legally. A ban would punish responsible pet owners without affecting wild populations.

Please distinguish domesticated pet R. rattus from wild pests in any future legislation, and vote against a blanket ban.

Thank you for your time,
[Your name, town]

Official sources

  • IDAPA 02.04.27 — Rules Governing Deleterious Exotic Animals (R. rattus not listed) — Idaho State Dept of Agriculture
  • Idaho Code §25-3900 et seq. — Deleterious Exotic Animals (authorizing statute) — Idaho Legislature
  • IDAPA 02.04.21 — Rules Governing the Importation of Animals (CVI) — Idaho State Dept of Agriculture
  • Idaho Senate Bill S1271 (2026) — 'Rodents of Unusual Size Act' (passed Senate, failed House 32–38) — Idaho Legislature

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Illinois? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Illinois

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the Illinois-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Illinois is silent. See United States.

Summary. Illinois does not specifically regulate the roof rat as a pet. It is not a 'dangerous animal' (720 ILCS 5/48-10 lists big cats, bears, wolves, primates), and as a captive-bred, tame animal it falls outside the Wildlife Code's definition of 'wildlife' (520 ILCS 5/1.2) and is on no injurious-species list — so no state possession permit is required. The caveats are commercial: selling rats you did not raise yourself can require an Animal Welfare Act pet-shop/dealer license (225 ILCS 605, which exempts someone who sells only animals they 'produced and raised'), and you may never release a pet rat. Because the conclusion rests on statutory silence (no rule names the genus), it's best labeled unregulated/unclear — effectively legal.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

No general exotic/wild-animal possession permit covers rodents. The dangerous-animal prohibition (720 ILCS 5/48-10) lists only large carnivores and primates — no rodent. A captive-bred, tame rat doesn't meet the Wildlife Code's 'wild by nature... living unconfined... without the care of man' definition (520 ILCS 5/1.2), and no injurious-species list names Rattus. Effectively legal, but it rests on statutory silence rather than a named exemption.

Sources: Illinois General Assembly, Illinois General Assembly / IL DNR

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Private hobby breeding isn't separately regulated (R. rattus isn't 'wildlife'/protected/injurious, nor a dangerous animal). Commercial scale can trigger the Animal Welfare Act (225 ILCS 605), but it exempts 'a person who sells only such animals that he has produced and raised' — sheltering a true hobby breeder.

Sources: Illinois General Assembly / IL Dept of Agriculture, Illinois General Assembly / IL DNR

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Someone who sells/gives away only rats they produced and raised is exempt from the Animal Welfare Act pet-shop-operator definition (225 ILCS 605/2). Buying-and-reselling, or retailing as a business, requires an IL Dept of Agriculture license (225 ILCS 605/3). No DNR sale permit applies (R. rattus isn't protected/injurious wildlife). Free vetted adoption of home-bred rats is the exempt path.

Sources: Illinois General Assembly / IL Dept of Agriculture

Transport & import   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

In-state movement of a legally kept pet rat isn't regulated. Illinois's import CVI framework targets livestock/dogs/cats; the AWA import rule (8 Ill. Adm. Code 25.47) applies to AWA licensees bringing animals in commercially, not a private owner moving a pet — and no rodent-specific CVI rule is published, so confirm with the State Veterinarian. Never release (520 ILCS 5/2.3).

Sources: Illinois Administrative Code / IL Dept of Agriculture, Illinois General Assembly / IL DNR

Restrictions & responsibilities

Selling rats you did NOT raise yourself, or retailing as a business, requires an IL Dept of Agriculture pet-shop/dealer license (225 ILCS 605). Selling/giving only your own home-bred rats is exempt ('produced and raised').
  • Stay within the 'produced and raised' exemption, or get an Animal Welfare Act license

Where: Illinois Dept of Agriculture, Bureau of Animal Health & Welfare

Source: Illinois General Assembly / IL Dept of Agriculture

Never release a pet rat outdoors (520 ILCS 5/2.3). Local ordinances (e.g., Chicago) may add limits — check yours.

Source: Illinois General Assembly / IL DNR

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Help change this

How to help in Illinois

In Illinois, keeping a domesticated, captive-bred roof rat (Rattus rattus) as a pet is effectively legal — but the law never says so out loud, and that silence creates needless uncertainty for owners, breeders, and the vets and shelters they deal with. Here is the actual picture, statute by statute: Illinois's dangerous-animal law (720 ILCS 5/48-10) lists only big cats, bears, wolves, and primates — no rodent of any kind. The Wildlife Code's definition of "wildlife" (520 ILCS 5/1.2) covers animals "wild by nature... living unconfined... without the care of man," which a tame, cage-raised pet rat plainly is not. And the state's injurious-species list (17 Ill. Adm. Code Part 805) names exactly one rodent as injurious — the multimammate rat, genus Mastomys — and does NOT name Rattus rattus, the roof rat, or the black rat. So no possession permit is required, and the genus appears on no prohibited, dangerous, or injurious list. The only real caveats are commercial and ordinary: a true hobby breeder who gives away or sells only rats they raised themselves is exempt from Animal Welfare Act pet-shop licensing under the "produced and raised" provision (225 ILCS 605), and no one may ever release a pet rat outdoors (520 ILCS 5/2.3). The problem is not a hostile rule — it's the absence of a plain, written confirmation that an owner can point to.

The ask: Ask the Illinois Department of Agriculture's Bureau of Animal Health & Welfare (the State Veterinarian's office) for a short written confirmation, in plain language, that: (1) the genus Rattus / Rattus rattus appears on no Illinois prohibited, dangerous-animal, "wildlife," or injurious-species list, and no state permit is required to keep one as a pet; (2) a hobby breeder who gives away or sells only home-bred pet rats is exempt from Animal Welfare Act licensing under the "produced and raised" provision (225 ILCS 605); and (3) whether a private owner bringing a pet rodent into Illinois needs a certificate of veterinary inspection or entry permit, or whether that requirement applies only to commercial licensees. A written reply turns "probably fine" into documented certainty you can show a vet, shelter, or landlord.

Where the lever really is: This is BRANCH (a): the bureaucracy under-documenting a permissive law, NOT a bad law that needs the legislature. The lever is the AGENCY — a written clarification / declaratory confirmation from the State Veterinarian — not a bill and not a public-comment window. Why, concretely for Illinois: there is no statute or rule to repeal, because none of them prohibit the roof rat. We verified the three places a ban would live and the rat is in none of them. (1) The dangerous-animal statute (720 ILCS 5/48-10) enumerates only large carnivores and primates — no rodent. (2) The Wildlife Code (520 ILCS 5/1.2) defines "wildlife" as animals living unconfined without the care of man, which excludes a tame, cage-raised pet. (3) The injurious-species list (17 Ill. Adm. Code Part 805), which we confirmed directly, names only the multimammate rat (Mastomys) as an injurious rodent and does NOT list Rattus rattus, the roof rat, or the black rat. Legality therefore rests on statutory silence, not on a misreading the agency is enforcing against owners. Because nothing is being applied against the species, going to the legislature would be solving a problem that does not exist — there is no list to be removed from. The right move is to ask the agency to put the already-true legal status in writing. (If, in the future, Illinois were to ADD Rattus to an injurious or prohibited list — e.g., via a Part 805 rulemaking — the lever would flip to branch (b): the official public-comment window for that rule. That is not the situation today.)

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Illinois Department of Agriculture — Bureau of Animal Health & Welfare (Office of the State Veterinarian), via the Department's official Contact Us inquiry form (executive / agency) — official contact page
    This is the agency that administers the Animal Welfare Act (225 ILCS 605) pet-shop/dealer licensing and the state's import/CVI program — exactly the office that can issue a written confirmation that captive-bred Rattus rattus needs no permit, that the 'produced and raised' breeder exemption applies, and whether a private pet-owner import CVI is required. Use the Department's official Contact Us inquiry form; the Bureau's direct line is (217) 782-4944. Direct your request to the office, not to any named individual.
  • Illinois Department of Natural Resources — general contact (Wildlife Code / injurious-species scope) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Secondary touchpoint. IDNR administers the Wildlife Code (520 ILCS 5) and the injurious-species rule (17 Ill. Adm. Code Part 805). A one-line confirmation from DNR that Rattus rattus is not 'wildlife' and is not on the injurious-species list closes the loop alongside the Department of Agriculture letter. Use the official contact form.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Illinois Department of Agriculture, Bureau of Animal Health & Welfare (Office of the State Veterinarian):

I keep a domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) as a pet and am writing to ask for written confirmation of its legal status in Illinois. My understanding is that Illinois does not regulate this animal as a pet, but I would like that in writing so I can show it to my veterinarian, landlord, or shelter if asked.

My reading of the law: the dangerous-animal statute (720 ILCS 5/48-10) lists no rodent; the Wildlife Code (520 ILCS 5/1.2) defines 'wildlife' as animals living unconfined without the care of man, which a tame pet rat is not; and the injurious-species list (17 Ill. Adm. Code Part 805) names only the multimammate rat (Mastomys), not Rattus rattus.

My rats are captive-bred, hand-tame, kept indoors in cages, and are never released outdoors. I do not sell rats I did not raise myself.

Could you please confirm in writing: (1) that the genus Rattus / Rattus rattus is on no Illinois prohibited, dangerous, 'wildlife,' or injurious list and needs no possession permit; (2) that a hobby breeder who gives away or sells only home-bred pet rats is exempt from Animal Welfare Act licensing under the 'produced and raised' provision (225 ILCS 605); and (3) whether a private owner needs a certificate of veterinary inspection or entry permit to bring a pet rodent into Illinois.

Thank you for your time.

[Your name]
[Your city, Illinois]
[Your email]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • 720 ILCS 5/48-10 — Dangerous animal or primate offense (no rodents) — Illinois General Assembly
  • 520 ILCS 5 — Wildlife Code (defn of 'wildlife' excludes tame/cared-for animals; §2.3 no-release) — Illinois General Assembly / IL DNR
  • 225 ILCS 605 — Animal Welfare Act (pet-shop/dealer licensing; 'produced and raised' exemption) — Illinois General Assembly / IL Dept of Agriculture
  • 8 Ill. Adm. Code 25.47 — Animals Imported Into Illinois (CVI + entry permit for AWA licensees) — Illinois Administrative Code / IL Dept of Agriculture

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

National law also applies. These are the Indiana-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Indiana is silent. See United States.

Summary. Indiana is permissive for the roof rat. The DNR Wild Animal Possession Permit (312 IAC 9-11) applies only to enumerated Class I/II/III animals — bears, big cats, native furbearers, venomous reptiles, etc. — none of which include rats or the genus Rattus, and DNR's permit authority reaches only protected-native or harmful/dangerous wildlife. The roof rat is also off the exotic-mammal and invasive-vertebrate lists. So keeping, breeding, and selling/giving are legal with no state permit (Indiana's commercial-breeder law is dog-only), and import needs no mandated pet-rodent CVI (rodents aren't a listed entry species) — though confirming with the Board of Animal Health is prudent. Never release one.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

The DNR Wild Animal Possession Permit scheme (312 IAC 9-11) applies only to the exhaustively enumerated Class I/II/III lists, which include no rats/Rattus; the authority (IC 14-22-26-3) reaches only protected-native or harmful/dangerous wildlife, and R. rattus is a non-native species Indiana neither protects nor lists as dangerous. It's also absent from the exotic-mammal rule (312 IAC 9-3-18.5) and invasive-vertebrate bans. No permit to keep one.

Sources: Indiana DNR / Indiana Code, Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII), Indiana Code (via Justia)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Because keeping is unregulated by DNR, breeding is too (no possession permit attaches to a non-listed pet rodent). Indiana's only commercial-breeder statute (IC 15-21) is dogs-only. No state breeding license for pet rats.

Sources: Indiana General Assembly, Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

No Indiana statute licenses or restricts selling pet rodents; the exotic/wild-animal sale rules don't list Rattus, and dealer/breeder registration (IC 15-21) is dogs-only. A seller of pet roof rats is not a regulated 'animal dealer' under state law (federal USDA/AWA can apply to some commercial dealers).

Sources: Indiana General Assembly, Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII)

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

In-state transport is unrestricted. The Board of Animal Health imposes entry CVI requirements only on enumerated species (livestock, poultry, dogs/cats/ferrets) — pet rodents aren't listed, so no CVI is mandated to bring a pet rat into Indiana; confirm with BOAH before interstate movement. Never release a non-native rodent.

Sources: Indiana State Board of Animal Health, Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Never release a roof rat — it's a non-native species; rehome responsibly. Local city/county ordinances may add limits — check yours.

Source: Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII)

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Kansas

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the Kansas-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Kansas is silent. See United States.

Summary. Kansas is among the most permissive states for the roof rat. The Dangerous Regulated Animals Act (K.S.A. 32-1301+) covers only big cats, bears, and non-native venomous snakes — no rodents. KDWP's exotic-wildlife rule (K.A.R. 115-20-3) AFFIRMATIVELY allows possessing, breeding, and selling non-native species with no permit (just confine them and never release). The Pet Animal Act covers rodents but exempts a resident home breeder who sells only animals raised on their own premises, and its dealer license targets dog/cat sellers. So keeping, breeding, and selling/giving a captive-bred roof rat is legal; the only open edge is whether an import CVI applies (pocket pets are exempt from the import permit; confirm the CVI with the Dept of Agriculture).

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

The Dangerous Regulated Animals Act (K.S.A. 32-1301/-1302) lists only big cats, bears, and non-native venomous snakes — no rodents. KDWP's exotic-wildlife rule (K.A.R. 115-20-3) permits possession of non-native species (confined, not released) with NO permit. KDWP's nuisance-control guidance states no permit is required for Norway rats or house mice. No statute restricts keeping a captive-bred roof rat.

Sources: Kansas Statute Revisor, KDWP (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

K.A.R. 115-20-3 permits possession/breeding of non-native species without a permit. The Pet Animal Act (K.S.A. 47-1701+) covers rodents but EXEMPTS a resident home breeder who sells only animals produced and raised on their own premises — so hobby breeding needs no license.

Sources: KDWP (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center), Kansas Statute Revisor

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

K.A.R. 115-20-3 expressly authorizes sale of exotic (non-native) wildlife with no KDWP permit. The Pet Animal Act's pet-shop license is needed for retail of animals NOT raised on your premises; a resident home breeder selling their own is exempt, and the 'animal distributor' license targets dog/cat dealers. Free adoption is unregulated.

Sources: KDWP (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center), Kansas Statute Revisor

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

K.A.R. 115-20-3 requires confinement but doesn't restrict intrastate movement. For IMPORT, the Dept of Agriculture exempts 'pocket pets' (rats/hamsters/gerbils/mice) from the zoo/exotic-animal import permit; whether the general 30-day CVI rule applies to pet rodents isn't explicit — confirm with the KDA Import Desk. Never release (K.A.R. 115-20-3 no-release).

Sources: KDWP (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center), Kansas Dept of Agriculture, Division of Animal Health

Restrictions & responsibilities

K.A.R. 115-20-3 requires exotic wildlife to be confined and never released into Kansas lands/waters. Importing? Pocket pets are exempt from the KDA import permit; confirm any CVI with the Import Desk. Check local ordinances.

Source: KDWP (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center)

item.dc:creator: admin

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Kentucky

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the Kentucky-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Kentucky is silent. See United States.

Summary. Kentucky is one of the clearest 'yes' states: its exotic-wildlife rule (301 KAR 2:082 §7) names 'domesticated races of rats (Rattus norvegicus or Rattus rattus)' by binomial as PERMIT-EXEMPT for importation, transport, and possession. So keeping, breeding, and transferring a captive-bred roof rat needs no state wildlife permit, and the roof rat is not on Kentucky's inherently-dangerous prohibited-species list. The only open edge is whether the Dept of Agriculture requires an import Certificate of Veterinary Inspection for pet rodents (rodents aren't named in its entry list — likely no, confirm with the State Vet). Never release one.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

301 KAR 2:082 §7 lists 'domesticated races of rats (Rattus norvegicus or Rattus rattus) or mice (Mus musculus)' as animals that 'shall not require permits... for importation, transportation into Kentucky, or possession.' R. rattus is named by species, and it is not on the inherently-dangerous prohibited-species list. No permit to keep one.

Sources: Kentucky Legislative Research Commission / KDFWR, Kentucky Dept of Fish & Wildlife Resources

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Because possession is permit-exempt, breeding needs no KDFWR permit; Kentucky's pet-breeder statutes (KRS ch. 258) cover dogs/cats/rabbits, not rodents. (Federal USDA/AWA can apply to large commercial dealers.)

Sources: Kentucky Legislative Research Commission / KDFWR

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

No state permit/dealer license applies to selling or giving away captive-bred roof rats; the permit-exempt status covers transfer, and KRS ch. 258 commercial-establishment licensing is dogs/cats/rabbits. General cruelty law (KRS 525) applies.

Sources: Kentucky Legislative Research Commission / KDFWR

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

301 KAR 2:082 §7 exempts R. rattus from the wildlife transportation/import permit. For animal health, the Dept of Agriculture entry rule (302 KAR 20:040) lists CVIs for specific species (dogs/cats/livestock); rodents aren't named, so a CVI is likely not required — confirm with the State Vet before interstate movement. Never release (301 KAR 2:082 bars liberation of exotic wildlife).

Sources: Kentucky Legislative Research Commission / KDFWR, Kentucky Dept of Agriculture, Office of State Veterinarian

Restrictions & responsibilities

Never release a roof rat into the wild — 301 KAR 2:082 prohibits liberating exotic wildlife, and it's an invasive species. Rehome responsibly. Check local county/city ordinances.

Source: Kentucky Legislative Research Commission / KDFWR

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Louisiana

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the Louisiana-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Louisiana is silent. See United States.

Summary. Louisiana has no law that expressly prohibits keeping a captive-bred roof rat. The 'potentially dangerous wild quadruped' ban (LAC 76:V-115) covers only big cats, bears, wolves, and primates; the 'outlaw quadruped' list is feral hogs, coyotes, and armadillos — no rodents. Both state and local definitions of 'wild or exotic animal' carve out 'laboratory rats... bred and raised in captivity which have never known the wild' and common 'pocket pets,' which a multi-generation captive-bred roof rat fits. So keeping, breeding, and giving are effectively legal, though R. rattus isn't named by species. The live edge is commercial sale: whether LDWF treats it as a 'nongame quadruped' needing a breeder license (29... §56:262) is unsettled — confirm before selling. Parish ordinances vary; never release one.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

R. rattus is on no Louisiana prohibited/dangerous list: the 'potentially dangerous wild quadruped' rule (LAC 76:V-115) lists only big cats/bears/wolves/primates, and 'outlaw quadrupeds' (RS 56:116.2) are feral hogs/coyotes/armadillos. Both state and local 'wild or exotic animal' definitions carve out 'laboratory rats bred and raised in captivity which have never known the wild' and 'pocket pets,' which a captive-bred roof rat fits. Effectively legal, but R. rattus isn't named by species and no LDWF guidance confirms the carve-out reaches it — hence unclear.

Sources: Louisiana Wildlife & Fisheries Commission (via Cornell LII), Louisiana Legislature

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Because keeping is unregulated/unclear, private hobby breeding of captive-born stock falls outside any explicit prohibition. The nongame-quadruped breeder license (RS 56:262) targets wild/fur-associated quadrupeds; a captive-bred non-native commensal rodent not taken from the wild sits in a definitional gap. No-release obligation applies (RS 56:20).

Sources: Louisiana Legislature

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Non-commercial giving/rehoming appears to need no permit. Commercial SALE may require a Nongame Quadruped Breeder License (RS 56:262, ~$25/yr) IF LDWF classifies R. rattus as a 'nongame quadruped' — an unresolved question. A commercially-minded seller should get a written LDWF determination first; free vetted adoption avoids the issue.

Sources: Louisiana Legislature

Transport & import   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

No rule specifically restricts intrastate transport of captive-bred R. rattus. Louisiana's animal-health import rules (LAC 7:XXI) cover dogs/cats (CVI + rabies) and livestock/poultry, not pet rodents; the 'wild or semi-wild animal' import-report rule likely doesn't apply because captive-bred lab-type rats are excluded from 'wild or exotic animal.' So no CVI appears required — confirm with the State Vet. Never release (RS 56:20).

Sources: Louisiana Dept of Agriculture & Forestry (via Cornell LII), Louisiana Legislature

Restrictions & responsibilities

Commercial sale MAY require a Louisiana Nongame Quadruped Breeder License (RS 56:262) if LDWF classifies R. rattus as a 'nongame quadruped' — unsettled, so get a written determination before advertising for sale. Free/private rehoming needs no permit. Parish ordinances may add limits.

Never release a roof rat (RS 56:20). Parish/municipal ordinances (e.g., Orleans Parish §6-100) define 'wild or exotic animal' and may add local rules — check your parish.

Source: Louisiana Legislature
