item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Massachusetts? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Massachusetts

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Massachusetts-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Massachusetts is silent. See United States.

Summary. Massachusetts is a strict 'prohibited-unless-listed' state — and the roof rat is NOT on the list. Its exemption list (321 CMR 9.01) and domestic-animals list (321 CMR 9.02) name only the Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus) and its laboratory strains — Rattus rattus appears nowhere. So a roof rat is treated as a non-listed undomesticated mammal that may not be kept without a MassWildlife permit, and MassWildlife states it 'will not be issued a permit for keeping a wild animal as a pet.' The result: keeping, breeding, selling, and importing a roof rat are effectively prohibited here — purely because the species isn't named, while its near-twin the fancy rat is. A textbook 'species-not-domestication' gap and a prime advocacy target.

Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Massachusetts Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (MassWildlife), written reply June 2026: confirmed that roof rats (Rattus rattus) are not a legal pet in Massachusetts, and directed us to the state's published 'Wildlife as pets' guidance. This confirms there is no general pet-keeping pathway for R. rattus in Massachusetts — even though its near-twin the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is exempt and fully legal. The barrier is that the species is simply absent from the state's exemption list, not a finding that domesticated roof rats are dangerous.
  • Massachusetts Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (MassWildlife), follow-up reply June 2026: confirmed that an educator may apply for a permit to possess roof rats, and provided the possession/importation application form. So while roof rats are not a general legal pet in Massachusetts, a documented educational or scientific keeper can apply to MassWildlife for a possession permit.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

R. rattus is not on the 321 CMR 9.01 exemption list nor the 321 CMR 9.02 domestic-animals list (both name only the Norway rat / laboratory rat derived from R. norvegicus). As a non-listed undomesticated mammal it may not be possessed without a MassWildlife license under M.G.L. c.131 §23 — and MassWildlife's own guidance states no permit is issued for keeping a wild animal as a pet, so there is no lawful pet pathway. Refined (assume-a-pathway re-audit): R. rattus isn't on the 321 CMR 9.01(12) exempt list (only R. norvegicus is), so possession needs a MassWildlife license under MGL c.131 §23 / 321 CMR 2.12 — BUT 2.12 requires DENIAL of applications to keep a wild animal 'as a pet' (MassWildlife: 'you will not be issued a permit for keeping a wild animal as a pet'). No private pet pathway; only a scientific/educational/commercial-propagator license (institutional). = restricted, not flat-prohibited. The operative trigger confirmed by Gemini DR (2026-06-10) is 321 CMR 9.02(2)(c): any vertebrate taxon not listed 'shall be presumed to be wild and shall be subject to the provisions of M.G.L. c. 131,' which is what subjects an unlisted R. rattus to the §23 licensing regime.

Sources: MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), Massachusetts General Court, MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife, MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)

Breeding   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Breeding an unlisted wild mammal requires a Class 4 Propagator's License under M.G.L. c.131 §23 / 321 CMR 2.12, which authorizes a holder to possess, maintain, propagate, buy, sell, or dispose of specified mammals — but acquisition is gated by an exhaustive application (scale diagrams/photos of enclosures, a written disposition plan and justification, documentary proof of professional husbandry qualifications, and a liability/inspection agreement). Critically, 321 CMR 2.12(9) MANDATES denial of any application to 'possess, maintain, propagate, or cultivate animals as pets,' or where the intent is 'purely on curiosity, impulse, novelty, or to provide personal amusement or entertainment.' There is therefore no hobby/small-breeder threshold: a Class 4 license for R. rattus is only structurally available for a certified non-pet purpose — scientific (recognized institution), educational (recognized institution), or commercial propagation for the agricultural/laboratory supply chain divorced from the pet trade. R. norvegicus needs none of this because it is exempt/domestic. Hobby/pet breeding is barred.

Sources: Massachusetts General Court, MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Commercial sale, offer for sale, barter, or transfer of a presumed-wild mammal requires a Class 6 Dealer's License or a Class 4 Propagator's License under 321 CMR 2.12(3) / M.G.L. c.131 §23. Because R. rattus is unlisted, the 'without a permit' privilege in 321 CMR 9.01 does not reach it. A second, independent barrier blocks the retail pet channel: under 330 CMR 12.00 (Licensing and Operation of Pet Shops), a licensed pet shop may sell only an 'Animal,' defined as a species that may be kept without a MassWildlife permit per 321 CMR 9.01/9.02 — so the roof rat falls outside what any pet shop may lawfully sell. The result is a closed regulatory loop: a Class 4/Class 6 holder may transfer R. rattus only to another permitted person or institution, permanently sequestering the species from public pet ownership. Private give-away/sale of a pet roof rat is not authorized; only a licensed non-pet dealer/propagator transfer is structurally possible.

Sources: Massachusetts General Court, MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Dept of Agricultural Resources (via Animal Legal & Historical Center)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Cross-border movement of R. rattus is treated as importation of 'wildlife' under 321 CMR 2.15 regardless of captive-bred origin. No person may import a live mammal without an Importation Permit from the Director (321 CMR 2.15(2)); the application must be filed at least ten days in advance with the originating/destination facility details and a signed certification that the export is lawful in the origin jurisdiction, and the Director may deny under 321 CMR 2.15(10) where importation is 'detrimental to the fish and wildlife resources of Massachusetts... and is not in the public interest' (a real risk given the roof rat's invasive-pest reputation), and may require zoonotic-disease/parasite health certificates; illegal or diseased imports may be seized and humanely destroyed (321 CMR 2.15(22)). Once lawfully in-state under permit, transport is allowed only with the permit accompanying the animal and subject to Director-imposed caging/safety conditions. Liberation is ABSOLUTELY barred — never release; release of a non-native presumed-wild rodent is a serious violation. So transport is permit-gated and restricted, not unregulated. (The MDAR animal-health/CVI layer is secondary to the wildlife-import permit.)

Sources: Massachusetts General Court, MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Dept of Agricultural Resources (via Cornell LII)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Because R. rattus is not on the Massachusetts exempt/domestic lists, there is no lawful way to keep it as a pet here — MassWildlife does not issue pet-keeping permits for wildlife. If you have a roof rat and move to Massachusetts, you cannot bring it; rehome it responsibly first. (The fancy rat, R. norvegicus, IS exempt and legal.)
  • Do not bring a roof rat into Massachusetts
  • If advocating: petition MassWildlife to add captive-bred R. rattus to the 321 CMR 9.02 / 9.01 lists

Where: Massachusetts Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (MassWildlife)

Source: MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife, MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Massachusetts. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Massachusetts

Massachusetts uses a "prohibited-unless-listed" system for keeping animals. The state's exemption list (321 CMR 9.01) and its domestic-animals list (321 CMR 9.02) name only the Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus) and the laboratory/fancy rat strains derived from it. The roof rat — Rattus rattus, also called the black rat — is not named anywhere on either list. The operative trigger is 321 CMR 9.02(2)(c): 'Any vertebrate taxa not listed in 321 CMR 9.02 shall be presumed to be wild and shall be subject to the provisions of M.G.L. c. 131.' So the state treats a roof rat as a non-listed wild mammal that can't be kept without a MassWildlife license, and MassWildlife's own guidance says it will not issue a permit to keep a wild animal as a pet. The practical result: a tame, captive-bred roof rat is effectively off-limits in Massachusetts — purely because the species name is missing from a list, while its near-identical cousin the fancy rat is fully legal. This is a species-not-domestication gap, not a judgment that domesticated roof rats are actually dangerous or different to care for.

The ask: Ask MassWildlife to add captive-bred Rattus rattus to the 321 CMR 9.01 exemption list (specifically subsection (12), List of Mammals) and/or the 321 CMR 9.02 domestic-animals list, the same regulatory route already used for the Norway rat / fancy rat. The state law that controls the list, M.G.L. c. 131 §23, lets the Director amend it after a public hearing using four criteria, and a domesticated, indoor-kept, captive-bred roof rat line meets all four: an established, already-naturalized species poses no new ecological risk from an escaped tame animal, it is harmless to people, its care is no more demanding than any common pet rodent, and pet-keeping of a captive-bred line has no effect on wild populations. You can raise this informally by email, or formally as a petition for rulemaking under G.L. c. 30A §4 directed to the Director of the Division of Fisheries & Wildlife and the Fisheries and Wildlife Board (Permit Section, 100 Cambridge Street, 6th Floor, Boston, MA 02114).

Where the lever really is: This is an AGENCY lever, not a legislative one. The barrier is a regulation the agency itself writes and controls: the exemption list lives in 321 CMR 9.01, a MassWildlife regulation, and the enabling statute M.G.L. c. 131 §23 expressly authorizes the Director of the Division of Fisheries & Wildlife to alter that list after a public hearing, applying four statutory criteria (no ecological harm from escape, no danger to people, care no harder than a common domestic animal, no impact on wild populations). The roof rat's absence is simply a gap — the species was never added — and the agency has both the power and a built-in mechanism to fix it; the Norway rat / fancy rat got onto the list the very same way, and sugar gliders, the four-toed hedgehog, and several chameleons and skinks were all later added to 321 CMR 9.01 through this exact process. So the right move is to ask MassWildlife to add captive-bred R. rattus, either informally by writing to the Division or formally by filing a petition for rulemaking under the Massachusetts Administrative Procedure Act (G.L. c. 30A §4), which gives any interested person the right to ask an agency to amend a regulation and obliges the agency to consider it. The procedural path after a meritorious petition is: agency scientific review → public hearing noticed at least 21 days in advance in the Massachusetts Register → written comment period → Small Business Impact Statement → Fisheries and Wildlife Board vote → final promulgation with the Secretary of the Commonwealth. A legislative bill is NOT the primary path here, because no statute names or bans the roof rat — the gap is administrative. (By contrast, if the species had been written into a statute by name, appealing to the agency would be pointless and you'd need the legislature; that is not the situation in Massachusetts.)

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Massachusetts Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (MassWildlife) (executive / agency) — Mass.Wildlife@mass.gov
    MassWildlife writes and maintains the 321 CMR 9.01 exemption list and the 9.02 domestic-animals list, and under M.G.L. c. 131 §23 its Director can add a species to that list after a public hearing. This is the office with the actual power to fix the gap. Mass.Wildlife@mass.gov is the agency's official general inbox (verified on mass.gov); start here to ask for clarification and to request that captive-bred Rattus rattus be added, the same way Rattus norvegicus already is.
  • MassWildlife — formal Petition for Rulemaking under G.L. c. 30A §4 (public comment) — Mass.Wildlife@mass.gov
    If an informal request stalls, the Massachusetts Administrative Procedure Act (G.L. c. 30A §4) gives any interested person the right to file a written petition asking an agency to amend a regulation, and the agency must consider it. A petition to add captive-bred R. rattus to 321 CMR 9.01(12) forces the Division to formally consider the request and respond, and any list change triggers the public hearing required by M.G.L. c. 131 §23 — your chance to make the case on the record. Route the written petition to the Director of the Division of Fisheries & Wildlife and the Fisheries and Wildlife Board via the Permit Section, MassWildlife, 100 Cambridge Street, 6th Floor, Boston, MA 02114 (and copy the official Mass.Wildlife@mass.gov inbox). Board communications can also be addressed to the Chairman, Fisheries and Wildlife Board, 1 Rabbit Hill Road, Westborough, MA 01581.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Massachusetts Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (Director and Permit Section),

I'm writing about a gap in the exemption list at 321 CMR 9.01. That list, and the domestic-animals list at 321 CMR 9.02, name the Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus) and its laboratory and fancy strains, but they do not name the roof rat (Rattus rattus, the black rat). Under 321 CMR 9.02(2)(c) any taxon not listed 'shall be presumed to be wild,' so because of that single omission a tame, captive-bred roof rat cannot be kept in Massachusetts, even though its near-identical cousin the fancy rat is fully legal.

These are domesticated, captive-bred animals: selectively bred for tameness, kept entirely indoors as pets, and never released. They are not wild-caught and are no more demanding to care for than any common pet rodent.

I respectfully ask the Division to add captive-bred Rattus rattus to the 321 CMR 9.01 exemption list (subsection (12), List of Mammals) and/or the 9.02 domestic-animals list, the same route already used for the Norway rat — and, more recently, for sugar gliders, the four-toed hedgehog, and several chameleons and skinks. Under M.G.L. c. 131 §23, a captive-bred domestic line appears to meet all four statutory criteria: (1) accidental release will not adversely affect the ecology of the Commonwealth — the roof rat is already established in the region and a tame, captive-bred animal poses no new risk (and, like other added species, is poorly suited to surviving unaided); (2) the animal in captivity or escaped poses no substantial danger to people by injury or disease; (3) its care is no more demanding in any major respect than common domestic animals; and (4) trade in a captive-bred line has no significant adverse effect on wild populations.

Could you tell me the exact administrative procedure, designated recipient, and expected timeline for docketing such a request — and whether I should submit it as a formal petition for rulemaking under G.L. c. 30A §4 for a Fisheries and Wildlife Board hearing? I would also welcome the Division's view on whether the presumption of wildness under 321 CMR 9.02(2)(c) is rebuttable on a showing of domestication, or whether a full rulemaking is the only remedy. Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your town]
[Your email]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • 321 CMR 9.01 — Exemption List (names only Norway Rat / R. norvegicus among rats; R. rattus absent) — MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)
  • 321 CMR 9.02 — List of Domestic Animals (laboratory rat derived from R. norvegicus only; 9.02(2)(c) presumes unlisted taxa wild) — MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)
  • M.G.L. c.131 §23 — propagation/dealing licenses; possession of undomesticated mammals; special exemption list + four criteria; alterable by Director after public hearing — Massachusetts General Court
  • G.L. c. 30A §4 — Administrative Procedure Act: any interested person may petition an agency to adopt, amend, or repeal a regulation — Massachusetts General Court
  • 321 CMR 2.12 — Artificial Propagation (Class 4 Propagator's / Class 6 Dealer's Licenses; 2.12(9) mandatory denial for pet/novelty purposes) — MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)
  • 321 CMR 2.15 — Importation, Liberation, and Transportation (2.15(2) import permit ≥10 days, 2.15(10) discretionary denial, 2.15(22) seizure; absolute liberation ban) — MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)
  • MassWildlife — Wildlife as pets ('will not be issued a permit... as a pet') — MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife
  • 330 CMR 12.00 — Licensing and Operation of Pet Shops (sellable 'Animal' limited to species kept without a MassWildlife permit per 321 CMR 9.01/9.02) — MA Dept of Agricultural Resources (via Animal Legal & Historical Center)
  • 330 CMR 30.08 — Imported Animals (OCVI requirement) — MA Dept of Agricultural Resources (via Cornell LII)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Maryland? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Maryland

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Maryland-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Maryland is silent. See United States.

Summary. Keeping, breeding, and selling a domesticated roof rat is legal in Maryland with no state permit. Maryland's 'dangerous animal' ban (Md. Criminal Law §10-621) lists big cats, bears, primates, and the like — no rodents — and the wildlife regulation (COMAR 08.03.09.03) expressly exempts 'domesticated rats and mice' from any import or possession restriction. No rodent-specific import certificate is mandated (Maryland's CVI/rabies rules cover only livestock, poultry, and dogs/cats/ferrets), though obtaining a general interstate CVI before importing is prudent and worth confirming with the State Veterinarian.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Md. Criminal Law §10-621(b)(1) lists the live animals a person may not possess, and no rodent appears on it. DNR's possession regulation COMAR 08.03.09.03(C) affirmatively states it does not prohibit possession of 'domesticated rats and mice,' which covers a captive-bred domesticated roof rat. No DNR captive-wildlife permit applies to domesticated rodents. Gemini DR-verified: rodents aren't in MD's dangerous-exotic ban (Crim. Law sec.10-621), but COMAR 08.03.09 requires a permit for 'live wildlife' with an exemption for 'domestic rats' that ISN'T taxonomically defined -- so whether captive-bred R. rattus qualifies (vs only R. norvegicus) is genuinely ambiguous and open to DNR officer interpretation.

Sources: Md. Code (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center), Maryland DNR (Division of State Documents)

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

§10-621 prohibits 'breed' only for the enumerated dangerous species; rodents are not enumerated. COMAR 08.03.09.03(C) exempts domesticated rats and mice from import/possession restrictions, and no DNR breeder license reaches domesticated rodents. (Federal USDA/AWA dealer licensing is a separate matter triggered only by commercial wholesale/sight-unseen thresholds — see United States.) Gemini DR-verified: private hobby breeding isn't state-regulated (game husbandry licenses cover game birds/mammals, not non-game rodents); county zoning/kennel/pet-shop rules are the layer.

Sources: Md. Code (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center), Maryland DNR (Division of State Documents)

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

§10-621 bars offering for sale/trade/barter/exchange only for the listed dangerous animals; rodents are not listed. DNR's sale/transfer rules apply to permit-acquired and native/regulated wildlife, not to captive-bred domesticated rodents exempted by COMAR 08.03.09.03(C). No Maryland state pet-dealer license is required for private rodent transfers. Gemini DR-verified: the state doesn't regulate rodent sales (the retail-sale ban targets dogs/cats); a LOCAL 'Commercial Animal Establishment' license is required and varies by county.

Sources: Md. Code (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center), Maryland DNR (Division of State Documents)

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

In-state transport of a domesticated rat is unregulated. For IMPORT, Maryland's rabies-import rule (COMAR 10.06.02.11) applies to dogs/cats/ferrets only, and MDA's admission rules require a CVI for livestock/poultry/dogs/cats/ferrets — there is no pet-rodent category. So no rodent-specific CVI is mandated, but a general interstate CVI is the customary document for any animal crossing state lines (note: since 2019 Maryland no longer accepts the federal APHIS 7001 'small animal' form), so confirm with MDA Animal Health before importing. Gemini DR-verified: importing any companion rodent needs an Interstate CVI issued within 30 days before entry (COMAR 15.14.05.01); private-traveler enforcement is historically lax but the ICVI is mandated.

Sources: Maryland Dept of Health (Division of State Documents), Maryland Dept of Agriculture — Animal Health Program, Maryland DNR (Division of State Documents)

Restrictions & responsibilities

No rodent-specific import certificate is required (Maryland's CVI/rabies rules cover only livestock, poultry, dogs/cats/ferrets), but a general interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection is the customary travel document — confirm with MDA Animal Health before importing a pet rat. Maryland no longer accepts the APHIS 7001 small-animal form (use an approved CVI form).
  • Confirm CVI expectations with MDA Animal Health before interstate movement

Where: Maryland Dept of Agriculture — Animal Health Program

Source: Maryland Dept of Agriculture — Animal Health Program

Never release a roof rat — it is a non-native species; rehome responsibly.

Source: Maryland DNR (Division of State Documents)

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Official sources

  • Md. Code, Criminal Law §10-621 — Dangerous-animal import/possession ban (no rodents listed) — Md. Code (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center)
  • COMAR 08.03.09.03 — exempts 'domesticated rats and mice' from import/possession prohibition — Maryland DNR (Division of State Documents)
  • COMAR 10.06.02.11 — Importation of Animals (rabies import certificate; dogs/cats/ferrets) — Maryland Dept of Health (Division of State Documents)
  • MDA Health Requirements Governing the Admission of Animals (CVI scope by species) — Maryland Dept of Agriculture — Animal Health Program

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Maine? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Maine

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the Maine-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Maine is silent. See United States.

Summary. Maine runs a three-tier captive-wildlife scheme (unrestricted / restricted / prohibited) under 12 M.R.S. §12152 + MDIFW Ch. 7. The Unrestricted Species List names 'Rattus norvegicus var.' (the domestic Norway/fancy rat) but NOT Rattus rattus. A species that's neither unrestricted nor prohibited defaults to RESTRICTED — meaning a Wildlife Possession/Importation Permit from MDIFW is required to keep, breed, sell, or import a roof rat. (R. rattus is also not on the prohibited list, so the permit pathway appears open rather than a flat ban.) Another 'Norway-rat-only' species trap, with an advocacy path: petition MDIFW to add captive-bred R. rattus to the Unrestricted list. A direct MDIFW call is the recommended first step.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

MDIFW's Unrestricted Species List (Ch. 7) names only 'Rattus norvegicus var.', not R. rattus, and R. rattus is not on the prohibited list (§7.18 = bears/canids/felids/primates) — so under the three-tier scheme it defaults to RESTRICTED, requiring a Wildlife Possession Permit (12 M.R.S. §12152). The 'wild animal' definition (§10001: 'wild by nature, whether or not bred in captivity') would likely capture R. rattus since it lacks a recognized domestic breed line like the fancy rat.

Sources: Maine Legislature, Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center), Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Ch. 7 requires a permit to propagate any restricted (non-unrestricted) species; R. rattus isn't on the Unrestricted List, so breeding needs an MDIFW possession/propagation permit. Maine's simpler 'small animal' DACF breeder pathway (7 M.R.S. §3907) is limited to species ON the MDIFW unrestricted list — which R. rattus is not.

Sources: Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center), Maine Legislature

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Unrestricted species may be sold by pet shops; R. rattus isn't unrestricted, so it can't be sold without the appropriate MDIFW permit (and possibly a DACF pet-shop license). Non-commercial transfer still requires both parties to hold valid possession permits for a restricted species.

Sources: Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center), Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Importing a non-unrestricted species requires an MDIFW Wildlife Importation Permit (Category 1/2) + an interstate CVI from the origin state (12 M.R.S. §12152). In-state transport of a restricted species requires the underlying possession permit. No specific R. rattus invasive-import ban was found, so the permit pathway appears open. Never release (§12152).

Sources: Maine Legislature, Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Because R. rattus isn't on MDIFW's Unrestricted Species List (only the Norway rat is), it defaults to the restricted tier — a Wildlife Possession/Importation Permit is required to keep, breed, sell, or import. Call MDIFW (207-287-5252) for the species' tier classification before acquiring one; consider petitioning to add captive-bred R. rattus to the Unrestricted list. Never release.
  • Ask MDIFW which tier R. rattus is in and the permit pathway
  • If pursuing reform: petition to add captive-bred R. rattus to the Unrestricted Species List

Where: Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife (MDIFW)

Source: Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center), Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Maine

Maine sorts every captive animal into three tiers — unrestricted, restricted, or prohibited — under 12 M.R.S. §12152 and the MDIFW "Wildlife in Captivity" rules (09-137 C.M.R. Ch. 7). The catch is purely a wording gap: the state's Unrestricted Species List names "Rattus norvegicus var." — the domestic Norway/fancy rat you can buy at any pet shop — but it never names "Rattus rattus," the domestic roof rat. Because the roof rat isn't on the unrestricted list AND isn't on the prohibited list (which covers bears, big cats, wild canids, and primates), it falls through to the default "restricted" tier. That means the exact same kind of animal — a captive-bred, hand-tame pet rat — needs a Wildlife Possession Permit just because of which species name made it onto a list, not because of anything about how the animal actually lives. This isn't a ban; the permit pathway appears open. It's a species trap: two domesticated pet rats treated differently for no behavioral or safety reason.

The ask: Ask MDIFW to add captive-bred domestic roof rats — "Rattus rattus var." — to the Unrestricted Species List, right alongside the domestic Norway/fancy rat ("Rattus norvegicus var.") and the house mouse that are already on it. The fix is a one-line addition to a list the Department already maintains and updates. Use MDIFW's existing species-categorization (reclassification) request process to make the request in writing, and ask for a written determination of how the Department currently classifies Rattus rattus so keepers know where they stand in the meantime.

Where the lever really is: THIS IS AN AGENCY PROBLEM, NOT A LEGISLATIVE ONE — the lever is MDIFW, not the Legislature. The roof rat is NOT named on any statute. It is missing from an administrative list — the Unrestricted Species List — that MDIFW itself creates, maintains, and amends under 09-137 C.M.R. Ch. 7. The statute (12 M.R.S. §12152) only sets up the three-tier permit framework and delegates the actual species sorting to the Department. The Department has demonstrably exercised that power before: in 2009 it added ~50 reptile and amphibian species to the unrestricted list, and its own "Wildlife in Captivity" page describes an explicit "Unclassified Species" category plus a "Species Categorization Requests" process for reviewing and recategorizing species. So this is not a case of an agency misreading a law — it's an agency correctly applying a framework, where a captive-bred domestic species simply hasn't been added to the exemption list yet. The right move is a written reclassification petition to MDIFW asking it to add "Rattus rattus var." to the unrestricted list (parallel to the fancy rat), plus a request for a written classification determination. Because no Maine statute names or bans the roof rat, going to the Legislature is NOT the primary path — a bill is unnecessary to change an agency-maintained list, and could even be slower. The Legislature is only a fallback if MDIFW declines and a keeper wants the change codified.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Maine Department of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife (MDIFW) — Wildlife Division / Captive Wildlife (executive / agency) — info.ifw@maine.gov
    MDIFW owns and amends the Unrestricted Species List under 09-137 C.M.R. Ch. 7 — this is the office that can actually fix the gap. Its captive-wildlife page describes a 'Species Categorization Requests' process for adding/recategorizing species (mail to Wildlife Division, 353 Water Street, Augusta, ME 04330), and it added ~50 species to the unrestricted list in 2009, so the pathway is real. Send the reclassification request here and ask for a written determination of how R. rattus is currently classified. General inbox info.ifw@maine.gov is confirmed on the official contact page.
  • Maine State Legislature — Contact Your Legislator (House & Senate) (legislature) — official contact page
    FALLBACK ONLY, not the primary lever. No Maine statute names or bans the roof rat, so a bill isn't needed to change an agency-maintained list. Use this only if MDIFW declines the reclassification request and you want the parity (fancy rat = roof rat) codified — a legislator can direct the Department or amend the underlying statute. Official 'find and contact your legislator' page for both chambers.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To: Maine Department of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife, Wildlife Division (Captive Wildlife)
Re: Request to add captive-bred domestic roof rats (Rattus rattus var.) to the Unrestricted Species List

Dear MDIFW Wildlife Division,

I am writing about a wording gap in the Unrestricted Species List under 09-137 C.M.R. Ch. 7. The list names "Rattus norvegicus var." — the domestic Norway/fancy rat sold in pet shops — but it does not name "Rattus rattus," the domestic roof rat. Both are the same kind of animal: captive-bred, hand-tame pet rats. The roof rats I am writing about are bred in captivity, gentle, kept entirely indoors as family pets, and never released to the wild.

Because the roof rat is absent from the list (and is not on the prohibited list), it appears to default to the restricted tier, so an identical pet needs a permit only because of which species name made it onto a list. That is a distinction based on label, not on how the animal lives or any risk it poses.

I respectfully request that the Department use its species-categorization process to add captive-bred domestic roof rats ("Rattus rattus var.") to the Unrestricted Species List, parallel to the domestic Norway rat and house mouse already on it. I would also be grateful for a written determination of how the Department currently classifies Rattus rattus, so keepers know where they stand in the meantime.

Thank you for your time and for maintaining this list.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your town, Maine]
[Your email / phone]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • 12 M.R.S. §12152 — Permit to possess/import wildlife in captivity (CVI for import) — Maine Legislature
  • 09-137 C.M.R. Ch. 7 — MDIFW Regulations for Wildlife in Captivity (unrestricted/restricted/prohibited tiers) — Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center)
  • MDIFW Unrestricted Species List (names 'Rattus norvegicus var.'; R. rattus absent) — Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

Summary. Michigan has no exotic/wild-animal possession permit that captures rodents. The Large Carnivore Act covers only big cats and bears; the roof rat is not on the NREPA Part 413 prohibited/restricted (invasive) list (only nutria and Russian boar are among prohibited mammals); and the Pet Shops Act excludes rodents from its licensing definition. So keeping, breeding, and selling/giving a roof rat is effectively legal/unregulated at the state level. The one concrete requirement is animal-health: importing a non-native rodent needs a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (no Michigan entry permit). Because no rule names the species, it's best labeled unregulated/unclear, and local ordinances may add limits.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

No general exotic-possession permit captures rodents. The only exotic-mammal possession ban (Large Carnivore Act, MCL 287.1101+) covers big cats/bears, and R. rattus is not on the NREPA Part 413 prohibited/restricted list (only nutria and Russian boar among prohibited mammals). No statute prohibits or licenses keeping one — but none affirmatively names/exempts the species either, so it's unregulated rather than expressly permitted.

Sources: Michigan Legislature, Michigan Invasive Species Program (DNR/MDARD/EGLE)

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

No Michigan statute requires a permit to breed pet rodents; the DNR captive-wildlife permit covers native game, not non-native rodents, and R. rattus is neither regulated game nor a prohibited invasive species. Breeding is unaddressed (effectively legal).

Sources: Michigan Invasive Species Program (DNR/MDARD/EGLE)

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Michigan's Pet Shops Act (MCL 287.331+) requires a license to sell animals, but its definition of 'animal' EXCLUDES rodents — so a rodent-only seller isn't a regulated pet shop. Selling a prohibited invasive species would be unlawful, but R. rattus isn't on that list. No state breeder/dealer license reaches rodents.

Sources: Michigan Legislature, Michigan Invasive Species Program (DNR/MDARD/EGLE)

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Importing a non-native rodent requires an official interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection from a USDA-accredited vet; Michigan issues NO entry permit for non-native rodents (no permit number needed). Intrastate transport is unregulated. Never release a roof rat.

Sources: Michigan Dept of Agriculture & Rural Development, Michigan Invasive Species Program (DNR/MDARD/EGLE)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Importing a non-native pet rodent into Michigan requires an interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (MDARD); no Michigan entry permit. No CVI for in-state movement.

Where: Michigan Dept of Agriculture & Rural Development (MDARD), Animal Industry Division

Source: Michigan Dept of Agriculture & Rural Development

Never release a roof rat. Local city/township/county ordinances may add limits — check yours.

Source: Michigan Invasive Species Program (DNR/MDARD/EGLE)

Help change this

How to help in Michigan

In Michigan, keeping, breeding, and rehoming a captive-bred pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) is effectively legal, but no state rule says so by name. The species sits in a gap: it is NOT on Michigan's prohibited or restricted invasive-species list under NREPA Part 413 (the only prohibited mammals are nutria and wild/Russian boar), the Large Carnivore Act covers only big cats and bears, and the Pet Shops Act's definition of "animal" excludes rodents entirely. So no permit captures it and no statute bans it — its lawful status is inferred from silence rather than written down anywhere. That leaves owners, vets, and rescues without a clear document to point to, and it leaves the door open for the species to be wrongly treated as a wild pest. The fix is a written confirmation from the state, not a new law.

The ask: Ask MDARD (with DNR for the wildlife-permit point) to confirm IN WRITING that captive-bred domestic roof rats are treated like other unregulated non-native pet rodents: (1) Rattus rattus is not a prohibited or restricted species under NREPA Part 413; (2) no DNR captive-wildlife permit or MDARD exotic-animal permit is required to keep, breed, or rehome them; and (3) the only state movement requirement is an interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection on import, with no Michigan entry permit. A short letter, email, or declaratory statement to that effect gives owners and veterinarians something concrete to rely on.

Where the lever really is: This is an AGENCY / bureaucracy-clarification case, NOT a law-change case. The Michigan law as written already leaves captive-bred roof rats unregulated: the species is absent from the NREPA Part 413 prohibited/restricted lists (only nutria and wild/Russian boar are prohibited mammals — verified), the Large Carnivore Act reaches only big cats and bears, and the Pet Shops Act excludes rodents from "animal." The problem is purely that no rule names the species, so its legal status is inferred from silence and is undocumented — exactly the kind of gap an agency can close with a written clarification or declaratory statement. The correct lever is therefore MDARD's Animal Industry Division (with the DNR confirming the captive-wildlife-permit point), asked to put the existing status in writing. Going to the Legislature here would be the WRONG move and could backfire: there is no defective statute to amend, and opening Part 413 or the exotic-pet statutes invites the species being ADDED to a prohibited list rather than affirmed as a legal pet. Pursue the agency confirmation; do not seek legislation.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Michigan Department of Agriculture & Rural Development (MDARD) — Contact MDARD / Animal Industry Division (State Veterinarian) (executive / agency) — MDA-Info@Michigan.gov
    MDARD's Animal Industry Division administers animal-movement and animal-health rules and is the right office to confirm in writing that captive-bred roof rats need no exotic-animal permit and that the only import requirement is an interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection. Use the official contact form (or the verified MDA-Info inbox / 800-292-3939) — this is the primary lever for a written clarification.
  • Michigan Department of Natural Resources (DNR) — Wildlife Permits / Invasive Species Program (executive / agency) — official contact page
    The DNR co-administers the NREPA Part 413 prohibited/restricted species list and issues captive-wildlife permits. A short note (or call to Wildlife Permits, 517-284-6210) asking the DNR to confirm that Rattus rattus is not a prohibited/restricted species and that captive-wildlife permits do not reach non-native pet rodents documents the second half of the status.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request to confirm in writing the legal status of captive-bred pet roof rats (Rattus rattus)

Dear MDARD Animal Industry Division,

I keep domesticated, captive-bred roof rats (Rattus rattus) as indoor pets. These animals are tame, born in captivity, kept entirely indoors, and never released to the wild. I am writing because Michigan law does not name this species anywhere, which leaves its pet status unclear on paper even though it appears to be unregulated.

From my reading, Rattus rattus is not on the NREPA Part 413 prohibited or restricted species list (only nutria and wild/Russian boar are prohibited mammals), the Large Carnivore Act covers only big cats and bears, and the Pet Shops Act excludes rodents. I am not asking for any change to the law.

Could you please confirm in writing that: (1) Rattus rattus is not a prohibited or restricted species under Part 413; (2) no DNR captive-wildlife permit or MDARD exotic-animal permit is required to keep, breed, or rehome captive-bred roof rats; and (3) the only state movement requirement is an interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection on import, with no Michigan entry permit?

A brief written confirmation would give owners and veterinarians a clear document to rely on. Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your city, Michigan]
[Your email / phone]

Summary. Minnesota is permissive for the roof rat. Its 'regulated animals' law (Minn. Stat. §346.155) targets only big cats, bears, and primates — not rodents — and DNR rule Minn. R. 6216.0270 affirmatively classifies BOTH Rattus rattus and Rattus norvegicus as 'unregulated nonnative species,' outside the invasive-species controls of ch. 84D. So keeping, breeding, and selling/giving a captive-bred roof rat needs no state permit. The one requirement is animal-health: importing a mammal needs a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (confirm the pet-rodent application with the Board of Animal Health). Never release one; check local ordinances.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Minn. Stat. §346.155 ('regulated animals') covers only Felidae (non-domestic cats), bears, and nonhuman primates — no rodents — and Minn. R. 6216.0270 explicitly lists R. rattus and R. norvegicus as 'unregulated nonnative species' not subject to ch. 84D. No DNR permit is required to keep one.

Sources: Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes, Minnesota DNR / Revisor of Statutes

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Minnesota's commercial-breeder licensing (Minn. Stat. §§347.58–347.60) covers dogs and cats only; no state license reaches rodent breeders. R. rattus is 'unregulated nonnative,' so ch. 84D propagation bans don't apply.

Sources: Minnesota DNR / Revisor of Statutes

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Pet-dealer protections (Minn. Stat. §325F.791) apply to dogs/cats; no state dealer license is required for rodents. The pet-rodent care standards (Minn. Stat. §346.41) bind commercial facilities, not private breeders rehoming animals.

Sources: Minnesota DNR / Revisor of Statutes

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Intrastate transport is unregulated for an unregulated-nonnative species. For IMPORT, Minn. R. 1721.0040 requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection for all imported mammals unless exempted; no rodent-specific exemption was confirmed, so carry a CVI — confirm the pet-rodent application with the Board of Animal Health. Releasing any nonnative animal is unlawful (Minn. Stat. ch. 84D).

Sources: Minnesota Board of Animal Health, Minnesota DNR / Revisor of Statutes

Restrictions & responsibilities

Importing a pet rat into Minnesota requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (Minn. R. 1721.0040, all mammals); confirm the pet-rodent application with the Board of Animal Health. No CVI for in-state movement.

Where: Minnesota Board of Animal Health

Source: Minnesota Board of Animal Health

Never release a roof rat (Minn. Stat. ch. 84D). Local city/county ordinances may add limits — check yours.

Source: Minnesota DNR / Revisor of Statutes

Summary. Keeping, breeding, and selling a roof rat is legal in Missouri with no state permit. The Wildlife Code expressly lets non-native mammals be 'bought, sold, possessed, transported, and exhibited without permit' (3 CSR 10-9.110), and the prohibited-species list (3 CSR 10-4.117) names other rodents (genus Mastomys) but NOT Rattus. It's not a 'dangerous wild animal' (RSMo 578.023 = large carnivores/reptiles), and the Animal Care Facilities Act licensing applies only to dogs/cats. The one requirement: importing a pet rodent needs a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (rodents = 'miscellaneous animals'). Check your city/county ordinance, and never release one.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Under 3 CSR 10-9.110, non-native mammals may be possessed without a Wildlife Code permit, except federally endangered species or those on the prohibited-species (3 CSR 10-4.117) / Class II (3 CSR 10-9.240) lists. R. rattus is non-native and on none of those (the prohibited list names genus Mastomys, not Rattus), and it's not a 'dangerous wild animal' under RSMo 578.023. No permit to keep one.

Sources: Missouri Dept of Conservation, Missouri Dept of Conservation, Missouri Revisor of Statutes

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

The 3 CSR 10-9.110 non-native exemption covers propagation too, and the Animal Care Facilities Act (RSMo 273.325) defines 'animal' as dogs/cats only — so no state breeder license reaches pet rats. General cruelty/care law still applies.

Sources: Missouri Dept of Conservation, Missouri Revisor of Statutes

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

3 CSR 10-9.110 expressly allows non-native mammals to be 'bought, sold... without permit,' and the ACFA pet-shop/dealer licensing turns on the dog/cat definition (RSMo 273.325), so selling or giving away pet rats triggers no state license.

Sources: Missouri Dept of Conservation, Missouri Revisor of Statutes

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Within Missouri, no Wildlife Code permit is needed (3 CSR 10-9.110). For IMPORT, the Dept of Agriculture (2 CSR 30-2.010) requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection within 30 days for animals entering Missouri; rodents are 'miscellaneous animals,' so a pet rat should travel with a CVI. The Wildlife Code's no-release rule (3 CSR 10-4.110) bars ever liberating one.

Sources: Missouri Dept of Conservation, Missouri Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Importing a pet rodent into Missouri requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (2 CSR 30-2.010; rodents = 'miscellaneous animals'). No CVI for in-state movement.

Where: Missouri Dept of Agriculture, Animal Health Division

Source: Missouri Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII)

Never release a roof rat (3 CSR 10-4.110). Local city/county ordinances (e.g., Kansas City, St. Louis) may add limits — check yours.

Source: Missouri Dept of Conservation

item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Northern Mariana Islands

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the Northern Mariana Islands-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Northern Mariana Islands is silent. See United States.

Summary. The Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) is NOT a closed-list ban on pet rats - it's a permit pathway. Its Animal Quarantine rules (NMIAC T85-20.1) require a written entry permit for ALL animal imports from the Chief of Animal Health & Industry, but the only prohibited pet/guard mammals are a NAMED list (skunks, bats, raccoons, foxes, coyotes, wolves, wild/feral canids and felids and crosses) - NEITHER Rattus rattus NOR R. norvegicus appears on it. DLNR's own import page treats non-cat/dog animals as case-by-case ('email us, regulations vary by species'), and Customs classifies all animals as 'permits-required,' not prohibited. So a rat can be imported under an entry permit + a vet health certificate (rodents need no rabies vaccine), plus a DFW wildlife import permit ($10/species); once lawfully imported, keeping isn't separately restricted. Federal overlay: R. rattus (unlike the exempt R. norvegicus) needs a USFWS Form 3-177 wildlife declaration and must route through a designated port (Honolulu) or get a Designated Port Exception Permit. Breeding/intra-island transfer are simply unaddressed by CNMI law.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Once a rat is lawfully imported under an entry permit, no CNMI statute prohibits keeping it - the T85-20.1 prohibited-pet-mammal list names only skunks/bats/raccoons/foxes/coyotes/wolves/wild canids+felids, not Rattus. CNMI PL 21-31 (cruelty/theft) doesn't restrict rat ownership.

Sources: CNMI Law Revision Commission, CNMI Dept of Lands & Natural Resources

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-07

No CNMI law addresses private captive breeding of pet rodents; the permit scheme governs import, not domestic breeding. The DFW non-native-release prohibition is an indirect constraint if stock escaped. Closed-colony breeding from lawfully-imported animals appears outside any specific prohibition but isn't affirmatively authorized - confirm with DLNR.

Sources: CNMI Law Revision Commission, CNMI Law Revision Commission

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-07

No CNMI statute specifically prohibits or permits intra-island sale/transfer of captive-born pet rats; the DFW permit regime is for import/export, and the cruelty law governs treatment, not sale. No commercial-pet licensing framework identified - confirm with DLNR.

Sources: CNMI Law Revision Commission

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Import requires an entry permit from the Chief of Animal Health & Industry (advance inquiry; permit fee; USDA-accredited vet health certificate within 10 days; rodents need no rabies vaccine) + a DFW wildlife import permit ($10/species). Federal: R. rattus needs a USFWS Form 3-177 + a USFWS-designated port (Honolulu) or a Designated Port Exception Permit (R. norvegicus is exempt). CNMI is outside US customs territory but USFWS/APHIS/CDC apply. Never release.

Sources: CNMI Law Revision Commission, CNMI Dept of Lands & Natural Resources, US Fish & Wildlife Service

Restrictions & responsibilities

To bring a rat into CNMI: email DLNR Animal Health in advance, obtain an entry permit from the Chief of Animal Health & Industry + a USDA-accredited vet health certificate (within 10 days; no rabies vaccine for rodents), and a DFW wildlife import permit ($10/species). For R. rattus add a USFWS Form 3-177 + route via a designated port (Honolulu) or a Designated Port Exception Permit. Never release.
  • Email CNMI DLNR Animal Health (cnmianimalhealth@gmail.com) with species/number/purpose
  • Obtain the entry permit + DFW import permit + USDA health certificate
  • For R. rattus: file USFWS Form 3-177 + designated-port/DPEP

Forms: USFWS Form 3-177 (wildlife declaration - R. rattus) · Where: CNMI DLNR - Division of Agriculture, Animal Health Section · Fees: CNMI entry permit fee + DFW $10/species

Source: CNMI Dept of Lands & Natural Resources, US Fish & Wildlife Service

Official sources

  • NMIAC Title 85-20.1 - Animal Quarantine Rules (entry permit for all imports; named prohibited-mammal list excludes Rattus) — CNMI Law Revision Commission
  • CNMI DLNR - Importing a Pet into the CNMI (case-by-case for non-cat/dog; Animal Health contact) — CNMI Dept of Lands & Natural Resources
  • NMIAC Title 85-30.1 - Non-Commercial Fish & Wildlife Regulations (DFW import permit $10/species; no-release rule) — CNMI Law Revision Commission
  • USFWS - Importers & Exporters (R. norvegicus exempt from Form 3-177; R. rattus NOT exempt -> declaration + designated port) — US Fish & Wildlife Service
  • CNMI Customs - Import Requirements (animals = permits-required, not prohibited) — CNMI Department of Finance / Customs

Summary. Mississippi does not prohibit keeping a roof rat. Its 'inherently dangerous to humans' wildlife list (Miss. Code §49-8-5 / MDWFP Rule 8.3) enumerates primates, big cats, bears, elephants, etc. — no rodents — and MDWFP classifies R. rattus as an unprotected pest. So keeping, breeding, and selling/giving captive-bred roof rats is effectively legal at the state level (no rule names the species, hence 'unregulated/unclear'). The one real hook is IMPORT: the Board of Animal Health's broad 'other exotic animals' rule (Ch. 12) requires a prior entry permit + a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection for non-native, non-livestock species — which likely captures an imported roof rat. We've queued an inquiry to confirm. Never release one.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Miss. Code §49-8-5 (and MDWFP Rule 8.3, rev. 2025) lists the species 'inherently dangerous to humans' requiring a permit — order Rodentia is absent. R. rattus is non-native and MDWFP-classified as an unprotected pest, outside the nongame-protection chapter. No statute restricts private possession; effectively legal, though no rule positively exempts the species (hence unclear).

Sources: Mississippi Legislature, MS Dept of Wildlife, Fisheries & Parks

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

No MDWFP propagation/breeder permit applies to a non-listed, non-native rodent (the Ch. 8 permit covers only inherently-dangerous species; the collection/propagation permit covers native nongame). No state breeder-dealer license for small exotic rodents was found. Hobby breeding is effectively unregulated.

Sources: Mississippi Legislature

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

No Mississippi pet-dealer license for captive-bred non-native rodents was found; the nongame sale prohibition covers native species taken from the wild (R. rattus is a non-native pest, outside it), and the Ch. 8 dangerous-animals permit doesn't reach rodents. Free rehoming and sale appear unrestricted at the state level (federal USDA/AWA may apply to commercial dealers).

Sources: Mississippi Legislature

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Intrastate movement is unregulated. For IMPORT, the Board of Animal Health (2 Miss. Code R. 101-2-12, Ch. 12) requires a prior entry permit + a CVI for 'other exotic animals' (non-domesticated, non-native, non-livestock) — a definition broad enough to capture an imported roof rat. R. rattus is not on the prohibited-entry list. Request the entry permit from the State Veterinarian before importing. Never release.

Sources: Mississippi Board of Animal Health, Mississippi Legislature

Restrictions & responsibilities

Importing a roof rat into Mississippi likely needs a prior entry permit + a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection under the Board of Animal Health 'other exotic animals' rule (Ch. 12). Request the entry permit from the State Veterinarian (601-359-1170). Confirm scope for pet rodents. Never release.
  • Contact MBAH State Veterinarian for an 'other exotic animals' entry permit + CVI

National law also applies. These are the Montana-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Montana is silent. See United States.

Summary. Montana law puts the roof rat clearly in the clear: MCA 87-5-702 defines 'domestic animal' to expressly include 'rodents,' which removes them from the Fish, Wildlife & Parks exotic-wildlife scheme entirely (prohibited/controlled/noncontrolled) — and no Rattus species is on the prohibited (ARM 12.6.2215) or controlled list. So keeping, breeding, and selling/giving a captive-bred roof rat is legal statewide with no FWP permit. The one procedural item is import (a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection for rodents under the Dept of Livestock rule, with an informal owner-pet waiver — confirm). ⚠️ BIG local exception: the City of Billings bans keeping/breeding/selling rats within city limits (Municipal Code §4-304) — a prime example of why you must check your city.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

MCA 87-5-702 defines 'domestic animal' to include 'livestock..., dogs, cats, rodents, Eurasian ferrets, and poultry' — so rodents (incl. R. rattus) are outside FWP's exotic-wildlife classification. R. rattus is on neither the prohibited (ARM 12.6.2215) nor controlled list, and no state dangerous-animal statute reaches captive rodents. No FWP permit to keep one. (Local ordinances can differ — see Billings.)

Sources: Montana Legislature, Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks, City of Billings, Montana

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Breeding follows lawful possession; because rodents are domestic animals outside the FWP exotic-wildlife scheme, no FWP breeder/dealer license applies, and no state livestock-breeder framework reaches pet rodents. (Billings §4-304 bans 'raising' rats within that city.)

Sources: Montana Legislature, City of Billings, Montana

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

No Montana state law prohibits selling or giving domestic-category rodents between private parties, and no FWP exotic-wildlife dealer license applies. (Billings §4-304 prohibits offering for sale / giving away rats within city limits.)

Sources: Montana Legislature, City of Billings, Montana

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Intrastate transport is unregulated by FWP (rodents are domestic animals). For IMPORT, the Dept of Livestock (MCA 81-2-703 / ARM 32.3.206) nominally requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection for rodents entering Montana within 30 days, but the Department may waive it where there's no significant health risk and informally does so for owner-traveled small pets — confirm in writing before crossing. Never release a roof rat.

Sources: Montana Legislature / Dept of Livestock, Montana Legislature

Restrictions & responsibilities

⚠️ City of Billings: Municipal Code §4-304 (since 1967) bans keeping, raising, selling, giving away, or transporting rats of any species within city limits, except as feed for raptors/reptiles or under a scientific/educational exception. Check your specific city/county ordinance — Montana state law is permissive, but municipalities can ban rats outright.
  • Check your city/county animal ordinance (Billings bans rats)

Where: Your municipality

Source: City of Billings, Montana

Importing a rodent into Montana nominally requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (MCA 81-2-703), though the Dept of Livestock may waive it for owner-traveled pets — confirm with livpermits@mt.gov. No CVI for in-state movement; never release.

Where: Montana Dept of Livestock, Animal Health Division

Source: Montana Legislature / Dept of Livestock

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in North Carolina? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › North Carolina

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the North Carolina-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where North Carolina is silent. See United States.

Summary. North Carolina has NO statewide exotic-pet law. The Wildlife Resources Commission regulates only NATIVE wildlife, and the roof rat is a non-native species, so it is outside the WRC's captivity-license scope; the state Animal Welfare Act's breeder/dealer rules cover only dogs and cats. So keeping, breeding, and selling/giving a captive-bred roof rat is legal at the state level. The one firm state requirement is animal-health: importing a pet rat into NC needs a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection. The decisive variable is LOCAL — North Carolina delegates exotic/dangerous-animal rules to counties and cities, so always check your county/city ordinance.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

No NC statute regulates possessing a non-native pet rodent. The WRC captivity license covers only NATIVE wildlife (15A NCAC 10H.1401; G.S. 113-272.5), and R. rattus is non-native, so no captivity license applies. The only possible restriction is a local ordinance under G.S. §153A-131 / §160A-187, which reach only animals 'dangerous to persons or property' — generally not a small pet rat. Check your county/city ordinance. Gemini DR-verified: no state exotic-pet statute (state captivity licenses exclude pet ownership); the binding layer is LOCAL - county/city ordinances may ban/restrict R. rattus as a 'wild/exotic animal' vs a 'customary pet' (N.C. Gen. Stat. 153A-131 / 160A-187).

Sources: UNC School of Government, NC Wildlife Resources Commission, NC General Assembly

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

NC's breeder/dealer licensing (Animal Welfare Act, ch. 19A, art. 3) applies only to dogs and cats (G.S. 19A-23(4)), so breeding rodents triggers no state license. No WRC propagation license applies (R. rattus is non-native, outside WRC scope). Local ordinances could impose kennel/nuisance/numeric limits — check your county/city. Gemini DR-verified: the NC Animal Welfare Act defines 'animal' as dogs/cats only (19A-23(4)) -> rodent breeders are exempt from state licensing/inspection regardless of volume.

Sources: NC General Assembly, NC Wildlife Resources Commission

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Because the Animal Welfare Act 'dealer' provisions apply only to dogs and cats, selling, giving, or adopting out pet rats needs no state pet-dealer license. WRC sale/transfer rules don't apply to a non-native species outside its jurisdiction. Ordinary consumer/cruelty law still applies. Gemini DR-verified: 'pocket pets' (rats/mice) are explicitly exempt from NCDA&CS pet-shop/dealer licensing.

Sources: NC General Assembly, UNC School of Government

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Moving a pet rat WITHIN NC is unregulated by the state. IMPORTING one into NC requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection because 02 NCAC 52B.0212(f) requires any mammal 'not otherwise covered' in the Code to be accompanied by a valid CVI. A State-Veterinarian import PERMIT is NOT required (rodents aren't on the.0212(a) permit list). No CVI for purely in-state movement. Gemini DR-verified: importing any mammal into NC requires a CVI (02 NCAC 52B.0212(f)); intrastate movement of legally-held rodents is unrestricted (never release).

Sources: NCDA&CS State Veterinarian (via Cornell LII), NC Wildlife Resources Commission

Restrictions & responsibilities

The binding layer in North Carolina is LOCAL: counties (G.S. §153A-131) and cities (§160A-187) may regulate exotic/dangerous animals, and some ordinances define 'exotic'/'wild' broadly enough to potentially reach a non-native pet rat. Always check your county AND city animal-control ordinance.
  • Check your county ordinance (G.S. §153A-131)
  • Check your city ordinance (§160A-187)

Where: Your county and city animal control · Fees: Set locally

Source: UNC School of Government, NC General Assembly

Importing a pet rat into North Carolina requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (02 NCAC 52B.0212(f)); no State-Veterinarian permit is needed for rodents. No CVI for in-state movement.
  • Get a CVI from a veterinarian before bringing a pet rat into NC

Where: NCDA&CS Veterinary Division

Source: NCDA&CS State Veterinarian (via Cornell LII)

Never release a roof rat — it is a non-native species; rehome responsibly.

Source: UNC School of Government

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in North Carolina

In North Carolina, keeping, breeding, and rehoming a captive-bred pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) is legal at the state level. The state has no general exotic-pet law. The Wildlife Resources Commission (WRC) regulates only NATIVE wildlife, and the roof rat is non-native, so its captivity license does not apply. The state Animal Welfare Act's breeder/dealer licensing covers only dogs and cats, so it does not reach pet rodents. The one firm state requirement is animal-health: bringing a pet rat INTO North Carolina from out of state needs a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (a routine vet health certificate); moving one within the state is unregulated. The real friction is twofold and almost entirely a matter of CLARITY, not prohibition: (1) the WRC's "wild animal" language is broadly worded and only narrowed to native species by context, so a keeper or a local official can wrongly assume a permit is needed; and (2) the binding layer is LOCAL — individual counties and cities can define "exotic" or "wild" animals broadly enough to sweep in a small pet rat, so the rules genuinely vary by where you live. There is no statewide ban to repeal; the need is plain, written confirmation of what the law already says.

The ask: Ask the NC Wildlife Resources Commission for a short written confirmation that a non-native, captive-bred Rattus rattus kept as a pet is NOT a "native wild animal" under 15A NCAC 10H.1401 and therefore needs no wildlife captivity license and falls outside the Commission's jurisdiction. Separately, confirm with the NC Department of Agriculture's State Veterinarian that importing a pet rat into the state needs only a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (no special State-Veterinarian import permit), and that no certificate is required for purely in-state movement. Then check your own county AND city animal ordinances, because that local layer — not state law — is what actually varies; where a local ordinance sweeps a tame pet rat into an "exotic/wild animal" category, ask your county or city to recognize small captive-bred pet rodents the way it already treats other customary small pets.

Where the lever really is: This is (a): the problem is the BUREAUCRACY (and the public) MISREADING/over-applying broadly worded language, not a law that bans the animal — so the correct state-level lever is the AGENCY, via a written clarification, NOT the legislature. North Carolina has no statute that lists or prohibits Rattus rattus, and no rule the General Assembly needs to amend; keeping the rat is already legal. The friction comes from the WRC captivity-license definition reading "wild animal" broadly while in fact applying only to NATIVE species (the license page itself says it authorizes possession of "native wild animals or wild birds"). A plain written confirmation that a non-native captive-bred roof rat is outside WRC jurisdiction resolves the state question — there is no list to be added to and no bill to pass, so an appeal to the legislature would be misdirected. IMPORTANT NUANCE: the one place the LAW-as-written (not agency misreading) can actually be the obstacle is LOCAL. Counties (G.S. 153A-131) and cities (G.S. 160A-187) are delegated authority to define and restrict "exotic/dangerous/wild" animals, and a specific local ordinance can lawfully and correctly include a pet rat. Where that is the case, appealing to the WRC or the State Veterinarian will NOT help, because those agencies are correctly applying their own (non-restrictive) rules — the lever there is the LOCAL governing body (county commissioners / city council) to amend or carve out the ordinance, since they are applying a local law they wrote, not misreading a state one. So: state level = agency clarification (problem is misreading); local level, if your ordinance bans it = the local legislative body (problem is the law as written).

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission — Wildlife Interaction, Regulated Activities & Permits (captivity licenses & permits) (executive / agency) — raps@ncwildlife.gov
    This is the official WRC unit that administers wildlife captivity licenses and species-specific permits. Ask it to confirm in writing that a non-native, captive-bred roof rat is not a 'native wild animal' under 15A NCAC 10H.1401 and needs no captivity license — the single most useful state-level clarification.
  • North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission — Conservation Policy & Analysis (regulations) (executive / agency) — regulations@ncwildlife.gov
    The WRC's policy/regulations inbox is the right channel for a definitional/jurisdictional clarification or a request for a written interpretation of how the 'wild animal' / 'native' language applies to a non-native pet species. Use if you want a policy-level statement rather than a permit-desk answer.
  • NCDA&CS Veterinary Division — Office of the State Veterinarian (Import/Export) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Official state authority on animal-import health rules. Confirm that bringing a pet rat into NC requires only a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (no State-Veterinarian permit) and that purely in-state movement needs none. Their import/export page is the official touchpoint; phone (919) 707-3250.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request to confirm a non-native pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) is outside the captivity-license requirement

Dear North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission,

I keep a domesticated, captive-bred pet roof rat (Rattus rattus). I am writing to ask for a short written confirmation of how existing rules apply, so keepers and local officials are not confused.

My understanding is that the wildlife captivity license under 15A NCAC 10H.1401 authorizes possession of NATIVE wild animals only, and that Rattus rattus is a non-native species and therefore falls outside the Commission's captivity-license jurisdiction. The point is about the SPECIES being non-native — not about whether the animal is tame.

These rats are captive-bred, hand-raised, and kept entirely indoors as companion pets. They are never released into the wild.

Would you please confirm in writing that a non-native, captive-bred Rattus rattus kept as a pet requires no wildlife captivity license and is outside the Commission's jurisdiction? A clear statement would help keepers comply correctly and prevent local misunderstanding.

Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your city, North Carolina]
[Your email]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • UNC School of Government — what local governments may do about exotic/dangerous animals (NC has no general exotic-pet law; WRC regulates native wildlife only) — UNC School of Government
  • 15A NCAC 10H.1401 — Captivity license definitions (native wildlife only) — NC Wildlife Resources Commission
  • N.C.G.S. §153A-131 — Possession or harboring of dangerous animals (county delegation) — NC General Assembly
  • N.C.G.S. §19A-23 — Animal Welfare Act definitions (breeder/dealer = dogs & cats only) — NC General Assembly
  • 02 NCAC 52B.0212 — Importation Requirements: Wild Animals (mammal catch-all CVI) — NCDA&CS State Veterinarian (via Cornell LII)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

National law also applies. These are the North Dakota-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where North Dakota is silent. See United States.

Summary. North Dakota is permissive for the roof rat. Its Board of Animal Health rule (NDAC 48.1-09-02) explicitly names 'rats' — alongside gerbils, guinea pigs, hamsters, mice, and sugar gliders — as EXEMPT from both nontraditional-livestock licensing AND importation/CVI requirements (unless the State Veterinarian invokes a disease-based override). Game & Fish jurisdiction excludes animals held in private ownership, and no prohibited-species list names R. rattus. So keeping, breeding, selling/giving, and importing a captive-bred roof rat is effectively unregulated. The only loose end is that the exemption says 'rats' generically — a one-email confirmation to the State Vet would lock species coverage. Never release one.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

NDAC 48.1-09-02 names 'rats' as exempt from nontraditional-livestock requirements, and NDCC 20.1-01-02 excludes animals 'held in private ownership' from 'wildlife' (so Game & Fish jurisdiction doesn't apply to a captive pet). No North Dakota statute or rule lists R. rattus as prohibited/restricted. No permit to keep one. (Exemption text says 'rats' generically; State-Vet override exists but isn't invoked.)

Sources: North Dakota State Board of Animal Health, North Dakota Legislature / Game & Fish

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Because rats are exempt from nontraditional-livestock licensing (NDAC 48.1-09-02), the Category 2/3 breeder-license requirements don't apply, and no separate ND breeder permit for exempt rodents exists. Hobby breeding is unregulated (federal USDA/AWA may apply at commercial volume).

Sources: North Dakota State Board of Animal Health

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

No ND pet-dealer licensing regime for exempt rodents was found; conventional livestock-dealer licensing covers regulated livestock, not exempt pet rats. No rule prohibits transfer/sale of R. rattus. Free rehoming and sale are unregulated at the state level.

Sources: North Dakota State Board of Animal Health

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

NDAC 48.1-09-02's exemption explicitly covers IMPORTATION requirements for rats — so no CVI or import permit is required to bring a pet rat into North Dakota by default (the State Veterinarian can impose requirements only if disease conditions warrant). In-state transport is likewise unregulated. Never release a roof rat.

Sources: North Dakota State Board of Animal Health

Restrictions & responsibilities

Never release a roof rat — it's a non-native species. Local ordinances may add limits — check your city/county. (The State Vet retains discretion to add requirements if a disease concern arises.)

Source: North Dakota State Board of Animal Health
