Summary. Nebraska is unusually clear: its statute defining 'wild mammals' (Neb. Rev. Stat. 37-246) EXCLUDES 'the black rat' by name (alongside the house mouse, Norway rat, fallow deer, and feral dogs/cats). 'Black rat' is the common name for Rattus rattus. Because the Captive Wildlife Permit system and the prohibited-species list (wolf/skunk/cats/bears) are scoped to 'wild mammals,' the roof rat falls entirely outside them — so keeping, breeding, and selling/giving is legal at the state level with no permit. The one procedural requirement is interstate IMPORT: the Dept of Agriculture lists rats among pet rodents needing a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection + an import permit. (Statute uses the common name, so a written Game & Parks confirmation is the only loose end.)

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Neb. Rev. Stat. 37-246 defines 'wild mammals' but EXCLUDES 'the black rat' (= Rattus rattus) by name. The Captive Wildlife Permit requirement (37-477) applies only to wild mammals/birds/nongame wildlife, and the prohibited list (37-479: wolf, skunk, Felidae, Ursidae) doesn't include rats — so no state permit is required to keep one.

Sources: Nebraska Legislature, Nebraska Legislature, Nebraska Legislature

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

The captive-wildlife propagation permits (37-477/37-480) reach only 'wild mammals' as defined; R. rattus is excluded, so breeding needs no permit. The Commercial Dog and Cat Act covers only dogs/cats. Hobby breeding is unregulated by the state.

Sources: Nebraska Legislature, Nebraska Legislature

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

The captive-wildlife sale/barter rules (37-480) apply only to 'wild mammals'; R. rattus is excluded, and no Nebraska pet-dealer license covers non-livestock rodents (the Commercial Dog and Cat Act is dogs/cats). Within-state gifting and small sales are unregulated; commercial scale may trigger federal USDA/AWA licensing.

Sources: Nebraska Legislature

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Within-state transport of a lawfully-owned pet is unregulated. For IMPORT, the Dept of Agriculture (Neb. Admin. Code Title 23 ch. 21) requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (within 30 days) + an import permit, and explicitly lists rats among the pet rodents covered. Confirm the single-pet process with the State Veterinarian. Never release a roof rat.

Sources: Nebraska Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian), Nebraska Legislature

Restrictions & responsibilities

Importing a pet rat into Nebraska requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (within 30 days) + an import permit from the State Veterinarian (NDA lists rats among covered pet rodents). No CVI for in-state movement; never release.

Where: Nebraska Dept of Agriculture, State Veterinarian

Source: Nebraska Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian)

Local (Lincoln/Omaha/county) ordinances may separately regulate rats — check your city. Never release a roof rat.

Source: Nebraska Legislature

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in New Hampshire? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › New Hampshire

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the New Hampshire-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where New Hampshire is silent. See United States.

Summary. New Hampshire is one of the most clearly favorable states: its Fish & Game rule N.H. Admin. Code Fis 804.02(b)(7) names 'Rats, domesticated (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus)' as NON-CONTROLLED wildlife — by binomial — meaning no permit is required to possess, breed, or import a captive-bred roof rat. (The rule was re-adopted effective 2026-04-20 with the listing unchanged.) Selling is unobstructed from the Fish & Game side; the only touchpoint is the Dept of Agriculture's 'pet vendor' license, a threshold-triggered business registration for selling small mammals at volume (free transfers can count toward the threshold). Never release one — that's the single firm prohibition.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

N.H. Admin. Code Fis 804.02(a) requires no permit to possess non-controlled wildlife, and Fis 804.02(b)(7) lists 'Rats, domesticated (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus)' as non-controlled — both species named. RSA 207:1 also defines 'wild animals' as all animals other than domestic, reinforcing that a captive-bred domestic rat needs no permit.

Sources: NH Fish & Game (via Cornell LII), NH General Court

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Non-controlled designation covers breeding (possession encompasses progeny); the propagation permit (Fis 806) applies to controlled/prohibited wildlife, not non-controlled species. Hobby/non-commercial breeding needs no Fish & Game permit. Breeding for sale at volume may bring the Dept of Agriculture pet-vendor license into play (see sell_give).

Sources: NH Fish & Game (via Cornell LII)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

No Fish & Game sale permit applies to non-controlled mammals (Fis 811 covers indigenous herps only). The Dept of Agriculture 'pet vendor' license (RSA 437; Agr 1701) is required to transfer small mammals 'to the public' above a threshold quantity set by rule — and RSA 437:1 counts transfers 'with or without a fee or donation,' so high-volume free adoption can count. Below the threshold, selling/giving is unregulated.

Sources: NH General Court / Dept of Agriculture, NH Fish & Game (via Cornell LII)

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

No Fish & Game import permit is required for non-controlled species (Fis 803). Imported animals must meet Dept of Agriculture (Agr 2100), USDA-APHIS, and USFWS rules; Agr 2100's CVI list enumerates livestock categories, not pet rodents, and APHIS has no interstate health-cert requirement for pet rodents — so no CVI is clearly required (confirm with the State Vet). Releasing R. rattus into the wild is prohibited (Fis 805 / RSA 207:14).

Sources: NH Fish & Game (via Cornell LII), NH General Court

Restrictions & responsibilities

Transferring small mammals 'to the public' above the Dept of Agriculture's threshold (Agr 1701.02; counts free transfers too) requires a NH pet-vendor license — a routine business registration, not a species restriction. Confirm the small-mammal threshold with the Division of Animal Industry.
  • Confirm the Agr 1701.02 small-mammal threshold; register as a pet vendor if you exceed it

Where: NH Dept of Agriculture, Markets & Food — Division of Animal Industry

Source: NH General Court / Dept of Agriculture

Never release a roof rat into the wild (Fis 805 / RSA 207:14). Check local ordinances.

Source: NH General Court

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in New Jersey? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › New Jersey

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the New Jersey-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where New Jersey is silent. See United States.

Summary. New Jersey is strict about exotic pets in general, but it expressly exempts the entire rat genus: its exempt-pet list (N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4) names 'Mice and Rats — Mus spp. and Rattus spp.' Because the exemption is written at the GENUS level, it covers Rattus rattus exactly as it covers the common fancy rat. So keeping and breeding a captive-bred roof rat is legal with no exotic/nongame permit (just cage it to prevent escape and never release it). Private rehoming/adoption is fine; COMMERCIAL selling triggers Fish & Wildlife pet-shop/dealer licensing. No pet-rat-specific state import certificate was found (the CVI rules cover livestock/poultry).

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4(a) lists species that 'may be possessed in this State without a permit,' and subsection (a)2.v lists 'Mice and Rats — Mus spp. and Rattus spp.' Because the exemption names the entire genus Rattus, captive-bred Rattus rattus falls within it and needs no exotic/nongame possession permit. The only condition (4.4(b)) is that the animal be caged to prevent escape. Rattus is absent from the permit-required list (7:25-4.3) and the potentially-dangerous-species list (7:25-4.8). Gemini DR-verified: N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4 exempts the entire genus Rattus from exotic-wildlife permitting (the model genus-level exemption).

Sources: NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

An exempt species under 7:25-4.4 is removed from the possession-permit scheme, and no NJ Fish & Wildlife rule imposes a hobby-breeding permit for an exempt pet rodent. Breeding is simply continued possession of exempt animals, so long as the no-escape housing rule (4.4(b)) is met and animals are never released (N.J.S.A. 23:4-63.3). Commercial-scale breeding for sale shifts into dealer/pet-shop licensing. Gemini DR-verified: no statewide hobby-breeder license for exempt rodents.

Sources: NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), NJ Revised Statutes (Justia)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Because Rattus spp. is exempt, transferring or giving an individual pet rat is not barred by the possession code. But anyone SELLING exotic/nongame wildlife commercially must hold the applicable NJ Fish & Wildlife permit — a Pet Shop–Retail Sales permit or an Animal Dealer–Wholesale permit ($100 each). Free adoption/rehoming via private transfer is the cleanest route and avoids the dealer question. Gemini DR-verified: private giving is unregulated; commercial sale needs a MUNICIPAL pet-shop license (local health dept), not a state exotic-dealer permit.

Sources: NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife, NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Intrastate transport of a lawfully-possessed exempt pet is not restricted. New Jersey's animal-import / CVI scheme (N.J.A.C. 2:3) is limited to livestock and poultry and does not impose a CVI on pet rodents. The binding statewide rules are the no-release prohibition (N.J.S.A. 23:4-63.3) and the no-escape caging rule (7:25-4.4(b)). Confirm import expectations with the State Veterinarian, as no rat-specific rule was located. Gemini DR-verified: intrastate unregulated; import of companion rodents isn't subject to a state CVI (livestock/poultry/dogs-focused) - a practical-legal gray area; commercial carriers may still require a CVI.

Sources: NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), NJ Revised Statutes (Justia)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Selling pet rats COMMERCIALLY requires a NJ Fish & Wildlife permit — a Pet Shop–Retail Sales permit (selling to individuals) or an Animal Dealer–Wholesale permit (selling to stores), $100 each, with recordkeeping. Private free adoption/rehoming does not.
  • For commercial sales: obtain the appropriate NJ Fish & Wildlife pet-shop/dealer permit
  • Private rehoming/adoption needs no permit

Forms: NJ Fish & Wildlife — Exotic & Nongame Wildlife Permit Applications · Where: NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife — Wildlife Permits Unit · Fees: $100 per permit

Source: NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife

Cage the rat to prevent escape (N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4(b)) and never release it (N.J.S.A. 23:4-63.3) — R. rattus is a non-native species. Rehome responsibly.

Source: NJ Revised Statutes (Justia), NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.3 — Exotic/nongame species requiring a permit (Rattus NOT listed) — NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)
  • N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.8 — Potentially dangerous species (rodents = prairie dogs & ground squirrels only) — NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)
  • N.J.S.A. 23:4-63.3 — Possession/release of certain animals (no-release rule) — NJ Revised Statutes (Justia)
  • NJ Fish & Wildlife — Exotic & Nongame Wildlife Permit Applications (pet-shop/dealer permits) — NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in New Mexico? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › New Mexico

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the New Mexico-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where New Mexico is silent. See United States.

Summary. New Mexico's importation/possession scheme makes the roof rat legally precarious. The Dept of Game & Fish (19.35.7 NMAC, under NMSA §17-3-32) sorts non-domesticated animals into four groups, and the key default rule is that ANY species not on the Director's list 'will be designated Group IV' — prohibited for the general public. The fancy rat (R. norvegicus) is treated as semi-domesticated (Group I, no permit); Rattus rattus is not a domesticated species in that sense and does not appear on the Group I list, so it almost certainly defaults to Group IV (prohibited without a special permit). So keeping/breeding/selling/importing a roof rat is restricted — likely prohibited or permit-at-best — pending an NMDGF determination. We've queued that inquiry. (The Livestock Board's CVI rules don't apply — rodents aren't 'livestock.')

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Under 19.35.7 NMAC, possessing a non-domesticated animal without an importation permit is unlawful, and the default rule designates any species not on the Director's Importation List as Group IV (prohibited for the general public; allowed only for science/zoo/etc.). R. rattus is not a selectively domesticated species like R. norvegicus and isn't on the Group I (semi-domesticated, no-permit) list — so it almost certainly defaults to Group IV. Keeping is therefore restricted/likely prohibited pending an NMDGF determination.

Sources: New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish, New Mexico Legislature

Breeding   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Breeding presupposes lawful possession; for a non-Group-I species that requires an importation/possession permit (with containment + health conditions), and if R. rattus is Group IV, breeding is prohibited for the general public. No separate NM small-rodent breeder license exists.

Sources: New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

19.35.7 NMAC lists 'purchase, barter, transfer, sell' as unlawful for Group II-IV species without a department permit/license. If R. rattus is Group IV, sale and transfer (including free gifting) are prohibited for the general public; if Group II/III, possible under permit.

Sources: New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

NMSA §17-3-32 makes it a misdemeanor to import any live non-domesticated animal without an NMDGF permit (only domesticated animals are exempt) — so crossing the state line with a roof rat without a permit is unlawful if it's non-domesticated/Group IV. The Livestock Board (21.32 NMAC) does NOT apply (rodents aren't 'livestock'), so no CVI route there. No-release rule applies.

Sources: New Mexico Legislature, New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish

Restrictions & responsibilities

Because R. rattus is not on NMDGF's semi-domesticated (Group I) list, it likely defaults to Group IV (prohibited for the general public). Do NOT acquire or import one before confirming its group with NMDGF; request the current Director's Species Importation List and consider petitioning to add captive-bred R. rattus to Group I. Never release.
  • Request the Director's Species Importation List + R. rattus's group from NMDGF (ispa@dgf.nm.gov)
  • If pursuing reform: petition to add captive-bred R. rattus to Group I

Where: New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish — Special Use Permits

Source: New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in New Mexico. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in New Mexico

In New Mexico, the domesticated pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) is in legal limbo not because any law names it as dangerous, but because of a paperwork gap. The Department of Game & Fish rule on importing live non-domesticated animals (19.35.7 NMAC, under NMSA 1978 Sec. 17-3-32) sorts species into four groups. The everyday "fancy rat" (Rattus norvegicus) and the house mouse are effectively treated as semi-domesticated (Group I), which needs no permit. The roof rat simply isn't written anywhere on the Director's Species Importation List. And the rule says any species that isn't on the list "will be designated group IV until such time as another determination is made by the director" — and Group IV is prohibited for the general public. So a tame, captive-bred roof rat is treated as prohibited purely by default, even though its close cousin the fancy rat is freely kept. The fix the rule itself describes is "another determination by the director" — exactly the lever pet keepers can ask for.

The ask: Ask the New Mexico Department of Game & Fish, in writing, to make a Director's determination adding captive-bred, domesticated Rattus rattus to Species Importation List Group I (semi-domesticated, no permit) — the same treatment already given to the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) and the house mouse. As a first step, request the current Director's Species Importation List and a written statement of what group Rattus rattus is in today, and whether captive-bred animals are treated differently from wild ones. The point to make: this is a species-listing gap, not a domestication question — captive-bred roof rats are tame, raised entirely indoors, and never released, so they meet the rule's own definition of "semi-domesticated" (a species "commonly tamed, raised, bred or sold in captivity").

Where the lever really is: BRANCH: This is an AGENCY problem (bureaucratic species-listing trap), NOT a law-as-written problem — so the lever is the Department of Game & Fish, and the agency CAN fix it without any legislation. Why, concretely for New Mexico: The roof rat is not named on any statutory prohibited list. Its prohibition is entirely a regulatory DEFAULT — 19.35.7.9 NMAC states any species not on the Director's Species Importation List "will be designated group IV until such time as another determination is made by the director." Two facts make this squarely an agency lever: (1) The same rule gives the Director explicit discretionary power to classify a species as semi-domesticated (Group I) "in those instances where individual members of such species are commonly tamed, raised, bred or sold in captivity" — which captive-bred roof rats plainly are, and which the Department already applied to the closely related fancy rat. (2) Because the Director assigns the list groups, the Director can move R. rattus off the default by a written determination — no statute needs to change. Appealing to the agency is therefore the RIGHT move; this is not a case where the agency is merely applying a fixed statutory list correctly. The legislature is only a distant backstop if the Department refuses; the primary, effective channel is a written petition / inquiry to NMDGF asking for a Director's determination (and the current list). Verified that the statute (NMSA 17-3-32) only creates the permit requirement and exempts domesticated animals — it does NOT itself list R. rattus as prohibited — confirming the trap lives in the agency's list, where the agency holds the cure.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • New Mexico Department of Game & Fish (Department of Wildlife) — general inquiries / Species Importation (executive / agency) — ispa@dgf.nm.gov
    Primary and decisive lever. The Director of this Department maintains the Species Importation List and has explicit regulatory authority (19.35.7 NMAC) to designate a species as semi-domesticated (Group I) by written determination — exactly the change needed for captive-bred R. rattus. This is the verified official inbox (ispa@dgf.nm.gov, shown on the Department's own contact page) and contact page; use it to request the current list, ask what group R. rattus is in, and petition to add it to Group I.
  • Director's Species Importation List (official current PDF) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Verified official download of the current list (last updated Jan 2023). Read it first to confirm R. rattus is absent (and thus defaulting to Group IV) and to cite the exact Group I entries for the fancy rat / house mouse as your precedent when you write to the Department.
  • New Mexico Legislature — Find My Legislator (legislature) — official contact page
    Secondary backstop ONLY. The agency can and should fix this itself, so go here only if the Department declines to make a Director's determination — your legislator can prompt the agency or, if ever needed, pursue a statutory clarification. Official tool to find and contact your own state representative and senator.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the New Mexico Department of Game & Fish, Director's Species Importation List:

I am writing about a gap in the Director's Species Importation List under 19.35.7 NMAC. The domesticated pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) does not appear on the list, so it defaults to Group IV (prohibited), even though the closely related fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) and the house mouse are treated as semi-domesticated Group I and need no permit.

The captive-bred roof rats kept by hobbyists are tame, raised entirely indoors, and never released to the wild. They meet the rule's own definition of a semi-domesticated species — one "commonly tamed, raised, bred or sold in captivity." This is a listing gap, not a question of domestication.

I respectfully request: (1) a copy of the current Director's Species Importation List and a written statement of what group Rattus rattus is in today; and (2) that the Director make a determination adding captive-bred, domesticated Rattus rattus to Group I, on the same basis as the fancy rat.

Thank you for your consideration.

[Your name]
[Your city, New Mexico]
[Your email]
Español
Al Departamento de Caza y Pesca de Nuevo Mexico, Lista de Importacion de Especies del Director:

Les escribo respecto a un vacio en la Lista de Importacion de Especies del Director, conforme a 19.35.7 NMAC. La rata de techo domesticada (Rattus rattus) no aparece en la lista, por lo que queda por defecto en el Grupo IV (prohibida), aunque la rata fancy estrechamente emparentada (Rattus norvegicus) y el raton domestico se tratan como semidomesticados del Grupo I y no requieren permiso.

Las ratas de techo criadas en cautiverio que mantienen los aficionados son mansas, se crian totalmente en interiores y nunca se liberan a la naturaleza. Cumplen con la propia definicion de la norma de especie semidomesticada: aquella "comunmente amansada, criada, reproducida o vendida en cautiverio". Se trata de un vacio en la lista, no de una cuestion de domesticacion.

Solicito respetuosamente: (1) una copia de la Lista de Importacion de Especies del Director vigente y una declaracion por escrito sobre en que grupo se encuentra hoy Rattus rattus; y (2) que el Director emita una determinacion para anadir a Rattus rattus domesticada y criada en cautiverio al Grupo I, sobre la misma base que la rata fancy.

Gracias por su atencion.

[Su nombre]
[Su ciudad, Nuevo Mexico]
[Su correo electronico]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • 19.35.7 NMAC — Importation of Live Non-Domesticated Animals (Group I-IV; unlisted defaults to Group IV) — New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish
  • NMSA 1978 §17-3-32 — Importing live animals; permits (misdemeanor without NMDGF permit; domesticated exempt) — New Mexico Legislature
  • Director's Species Importation List — NMDGF — New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Nevada? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Nevada

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the Nevada-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Nevada is silent. See United States.

Summary. Nevada is permissive and the roof rat is almost certainly fine — but there's a wording gap. NRS 501.097 defines 'wildlife' to include wild mammals 'whether raised in captivity or not,' and the key exemption (NAC 503.140) frees 'domesticated races of rats and mice' from any NDOW permit. R. rattus is NOT on Nevada's prohibited-species list (only the African multimammate rat is). The open question is whether NDOW reads 'domesticated races of rats' to include captive-bred R. rattus (it clearly covers the fancy rat). If yes — as is likely — keeping, breeding, selling, and transporting are fully legal with no permit. We've asked NDOW to confirm.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

NAC 503.140 exempts 'domesticated races of rats and mice' from NDOW possession licensing; if captive-bred R. rattus is a 'domesticated race,' no license is needed. R. rattus is not on the NAC 503.110 prohibited list (only Mastomys is), so prohibition is unlikely — but NDOW hasn't published a ruling confirming the exemption reaches R. rattus specifically (vs. just R. norvegicus). Likely legal; confirm with NDOW.

Sources: Nevada Legislature, Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII), Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

If R. rattus qualifies under the NAC 503.140 exemption, breeding needs no NDOW permit; if not, a NAC 504 possession license would apply. No species-specific breeding prohibition exists. Commercial-scale operations may need a local business/breeder permit regardless of species.

Sources: Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII)

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

NAC 503.140 expressly allows lawfully-acquired exempt species to be sold in Nevada without an NDOW dealer permit; if R. rattus is within 'domesticated races,' private sale/free adoption is fine. Local business licenses apply to commercial activity.

Sources: Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII)

Transport & import   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

NAC 503.140 species may be transported and imported without an NDOW permit/CVI; if R. rattus is exempt, no importation permit is needed. If treated as non-exempt wildlife, an NDOW importation permit + CVI would apply. The NDA's separate import rules don't appear to require a CVI for small pet rodents — confirm. Never release (R. rattus is a pest under NRS 567).

Sources: Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII), Nevada Dept of Wildlife

Restrictions & responsibilities

Never release a roof rat — it's treated as a pest in the wild (NRS 567). Local (Clark County / Las Vegas / Henderson) business or breeder permits apply to commercial activity regardless of species.

Source: Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII)

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Help change this

How to help in Nevada

Good news first: in Nevada, keeping a pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) is almost certainly already legal. The roof rat is NOT on Nevada's prohibited-species list (NAC 503.110 lists only the African multimammate rat, Mastomys), and a state regulation, NAC 503.140, exempts "domesticated races of rats and mice" from any Nevada Department of Wildlife (NDOW) permit or license — the same rule that covers the ordinary pet "fancy rat." So this is not a case of a law banning the animal. The single gap is a wording/interpretation question. Nevada's wildlife definition (NRS 501.097) sweeps in wild mammals "whether raised in captivity or not." NDOW has not published anything confirming that its "domesticated races of rats and mice" exemption reaches captive-bred R. rattus specifically (everyone agrees it covers R. norvegicus, the fancy rat). Until NDOW says so in writing, an owner, breeder, or seller of pet roof rats is left guessing whether they need a possession license or an importation permit — even though the most natural reading is that multi-generational, captive-bred, tame roof rats are exactly the "domesticated races of rats" the regulation already exempts.

The ask: Ask NDOW to confirm, in writing, that the NAC 503.140 exemption for "domesticated races of rats and mice" includes captive-bred Rattus rattus kept as companion animals — so that possessing, breeding, gifting/selling, and importing pet roof rats requires no NDOW permit or license, exactly as for the fancy rat. A short written confirmation (or a declaratory ruling) closes the gap. If NDOW will not read the existing exemption that way, ask it to bring a rule petition to the Board of Wildlife Commissioners to add R. rattus by name to the NAC 503.140 exemption list. Separately, ask the Nevada Department of Agriculture whether any certificate of veterinary inspection or entry permit applies to a small pet rodent brought into Nevada.

Where the lever really is: This is an AGENCY-clarification lever, not a legislative one — and that distinction is the whole point in Nevada. The roof rat is not on any statutory or regulatory prohibited list, so there is no "bad law" to repeal: appealing to the Legislature would be aimed at a ban that does not exist. The real obstacle is interpretive — whether NDOW reads its own already-on-the-books exemption (NAC 503.140, "domesticated races of rats and mice") to reach captive-bred R. rattus. Because the exemption text and the absence of R. rattus from the NAC 503.110 prohibited list both already point toward "legal," the correct first move is to ask NDOW for a written confirmation or declaratory ruling that the exemption covers the captive-bred roof rat. That is something the AGENCY can do today without any new rule. The optional, second-line lever is quasi-legislative within the agency: if NDOW declines to confirm by interpretation, a member of the public can petition the Board of Wildlife Commissioners (the body that adopts and amends NAC wildlife regulations) to add R. rattus by name to the NAC 503.140 exemption — a rulemaking/public-comment route, not an ordinary statute. We are NOT asking NDOW to override a law it is correctly applying; we are asking it to map an exemption it already administers onto a species the law does not prohibit. Keep the request that modest and it is well within NDOW's authority.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Nevada Department of Wildlife (NDOW) — general inquiry / Wildlife Diversity (executive / agency) — ndowinfo@ndow.org
    Primary lever. NDOW administers the NAC 503.140 exemption and the prohibited-species list. Its contact form lets you direct the inquiry to the Wildlife Diversity division; ask for a written confirmation (or declaratory ruling) that the 'domesticated races of rats and mice' exemption covers captive-bred Rattus rattus. The form is preferable; ndowinfo@ndow.org is the verified general inbox if you'd rather email.
  • Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners — written public comment / rule petition (executive / agency) — wildlifecommission@ndow.org
    Second-line / escalation lever. If NDOW will not confirm by interpretation, the Commission is the body that adopts and amends NAC wildlife regulations. This verified address receives written public comment and petition correspondence; use it to ask the Commission to add Rattus rattus by name to the NAC 503.140 exemption through its rulemaking process.
  • Nevada Department of Agriculture — Animal Disease / Entry Permits (executive / agency) — entrypermits@agri.nv.gov
    Narrow, separate question only: whether a certificate of veterinary inspection or entry permit applies to a small pet rodent brought into Nevada. (Email carried from prior research; confirm before relying on it.)

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Nevada Department of Wildlife, Wildlife Diversity Division:

I am writing to ask for a written clarification about pet roof rats (Rattus rattus). I keep these animals as companion pets, and I want to be sure I am following Nevada law.

Roof rats kept as pets are captive-bred over many generations, hand-tame, housed indoors in cages, and never released into the wild. They are kept exactly like the ordinary pet "fancy rat" (Rattus norvegicus).

My question is one of wording, not of any ban: R. rattus is not on the NAC 503.110 prohibited-species list, and NAC 503.140 already exempts "domesticated races of rats and mice" from any NDOW permit or license. Captive-bred pet roof rats appear to be exactly such a "domesticated race of rats."

Would NDOW please confirm in writing that the NAC 503.140 exemption includes captive-bred Rattus rattus kept as companion animals, so that possessing, breeding, gifting, and importing them requires no NDOW permit or license? If NDOW reads the exemption otherwise, would it consider a rule petition to add R. rattus by name to that list?

Thank you for your time and for the work you do.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your city, Nevada]
[Your email / phone]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • NRS 501.097 — 'Wildlife' defined (wild mammals, whether raised in captivity or not) — Nevada Legislature
  • NAC 503.140 — Species exempt from permit/license ('domesticated races of rats and mice'); sale of exempt species allowed — Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII)
  • NAC 503.110 — Prohibited species (Mastomys multimammate rat listed; R. rattus absent) — Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW
  • NDOW Wildlife Importation Permit instructions (CVI for wildlife; NAC 503.140 species exempt) — Nevada Dept of Wildlife

item.dc:creator: admin

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › New York

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the New York-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where New York is silent. See United States.

Summary. Keeping, breeding, and selling pet roof rats is legal in New York — both statewide and in New York City. The state classifies Rattus rattus as 'unprotected wildlife,' which may be possessed and sold without restriction (ECL §11-0917(2)); it is not a prohibited 'wild animal' and not on the invasive-species list. NYC's Health Code bans only 'large rodents,' so small pet rats are allowed (a Class P pet-shop permit is needed only for commercial retail). Bringing a rat into NY from another state needs a 30-day vet health certificate; international movement is federally restricted.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

New York classifies Rattus rattus as 'unprotected wildlife,' which ECL §11-0917(2) says 'may be possessed, transported, bought and sold without restriction.' It is not a prohibited 'wild animal' (ECL §11-0512 / §11-0103(6)(e) lists primates, big cats, canids, bears, venomous reptiles, crocodilians — not rodents) and is not on the state invasive-species list (6 NYCRR Part 575). New York CITY allows it too: the NYC Health Code (Art. 161.01(b)(14)) bans only 'large rodents' (beaver, capybara, prairie dog, porcupine, etc.); small domestic rats are permitted.

Sources: NY State Senate (Consolidated Laws), NY State Senate, NYC DOHMH

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

No New York breeder license for rodents — the 'Pet Dealer' law (Agriculture & Markets Law Art. 26-A, §400) defines 'animal' as only dogs and cats, so breeding rats at any volume is outside it; only the general anti-cruelty rules apply. In NYC, hobby breeding is fine, but sanitation/nuisance rules (odor, escapes) apply.

Sources: NY Consolidated Laws

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Statewide, selling roof rats is legal — a retailer must just give buyers written/digital care instructions for 'small animals' (which the law lists as including rats), per General Business Law §391-t. In New York CITY, a commercial retail seller needs a Class P 'Pet Shop' permit (NYCHC §161.09); NYC's Local Law 132 (2024) banned the retail sale of dogs, cats, guinea pigs and rabbits, but rats remain sellable. Giving rats away or private/face-to-face placement needs no permit. (Federal USDA licensing applies to wholesale/sight-unseen sales — see United States.)

Sources: NY State Senate, NYC DOHMH

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Within New York, no permit is required. Bringing a rat INTO New York from another state requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (health certificate) issued within 30 days (1CRR-NY 67.2); no rabies vaccine is required for rodents, and enforcement against a private owner with a single pet is reportedly minimal. International import/export is restricted at the federal level (USFWS Form 3-177; CDC African-rodent ban) — see United States.

Sources: NY Dept. of Agriculture & Markets

Restrictions & responsibilities

In New York CITY, a commercial retail seller of rats needs a Class P 'Pet Shop' permit from DOHMH (facility inspections; integrated pest management). Rats remain legally sellable in NYC even after Local Law 132 (2024) banned retail sale of dogs/cats/guinea pigs/rabbits. Private/face-to-face placement and giveaways need no permit.
  • If running an NYC retail storefront, obtain a DOHMH Class P pet-shop permit

Forms: NYC Health Code Ch. 5 — Pet Shops · Where: NYC DOHMH · Fees: Municipal pet-shop permit fee

Source: NYC DOHMH

Statewide, a retailer selling rats must give the buyer written or digital care instructions for the species at the time of sale (GBS §391-t), and keep copies on file.

Source: NY State Senate

Bringing a rat into New York from another state requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) issued within 30 days by a USDA-accredited vet (1CRR-NY 67.2). No rabies vaccine is required for rodents.
  • Have a USDA-accredited vet issue a CVI within 30 days of entry

Forms: NY Companion Animal Import & Export · Where: Carried with the animal · Fees: Veterinary fee

Source: NY Dept. of Agriculture & Markets

Keep rats in escape-proof caging — an escaped pet rat is legally indistinguishable from a feral pest under NYC's rodent-control rules (Art. 151), and harborage/active-rodent-signs carry fines. Never release a nonnative species.

Source: NYC DOHMH

Summary. Keeping, breeding, and selling a roof rat is legal in Ohio. The Dangerous Wild Animals Act (ORC ch. 935, post-Zanesville) lists big cats, bears, primates, large constrictors and the like — no rodents. The roof rat is not native wildlife regulated by ODNR (it's actually named a nuisance pest), no Ohio prohibited/exotic list captures the genus Rattus, and Ohio's commercial breeder/dealer licensing (ORC ch. 956) is dogs-only. The one nuance is interstate IMPORT: Ohio's general animal-import rule likely requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection for an incoming pet rat (rodents aren't named in either the domestic or non-domestic import rule), so confirm with the State Veterinarian.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

R. rattus is not a 'dangerous wild animal' under ORC 935.01 (20 enumerated categories; no rodents), not native wildlife regulated by ODNR (it is named a nuisance pest in OAC 1501:31-15-03), and on no Ohio prohibited/exotic-species list (OAC 1501:31-19-01). No statute restricts private possession.

Sources: Ohio General Assembly, ODNR Division of Wildlife, ODNR Division of Wildlife

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

No Ohio statute restricts breeding rodents; commercial breeder/retailer licensing (ORC ch. 956) is limited to dogs. R. rattus is outside ch. 935 and ODNR's regulated-wildlife scope, so breeding is unregulated (local zoning/nuisance aside).

Sources: Ohio General Assembly, Ohio General Assembly

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Ohio's animal sales/dealer licensing (ORC ch. 956) covers only dogs and dog pet-stores; no state license attaches to selling or giving away pet rats, and R. rattus is on no restricted/dangerous list. General humane law (ORC ch. 959) applies to all animals.

Sources: Ohio General Assembly, ODNR Division of Wildlife

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

In-state transport is unregulated. For IMPORT, ODA's general rule (OAC 901:1-17-01) requires a CVI for 'domestic animals' entering Ohio; a captive-bred pet rat plausibly reads as 'domestic,' but rodents aren't named in either the domestic or non-domestic (901:1-17-12) import rule, so confirm the exact paperwork with the State Veterinarian.

Sources: Ohio Dept of Agriculture, Division of Animal Health

Restrictions & responsibilities

Importing a pet rat into Ohio likely needs a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (OAC 901:1-17-01); rodents aren't named, so confirm with the ODA State Veterinarian. No CVI for in-state movement.

Where: Ohio Dept of Agriculture, Division of Animal Health

Source: Ohio Dept of Agriculture, Division of Animal Health

Never release a roof rat — it's a non-native species (and a declared nuisance in Ohio). Rehome responsibly.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Oklahoma? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Oklahoma

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Oklahoma-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Oklahoma is silent. See United States.

Summary. Oklahoma is now AGENCY-CONFIRMED, and the answer is clean and favorable. The Oklahoma Department of Wildlife Conservation (Wildlife Diversity Program together with its Law Enforcement Division) confirmed in writing (June 2026) that OAC 800:25-25-3(a)(25) exempts BOTH the Norway rat and the roof rat (Rattus rattus) from ODWC's import/export permit, its commercial breeder license, and its noncommercial breeder license. Keeping, breeding, and selling or trading roof rats are NOT prohibited and require NO ODWC permit; importing or exporting requires no permit and no health certificate. ODWC treats R. rattus as 'not normally found in the wild' (a non-native species) for purposes of that exemption, which resolves the earlier feral-population ambiguity in the keeper's favor. ODWC recommends standard biosecurity to prevent accidental escapes (never release one). The only open thread is the Oklahoma Department of Agriculture, Food & Forestry (ODAFF), which ODWC suggested contacting in case it enforces separate rules; that inquiry has been sent.

Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Oklahoma Department of Wildlife Conservation (Wildlife Diversity Program and Law Enforcement Division), written reply June 2026: OAC 800:25-25-3(a)(25) exempts both the Norway rat and the roof rat (Rattus rattus) from ODWC's import/export permit, commercial breeder license, and noncommercial breeder license. Keeping, breeding, and selling or trading roof rats are not prohibited and require no ODWC permit; importing or exporting requires no permit and no health certificate. ODWC considers R. rattus a non-native species 'not normally found in the wild' for purposes of that exemption, and recommends standard biosecurity measures to prevent accidental escape.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

ODWC confirmed in writing (June 2026) that keeping a roof rat is not prohibited and requires no permit. OAC 800:25-25-3(a)(25)'s exemption for 'rats (except those species normally found in the wild)' was confirmed by the agency to cover both Rattus species widely kept in captivity (R. rattus and R. norvegicus): ODWC treats R. rattus as a non-native species 'not normally found in the wild,' so it falls inside the exemption despite scattered semi-naturalized populations. The earlier 'unregulated/unclear' reading is superseded by this agency confirmation.

Sources: Oklahoma Dept of Wildlife Conservation (via Cornell LII)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

ODWC confirmed (June 2026) that breeding roof rats requires no permit. OAC 800:25-25-3(a)(25) exempts the roof rat from ODWC's commercial breeder license AND its noncommercial breeder license. (The native-wildlife breeder statute 4 O.S. §4-107 never applied — R. rattus is non-native — and the Commercial Pet Breeders Act covers dogs/cats only.)

Sources: Oklahoma Dept of Wildlife Conservation (via Cornell LII)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

ODWC confirmed (June 2026) that selling or trading roof rats is not prohibited and requires no permit. The OAC 800:25-25-3(a)(25) exemption removes them from ODWC's breeder-license and import/export-permit framework, and no other Oklahoma statute imposes a sale prohibition or permit on captive-bred R. rattus.

Sources: Oklahoma Dept of Wildlife Conservation (via Cornell LII)

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

ODWC confirmed (June 2026) that importing or exporting roof rats requires no ODWC permit, and because of that exemption ODWC does not require a health certificate to accompany these animals. Internal movement of a lawfully held pet is unrestricted. (One open item below: ODAFF, the agriculture department, may have separate animal-movement rules — an inquiry has been sent.) Never release a roof rat.

Sources: Oklahoma Dept of Wildlife Conservation (via Cornell LII), Oklahoma Dept of Agriculture, Food & Forestry

Restrictions & responsibilities

ODWC confirmed (June 2026) that no permit or license is required to keep, breed, sell/trade, import, or export a roof rat in Oklahoma, and none of these is prohibited. ODWC recommends standard biosecurity to prevent accidental escape. Never release a roof rat. One open item: the Oklahoma Department of Agriculture, Food & Forestry may enforce separate rules; an inquiry has been sent at ODWC's suggestion.
  • Use standard biosecurity (secure caging) to prevent escapes — never release a roof rat
  • (Pending) Confirm with the Oklahoma Department of Agriculture, Food & Forestry that no separate agriculture rule applies

Where: No ODWC filing required; ODAFF inquiry pending · Fees: None (no ODWC permit required)

Source: Oklahoma Dept of Wildlife Conservation (via Cornell LII)

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Pennsylvania? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Pennsylvania

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the Pennsylvania-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Pennsylvania is silent. See United States.

Summary. Keeping, breeding, and rehoming a captive-bred roof rat appears legal in Pennsylvania with no permit. The state's 'exotic wildlife' permit list (34 Pa.C.S. §2961) covers only large carnivores (bears, big cats, wolves, coyotes), and the Game Commission's import/possession ban (58 Pa. Code §137.1) is a closed list that doesn't include any rat or rodent. One technicality: the Game Code's literal 'wild animal' definition could label any rat (even the common fancy rat) 'wildlife,' but no active rule turns that into a ban or permit for pet rodents — so it's best treated as legal-but-worth-confirming with the Game Commission. Importing a pet rat may call for a vet health certificate; never release one.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

No Pennsylvania statute/regulation requires a permit to keep a pet rat. R. rattus is not 'exotic wildlife' (34 Pa.C.S. §2961 lists only large carnivores) and is not on the §137.1 possession-prohibition list (felids, canids, ursids, raccoons, nutria, skunks, primates, listed T&E/injurious). The only caveat: the literal §102 / 1 Pa.C.S. §1991 definition technically labels any non-(equine/bovine/sheep/goat/pig) mammal a 'wild animal,' but no active rule converts that into a rodent permit/ban.

Sources: Pennsylvania General Assembly, Pennsylvania General Assembly, PA Game Commission / PA Code & Bulletin

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

No propagation/breeding permit applies to pet rodents — the Game Commission's propagation and exotic-wildlife-dealer permits attach to enumerated game/furbearer and exotic-carnivore species, not rats. Breeding captive-bred roof rats is unregulated (same definitional caveat as keeping).

Sources: Pennsylvania General Assembly, PA Game Commission / PA Code & Bulletin

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling/giving a pet rat is not 'exotic wildlife dealer' activity (that permit covers only §2961 carnivores) and rats aren't on the §137.1 sale-prohibition list. A high-volume commercial animal dealer could fall under PA's Domestic Animal Law dealer license (3 Pa.C.S.; broad 'domestic animal' incl. captive wild animals), but ordinary private placement/free adoption is outside it.

Sources: Pennsylvania General Assembly, PA Game Commission / PA Code & Bulletin

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Intrastate transport isn't restricted. For IMPORT, PDA (Bureau of Animal Health) animal-health rules govern; a CVI is the general interstate mechanism but PDA notes not all states require a CVI for small/pocket pets, so treat it as recommended/possibly required and confirm with BAHDS. Game Commission §137.1 import-permit rules don't apply (rats aren't listed). Never release a pet rat (58 Pa. Code §137.1/§137.2).

Sources: PA Dept of Agriculture, BAHDS, PA Game Commission / PA Code & Bulletin

Restrictions & responsibilities

A veterinary health certificate (CVI) may be requested to bring a pet rat into Pennsylvania but isn't clearly required for pocket pets — confirm with PDA-BAHDS. Never release a pet rat into the wild (58 Pa. Code §137.1/§137.2) — it's illegal and ecologically harmful.

Where: PA Dept of Agriculture, Bureau of Animal Health & Diagnostic Services

Source: PA Dept of Agriculture, BAHDS, PA Game Commission / PA Code & Bulletin

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Pennsylvania

In Pennsylvania, keeping, breeding, and rehoming a captive-bred, domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) appears to be perfectly legal with no permit required. The state's "exotic wildlife" permit list (34 Pa.C.S. §2961) names only large carnivores — bears, big cats, wolves, coyotes — and the Game Commission's import/possession prohibition (58 Pa. Code §137.1) is a closed, enumerated list that contains no rat or rodent of any kind. The one snag is purely definitional: the Game Code's broad "wild animal" wording (34 Pa.C.S. §102, via 1 Pa.C.S. §1991) literally sweeps in every mammal that isn't a horse, cow, sheep, goat, or pig — which on paper would label even the ordinary pet "fancy" rat (Rattus norvegicus) "wildlife" too. No active rule turns that wording into a permit or ban for pet rodents, but the gap leaves owners unsure. The issue here is not a bad law that bans the species; it is the absence of a plain written confirmation from the agency that captive-bred pet rats fall outside the exotic-wildlife and §137.1 schemes.

The ask: Ask the Pennsylvania Game Commission for a short written confirmation (an informal clarification letter or a formal declaratory ruling) stating that a captive-bred, domesticated roof rat kept as a pet is NOT regulated "exotic wildlife" under 34 Pa.C.S. §2961 and is NOT on the §137.1 importation/possession-prohibition list, and therefore may be kept, bred, and rehomed without an exotic-wildlife possession permit, an importation permit, or any other Commission authorization — notwithstanding the literal "wild animal" definition. Separately, ask the PA Department of Agriculture (BAHDS) whether a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection is required to bring a pet rodent into the state.

Where the lever really is: This is a BUREAUCRACY/clarification problem, NOT a bad-law problem — so the lever is the AGENCY, not the legislature. Concretely for Pennsylvania: the statute and regulation that would have to list roof rats for a ban or permit to exist simply do not. 34 Pa.C.S. §2961 defines "exotic wildlife" as a short, closed set of large carnivores; 58 Pa. Code §137.1 is likewise a closed, enumerated import/possession list — neither contains any rodent. There is no statutory list to be added to and no on-point law being misapplied; the only live ambiguity is the over-broad definitional language in 34 Pa.C.S. §102 / 1 Pa.C.S. §1991, which the Commission does not actually enforce against pet rodents. The right fix is therefore a written agency clarification or a declaratory ruling confirming that pets like R. rattus sit outside the exotic-wildlife/§137.1 scheme — which the Commission can issue without any legislative change. Going to the legislature would be the wrong tool here, because there is no prohibition statute to repeal and no positive list to amend; a bill is only worth considering as a fallback IF the Commission were to take the position that the literal "wild animal" definition does ban or burden pet rodents (it currently does not). Use the legislature contact only in that contingency.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Pennsylvania Game Commission — Contact Us / staff inquiry form (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Official PGC public contact form (linked from the Commission's own Contact Information page) for routing a question to staff. Use it to request written confirmation that a captive-bred pet roof rat is outside the §2961 exotic-wildlife and §137.1 prohibition schemes and needs no Commission permit.
  • Pennsylvania Game Commission — License Division (executive / agency) — pgclicdiv@pa.gov
    Verified official Commission inbox (listed on the PGC Contact Information page) handling licensing/permit questions; the right place to ask, in writing, whether any exotic-wildlife or importation permit applies to a pet rodent — and to request that the answer be put in writing.
  • Pennsylvania General Assembly — Find My Legislator (fallback only) (legislature) — official contact page
    Official tool to identify and contact your state senator and representative. Use ONLY as a contingency — i.e., if the Commission ever asserts the literal 'wild animal' definition bans or burdens pet rodents — to seek a statutory clarification exempting domesticated pet rats. Not needed to fix anything today.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Pennsylvania Game Commission,

I am writing to request a written clarification about keeping a captive-bred, domesticated pet roof rat (Rattus rattus). I want to comply fully, and I would like the Commission's position in writing.

As I read the law, roof rats are not regulated 'exotic wildlife' under 34 Pa.C.S. §2961, which lists only large carnivores, and no rat or rodent appears on the closed importation/possession list in 58 Pa. Code §137.1. The only ambiguity I see is the broad 'wild animal' definition in 34 Pa.C.S. §102, which would literally reach even the common pet fancy rat — yet no active rule appears to apply it to pet rodents.

The rats I am asking about are captive-bred, hand-tame, kept entirely indoors as pets, and never released into the wild. The concern is the species label, not the animal's tameness.

Would the Commission please confirm in writing that a captive-bred pet roof rat may be kept, bred, and rehomed without an exotic-wildlife possession permit, an importation permit, or any other Commission authorization? A short clarification letter or declaratory ruling would settle the question for many responsible owners.

Thank you for your time and guidance.

[Your name]
[Your county / contact information]

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Puerto Rico? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Puerto Rico

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Preliminary — independently researched, not yet agency-confirmed. We compiled this from official sources but are still verifying it (and, where useful, asking the agencies directly). Treat it as a starting point and confirm with the official source. Know the local rule? Tell us.
National law also applies. These are the Puerto Rico-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Puerto Rico is silent. See United States.

Summary. In Puerto Rico, keeping a captive-bred roof rat ('rata negra') is currently legal without a DRNA permit: the species is named — with no restrictive asterisk — in Apéndice 4 of the DRNA wildlife regulation (Reg. 6765/6766), the list of low-risk exotics eligible for import, possession, sale, and captive breeding WITHOUT a permit. Only releasing them into the wild is flatly prohibited. Importing into PR still requires a veterinary health certificate and a PR Dept of Agriculture import permit (PR runs its own agricultural quarantine even though it's inside the US customs area). A standing commercial rattery (vs. free private adoption) would also need DRNA's $150 exotic-species dealer permit. WATCH-ITEM: a 2025 law (Ley 93-2025) creates a new prohibited/restricted/unrestricted classification scheme to be filled in by a forthcoming DRNA regulation — so confirm the current status directly with DRNA.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

R. rattus ('rata negra') is expressly listed in Apéndice 4 of DRNA Reg. 6765/6766 — low-risk exotics eligible for import, possession, and sale WITHOUT a permit. Art. 7 makes it illegal to possess only exotics NOT on Apéndice 4; R. rattus is on it (no asterisk). Ley 93-2025 has not yet produced an implementing list reclassifying it, and its Art. 13 excludes domestic/naturalized species.

Sources: Departamento de Recursos Naturales y Ambientales (DRNA), Asamblea Legislativa de PR / DRNA

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Art. 7 expressly permits captive reproduction of Apéndice 4 species; only species marked with a double asterisk (**) need prior DRNA permission to breed, and R. rattus carries no asterisk. The regulation also expects only captive-born individuals to be imported/sold.

Sources: Departamento de Recursos Naturales y Ambientales (DRNA)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Apéndice 4 species may be sold 'sin permiso' (Art. 7), so private sale, giving, or free adoption of captive-bred black rats is permitted (only captive-born individuals). BUT operating a buy/sell BUSINESS in exotics needs a $150 DRNA dealer permit (Art. 7.01); the exemption from that business permit applies only to asterisk-marked agricultural/domestic species, and R. rattus is not asterisk-marked. Free vetted adoption is the unregulated private path.

Sources: Departamento de Recursos Naturales y Ambientales (DRNA)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Intra-PR transport of a permit-free Apéndice 4 species isn't separately restricted. For IMPORT, DRNA Art. 7 requires a veterinary certificate and limits import to captive-born animals, AND the PR Dept of Agriculture (DA-SAHO) requires a pre-shipment import permit + a 30-day veterinary inspection certificate (the DA routes exotic species to DRNA, $50 fee). Although PR is inside the US customs area, its agricultural quarantine is independent. Release into the environment is absolutely prohibited (24-hr escape reporting).

Sources: Departamento de Recursos Naturales y Ambientales (DRNA), Departamento de Agricultura de PR (SAHO)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Importing a roof rat into Puerto Rico needs a veterinary health certificate + a PR Dept of Agriculture import permit (exotic species routed to DRNA, ~$50); only captive-born animals. Never release one (24-hour escape reporting).
  • Obtain the PR Dept of Agriculture import permit (DRNA-routed for exotics)
  • Carry a veterinary health certificate

Where: DRNA (exotic species); PR Dept of Agriculture (DA-SAHO) · Fees: ~$50 import permit

Source: Departamento de Agricultura de PR (SAHO), Departamento de Recursos Naturales y Ambientales (DRNA)

A standing commercial exotic-species buy/sell business needs DRNA's $150 dealer permit (Art. 7.01). Private sale and FREE vetted adoption of captive-bred black rats need no permit.

Where: DRNA · Fees: $150 dealer permit (commercial only)

Source: Departamento de Recursos Naturales y Ambientales (DRNA)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Puerto Rico

In Puerto Rico, keeping a captive-bred, tame pet roof rat ("rata negra," Rattus rattus) is legal right now — and that's not a loophole. The species is named, with no restrictive asterisk, in Apéndice 4 of the DRNA wildlife regulation (Reglamento 6765/6766), the list of lower-risk exotics you may import, possess, sell, and breed in captivity WITHOUT a permit. Only releasing one into the wild is flatly prohibited. So the agency is currently reading the law correctly, and there is nothing for it to "fix" today. The real issue is on the horizon: a 2025 statute, Ley Núm. 93-2025 (Ley para el Manejo de Especies Introducidas), tells the DRNA to write a NEW regulation that will sort introduced species into "prohibida," "restringida," or "no restringida" — and the law's own findings name the rata negra. If that future regulation lumps tame, captive-bred pet lines together with feral pest populations, permit-free keeping could disappear. The danger is in a coming RULE under a NEW LAW, not in any misreading of today's rule.

The ask: Two things, aimed at the future rule rather than today's status. (1) When the DRNA publishes its draft Ley 93-2025 classification regulation for public comment, ask in writing that Rattus rattus kept as a captive-bred pet be classified "no restringida" — or that captive-bred, indoor pet lines be expressly distinguished from feral/invasive populations — consistent with the species already being on Apéndice 4 and with Ley 93-2025 Art. 13, which excludes domestic and already-naturalized species. (2) Tell your senator and representative the same thing: pet roof rats are domesticated companion animals, like the fancy rat, and the implementing regulation should not strip permit-free status from responsible keepers of captive-bred animals. Make the point that these animals are captive-bred, hand-tame, kept strictly indoors, and never released — they are not the source of feral establishment.

Where the lever really is: This is a LEGISLATURE / RULEMAKING lever, not an agency-misreading lever — and it's important to be honest about why. Today the DRNA is applying its wildlife regulation correctly: Rattus rattus sits on Apéndice 4 of Reg. 6765/6766 with no restrictive asterisk, so keeping/breeding/selling captive-bred animals is permit-free, and only release is prohibited. There is therefore NOTHING for the agency to reinterpret right now; writing to DRNA asking it to "clarify that the rat is legal" would just confirm a status that is already correct, and could not change a law the agency is applying properly. The actual risk and the actual lever both live upstream, in a new statute: Ley Núm. 93-2025 (verified — passed Aug 2025) directs DRNA to promulgate a regulation classifying introduced species as prohibida/restringida/no restringida, and the statute's findings explicitly name the rata negra. That reclassification will be done through a DRNA RULEMAKING with a public-comment window (Ley 93-2025 Art. 5). As of this writing, DRNA's official "Propuestas de reglamento" page shows NO posted draft implementing Ley 93-2025, so the comment window is not yet open. The right play is therefore twofold: (a) WATCH the DRNA rulemaking page and file a comment the moment the draft appears, and (b) reach the LEGISLATURE, because Ley 93-2025 is the enabling statute and legislators can shape both the mandate and the agency's posture. The science-based ask — captive-bred indoor pet lines are not the source of feral establishment, the species is already naturalized, and Art. 13 already excludes domestic/naturalized species — belongs in that rulemaking comment and in messages to legislators, NOT in a request for the agency to override its current correct reading.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • DRNA — Propuestas de Reglamento (official proposed-regulations / public-comment page) (public comment) — official contact page
    This is the official page where DRNA posts draft regulations for public comment. The Ley 93-2025 introduced-species classification rule will appear here, with its comment deadline and any public hearing. Check it periodically; as of now no Ley 93-2025 draft is posted, so the comment window is not yet open. When the draft appears, submit the comment asking that captive-bred pet Rattus rattus be classified 'no restringida' / distinguished from feral populations. This is the single most decisive touchpoint because it is where the actual rule gets written.
  • Directorio Legislativo — Oficina de Servicios Legislativos de Puerto Rico (official find-and-contact-your-legislator portal) (legislature) — official contact page
    Verified official OSLPR directory (2025-2028 term) that lets any member of the public look up and contact senators and representatives by name, district, or chamber, with phone and email on each profile. Because Ley 93-2025 is the enabling STATUTE behind the coming reclassification, legislators are the right audience for the message that pet roof rats are domesticated companion animals and the implementing rule should preserve permit-free keeping of captive-bred animals.
  • DRNA — Oficina de Permisos de Vida Silvestre (Especies Exóticas) — wildlife/exotic-species permits office (executive / agency) — official contact page
    The substantive wildlife authority for exotic/introduced species and the office that will administer the Ley 93-2025 rule. Its public page lists only phone (787-999-2200, ext. 2750/2783 for wildlife) and a mailing address — NO official email or online form — so treat it as a monitoring/inquiry touchpoint (call or mail) to confirm the rule's status and timing, not as a lever to change the law it is correctly applying.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Keep captive-bred pet roof rats classified as lower-risk under the Ley 93-2025 regulation

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing about the introduced-species classification regulation the DRNA must adopt under Ley Núm. 93-2025. I respectfully ask that the captive-bred domestic roof rat (Rattus rattus, "rata negra") kept as a pet be classified "no restringida" — or that captive-bred, indoor pet lines be expressly distinguished from feral populations.

This is consistent with current law: the species is already on Apéndice 4 of Reglamento 6765/6766 as a lower-risk exotic, and Ley 93-2025 (Art. 13) already excludes domestic and naturalized species.

The animals I am writing about are captive-bred, hand-tame, kept strictly indoors, and never released. Like the fancy rat, the pet roof rat is a domesticated companion animal — it is not the source of any feral population, and the distinction is the species' lineage and use, not its name.

I ask that the forthcoming regulation preserve permit-free keeping of captive-bred pet roof rats. Please let me know when the draft regulation opens for public comment.

Thank you for your time and service.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your municipality, Puerto Rico]
[Your email]
Español
Asunto: Mantener a la rata negra de compañía criada en cautiverio como especie de menor riesgo en el reglamento de la Ley 93-2025

Estimado señor o señora:

Le escribo sobre el reglamento de clasificación de especies introducidas que el DRNA debe adoptar conforme a la Ley Núm. 93-2025. Respetuosamente solicito que la rata negra doméstica (Rattus rattus) criada en cautiverio y mantenida como mascota se clasifique como "no restringida" — o que las líneas de mascota criadas en cautiverio y mantenidas bajo techo se distingan expresamente de las poblaciones asilvestradas.

Esto es congruente con el derecho vigente: la especie ya figura en el Apéndice 4 del Reglamento 6765/6766 como exótico de menor riesgo, y la propia Ley 93-2025 (Art. 13) excluye a las especies domésticas y naturalizadas.

Los animales a los que me refiero son criados en cautiverio, mansos, mantenidos estrictamente bajo techo y nunca liberados. Al igual que la rata fancy, la rata negra de compañía es un animal doméstico de compañía — no es el origen de ninguna población asilvestrada, y la diferencia está en el linaje y el uso de la especie, no en su nombre.

Solicito que el reglamento próximo a adoptarse conserve la tenencia sin permiso de ratas negras de compañía criadas en cautiverio. Le agradeceré me informe cuándo el borrador del reglamento se abra a comentarios públicos.

Gracias por su tiempo y servicio.

Atentamente,
[Su nombre]
[Su municipio, Puerto Rico]
[Su correo electrónico]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Reglamento 6765/6766 (DRNA) — conservación y manejo de Vida Silvestre y Especies Exóticas (Art. 7; Apéndice 4 lista 'Rattus rattus – Rata negra') — Departamento de Recursos Naturales y Ambientales (DRNA)
  • Ley Núm. 93 de 2025 — Ley para el Manejo de Especies Introducidas (clasificación; Art. 13 exclusión domésticas/naturalizadas) — Asamblea Legislativa de PR (via LexJuris)
  • Requisitos para que animales ingresen a Puerto Rico (DA-SAHO; permiso + CVI; exóticos → DRNA) — Departamento de Agricultura de PR (SAHO)
  • Ley Núm. 241 de 1999 — Nueva Ley de Vida Silvestre de Puerto Rico — Asamblea Legislativa de PR / DRNA
