item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Vermont? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Vermont

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Vermont-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Vermont is silent. See United States.

Summary. Vermont is permissive and unusually explicit for the roof rat. Its 'prohibited-unless-listed' wildlife regime (10 V.S.A. §4709; Reg. 881 / 10 App. V.S.A. §18) bans possessing or importing a wild animal without a permit unless the species is on the Fish & Wildlife exemption lists — and the July 2025 Unrestricted Wild Animal List names Rattus rattus by exact scientific name (common name 'Domesticated rat'), right alongside Rattus norvegicus. So there is no species trap: keeping, breeding, importing, and transporting a roof rat need no Fish & Wildlife permit. Breeding is also outside commercial law (the 'Pet Dealer' rule covers only dogs/cats/wolf-hybrids), and home sales are exempt; only a non-residential retail storefront needs a state Pet Shop License. Keepers remain bound by animal-cruelty law (13 V.S.A. ch. 8) and may never release a roof rat.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

10 V.S.A. §4709 bars possessing any wild animal without a Fish & Wildlife permit, but Reg. 881 (10 App. V.S.A. §18) exempts any species on the Unrestricted Wild Animal List. The July 2025 list names Rattus rattus to the exact species level (Genus Rattus / species rattus, common name 'Domesticated rat'), so no importation or possession permit is required to keep a roof rat. The earlier 'is rat = which species?' ambiguity is fully resolved by the explicit listing.

Sources: Vermont General Assembly, Vermont Fish & Wildlife Board, Vermont Fish & Wildlife Department

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Breeding roof rats is unregulated at the state level. Because R. rattus is on the Unrestricted List it falls outside the wild-animal permit scheme, and Vermont's commercial breeder law applies only to other species: a 'Pet Dealer' (20 V.S.A. §3901(7)) is defined strictly as someone selling cats, dogs, or wolf-hybrids from three or more litters — rodents are deliberately omitted, so a home breeder of any scale never triggers municipal Pet Dealer permitting. Commercial-scale sale from a storefront is handled under the Pet Shop license (see sell_give); federal USDA/AWA licensing can apply to wholesale/sight-unseen sales (see United States).

Sources: Vermont Fish & Wildlife Department, Vermont General Assembly, Vermont General Assembly

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Private/face-to-face sales and giveaways are unregulated: a roof rat breeder is exempt from the Pet Dealer rule (rodents excluded, 20 V.S.A. §3901(7)) AND from the Pet Shop rule when selling 'from a private dwelling' (20 V.S.A. §3901(11) explicitly excludes a private dwelling from the Pet Shop definition). Only a non-residential retail operation — a storefront, a flea-market booth, or a detached commercial building — is a 'Pet Shop' (rodents ARE included in that definition) and needs a state Pet Shop License with inspection. Status is set to legal_with_permit to capture that commercial-storefront layer; ordinary hobbyist placement needs no license. (Federal USDA/AWA licensing applies to wholesale/sight-unseen sales — see United States.)

Sources: Vermont General Assembly, Vermont General Assembly

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Because R. rattus is on the Unrestricted Wild Animal List, no Fish & Wildlife import permit is needed to bring or move one into/within Vermont (10 V.S.A. §4709; Reg. 881). The list's '(Captive Bred Only)' tag — which would trigger a statement-of-origin/CVI — is applied species-by-species and is NOT placed on either Rattus line, so no CVI is mandated by Fish & Wildlife for a pet roof rat. VAAFM's domestic-animal import rule (Rule #98074) requires a CVI in practice mainly for livestock, poultry, and rabies-vector species (dogs/cats/ferrets); private small companion rodents are not subject to border CVI enforcement. Never release a roof rat.

Sources: Vermont General Assembly, Vermont Fish & Wildlife Board, Vermont Fish & Wildlife Department, Vermont Agency of Agriculture, Food & Markets

Restrictions & responsibilities

Selling roof rats from a non-residential retail space — a storefront, a flea-market booth, or a detached commercial building (anything 'not part of a private dwelling') — makes the operation a 'Pet Shop' under 20 V.S.A. §3901(11) (rodents are included) and requires a state Pet Shop License plus a pre-licensing inspection, records, and caging standards. Selling/giving roof rats from your own home is exempt and needs no license.
  • If selling only from your private dwelling: no Pet Shop license needed — you're statutorily exempt.
  • If operating any non-residential retail space (storefront, flea-market booth, detached building): apply for a Pet Shop License and pass the pre-licensing inspection.
  • Confirm which agency currently processes the application during the Act 167 transition (legacy VAAFM Animal Health vs. the new DPS Division of Animal Welfare).

Where: Vermont Pet Shop licensing — currently transitioning from VAAFM (Animal Health Section) to the DPS Division of Animal Welfare (Act 167, phased 2024–2025) · Fees: Pet Shop license historically ~$150/yr (plus inspection); civil penalties up to $1,000/violation under Act 167. No fee for private-dwelling sales.

Source: Vermont General Assembly, Vermont General Assembly

A captive roof rat is the keeper's personal property and is protected by Vermont's animal-cruelty law (13 V.S.A. ch. 8 — §352 sustenance/care, no abandonment; §362 bars poisoning a captive animal). Releasing or abandoning a roof rat is both criminal cruelty and an illegal release of a non-native species — never release one. If you can no longer keep it, rehome it, surrender it to a shelter/rescue, or arrange humane euthanasia by a veterinarian.
  • Provide food, water, shelter, and veterinary care
  • Never release or abandon a roof rat — rehome or surrender responsibly

Source: Vermont General Assembly

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • 10 V.S.A. §4709 — Transport, importation, possession of wild animals; permit requirement — Vermont General Assembly
  • Reg. 881 / 10 App. V.S.A. §18 — Governing the importation and possession of wild animals (prohibited-unless-listed; exemption via Unrestricted List) — Vermont Fish & Wildlife Board
  • Unrestricted Wild Animal List (July 2025) — names Rattus rattus ('Domesticated rat') AND Rattus norvegicus; no '(Captive Bred Only)' tag on either — Vermont Fish & Wildlife Department
  • 20 V.S.A. ch. 194 — §3901 (Pet Dealer excludes rodents; Pet Shop includes rodents but excludes private dwelling), §3906 (Pet Shop license) — Vermont General Assembly
  • 20 V.S.A. §3681 — Pet dealer permit (municipal; dogs/cats/wolf-hybrids only) — Vermont General Assembly
  • Act 167 (H.626, 2024) — transfers pet-shop/welfare oversight from VAAFM to DPS Division of Animal Welfare — Vermont General Assembly
  • 13 V.S.A. ch. 8 — Animal cruelty (§352 care/no abandonment; §362 poisoning a captive animal) — Vermont General Assembly
  • VAAFM Rule #98074 — Rules Governing the Importation of Domestic Animals, Including Livestock and Poultry (CVI mainly for livestock/rabies-vector species) — Vermont Agency of Agriculture, Food & Markets

item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Washington

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Washington-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Washington is silent. See United States.

Summary. Washington is now DR-verified and is cleanly legal at the state level. The wildlife statute excludes "old world rats and mice of the family Muridae" from the definition of "wildlife" (RCW 77.08.010(74)), so the roof rat (Rattus rattus) is outside WDFW jurisdiction with no species trap (R. rattus and R. norvegicus are treated identically), and it is on neither the dangerous-wild-animal list (RCW 16.30.010) nor the deleterious-exotic-wildlife list (WAC 220-640-200). Keeping, breeding, and selling are unregulated by the state (WSDA licenses no breeders; a rat sale is treated as personal property) — commercial breeding/retail defer to LOCAL zoning and animal-business codes. Importing one requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection as a "pocket pet" (WAC 16-54-170 / WSDA), but no exotic entry permit. Never release a roof rat (it is a recognized invasive species; WAC 220-450-010).

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

The roof rat is excluded from the statutory definition of "wildlife" — RCW 77.08.010(74) excludes "old world rats and mice of the family Muridae" — so WDFW has no jurisdiction. It is also absent from the dangerous-wild-animal list (RCW 16.30.010) and the deleterious-exotic-wildlife list (WAC 220-640-200). No state permit, caging, or inspection (only general anti-cruelty, RCW 16.52). Local exotic-pet ordinances may still apply.

Sources: Washington State Legislature, WA Dept of Fish & Wildlife

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

No state rodent breeder license: WDFW breeding rules cover only dangerous/deleterious species (neither covers R. rattus), and the WSDA does not license, register, or regulate breeders of any species. Hobby breeding is unrestricted; commercial breeding defers to LOCAL county/municipal animal-business and zoning codes.

Sources: WA Dept of Fish & Wildlife

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

No state pet-dealer license applies to rodents — a roof rat sale is treated as the sale of personal property, not classified wildlife. Statewide pet-dealer bills historically targeted dog/cat volume breeders, not rodents. Retail sale defers to a local business/pet-shop license; private transfer is unregulated.

Sources: WA Dept of Fish & Wildlife

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Intrastate transport of an owned pet is unregulated (only humane-transport rules, RCW 16.52.080). IMPORT into Washington requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection within 30 days, with the roof rat handled administratively as a "pocket pet" (WAC 16-54-170 / WSDA small-animal import) — no exotic entry permit needed via that route; rodents are exempt from rabies vaccination. Never release a roof rat.

Sources: Washington State Dept of Agriculture, WA Dept of Fish & Wildlife

Restrictions & responsibilities

Importing a pet rat ('pocket pet') into Washington requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (WSDA). No CVI for in-state movement.

Where: WA State Dept of Agriculture, Animal Health Program

Source: Washington State Dept of Agriculture

Never release a roof rat — it's a non-native species; rehome responsibly.

Source: WA Dept of Fish & Wildlife

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Wisconsin? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Wisconsin

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Wisconsin-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Wisconsin is silent. See United States.

Summary. Wisconsin is now DR-verified. Keeping and breeding a pet roof rat are legal and largely deregulated: the DNR exempts non-native, non-harmful wild animals from possession and captive-wildlife-farm licensing (Wis. Stat. ch. 169), and the roof rat is not on the 'harmful wild animal' list. The open question is on the agriculture side: commercial SALE may require a DATCP Animal Dealer license, and IMPORT may require a Wild Animal Import Permit (on top of the standard veterinary certificate), depending on whether DATCP classifies a captive-bred R. rattus as a 'domestic animal' (ATCP 10.02(8)) or a 'wild animal' — a definition DATCP has not pinned down for R. rattus. (Local ordinances can also restrict exotic pets.)

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Rattus rattus is a non-native wild animal that is not endangered and not a designated 'harmful wild animal', so it is statutorily exempt from any DNR possession license (Wis. Stat. 169.04(4)(b); the harmful-wild-animal list, 169.11(1)(a), names only cougars, bears, and wild/feral swine). No permit, testing, or inspection by the DNR. Note: municipalities may impose stricter local exotic-pet rules (169.11(3)).

Sources: Wisconsin Legislature / DNR, Wisconsin DNR

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Propagation is tied to the possession exemption: Wis. Stat. 169.08(2) exempts from the Captive Wild Animal Farm License any animal exempt under 169.04(4)(b). So hobby and commercial breeding of roof rats need no DNR breeding permit, inspection, or fee (and the NR 16.30 caging standards apply only to ch.169-licensed animals, so they do not bind roof-rat keepers).

Sources: Wisconsin Legislature / DNR

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-10

The DNR requires no sales license (169.10(1)(b), via the same exemption). BUT commercial selling may trigger a DATCP Animal Dealer license ($220/yr; Wis. Stat. 95.69, ATCP 12.03) IF DATCP classifies R. rattus as a 'wild animal' rather than a 'domestic animal' (ATCP 10.02(8)). DATCP's pet-movement guidance lists the 'domestic rat' as a household pet, but it is unconfirmed whether that covers R. rattus or only R. norvegicus. Giving away privately is unproblematic; commercial sale is the gray zone.

Sources: Wisconsin Legislature / DNR

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-10

Intrastate movement of a healthy pet is unregulated. IMPORT into Wisconsin requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection for every animal (ATCP 10.06(1)) — no rabies/test requirement for rodents — and MAY additionally require a Wild Animal Import Permit (ATCP 10.84) if DATCP treats R. rattus as a 'wild animal' rather than 'domestic'. Never release a roof rat.

Sources: Wisconsin DATCP, Wisconsin DNR

Restrictions & responsibilities

Importing a pet rat into Wisconsin requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (ATCP 10.06); no special tests or import permit for a domestic-rodent household pet. No CVI for in-state movement.

Where: Wisconsin DATCP, Division of Animal Industry

Source: Wisconsin DATCP

Never release a roof rat (Wis. Stat. §169.30 / NR 40). Local city/village/county ordinances may be stricter (Wis. Stat. §169.11(3)) — check yours.

Source: Wisconsin Legislature / DNR

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Wisconsin

Keeping and breeding roof rats in Wisconsin are clearly legal (the DNR exempts non-native, non-harmful animals). But the commercial sale and import sit in a gray zone: the agriculture department (DATCP) regulates dealers and importers of 'wild animals' while exempting 'domestic' ones, and it is unconfirmed whether DATCP's 'domestic rat' covers captive-bred Rattus rattus or only the fancy rat (R. norvegicus).

The ask: Ask DATCP's Division of Animal Health to confirm in writing that a captive-bred, domesticated Rattus rattus is a 'domestic animal' under ATCP 10.02(8) — so selling it needs no $220 Animal Dealer license (ATCP 12) and importing it needs only a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection, not a Wild Animal Import Permit (ATCP 10.84).

Where the lever really is: This is a bureaucratic-clarification case (agency), not a law-as-written one: the rules already exempt 'domestic' animals; the only open question is whether DATCP reads 'domestic rat' to include R. rattus. The lever is a written determination from DATCP, not the legislature.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Wisconsin DATCP — Division of Animal Health (executive / agency) — official contact page
    DATCP decides whether R. rattus is 'domestic' (ATCP 10.02(8)) for Animal Dealer-license and import-permit purposes. Reach the Division of Animal Health via its Animal Imports / Movement contact on datcp.wi.gov.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Wisconsin DATCP, Division of Animal Health,

I keep and, on a small scale, breed domesticated roof rats (Rattus rattus) as pets. Wisconsin's DNR exempts them from wildlife licensing as non-native, non-harmful animals. I am writing to confirm how DATCP classifies them for commercial and import purposes.

Specifically: is a captive-bred, domesticated Rattus rattus a "domestic animal" under ATCP 10.02(8) (like the domestic rat/mouse in your pet-movement guidance), so that (a) selling them does not require an Animal Dealer license under ATCP 12, and (b) importing one requires only a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection, not a Wild Animal Import Permit under ATCP 10.84?

These animals are captive-bred over generations for tameness, kept indoors, and never released. A written confirmation I can rely on would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you,
[Your name]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Wis. Stat. §169.04 — Possession of live wild animals (nonnative exemption §169.04(5)) — Wisconsin Legislature / DNR
  • Wis. Admin. Code NR 40 — Invasive Species (prohibited mammals: nutria, feral swine, monk parakeet; Rattus absent) — Wisconsin DNR
  • Wis. Admin. Code ATCP 10.06 / 10.01 — Animal import CVI + household-pet 'domestic rodent' definition — Wisconsin DATCP

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › West Virginia

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the West Virginia-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where West Virginia is silent. See United States.

Summary. West Virginia is now DR-verified, and it is one of the cleanest 'legal' cases in the country. The state's wildlife code defines 'wild animals' as native mammals EXCEPT 'house mice or rats' (W. Va. Code 20-1-2) — so the roof rat is excluded from the DNR's captive-wildlife scheme by name, and there is no species trap (R. rattus and R. norvegicus are treated identically). No rodents appear on the Dangerous Wild Animal List (74 CSR 1), and a domesticated rat also meets the Act's 'domestic animal' (genetic-change) exemption. Keeping, breeding, and selling are all unregulated at the state level (the only commercial-breeder law, 19-20-26, covers dogs only). Importing rodents is a minor gray area (the agriculture CVI rules omit rodents but use conflicting 'animal' definitions). Never release one.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

West Virginia's wildlife code defines 'wild animals' as mammals NATIVE to the state EXCEPT 'house mice or rats' (W. Va. Code 20-1-2). The roof rat is both non-native AND within the 'rats' carve-out, so the DNR has no jurisdiction (no permit, caging, or inspection). It is also not on the Dangerous Wild Animal List (74 CSR 1-3 lists zero rodents), and a domesticated rat independently meets the Act's 'domestic animal' genetic-change exemption (19-34-2).

Sources: West Virginia Legislature, WV Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

No rodent breeder license exists. West Virginia's commercial-breeding statute (W. Va. Code 19-20-26) regulates dogs only (11+ unsterilized dogs); by expressio unius, rodents are excluded. Even warehouse-scale roof-rat breeding needs no state facility license (federal USDA wholesale rules can still apply — see United States).

Sources: West Virginia Legislature

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

No state pet-dealer or pet-shop license exists for rodents (historical exotic-pet-dealer bills failed). Selling or giving roof rats is unregulated at the state level (federal USDA wholesale/sight-unseen rules apply on top — see United States).

Sources: West Virginia Legislature, WV Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII)

Transport & import   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-10

Intrastate transport of a healthy pet is unregulated. For IMPORT, the agriculture CVI rules (W. Va. C.S.R. 61-1-8) mandate Certificates of Veterinary Inspection for many species but omit rodents, while conflicting definitions of 'animal' leave a minor ambiguity — so a CVI may or may not be demanded for a pet rat. Never release a roof rat.

Sources: WV Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII), West Virginia Legislature

Restrictions & responsibilities

Never release a roof rat — it's a non-native species. Local county/municipal ordinances may add limits — check yours.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Wyoming? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Wyoming

Research aid, not legal advice. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Wyoming-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Wyoming is silent. See United States.

Summary. Wyoming is one of the clearest 'yes' states for the roof rat — it names the species. Game & Fish Commission Regulation Chapter 10 §2(j) lists 'Domesticated rat (Rattus norvegicus AND Rattus rattus)' by binomial name in its 'Domesticated Animals' category, and §16 exempts domestic/domesticated animals from all importation/possession permits. So keeping a captive-bred roof rat is legal statewide with no wildlife permit, and there's no by-name disparity vs the fancy rat. Breeding and selling/giving are also unregulated at the state level — Wyoming licenses no pet breeders, kennels, or pet shops (LSO report 10 RM 017). The one real requirement is INTERSTATE IMPORT: the Livestock Board (Chapter 8) requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) for any vertebrate entering the state, and rodents are NOT in the dog/cat/ferret travel waiver — but no separate entry permit is needed for a pet rat. Intrastate movement is unregulated. Never release one (a released roof rat loses its 'domesticated' protection and becomes a takeable pest); watch local 'harboring rodents' ordinances.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

WGFD Commission Regulation Chapter 10 §2(j) expressly lists 'Domesticated rat (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus)' as a 'Domesticated Animal,' and §16(a) states that animals in the domestic/domesticated categories 'do not require an importation or possession permit from the Department.' Wyoming distinguishes 'Domestic Animals' (§2(i), genetic divergence) from 'Domesticated Animals' (§2(j), tame/tractable, with an explicit species list that includes R. rattus) — so a captive roof rat is legally indistinguishable from a fancy rat. No caging/facility standards for private keeping (only general anti-cruelty, Title 6).

Sources: Wyoming Game & Fish Commission, Wyoming Game & Fish Department

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

Wyoming licenses/regulates no pet breeding kennels, boarding kennels, grooming shops, or pet shops at the state level (Legislative Service Office research report 10 RM 017), and there is no propagation quota for exempt companion rodents. Hobby and commercial breeding of R. rattus are both unregulated by the state (federal USDA Animal Welfare Act applies only to sight-unseen/wholesale operations).

Sources: Wyoming Game & Fish Commission, Wyoming Legislative Service Office

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

No Wyoming pet-shop, pet-dealer, or secondhand-dealer license exists — commercial and private transfers of domesticated rodents are structurally unregulated (LSO 10 RM 017; Wolters Kluwer business-license survey). A hobbyist giving a roof rat away and a commercial seller face the same absence of state animal-sales licensing (general business registration + sales tax aside).

Sources: Wyoming Game & Fish Commission, Wyoming Legislative Service Office

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

INTRASTATE movement is fully unregulated (exempt species). INTERSTATE IMPORT: once across the line, jurisdiction shifts to the Wyoming Livestock Board (Chapter 8 Import Rules), which requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) for 'any living vertebrate' entering the state (Ch. 8 §5(b)); a roof rat — exempt from WGFD wildlife status — defaults to this broad 'Animal' definition. The §8-9 pet travel waiver (rabies cert instead of CVI) covers ONLY dogs, cats, and ferrets, so by expressio unius it does NOT extend to rodents → a CVI is legally required. However, NO entry permit is needed (those apply only to cattle/sheep/swine/bison). Export is unregulated by Wyoming. (Open: how strictly the CVI is enforced against private 'pocket pets' in passenger vehicles — a discretion question, not a legal exemption.) Never release.

Sources: Wyoming Livestock Board, Wyoming Game & Fish Commission

Restrictions & responsibilities

To bring a roof rat INTO Wyoming, carry a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) from an accredited vet in the origin state (valid ~30 days) — rodents are NOT covered by the dog/cat/ferret travel waiver. No entry permit is needed. No paperwork for in-state movement. NEVER release a roof rat: a released/escaped one loses its 'domesticated' protection (W.S. 11-20-101 feral definition) and becomes a takeable pest. Watch local 'harboring rodents' nuisance ordinances (e.g., Thermopolis) — keep enclosures hygienic + secure.
  • For interstate import: obtain a CVI from an accredited veterinarian before entering Wyoming

Where: Wyoming Livestock Board (Animal Health Division) · Fees: veterinary fee for the CVI

Source: Wyoming Livestock Board
